Chapter 1 - From Software Architecture to AI Architecture

Why established architecture remains necessary—but is no longer sufficient

Related chapters: Chapters 0, 2, and 3

AI architecture did not emerge because software architecture failed. It emerged because software systems acquired new forms of uncertainty, behaviour, and authority that established architecture alone could not fully govern.

1. Why This Chapter Matters

Artificial intelligence is often presented as a clean break from conventional software engineering.

That framing is misleading.

An AI application still depends on:

  • networks;
  • APIs;
  • databases;
  • identity and access control;
  • distributed coordination;
  • deployment pipelines;
  • monitoring;
  • security;
  • resilience;
  • cost management.

A poorly designed software system does not become well designed merely because an advanced model is placed inside it.

At the same time, AI cannot be treated as an ordinary library that receives an input and returns a consistently predictable output. Modern AI workloads introduce nondeterministic behaviour, dependence on models and data, changing output quality, probabilistic failure, and new operational requirements. Microsoft’s current Well-Architected guidance explicitly identifies nondeterministic functionality, data and application design, and operations as distinctive challenges of AI workloads.

The architect must therefore preserve the strengths of conventional software architecture while extending them to address uncertainty.

That is the central argument of this chapter:

Software architecture manages complexity. AI architecture manages complexity plus uncertainty.

2. Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • Explain how AI architecture evolved from software, cloud, data, and machine-learning architecture.
  • Distinguish deterministic, probabilistic, and hybrid system behaviour.
  • Identify architectural concerns that remain unchanged in AI systems.
  • Recognise concerns that AI introduces or amplifies.
  • Explain why model quality is not equivalent to system quality.
  • Apply the AI Trust Triangle to diagnose an AI architecture.
  • Defend the proposition that AI architecture extends rather than replaces software architecture.
  • Evaluate whether an organisation is treating AI as a component, a workload, or a governed system.

Part I — Architecture Before AI

3. What Software Architecture Has Always Been Solving

Software architecture exists because non-trivial systems must satisfy competing requirements.

A system must often be:

  • useful;
  • reliable;
  • secure;
  • responsive;
  • maintainable;
  • scalable;
  • affordable;
  • adaptable.

These qualities influence one another. Improving one may weaken another.

For example:

  • Strong consistency may increase latency.
  • Greater isolation may increase operational overhead.
  • More abstraction may improve portability while making debugging harder.
  • Additional redundancy may improve availability while increasing cost.

Architecture is therefore not the search for a universally correct structure.

It is the disciplined selection of trade-offs for a particular context.

This remains true when AI is introduced.

4. The Evolution of Architectural Responsibility

Software architecture did not move through perfectly separated eras. Monoliths, service-oriented systems, cloud platforms, data systems, and machine-learning workloads continue to coexist.

However, each stage expanded the architect’s field of responsibility.

Application Structure
        │
        ▼
Distributed Coordination
        │
        ▼
Elastic Infrastructure
        │
        ▼
Data and Learning Systems
        │
        ▼
Generative Behaviour
        │
        ▼
Tool-Using and Agentic Systems

4.1 Application Architecture

Early enterprise architecture concentrated heavily on organising application logic:

  • presentation;
  • business rules;
  • data access;
  • transactions;
  • integration boundaries.

The dominant uncertainty was usually requirements uncertainty:

Do we understand what the software should do?

Once a requirement was encoded, the software was generally expected to perform that operation predictably.

4.2 Distributed Systems

As applications were decomposed across processes, services, machines, and regions, new problems appeared:

  • partial failure;
  • network latency;
  • retries;
  • duplicate delivery;
  • eventual consistency;
  • concurrency;
  • service discovery;
  • distributed transactions.

The architect now had to reason about systems in which one component could fail while others continued operating.

The dominant uncertainty expanded:

What happens when communication, timing, or coordination fails?

4.3 Cloud-Native Systems

Cloud platforms introduced elastic infrastructure, managed services, automated provisioning, and global-scale deployment.

The architect’s concerns expanded again:

  • infrastructure as code;
  • autoscaling;
  • multiregion design;
  • shared responsibility;
  • identity-centric security;
  • observability;
  • resilience engineering;
  • consumption-based cost.

Cloud architecture did not remove traditional architecture. It extended it with new operational and economic constraints.

4.4 Data and Machine-Learning Systems

Machine learning introduced systems whose behaviour was partly learned from data rather than fully specified in source code.

This created additional dependencies:

  • training data;
  • feature pipelines;
  • labels;
  • model versions;
  • training infrastructure;
  • distribution shifts;
  • performance metrics;
  • retraining cycles.

The system could now degrade even when no application code had changed.

A model might perform well during development but deteriorate because production data changed.

The central question became:

Does the learned behaviour remain valid in the environment where the system operates?

4.5 Generative AI Systems

Generative models expanded the problem further.

Rather than choosing among a predefined set of outputs, the model could produce new text, code, images, plans, summaries, or decisions.

This introduced:

  • open-ended outputs;
  • prompt sensitivity;
  • context sensitivity;
  • hallucination;
  • subjective quality criteria;
  • variable latency and token cost;
  • safety concerns;
  • difficult-to-reproduce failures.

Microsoft describes AI workloads as combining code and data into models that exhibit nondeterministic behaviour. AWS and Google have similarly extended their general Well-Architected guidance with AI-specific perspectives rather than treating AI as independent of established architectural pillars.

4.6 Agentic Systems

Agentic systems add another architectural transition.

The model may no longer only generate information. It may:

  • select tools;
  • call APIs;
  • query databases;
  • modify files;
  • create tickets;
  • send messages;
  • schedule actions;
  • initiate workflows;
  • make decisions within delegated authority.

AWS’s Agentic AI Lens describes the production challenge as moving from whether an agent can be built to whether agents can be operated reliably, securely, and cost-effectively at scale.

The central question becomes:

What authority should a probabilistic system possess, and what controls must accompany that authority?

Part II — What Changed?

5. Deterministic and Probabilistic Behaviour

Traditional application logic is usually designed to be deterministic.

Given the same:

  • input;
  • state;
  • code version;
  • configuration;

the system should normally produce the same result.

Input
  │
  ▼
Defined Logic
  │
  ▼
Expected Output

An AI model may produce different outputs for the same apparent request because its behaviour is influenced by:

  • sampling configuration;
  • prompt wording;
  • context ordering;
  • model version;
  • retrieved information;
  • conversation state;
  • tool results;
  • hidden platform changes.
Input
  │
  ├── Model
  ├── Prompt
  ├── Context
  ├── Retrieval
  ├── Tools
  ├── Sampling
  └── Policy
          │
          ▼
     Variable Output

Azure’s GenAIOps guidance explicitly notes that AI workloads are inherently nondeterministic and may produce different responses to the same inquiry.

This does not mean AI systems are uncontrollable.

It means control must be established through system design rather than assumed from the model.

6. Three Behavioural Zones

A useful AI architecture separates the system into three zones.

Zone 1 — Deterministic

These operations should be governed by explicit logic:

  • authentication;
  • authorisation;
  • payment execution;
  • entitlement checks;
  • transaction limits;
  • policy enforcement;
  • schema validation;
  • irreversible writes;
  • audit recording.

Zone 2 — Probabilistic

These operations can benefit from interpretation or generation:

  • classification;
  • summarisation;
  • extraction from ambiguous language;
  • recommendation;
  • drafting;
  • semantic matching;
  • planning suggestions.

Zone 3 — Governed Transition

This is the boundary where probabilistic output may influence deterministic action.

Examples:

  • An agent proposes a refund, but a policy engine verifies eligibility.
  • A model generates SQL, but a validator restricts permitted operations.
  • An incident agent recommends remediation, but approval is required before execution.
  • A document assistant extracts a monetary value, but deterministic checks validate the format and allowable range.
Probabilistic Interpretation
            │
            ▼
   Validation and Policy
            │
            ▼
   Deterministic Execution

This boundary is one of the most important objects in AI architecture.

It is the point where uncertainty can become consequence.

Architect’s Notebook

Do not ask only where AI is used. Ask where AI-generated uncertainty crosses into business state.

A generated paragraph may be wrong and inconvenient.

A generated bank transfer may be wrong and catastrophic.

The model can be identical in both cases. The architecture cannot.

Part III — What Remains the Same?

7. AI Systems Are Still Software Systems

The presence of a model does not remove foundational engineering concerns.

An AI workload still requires:

Security

  • identity;
  • access control;
  • encryption;
  • secrets management;
  • network boundaries;
  • least privilege;
  • auditability.

AWS’s current Generative AI Lens applies least privilege across models, data stores, endpoints, and agent workflows, demonstrating that established security principles remain central in AI architecture.

Reliability

  • retries;
  • timeouts;
  • circuit breakers;
  • fallback behaviour;
  • redundancy;
  • state recovery;
  • graceful degradation.

Performance

  • latency budgets;
  • throughput;
  • concurrency;
  • caching;
  • batching;
  • capacity planning.

Cost

  • infrastructure consumption;
  • model tokens;
  • retrieval;
  • storage;
  • evaluation;
  • logging;
  • human review;
  • support overhead.

Google’s AI and ML Well-Architected perspective retains the established pillars of operational excellence, security, reliability, cost optimisation, and performance optimisation.

Maintainability

  • modular boundaries;
  • testability;
  • version control;
  • deployment safety;
  • documentation;
  • ownership;
  • replaceability.

The first law of our handbook therefore stands:

Every AI system is a software system first.

Part IV — What AI Adds

8. Model Dependency

Conventional applications depend on libraries and services.

AI systems additionally depend on model behaviour.

This introduces questions such as:

  • Which model version produced the output?
  • Has the provider changed model behaviour?
  • Does a replacement model interpret instructions differently?
  • Is the model equally capable across languages or domains?
  • Does the fallback model preserve the required safety behaviour?

A model is not merely a deployment dependency.

It is a behavioural dependency.

9. Data and Context Dependency

AI behaviour depends not only on the model but also on the information supplied at runtime.

That may include:

  • user prompts;
  • system instructions;
  • retrieved documents;
  • conversation history;
  • tool descriptions;
  • database results;
  • memory;
  • policy text.

A defect in any of these may appear to the user as a model failure.

For example:

The answer is wrong.

Possible causes:

  • the model could not reason correctly;
  • retrieval returned the wrong document;
  • the right document was ranked too low;
  • the context was truncated;
  • a tool returned stale data;
  • the system prompt created conflicting instructions;
  • the output validator accepted an invalid answer.

The architect must reason about the complete evidence path.

10. Evaluation Dependency

Traditional software testing asks whether the implementation matches specified behaviour.

AI evaluation often asks whether the behaviour is acceptable across a representative distribution of cases.

The expected answer may not always be a single exact value.

Evaluation may involve:

  • factuality;
  • relevance;
  • task completion;
  • groundedness;
  • safety;
  • style;
  • citation correctness;
  • tool selection;
  • business outcome.

NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework is designed to incorporate trustworthiness considerations across the design, development, use, and evaluation of AI systems. Its core functions are Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.

Evaluation is therefore not an optional testing phase.

It is part of the architecture.

11. Continuous Behavioural Change

Traditional application behaviour usually changes because:

  • code changes;
  • configuration changes;
  • dependencies change;
  • infrastructure changes.

AI behaviour can also change because:

  • the model changes;
  • the knowledge base changes;
  • retrieval indexes change;
  • data distribution changes;
  • user behaviour changes;
  • prompts change;
  • safety policies change;
  • tools change.

This means the system can regress without a conventional code defect.

AI operations must therefore monitor behaviour, not only infrastructure.

12. Expanded Attack Surface

AI systems introduce additional attack paths:

  • prompt injection;
  • malicious documents;
  • data poisoning;
  • tool manipulation;
  • excessive agency;
  • sensitive-data leakage;
  • insecure output handling;
  • model supply-chain risk.

The NIST Generative AI Profile was created specifically to identify risks distinctive to generative AI and propose corresponding risk-management actions.

Security can no longer stop at protecting the API endpoint.

The system must also protect the decision path.

13. Authority and Autonomy

A chatbot that writes a draft has limited authority.

An agent that can execute commands, alter records, or communicate externally has greater authority.

As authority increases, architecture must add proportionate:

  • policy;
  • identity;
  • approval;
  • isolation;
  • monitoring;
  • audit;
  • rollback;
  • incident response.

This leads to one of the handbook’s core principles:

Every autonomous capability requires a corresponding governance capability.

Part V — A New Definition of System Quality

14. Model Quality Is Not System Quality

A common mistake is to treat the model benchmark as the quality of the application.

The model may be highly capable while the system remains poor.

Consider a support assistant using a frontier model.

It may still fail because:

  • the knowledge base is outdated;
  • retrieval excludes relevant policies;
  • access controls expose the wrong documents;
  • citations point to irrelevant passages;
  • escalation rules are missing;
  • latency makes the interface unusable;
  • the system cannot recognise when it lacks evidence.

Conversely, a smaller model inside a well-designed system may deliver better business outcomes because it has:

  • better context;
  • reliable tools;
  • constrained tasks;
  • deterministic validation;
  • effective escalation;
  • strong evaluation.

Therefore:

System Quality
    ≠
Model Quality

A more useful representation is:

System Quality
    =
Model Capability
+ Evidence Quality
+ Workflow Design
+ Evaluation
+ Controls
+ Operations
+ User Experience

This is conceptual, not a literal mathematical formula.

Its purpose is to remind the architect that the model is only one contributor.

Part VI — The AI Trust Triangle

15. Applying the Triangle

The AI Trust Triangle evaluates three concerns:

                Capability
                     ▲
                    /                    /                     /             Confidence ----- Evidence

Capability

Can the system perform the task at the required level?

This includes:

  • reasoning;
  • language understanding;
  • planning;
  • tool use;
  • domain competence.

Evidence

What grounds, verifies, or constrains the result?

This may include:

  • retrieved sources;
  • API responses;
  • database records;
  • calculations;
  • policy rules;
  • provenance;
  • human input.

Confidence

What level of reliance is justified?

Confidence is not the model announcing a percentage.

It is a system-level judgement based on:

  • evaluations;
  • validation;
  • evidence quality;
  • task risk;
  • historical performance;
  • controls;
  • human review.

16. Diagnosing Common Failures

High Capability, Weak Evidence

The system generates plausible answers but cannot demonstrate why they are correct.

Diagnosis: The Hallucination Trap

Architectural response:

  • improve retrieval;
  • require sources;
  • introduce tool use;
  • constrain unsupported claims;
  • add escalation.

Strong Evidence, Weak Capability

The system retrieves correct information but cannot synthesise or reason over it effectively.

Diagnosis: The Inadequate Analyst

Architectural response:

  • improve task decomposition;
  • use a more capable model selectively;
  • simplify the task;
  • add deterministic computation;
  • improve context organisation.

Capability and Evidence, Weak Confidence

The system often produces good results, but the organisation cannot justify trusting it.

Diagnosis: The Unproven System

Architectural response:

  • create representative evaluations;
  • establish acceptance thresholds;
  • measure production outcomes;
  • define escalation rules;
  • calibrate human oversight.

Capability, Evidence, and Justified Confidence

The system can perform the task, ground its output, and demonstrate acceptable reliability for the risk level.

Target state: The Trusted Assistant

The word assistant is deliberate. Higher-risk autonomy must still be earned through evaluation, governance, and operating experience.

Part VII — A Practical Example

17. Designing an AI Invoice-Processing System

A company wants AI to process emailed invoices.

A superficial design might be:

Email → LLM → Accounting System

This architecture places probabilistic interpretation directly next to financial execution.

A stronger design separates concerns.

Invoice
   │
   ▼
Document Parsing
   │
   ▼
AI Extraction
   │
   ▼
Schema Validation
   │
   ▼
Supplier Verification
   │
   ▼
Duplicate Check
   │
   ▼
Policy and Threshold Rules
   │
   ├── Low Risk ──► Controlled Processing
   │
   └── High Risk ─► Human Review

Deterministic responsibilities

  • supplier identity;
  • account validation;
  • duplicate detection;
  • approval threshold;
  • tax calculation;
  • ledger write;
  • audit record.

Probabilistic responsibilities

  • document classification;
  • field extraction;
  • line-item interpretation;
  • anomaly suggestion;
  • natural-language explanation.

Governed transition

AI-extracted information is validated before it can affect financial state.

This is the defining move of good AI architecture:

Use probabilistic capability to interpret the world, but require governed mechanisms before changing it.

18. Trust Triangle Review

Capability

Can the extraction system understand the invoice formats, languages, and line items encountered in practice?

Evidence

Can each extracted field be traced to a document region or source value?

Confidence

Have evaluations demonstrated acceptable performance for each supplier type and risk category?

The design review should not ask only:

Which model are we using?

It should ask:

Which corner of the Trust Triangle is weakest, and what is the consequence if it fails?

Part VIII — Architectural Smells

19. Smell: The Model as the Architecture

User → Model → Answer

This may be sufficient for a prototype.

It is rarely a complete production architecture.

Missing concerns may include:

  • identity;
  • context;
  • validation;
  • retrieval;
  • policy;
  • safety;
  • evaluation;
  • observability;
  • fallback;
  • audit.

20. Smell: Deterministic Expectations from a Probabilistic Component

The team expects identical wording, classification, or reasoning from a generative model without constraining the task or validating the result.

Typical symptom:

It worked yesterday. Why did the same prompt behave differently today?

21. Smell: Probabilistic Enforcement

The model is asked to enforce a rule that should be implemented deterministically.

Examples:

  • “Decide whether the user is authorised.”
  • “Ensure the refund never exceeds £500.”
  • “Do not reveal records from other departments.”
  • “Determine whether this transaction is legally permitted.”

The model may help interpret supporting information.

It should not become the only enforcement mechanism.

22. Smell: Benchmark Substitution

A model performs well on a public benchmark, so the team assumes it will perform well on the organisation’s use case.

Public benchmarks can inform model selection.

They cannot replace task-specific evaluation.

23. Smell: Invisible Behavioural Change

The system records infrastructure metrics but does not track:

  • response quality;
  • retrieval quality;
  • tool-selection errors;
  • refusal behaviour;
  • escalation rates;
  • business outcomes.

The service remains technically available while its usefulness deteriorates.

Part IX — Architecture Review

24. Scenario

A company has built an AI customer-service agent.

The current architecture:

  • sends every request to one large model;
  • injects several policy documents into the prompt;
  • allows the model to issue refunds through an API;
  • stores only the final response;
  • has no representative evaluation set;
  • escalates only when the user asks for a human;
  • measures availability and average latency.

25. ARB Review

Finding 1 — Policy is not enforcement

Policy text inside a prompt does not replace deterministic refund rules.

Finding 2 — Authority exceeds demonstrated reliability

The agent can create financial consequences without sufficient evidence, evaluation, or approval.

Finding 3 — Auditability is incomplete

The organisation records the final answer but not:

  • retrieved context;
  • tool arguments;
  • policy decisions;
  • model version;
  • approval state.

Finding 4 — Evaluation is absent

Availability shows whether the service responded.

It does not show whether the service resolved the customer’s problem correctly.

Finding 5 — Escalation is user-driven

The system has no risk-based or confidence-based escalation mechanism.

26. Recommended Redesign

Customer Request
       │
       ▼
Intent Classification
       │
       ▼
Knowledge Retrieval
       │
       ▼
Response or Action Proposal
       │
       ▼
Policy Engine
       │
       ├── Informational ─► Respond
       │
       ├── Low-Risk Action ─► Execute + Audit
       │
       └── High-Risk Action ─► Human Approval

Add:

  • task-specific evaluation;
  • retrieval metrics;
  • action-level audit;
  • model and prompt versioning;
  • refund thresholds;
  • risk-based escalation;
  • production outcome monitoring.

Part X — Interview Preparation

27. Foundational Questions

Question 1

How is AI architecture different from software architecture?

A strong answer should say:

  • AI architecture retains software architecture fundamentals.
  • It adds model, data, context, evaluation, nondeterminism, and governance concerns.
  • The distinction is not that everything is new.
  • The distinction is that learned or generated behaviour must be managed as part of the system.

Weak answer:

AI architecture uses LLMs, vector databases, and agents.

That lists technologies without explaining the architectural difference.

Question 2

Why is a highly capable model not sufficient for a reliable AI system?

A strong answer should discuss:

  • evidence;
  • workflow design;
  • deterministic controls;
  • task-specific evaluation;
  • monitoring;
  • user experience;
  • business outcomes.

Question 3

Where should deterministic logic end and probabilistic logic begin?

A strong answer should distinguish:

  • interpretation from enforcement;
  • recommendation from execution;
  • generation from validation;
  • low-risk from high-impact decisions.

Question 4

What makes AI workloads operationally different?

A strong answer should mention:

  • behavioural variation;
  • model and data versioning;
  • evaluation in production;
  • prompt and context changes;
  • drift;
  • quality metrics;
  • cost variability;
  • traceability.

Question 5

How would you explain AI nondeterminism to a business stakeholder?

A strong answer:

Traditional software follows explicitly written instructions. AI models learn patterns and generate the most appropriate response from several plausible possibilities. We therefore control reliability through evidence, testing, validation, constraints, and human oversight rather than assuming every response will be identical.

28. Senior-Level Questions

Question 6

An AI application’s factual accuracy has fallen, but the model has not changed. How would you investigate?

Look beyond the model:

  • retrieval corpus changes;
  • indexing failures;
  • ranking changes;
  • stale sources;
  • context truncation;
  • prompt changes;
  • tool failures;
  • user-distribution changes;
  • evaluation defects.

Question 7

How do you prevent an AI architecture from becoming vendor-dependent?

Discuss:

  • business logic outside model adapters;
  • canonical message and tool schemas;
  • model gateways;
  • evaluation suites;
  • provider-neutral telemetry;
  • portable data;
  • capability-based routing;
  • explicit acceptance of unavoidable dependencies.

Question 8

When is nondeterminism acceptable?

It is more acceptable when:

  • outputs are advisory;
  • mistakes are reversible;
  • evidence is visible;
  • users can correct the result;
  • consequences are limited;
  • escalation is available.

It is less acceptable when:

  • the system controls access;
  • executes irreversible transactions;
  • affects safety;
  • makes regulated decisions;
  • cannot be audited.

Question 9

Should an AI agent be allowed to write directly to a production database?

A mature answer avoids an unconditional yes or no.

It considers:

  • scope of access;
  • operation type;
  • reversibility;
  • validation;
  • least privilege;
  • approval;
  • audit;
  • sandboxing;
  • idempotency;
  • compensation;
  • blast radius.

Question 10

What would you evaluate before increasing an agent’s autonomy?

Use the Principle of Earned Autonomy:

  • task success;
  • failure distribution;
  • evidence quality;
  • tool correctness;
  • policy compliance;
  • monitoring;
  • rollback;
  • incident handling;
  • organisational accountability.

Part XI — Whiteboard Challenge

29. Exercise

Design an AI system that reviews proposed software changes and may approve low-risk deployments.

Constraints

  • 400 engineering teams;
  • multiple programming languages;
  • regulated production systems;
  • deployments occur continuously;
  • high-risk changes require a human;
  • the system must explain every recommendation;
  • teams may use different source-control platforms.

Discuss

  • Where is AI useful?
  • Which decisions remain deterministic?
  • What constitutes evidence?
  • How is confidence established?
  • How is risk classified?
  • What is the rollback path?
  • What is recorded for audit?
  • How does the design behave when the model is unavailable?
  • What changes at ten times the deployment volume?

Evaluation rubric

A strong architecture should include:

  • a deterministic policy layer;
  • scoped repository access;
  • code and deployment evidence;
  • task-specific evaluation;
  • risk-based approval;
  • human escalation;
  • full traceability;
  • model abstraction;
  • fallback behaviour;
  • measurable business outcomes.

Part XII — Questions to Take Back to Your Team

  1. Where does probabilistic behaviour enter our architecture?
  2. Where can AI output change business state?
  3. Which rules are currently enforced only through prompts?
  4. Can we reconstruct why the system produced a particular decision?
  5. Do we monitor behaviour as well as infrastructure?
  6. What can change the system’s behaviour without a code deployment?
  7. Which corner of the AI Trust Triangle is weakest?
  8. Does our level of autonomy exceed our evidence and evaluation maturity?
  9. Could we replace the current model without rewriting business logic?
  10. What business outcome proves that the AI system is useful?

From the Architect’s Desk

The arrival of AI does not excuse us from the disciplines we learned while building conventional systems. It makes those disciplines more important.

An AI system still needs boundaries, ownership, security, resilience, and clear operating responsibility. But it also requires us to acknowledge something software teams have traditionally tried to eliminate: meaningful uncertainty inside the execution path.

The inexperienced response is to hide that uncertainty behind a confident interface. The architectural response is to expose it, constrain it, measure it, and decide where it is acceptable.

You will often be asked which model an organisation should adopt. Treat that as the beginning of the conversation, not the decision. Ask where the knowledge comes from, what evidence supports the result, what happens when the output is wrong, and who is accountable when the system acts.

The model may be the most visible component, but the invisible structure around it determines whether the result becomes a prototype, a product, or a liability.

If I Were the Architect

You inherit an AI assistant that users like.

It is fast, articulate, and inexpensive.

However:

  • there is no evaluation dataset;
  • outputs are not traceable to evidence;
  • the provider changes models automatically;
  • business teams are beginning to use its recommendations for high-impact decisions.

What do you do first?

A model-centric answer asks whether a better model is available.

An architectural answer first establishes:

  1. where the system is being trusted;
  2. what evidence supports that trust;
  3. what consequences follow from failure;
  4. what controls are required before use expands.

That is the transition from building AI features to practising AI architecture.

Key Takeaways

  • AI architecture extends software architecture; it does not replace it.
  • Established concerns such as reliability, security, performance, cost, and maintainability remain essential.
  • AI introduces model, data, context, evaluation, behavioural, and governance dependencies.
  • Deterministic and probabilistic responsibilities should be separated deliberately.
  • The most critical boundary is where probabilistic interpretation can change business state.
  • Model quality is only one contributor to system quality.
  • AI systems must be monitored for behavioural quality, not merely technical availability.
  • Autonomy should increase only when evidence, evaluation, observability, and governance can support it.
  • The AI Trust Triangle helps diagnose whether capability, evidence, or justified confidence is weakest.
  • The architect’s task is not to remove all uncertainty, but to decide where it is valuable, where it is dangerous, and how it will be controlled.
