Chapter 2 - The Architecture of an AI Decision

How a model response becomes a governed system outcome

Related chapters: Chapters 3, 4, 5, 7, and 13

A model produces a response. A system makes a decision only when intent, evidence, policy, authority, action, and accountability are connected around that response.

1. Why This Chapter Matters

An application sends a prompt to a model and receives an answer.

What happened?

At the API boundary, an inference request completed.

At the user interface, text appeared.

But did the system make a decision?

Not necessarily.

A model response may be:

  • a draft;
  • a classification;
  • a recommendation;
  • a proposed plan;
  • an extracted value;
  • a tool request;
  • a refusal;
  • a plausible but unsupported guess.

A system decision exists only when the surrounding architecture determines:

  • what the task actually is;
  • which context and evidence are permitted;
  • how the output will be validated;
  • which policy applies;
  • who or what has authority;
  • whether an action may occur;
  • how the outcome will be observed;
  • how the event can be reconstructed;
  • what the system learns from the result.

This distinction becomes critical as AI moves from generating information to influencing or changing real-world state.

Current agentic architecture guidance treats identity, permission boundaries, tiered human oversight, auditability, behavioural monitoring, and bounded autonomy as first-class concerns. NIST similarly asks organisations to map how AI capabilities affect downstream decision-making, define human roles and delegated authority, evaluate oversight procedures, and document performance and accountability.[1][2][3]

The central argument of this chapter is:

The model call is one stage of an AI decision. It is not the decision architecture.

2. Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish a model output, recommendation, decision, and action;
  • decompose an AI decision into explicit architectural stages;
  • define a task contract before model execution;
  • identify the difference between context and evidence;
  • place validation outside the probabilistic reasoning path where appropriate;
  • design authority and identity boundaries for AI actions;
  • classify actions by impact and reversibility;
  • create a decision trace without indiscriminately storing sensitive content;
  • model the decision as a state machine;
  • diagnose failures at the correct stage rather than blaming the model;
  • design outcome and feedback mechanisms;
  • answer current architecture interview questions about agent actions, approvals, audit, idempotency, and observability.

Part I — What Is an AI Decision?

3. Response, Recommendation, Decision, and Action

These terms are often used interchangeably. They should not be.

Response

A model or service returns an output.

Example:

“The invoice total appears to be £12,480.”

A response has been produced. No decision has necessarily been made.

Recommendation

The system proposes a course of action.

Example:

“This invoice should be routed for manual review because the amount exceeds the supplier’s historical range.”

The system has expressed a preference, but authority may remain elsewhere.

Decision

An authorised actor or mechanism selects an outcome under applicable policy.

Example:

“Route the invoice to enhanced review.”

The decision may be made by:

  • deterministic policy;
  • a human;
  • an AI-assisted workflow;
  • an autonomous agent operating within delegated authority;
  • a combination of these.

Action

The system changes state or affects the external world.

Example:

  • creates a review case;
  • places a payment hold;
  • sends a message;
  • modifies a record;
  • deploys software;
  • restarts a service.

A decision may exist without action. An action should not exist without an authorised decision.

Model Response
      │
      ▼
Recommendation
      │
      ▼
Authorised Decision
      │
      ▼
Controlled Action
      │
      ▼
Observed Outcome

Architectural principle — Do not collapse the verbs

Generate, recommend, decide, authorise, and execute are different responsibilities even when one runtime appears to perform all of them.

Collapsing these responsibilities hides control points and makes incident reconstruction difficult.

4. Five Levels of AI Influence

AI systems can influence a workflow at different levels.

Level 1 — Describe

The system explains or summarises existing information.

Example:

“Three services began returning errors after the deployment.”

Level 2 — Interpret

The system classifies, extracts, or infers meaning.

Example:

“The incident is likely related to database connection exhaustion.”

Level 3 — Recommend

The system proposes an action.

Example:

“Roll back deployment version 4.8.2.”

Level 4 — Decide within policy

The system selects an option under delegated rules.

Example:

“The rollback is permitted because the service is stateless, the release is under ten minutes old, and the rollback runbook has passed validation.”

Level 5 — Act

The system invokes the rollback tool and changes production state.

Each level adds consequence.

The model may be technically capable of all five, but capability does not establish permission.

Part II — The AI Decision Pipeline

5. The Core Pipeline

This handbook models an AI decision as nine architectural stages:

Intent
  ↓
Context
  ↓
Evidence
  ↓
Reasoning
  ↓
Validation
  ↓
Authority
  ↓
Action
  ↓
Outcome
  ↓
Learning

The stages are logical responsibilities, not a mandatory deployment topology.

A simple system may combine several stages in one service. A high-risk system may separate them across independently owned components.

The value of the model is not that it forces every system into nine boxes.

Its value is that it prevents important responsibilities from disappearing inside “the agent.”

6. Why a Pipeline Is Better Than “Prompt → Model → Tool”

The simplified agent diagram is often:

Prompt → Model → Tool

That diagram is useful for teaching mechanics.

It is insufficient for architecture because it does not reveal:

  • who defined the task;
  • whether the requester is authorised;
  • which evidence the model used;
  • whether the tool arguments were valid;
  • which policy permitted the action;
  • whether approval was required;
  • whether the action was idempotent;
  • what outcome occurred;
  • whether the result improved the original objective.

AWS’s current Agentic AI Lens explicitly notes that one request can trigger multiple model calls, tool invocations, memory retrievals, and communications, each adding latency, cost, and failure surface. It therefore treats bounded autonomy, auditability, tiered oversight, evaluation, identity, and tool access as architectural concerns rather than optional wrappers.[2]

Part III — Stage 1: Intent

7. Establish the Task Contract

Before a model reasons, the system must determine what it is being asked to do.

A useful task contract contains:

  • objective — the outcome sought;
  • requester — who or what initiated it;
  • subject — the resource, customer, service, document, or case involved;
  • scope — what is included and excluded;
  • constraints — policy, time, cost, privacy, and safety limits;
  • success criteria — what completion means;
  • risk class — consequence if wrong;
  • expiry — when the request or evidence becomes stale;
  • allowed actions — what the workflow may propose or execute;
  • escalation path — when authority must move elsewhere.

Example:

objective: restore checkout availability
requester: incident_commander_482
subject: checkout-api-production
scope:
  - investigate deployment 4.8.2
  - inspect current telemetry
excluded:
  - database schema changes
  - customer data modification
success:
  - error rate below 1 percent for 10 minutes
risk_class: high
allowed_actions:
  - read_telemetry
  - compare_deployment
  - propose_rollback
execution_requires: human_approval
expires_at: 2026-08-02T15:30:00Z

This is not necessarily the exact wire format.

It illustrates the architectural idea: the system should reason inside an explicit contract rather than infer unlimited authority from a natural-language request.

8. Intent Is Not the Prompt

A prompt is one representation of intent.

Intent may also be derived from:

  • an event;
  • an API request;
  • a workflow state;
  • a support ticket;
  • an incident alert;
  • a user interface selection;
  • a scheduled policy;
  • a human instruction.

Natural language is ambiguous.

A user who says, “Fix the service,” may mean:

  • diagnose the incident;
  • recommend remediation;
  • execute a safe runbook;
  • restore service at any cost;
  • make no irreversible changes;
  • keep them informed.

The architect should avoid forcing the model to infer both the objective and the authority from one sentence.

Architecture smell — Intent laundering

A vague user request is transformed into a high-impact action without an explicit task contract, scope boundary, or confirmation of authority.

9. Validate Intent Before Reasoning

Intent checks may include:

  • requester authentication;
  • subject existence;
  • scope validation;
  • conflict detection;
  • rate or budget limits;
  • required information;
  • policy eligibility;
  • risk classification;
  • approval prerequisites.

A task that is invalid should fail before expensive reasoning begins.

This reduces:

  • wasted model cost;
  • accidental scope expansion;
  • confused-deputy behaviour;
  • unauthorised action proposals;
  • downstream ambiguity.

Part IV — Stage 2: Context

10. Context Is the Working Situation

Context is the information the system makes available to perform the task.

It may include:

  • conversation history;
  • user profile;
  • workflow state;
  • system instructions;
  • tool descriptions;
  • memory;
  • prior decisions;
  • retrieved documents;
  • current telemetry;
  • policy;
  • environmental state.

Context answers:

What does the system need to know right now to work on this task?

Context engineering is therefore an architectural responsibility involving selection, ordering, compression, freshness, access control, and conflict handling.

Microsoft’s current AI application guidance recommends explicit layer boundaries, business-outcome-first design, auditable controls, observability, and clear isolation around agent capabilities and tools.[4]

11. Context Has a Budget

More context is not always better.

Additional context can introduce:

  • latency;
  • token cost;
  • contradictory instructions;
  • irrelevant detail;
  • privacy exposure;
  • stale information;
  • prompt injection;
  • attention dilution;
  • difficult reconstruction.

A context budget should allocate space by importance:

Task and Policy
      │
Authoritative Evidence
      │
Current State
      │
Relevant History
      │
Examples and Preferences

The ordering will vary by use case.

The principle is that context should be purpose-built, not accumulated indefinitely.

12. Context Integrity

Context should be assessed for:

  • identity — whose context is this?
  • provenance — where did it come from?
  • freshness — is it still valid?
  • authority — is it advisory or binding?
  • confidentiality — may this actor access it?
  • integrity — can it be trusted?
  • priority — which source wins during conflict?
  • retention — should it persist after the task?

A policy document, customer message, retrieved web page, and model-generated memory should not all receive equal authority.

Architectural principle — Context is typed

Treat context items as typed inputs with provenance, authority, freshness, and access rules—not as undifferentiated text.

13. Context Failure Modes

Context starvation

The model lacks information needed to complete the task.

Context flooding

The model receives too much information to reliably focus on what matters.

Context poisoning

Untrusted content manipulates reasoning or tool selection.

Context collision

Two sources provide conflicting instructions or facts.

Context leakage

Information is exposed across users, tenants, cases, or security domains.

Context staleness

The information was valid when stored but is no longer valid at decision time.

A robust design handles these as data and control problems, not merely prompt problems.

Part V — Stage 3: Evidence

14. Context Is Not Evidence

All evidence may appear in context, but not all context is evidence.

Examples of context:

  • user preference;
  • conversation history;
  • style instruction;
  • previous draft;
  • tool schema.

Examples of evidence:

  • signed transaction record;
  • current database result;
  • approved policy;
  • deployment diff;
  • telemetry window;
  • cited document passage;
  • deterministic calculation.

Evidence answers:

What supports the claim or proposed action?

This distinction is central to the AI Trust Triangle.

A highly capable model may operate with abundant context and still lack the evidence needed to justify reliance.

15. Evidence Quality Dimensions

Evaluate evidence across:

Relevance

Does it address the actual task?

Authority

Is the source entitled to establish the fact or rule?

Freshness

Is it current enough for the decision?

Completeness

Is important counter-evidence missing?

Integrity

Has the source been altered or manipulated?

Access legitimacy

Was the evidence obtained under appropriate permission?

Traceability

Can the result be linked back to the source?

Consistency

Does it conflict with other authoritative evidence?

Resolution

Is the evidence sufficiently precise?

A retrieved paragraph may be relevant but outdated. A database value may be current but incomplete. A human statement may be authoritative for intent but not for financial policy.

16. Evidence Acquisition Patterns

Retrieval

Search a corpus and return source passages.

Tool query

Ask an authoritative system for current state.

Deterministic calculation

Compute a value from validated inputs.

Policy evaluation

Evaluate a decision against explicit rules.

Sensor or telemetry read

Observe the environment.

Human attestation

Obtain confirmation from an accountable person.

Multi-source corroboration

Require agreement across independent sources.

The architect chooses an evidence pattern based on risk and task.

17. Evidence Gaps Must Be First-Class

A dangerous system converts missing evidence into confident completion.

A trustworthy system can represent:

  • evidence found;
  • evidence conflicting;
  • evidence stale;
  • evidence inaccessible;
  • evidence insufficient;
  • evidence not required.

The workflow should have a deliberate response to each state:

  • continue;
  • retrieve again;
  • use an alternate source;
  • narrow the claim;
  • request user input;
  • escalate;
  • refuse;
  • postpone until fresh evidence is available.

Architecture smell — Absence becomes invention

The model fills missing evidence with a plausible answer because the system lacks an explicit “insufficient evidence” state.

Part VI — Stage 4: Reasoning

18. Reasoning Transforms Evidence into a Proposal

Reasoning may involve:

  • classification;
  • extraction;
  • synthesis;
  • comparison;
  • planning;
  • hypothesis generation;
  • tool selection;
  • decomposition;
  • ranking;
  • explanation.

The model’s role is to transform the task, context, and evidence into a candidate output or action proposal.

The word candidate matters.

The reasoning stage should not silently inherit authority to execute.

19. Choose the Simplest Reasoning Mechanism

Possible mechanisms include:

  • deterministic rules;
  • SQL;
  • search and ranking;
  • statistical models;
  • small language models;
  • frontier reasoning models;
  • workflow graphs;
  • optimisers;
  • human judgment;
  • combinations.

Use a model only where its capability adds value.

Examples:

  • calculate tax with deterministic logic;
  • interpret an ambiguous invoice description with a model;
  • retrieve policy through search;
  • determine permitted amount through a policy engine;
  • ask a human to adjudicate an exceptional case.

Architectural principle — Intelligence is allocated

Use the least expensive and least variable mechanism that satisfies the required capability and risk level.

This includes more than financial cost. It includes latency, explainability, operability, and failure complexity.

20. Reasoning Boundaries

The reasoning component should receive:

  • a defined task;
  • bounded evidence;
  • explicit tool contracts;
  • policy-relevant constraints;
  • a required output schema;
  • a budget;
  • stop conditions.

Budgets may include:

  • maximum model calls;
  • maximum tokens;
  • tool-call limit;
  • retry limit;
  • elapsed time;
  • cost;
  • maximum planning depth;
  • human escalation deadline.

These budgets prevent a stochastic workflow from becoming an unbounded loop.

21. Structured Output Is a Contract, Not Proof

A schema can require:

{
  "recommendation": "rollback",
  "evidence_ids": ["deploy-4.8.2", "metric-window-937"],
  "risk": "high",
  "requires_approval": true
}

This improves interoperability and validation.

It does not prove that:

  • the recommendation is correct;
  • the evidence supports it;
  • the risk is classified properly;
  • the actor is authorised;
  • the action is safe.

A valid shape can contain an invalid decision.

22. Reasoning Failure Modes

Goal drift

The workflow optimises a proxy rather than the intended outcome.

Tool-selection error

The model chooses an inappropriate capability.

Unsupported inference

The conclusion goes beyond the evidence.

Planning loop

The agent repeatedly reasons without making progress.

Premature commitment

The system selects a hypothesis too early and ignores alternatives.

Role confusion

One agent or component performs conflicting responsibilities such as proposing, approving, and auditing its own action.

Explanation substitution

A fluent rationale is mistaken for evidence that the reasoning was sound.

Part VII — Stage 5: Validation

23. Validation Challenges the Candidate Output

Validation asks whether the proposed result is acceptable before authority or execution.

Possible checks include:

  • schema validity;
  • allowed values;
  • required evidence;
  • citation support;
  • numerical constraints;
  • policy compliance;
  • security rules;
  • privacy filters;
  • risk threshold;
  • duplicate detection;
  • simulation;
  • sandbox execution;
  • independent evaluator;
  • human review.

Validation should be placed outside the same untrusted reasoning path where possible.

24. Deterministic Validation First

A useful ordering is:

Candidate Output
      │
      ▼
Deterministic Invariants
      │
      ▼
Evidence and Policy Checks
      │
      ▼
Probabilistic Quality Evaluation
      │
      ▼
Human Review if Required

Examples of deterministic invariants:

  • refund must not exceed policy limit;
  • database operation must be read-only;
  • deployment target must match the approved environment;
  • file path must stay inside an allowed root;
  • every claim must reference an existing evidence identifier;
  • action parameters must conform to a schema.

A probabilistic evaluator should not override a violated invariant.

25. Validator Independence

A validator is weak when it shares all the same assumptions as the generator.

Independence can come from:

  • different mechanism;
  • different model;
  • deterministic rules;
  • separate evidence;
  • different prompt and role;
  • human expertise;
  • sandbox outcome;
  • authoritative policy service.

Complete independence is not always possible or affordable.

The architect should identify correlated failure.

Architecture smell — The model marks its own exam

The same model generates, validates, and approves a consequential output without independent evidence or controls.

26. Validation Outcomes

Validation should produce explicit states:

  • pass;
  • fail;
  • repairable;
  • insufficient evidence;
  • policy review required;
  • human review required;
  • expired.

Avoid a single boolean when the recovery behaviour differs.

For example:

  • schema failure may be repaired automatically;
  • missing evidence may require retrieval;
  • policy conflict may require escalation;
  • expired telemetry may require a fresh read;
  • prohibited action should fail permanently.

Part VIII — Stage 6: Authority

27. Capability Is Not Authority

A tool-capable agent may be able to call an API.

That does not mean it is authorised to do so.

Authority answers:

  • who may make this decision?
  • on whose behalf?
  • within which scope?
  • under which policy?
  • for how long?
  • with which permissions?
  • under which approval?
  • with what revocation path?

AWS’s current guidance recommends distinct agent identities, signed propagation of user context, short-lived credentials, minimum permissions, clear audit attribution, and controls that prevent agents from assuming human identities.[3]

28. Actor, Principal, and Subject

These roles should be distinguished.

Requesting principal

The human or service asking for the task.

Acting workload

The agent or service performing computation.

Authorising principal

The policy engine, human approver, or delegated authority permitting action.

Subject

The resource or person affected by the decision.

Executing service

The deterministic system that applies the action.

Example:

Incident Commander
    requests
        │
        ▼
Remediation Agent
    proposes
        │
        ▼
Policy + Human Approver
    authorise
        │
        ▼
Deployment Service
    executes on
        │
        ▼
Checkout Production

A single person or service may hold multiple roles, but the architecture should make this explicit.

29. The Impact–Reversibility Matrix

Action governance should be proportional to consequence.

                         REVERSIBILITY
                  High                    Low
IMPACT
Low          Autonomous / log       Notify or approve
High         Notify / approve       Explicit approval,
                                      dual control, or prohibit

This matrix is a synthesis grounded in current agentic guidance that recommends classifying actions by impact and reversibility into autonomous, notify, and approve tiers.[1]

High reversibility

The action can be reliably undone within the required time and without hidden harm.

Low reversibility

The action is difficult, slow, incomplete, legally constrained, or impossible to undo.

Low impact

Failure has limited consequence and blast radius.

High impact

Failure can affect safety, finance, rights, security, customers, regulated records, or critical operations.

Important constraint

Reversibility is not merely the presence of an “undo” button.

A message can be deleted but still seen. A database change can be rolled back but still trigger downstream events. A production action can be reversed but still violate an SLA.

30. Tiered Oversight

A practical policy can classify actions as:

Autonomous

Low impact, bounded, observable, and reliably reversible.

Notify

The action may proceed, but an operator receives timely visibility.

Approve

Execution is blocked until explicit authority is granted.

Prohibit

The action is outside the system’s delegated authority.

AWS recommends structured review requests, timeouts, escalation paths, safe fallbacks, and logging of reviewer identity, rationale, and timestamp.[1]

Architectural principle — Approval is a workflow

Human approval requires evidence, context, authority, timeout, escalation, and a recorded decision. A pause button alone is not governance.

31. Authority Expiry and Revocation

Authority should be bounded by:

  • time;
  • task;
  • subject;
  • environment;
  • action type;
  • amount;
  • region;
  • risk;
  • approval;
  • evidence version.

A rollback approval based on telemetry from twenty minutes ago may no longer be valid.

The architecture should answer:

  • when does authority expire?
  • what evidence invalidates it?
  • can it be revoked during execution?
  • how is revocation propagated?
  • what happens to in-flight work?

Part IX — Stage 7: Action

32. Execute Through Controlled Interfaces

The action layer should expose narrow, explicit capabilities.

Prefer:

restart_service(service_id, approved_change_id)

over:

run_shell(command)

Prefer:

create_refund(order_id, amount, reason_code)

over generic database write access.

Narrow tools reduce:

  • ambiguity;
  • prompt injection impact;
  • privilege;
  • invalid parameters;
  • audit complexity;
  • blast radius.

33. Idempotency

An action is idempotent when retrying it with the same request does not create additional unintended effects.

This matters because agentic workflows may retry after:

  • timeout;
  • network failure;
  • uncertain response;
  • worker restart;
  • duplicated event;
  • human resubmission.

Examples:

  • create one ticket with an idempotency key;
  • set desired deployment version rather than “deploy again”;
  • record payment intent before execution;
  • reject duplicate refund requests.

AWS’s Agentic AI Lens includes idempotency as a core reliability concept for safe retries and duplicate prevention.[2]

34. Atomicity and Compensation

Some actions cannot be completed atomically across all systems.

The workflow may need a saga-like pattern:

Reserve Resource
      │
      ▼
Perform Action
      │
      ▼
Update Record
      │
      ├── success → close
      └── failure → compensate / escalate

The architect should define:

  • commit point;
  • partial-success states;
  • compensation;
  • manual recovery;
  • retry ownership;
  • timeout;
  • duplicate handling.

Do not assume the model will reason its way out of an inconsistent distributed state.

35. Pre-Execution and Post-Execution Checks

Pre-execution

  • authority still valid;
  • evidence still fresh;
  • target still matches;
  • policy still permits;
  • parameters valid;
  • budget available;
  • approval present;
  • action not already completed.

Post-execution

  • response received;
  • expected state changed;
  • unintended state unchanged;
  • audit event recorded;
  • outcome observation scheduled;
  • compensation ready if needed.

Execution success does not prove outcome success.

An API may return HTTP 200 while the wrong service was restarted.

Part X — Stage 8: Outcome

36. Action Completion Is Not Goal Completion

The tool call completed.

Did the situation improve?

This is the difference between:

  • execution metric — the operation ran;
  • task metric — the requested task was completed;
  • outcome metric — the real-world condition improved.

Example:

Restart API succeeded      → execution
Error rate fell            → task effect
Checkout conversions rose  → business outcome

A system that observes only execution may optimise for activity rather than value.

37. Define Outcome Windows

Some outcomes are immediate.

Others require observation over time.

Examples:

  • service error rate for ten minutes;
  • refund dispute rate over thirty days;
  • customer repeat-contact within seven days;
  • deployment incident rate over one quarter;
  • document-review correction rate after human audit.

The task contract should define:

  • observation metric;
  • baseline;
  • expected direction;
  • threshold;
  • time window;
  • confounding factors;
  • owner.

38. Outcomes Can Contradict the Decision

A technically correct action may produce an undesirable outcome.

Examples:

  • a rollback restores availability but reintroduces a security defect;
  • a support agent reduces handling time but increases repeat contact;
  • a fraud model blocks losses but harms legitimate customers;
  • an optimisation agent lowers infrastructure cost but increases latency.

The system should preserve the ability to compare:

  • intended outcome;
  • actual outcome;
  • side effects;
  • residual risk.

Part XI — Stage 9: Learning

39. Learning Closes the Loop

Production evidence should update:

  • evaluations;
  • policies;
  • prompts;
  • retrieval;
  • tool contracts;
  • risk classifications;
  • approval thresholds;
  • runbooks;
  • architecture decisions.

NIST treats risk management as continuous throughout the AI lifecycle, and OpenTelemetry’s generative-AI conventions support standardised traces, metrics, and events for model requests, tokens, tool calls, tool results, and related operations.[5][6]

Learning does not necessarily mean online model training.

Often the safest improvements occur in the surrounding system.

40. Separate Feedback Types

User preference

“I prefer shorter summaries.”

Quality correction

“The answer cited the wrong policy.”

Outcome evidence

“The recommended rollback did not reduce error rate.”

Safety signal

“The agent attempted a prohibited action.”

Operational signal

“Tool latency caused three retries.”

Governance signal

“Reviewers override this decision category 40% of the time.”

These signals should not all feed the same update mechanism.

A preference should not silently weaken policy. A user correction should not automatically become global truth. A malicious rating should not poison future decisions.

41. Feedback Integrity

Evaluate feedback for:

  • source identity;
  • expertise;
  • conflict of interest;
  • representativeness;
  • delay;
  • ambiguity;
  • manipulation;
  • privacy;
  • linkage to the original decision.

Architecture smell — Learning from applause

The system optimises for immediate positive feedback without measuring whether the decision was correct, safe, or valuable.

Part XII — The Decision Envelope

42. Package the Decision Context

A decision envelope is the minimum structured information required to move a candidate decision safely between stages.

Example:

decision_id: dec_01J8M8...
task_id: incident_7432
objective: restore checkout availability
subject: checkout-api-production
requesting_principal: user_482
acting_workload: remediation-agent-v3
candidate:
  action: rollback
  target_version: 4.8.1
evidence:
  - deploy_diff_4.8.2
  - metric_window_937
policy:
  risk_tier: approve
  matched_rules:
    - prod_change_requires_human
validation:
  schema: pass
  evidence_support: pass
  target_check: pass
authority:
  status: pending
  required_role: incident_commander
expires_at: 2026-08-02T15:30:00Z
trace_id: 7ce1...

The envelope is not intended to expose private chain-of-thought.

It records operationally meaningful facts:

  • task;
  • actors;
  • proposal;
  • evidence;
  • policy;
  • validation;
  • authority;
  • expiry;
  • trace.

ARB constraint

The envelope is a handbook synthesis, not a universal standard. Implementations should adapt fields to their domain and privacy obligations.

43. Why the Envelope Matters

It supports:

  • policy evaluation;
  • approval UI;
  • audit;
  • retry;
  • handoff;
  • observability;
  • incident reconstruction;
  • expiry;
  • replay in evaluation;
  • separation of model and execution.

Without it, critical information may be scattered across prompts, logs, memory, and application state.

Part XIII — Decision State Machine

44. Decisions Have State

A useful decision lifecycle is:

Requested
   ↓
Framed
   ↓
Evidence Ready
   ↓
Proposed
   ↓
Validated
   ↓
Authorised
   ↓
Executing
   ↓
Observed
   ↓
Closed

Alternative terminal or exceptional states include:

  • rejected;
  • insufficient evidence;
  • expired;
  • cancelled;
  • failed;
  • partially completed;
  • compensating;
  • rolled back;
  • escalated.

A state machine makes transitions explicit.

45. Transition Guards

Examples:

Proposed → Validated
  only if schema passes and evidence is sufficient

Validated → Authorised
  only if matching policy and required approval exist

Authorised → Executing
  only if authority and evidence are not expired

Executing → Observed
  only if execution record is durable

Observed → Closed
  only if outcome criteria are assessed

This prevents conversational state from becoming the only source of workflow truth.

Architecture smell — Chat history as transaction log

The system relies on an agent’s conversation history to determine whether an action was approved, executed, or already retried.

Use durable state and explicit identifiers for consequential workflows.

Part XIV — Decision Trace and Observability

46. Trace the System, Not Only the Model

A useful trace may include:

  • task creation;
  • identity resolution;
  • context assembly;
  • retrieval query;
  • evidence identifiers and scores;
  • model request and response metadata;
  • tool calls;
  • validation results;
  • policy decision;
  • approval;
  • execution;
  • outcome observation;
  • retry;
  • escalation;
  • cost and latency.

OpenTelemetry’s generative-AI conventions are intended to standardise traces, metrics, and events for AI operations, including model information, token use, tool calls, and—in controlled configurations—content and tool results.[5][6]

47. Content Capture Requires Deliberate Policy

Full prompts, completions, retrieved content, and tool results can improve debugging.

They can also expose:

  • personal data;
  • secrets;
  • regulated records;
  • intellectual property;
  • security-sensitive instructions.

Decide:

  • which fields are captured;
  • whether content is redacted;
  • sampling rate;
  • encryption;
  • retention;
  • access;
  • regional storage;
  • deletion;
  • use in evaluation;
  • consent and disclosure where required.

Architectural principle — Trace enough, not everything

Capture the minimum information required to reconstruct and improve the decision at the relevant risk level.

48. Three Observability Planes

Technical plane

  • availability;
  • latency;
  • errors;
  • retries;
  • tokens;
  • cost;
  • resource usage.

Behavioural plane

  • task success;
  • evidence support;
  • tool selection;
  • policy compliance;
  • refusal;
  • loop rate;
  • escalation;
  • evaluator results.

Outcome plane

  • user success;
  • operational improvement;
  • business KPI;
  • side effects;
  • incident rate;
  • override rate.

An agent can be healthy on the technical plane and failing on the outcome plane.

Part XV — Failure Taxonomy

49. Intent Failures

  • ambiguous objective;
  • wrong requester;
  • unauthorised scope;
  • conflicting goals;
  • stale task;
  • missing success criteria.

50. Context Failures

  • leakage;
  • poisoning;
  • collision;
  • staleness;
  • flooding;
  • missing history.

51. Evidence Failures

  • irrelevant source;
  • incomplete retrieval;
  • low-authority source;
  • outdated state;
  • fabricated citation;
  • missing counter-evidence.

52. Reasoning Failures

  • unsupported inference;
  • wrong tool;
  • planning loop;
  • goal drift;
  • premature conclusion;
  • role confusion.

53. Validation Failures

  • validator shares generator failure;
  • invariant missing;
  • policy version stale;
  • false pass;
  • repair loop;
  • evaluator over-trusted.

54. Authority Failures

  • shared credentials;
  • confused deputy;
  • user context lost;
  • approval expired;
  • excessive privilege;
  • actor attribution unclear.

55. Action Failures

  • duplicate side effect;
  • partial completion;
  • wrong target;
  • non-idempotent retry;
  • timeout uncertainty;
  • compensation failure.

56. Outcome Failures

  • execution mistaken for success;
  • observation window too short;
  • side effect ignored;
  • wrong KPI;
  • delayed harm;
  • no baseline.

57. Learning Failures

  • malicious feedback;
  • preference treated as truth;
  • local correction applied globally;
  • incident not added to evaluation;
  • policy weakened by popularity;
  • feedback not linked to decision.

Diagnostic rule

Name the failed stage before proposing the fix.

“The agent is unreliable” is too broad to guide architecture.

“The evidence layer returned a stale runbook, and authority did not expire when the evidence changed” points to correct controls.

Part XVI — Worked Example: Incident Remediation

58. Scenario

A production alert reports that checkout errors increased after a deployment.

The organisation wants an AI system to investigate and, when safe, remediate.

59. Weak Architecture

Alert → Agent → Shell Tool → Production

Problems:

  • alert text becomes unlimited intent;
  • no explicit requester or authority;
  • shell access is broad;
  • evidence is not distinguished from model memory;
  • approval is unclear;
  • retries can duplicate action;
  • API success may be mistaken for incident resolution;
  • trace may not identify the human or agent actor.

60. Decision-Pipeline Architecture

Intent

Objective: restore checkout availability
Scope: checkout service and latest deployment
Prohibited: schema changes, customer-data writes
Success: error rate <1% for 10 minutes

Context

  • current incident state;
  • service ownership;
  • runbooks;
  • deployment history;
  • allowed tools;
  • policy;
  • prior remediation attempts.

Evidence

  • error-rate telemetry;
  • deployment diff;
  • dependency health;
  • logs;
  • approved rollback runbook;
  • blast-radius data.

Reasoning

The model:

  • compares hypotheses;
  • selects diagnostic tools;
  • proposes rollback;
  • identifies risk and required evidence.

Validation

Deterministic checks confirm:

  • target deployment exists;
  • previous version is deployable;
  • no database migration blocks rollback;
  • evidence is fresh;
  • action parameters match schema.

Authority

Policy classifies production rollback as:

  • high impact;
  • reasonably reversible;
  • approval required.

An incident commander receives:

  • proposed action;
  • supporting evidence;
  • expected impact;
  • rollback-of-rollback plan;
  • execution history;
  • expiry.

Action

A narrow deployment API:

rollback_service(
  service="checkout-api",
  from_version="4.8.2",
  to_version="4.8.1",
  approval_id="appr_9182",
  idempotency_key="incident_7432_rollback_1"
)

Outcome

Observe:

  • error rate;
  • latency;
  • checkout completion;
  • dependent-service health;
  • new alerts;
  • observation window.

Learning

Record:

  • hypothesis quality;
  • evidence used;
  • approval;
  • action;
  • outcome;
  • unexpected effects;
  • whether the scenario should enter regression evaluation.

61. Trust Triangle Review

Capability

Can the system diagnose the relevant class of incidents and choose appropriate tools?

Evidence

Are telemetry, deployment state, and runbooks current, authoritative, and traceable?

Confidence

What evaluation and production history justify allowing recommendation, approval routing, or autonomous remediation?

The strongest model cannot compensate for stale telemetry or excessive authority.

Part XVII — Architecture Review

62. Scenario

A financial-services company builds a loan-document assistant.

It:

  • extracts applicant information;
  • calculates affordability through a model;
  • recommends approval;
  • stores the final answer;
  • lets a reviewer click approve;
  • uses the same model to check its own work;
  • has broad access to customer files;
  • retrains prompts from reviewer feedback.

63. ARB Findings

Finding 1 — Calculation is probabilistic

Affordability calculation should use validated deterministic logic.

Finding 2 — Context and evidence are mixed

Applicant statements, verified income, and policy rules are treated as equivalent text.

Finding 3 — Reviewer lacks decision evidence

The reviewer sees a recommendation but not source fields, conflicts, validation, or uncertainty.

Finding 4 — Validator is correlated

The same model generates and evaluates the recommendation.

Finding 5 — Authority boundary is unclear

The system’s recommendation may become de facto approval through automation bias.

Finding 6 — Audit is incomplete

Only the final answer is stored, not the decision envelope.

Finding 7 — Feedback can corrupt policy

Reviewer preference is used for prompt adaptation without distinguishing correction, exception, and policy change.

64. Recommended Redesign

  • explicit task contract;
  • typed evidence with provenance;
  • deterministic affordability service;
  • policy engine;
  • independent validation;
  • reviewer interface showing evidence and conflicts;
  • separate recommendation and approval;
  • least-privilege document access;
  • decision trace;
  • feedback classification;
  • outcome review;
  • appeal and correction path.

Part XVIII — Interview Preparation

65. Foundational Questions

Question 1

What is the difference between a model output and a system decision?

A strong answer explains that a system decision adds task framing, evidence, validation, policy, authority, and accountability around the model output.

Question 2

Why should context and evidence be separated?

Context helps the system work. Evidence justifies the claim or action. Context may contain preferences, instructions, and history that do not establish truth.

Question 3

Where should validation occur?

Outside the same probabilistic path where possible, with deterministic invariants first, followed by evidence, policy, probabilistic quality evaluation, and human review according to risk.

Question 4

Why is structured output insufficient for reliability?

A schema proves shape, not truth, support, authority, or safety.

Question 5

How do you decide whether an action requires human approval?

Discuss impact, reversibility, evidence, policy, confidence, blast radius, and organisational accountability.

66. Senior-Level Questions

Question 6

Design the identity model for an agent acting on behalf of a user.

A strong answer separates user identity, agent workload identity, delegated claims, least privilege, short-lived credentials, attribution, revocation, and downstream authorisation.[3]

Question 7

An agent timed out after calling a payment API. How do you retry safely?

Discuss idempotency keys, durable intent, payment status query, duplicate prevention, uncertain outcome state, and reconciliation before retry.

Question 8

What should be included in an approval request?

  • task objective;
  • proposed action;
  • subject;
  • evidence;
  • validation;
  • risk and impact;
  • reversibility;
  • prior actions;
  • expiry;
  • alternatives;
  • reviewer options.

Question 9

How do you observe whether an agent succeeded?

Separate technical, behavioural, task, and outcome metrics. Trace model calls, tools, policy, approval, action, and observed result.

Question 10

How do you prevent a model from fabricating evidence?

Use evidence identifiers from controlled retrieval or tools, verify identifier existence, require claim-to-source linkage, block unsupported actions, and represent insufficient evidence explicitly.

Question 11

Should reasoning traces be stored?

Avoid treating private chain-of-thought as a required audit artifact. Store operationally meaningful task, evidence, tool, validation, policy, approval, action, and outcome data. Capture sensitive content only under deliberate privacy and retention policy.

Question 12

How do you design for authority expiry?

Bind authority to task, action, subject, evidence version, risk, approver, and time. Revalidate immediately before execution and cancel or reapprove when material inputs change.

67. Principal-Level Questions

Question 13

How would you create an enterprise standard for agent actions?

A strong answer includes:

  • action taxonomy;
  • impact–reversibility classification;
  • tool contracts;
  • workload identity;
  • least privilege;
  • decision envelope;
  • policy gateway;
  • approval tiers;
  • idempotency;
  • trace standard;
  • outcome measurement;
  • incident and revocation process.

Question 14

What belongs in a platform and what belongs in a product team?

Platform candidates:

  • identity;
  • model gateway;
  • trace conventions;
  • policy enforcement;
  • approval primitives;
  • tool registry;
  • secret brokering;
  • evaluation infrastructure.

Product responsibilities:

  • task definition;
  • domain evidence;
  • success criteria;
  • risk classification;
  • domain validation;
  • outcome ownership.

Avoid centralising domain judgment into a generic platform.

Question 15

How would you challenge the proposed nine-stage decision pipeline?

A mature answer may argue that:

  • not all generative workloads make decisions;
  • stages can be combined;
  • some systems require additional perception or planning stages;
  • human decisions may occur earlier;
  • outcome may be delayed;
  • learning may be organisational rather than automated.

The response should preserve the responsibilities even if the topology changes.

Part XIX — Whiteboard Challenge

68. Design an AI Procurement Agent

The system may:

  • identify suppliers;
  • request quotations;
  • compare offers;
  • recommend a supplier;
  • create a purchase order below a threshold.

Constraints

  • multiple countries and currencies;
  • approved-supplier policy;
  • sanctions screening;
  • budget ownership;
  • confidential bids;
  • delivery deadlines;
  • human approval for exceptions;
  • supplier data can be stale;
  • procurement decisions may be audited months later.

Discuss

  1. Define the task contract.
  2. Separate context and evidence.
  3. Identify deterministic services.
  4. Model supplier and user identity.
  5. Define the impact–reversibility policy.
  6. Design the decision envelope.
  7. Define approval evidence.
  8. Handle tool timeout and duplicate orders.
  9. Define outcome metrics.
  10. Create the trace and retention policy.
  11. Describe safe degradation.
  12. Explain how reviewer feedback becomes learning.

Strong-answer characteristics

  • procurement policy is deterministic;
  • supplier data provenance is visible;
  • budget and sanctions checks use authoritative systems;
  • model compares narrative and ambiguous factors;
  • purchase order tool is narrow and idempotent;
  • authority is amount-, country-, and category-bounded;
  • high-risk exceptions require meaningful approval;
  • decision and evidence are reconstructable;
  • outcome includes delivery, quality, price, and dispute rate.

Part XX — Questions to Take Back to Your Team

  1. Are we calling a model response a decision?
  2. Where is the task contract stored?
  3. Which context items are authoritative evidence?
  4. How do we represent insufficient or conflicting evidence?
  5. Which invariants are checked deterministically?
  6. Can the generator approve its own output?
  7. Who is the requesting, acting, authorising, and executing principal?
  8. What limits authority by time, subject, action, and evidence?
  9. Which actions are low impact and reliably reversible?
  10. Are retries idempotent?
  11. Can we reconstruct the decision without relying on chat history?
  12. Do we observe outcome or only tool completion?
  13. How is feedback classified before it changes the system?
  14. What is the safe degraded mode?
  15. Which stage fails most often in production?

Architect’s Notebook — The Missing Middle

Teams often discuss two endpoints:

  • the user request;
  • the final action.

The architectural risk lives in the missing middle.

That middle contains:

  • interpretation;
  • context;
  • evidence;
  • policy;
  • validation;
  • authority;
  • state;
  • retries;
  • observation.

The more capable the model becomes, the easier it is to hide this middle behind a conversational interface.

Do not confuse invisibility with absence.

From the Architect’s Desk

Early AI applications could often be reviewed as information systems. The model produced text, and a human decided what to do with it. Agentic systems compress that distance. A generated proposal can become a tool call within milliseconds.

That compression is useful, but it removes the natural pauses where people previously checked evidence, applied policy, confirmed authority, and noticed that the situation had changed. Good architecture puts those responsibilities back deliberately.

Do not ask only whether the model can perform an action. Ask who authorised it, which evidence was current, which policy applied, whether the action could be reversed, and how you will know that it improved the outcome.

A model can produce a compelling reason. It cannot grant itself authority. A tool can return success. It cannot prove that the objective was achieved. A trace can record activity. It cannot replace accountability.

The architecture of an AI decision is the structure that connects capability to consequence without losing control of the space between them.

If I Were the Architect

You inherit an agent that manages cloud costs.

It can:

  • resize workloads;
  • delete unused resources;
  • alter retention;
  • purchase reservations;
  • change autoscaling policies.

The finance team loves the savings.

Engineering reports occasional outages and missing logs.

The agent’s dashboard shows a 96% task-success rate.

What do you do first?

Do not begin by changing the model.

Reconstruct the decision architecture:

  1. What objective is the agent optimising?
  2. Which side effects are represented?
  3. Which evidence determines “unused”?
  4. Which actions are reversible?
  5. Which policies protect reliability and retention?
  6. Who authorised each action category?
  7. Are retries idempotent?
  8. Does the trace show proposal, validation, approval, and action?
  9. What outcome window captures reliability harm?
  10. Which failure cases are missing from evaluation?

A system can be highly successful against the wrong objective.

The architect’s responsibility is to connect optimisation to the whole outcome.

Key Takeaways

  • A model response is not automatically a system decision.
  • Generate, recommend, decide, authorise, execute, and observe are distinct responsibilities.
  • The AI Decision Pipeline contains intent, context, evidence, reasoning, validation, authority, action, outcome, and learning.
  • Intent should be represented as a bounded task contract.
  • Context helps the system work; evidence justifies reliance.
  • Evidence gaps and conflicts need explicit workflow states.
  • Structured output validates shape, not correctness.
  • Deterministic invariants should be checked before probabilistic quality judgments.
  • Capability does not grant authority.
  • Agent and user identities should remain distinct and attributable.
  • Human oversight should be tiered according to impact and reversibility.
  • Approval is a structured workflow, not merely a pause.
  • Actions require narrow interfaces, idempotency, durable state, and recovery.
  • Execution success is not outcome success.
  • Learning signals must be classified and protected from manipulation.
  • A decision envelope and state machine make consequential workflows reconstructable.
  • Observability should cover technical, behavioural, and outcome planes.
  • Diagnose the failed stage before proposing a fix.
