Chapter 3 - Quality Attributes for AI Systems

Turning “good AI” into measurable architectural requirements

Related chapters: Chapters 2, 4, 9, and 10

An AI system is not high quality because it is intelligent. It is high quality when it delivers the required outcome, under the required conditions, with acceptable cost, risk, and operational behaviour.

1. Why This Chapter Matters

Teams often begin AI evaluation with a model question:

How accurate is it?

The question is necessary.

It is rarely sufficient.

A highly accurate model can still sit inside a system that is:

  • unavailable when users need it;
  • too slow for the workflow;
  • too expensive to operate;
  • insecure;
  • impossible to audit;
  • difficult to change;
  • unfair across affected groups;
  • unsafe when inputs are adversarial;
  • poorly grounded in current evidence;
  • unable to recognise when it should stop.

The inverse is also possible. A technically reliable service can return the wrong answer quickly, consistently, and cheaply.

Architecture exists because system quality is multidimensional.

ISO/IEC 25010 defines a product quality model that can be used to specify, measure, and evaluate quality throughout the lifecycle.[1] The SEI Quality Attribute Workshop derives architecture-critical qualities from mission and business goals, develops real-world scenarios, and prioritises them before an architecture is fixed.[2]

AI does not replace these practices. It introduces learned and generative behaviour whose quality depends on models, data, context, evidence, tools, policy, users, and operating conditions.

NIST describes trustworthy AI through characteristics including validity and reliability, safety, security and resilience, accountability and transparency, explainability and interpretability, privacy, and fairness. It also warns that these qualities involve trade-offs, do not apply equally in every context, and must be balanced according to intended use.[3]

The central argument of this chapter is:

Quality attributes must be expressed as prioritised, measurable scenarios. A list of desirable qualities is not an architecture requirement.

2. Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish functional capability from system quality;
  • explain why AI quality is a property of the socio-technical system rather than the model alone;
  • identify inherited software quality attributes and AI-elevated attributes;
  • turn vague goals such as “reliable,” “safe,” and “explainable” into scenarios;
  • define response measures for deterministic and probabilistic behaviour;
  • separate service-level indicators from task and outcome evaluations;
  • prioritise quality attributes from business goals, risk, and context of use;
  • identify trade-offs and sensitivity points;
  • choose architectural tactics for important qualities;
  • define quality gates for release and continued operation;
  • avoid aggregate metrics that conceal important failures;
  • answer architecture interview questions about quality, SLOs, evaluation, fairness, safety, performance, and cost.

Part I — Quality Is Contextual

3. Quality Is Fitness for a Particular Use

The phrase “high-quality AI” has no useful meaning without context.

Consider the same language model in three systems:

Creative writing assistant

The system may value:

  • novelty;
  • responsiveness;
  • style control;
  • low cost;
  • user editability.

A factually imaginative answer may be acceptable.

Internal policy assistant

The system may value:

  • groundedness;
  • current evidence;
  • access control;
  • citation quality;
  • refusal when evidence is missing.

Creative invention is a defect.

Medication information assistant

The system may require:

  • authoritative evidence;
  • careful scope;
  • safety;
  • traceability;
  • conservative escalation;
  • clear limitations;
  • human accountability.

The same output behaviour can be useful in one context and unacceptable in another.

Quality therefore depends on:

  • task;
  • users;
  • affected parties;
  • environment;
  • consequence;
  • evidence;
  • operating model;
  • legal and organisational obligations;
  • acceptable error.

ISO/IEC 25019 similarly treats context of use as a prerequisite for evaluating quality in use.[4]

Architectural principle — Quality belongs to a context

No quality target is meaningful until the system, user, environment, stimulus, and consequence are specified.

4. Capability Is Not the Whole Quality Model

Capability asks:

Can the system perform the task?

Quality asks broader questions:

  • Does it perform the correct task?
  • Under which conditions?
  • For whom?
  • How often?
  • With which evidence?
  • At what latency and cost?
  • How safely?
  • How consistently?
  • How is failure detected?
  • Can the system recover?
  • Can the behaviour be changed?

A model may demonstrate capability on a benchmark while the application fails in production because:

  • context is incomplete;
  • retrieval is stale;
  • tool permissions are wrong;
  • latency exceeds user tolerance;
  • costs scale badly;
  • evaluators do not represent real cases;
  • users over-rely on confident wording;
  • outcomes are not monitored.

The architecture must treat quality as an end-to-end property.

5. Model, System, and Outcome Quality

It is useful to distinguish three levels.

Model quality

Properties of the model under a defined evaluation:

  • predictive or generative performance;
  • robustness;
  • calibration;
  • reasoning capability;
  • language coverage;
  • harmful-output behaviour.

System quality

Properties of the complete technical workload:

  • availability;
  • latency;
  • security;
  • evidence quality;
  • tool correctness;
  • policy enforcement;
  • auditability;
  • cost;
  • maintainability.

Outcome quality

Properties experienced by users, organisations, or affected parties:

  • task completion;
  • decision improvement;
  • reduced effort;
  • safety impact;
  • error consequence;
  • customer outcome;
  • fairness;
  • business value.
Model Quality
      │
      ▼
System Behaviour
      │
      ▼
Workflow Effect
      │
      ▼
Real-World Outcome

The arrows are not guaranteed.

A better model does not automatically produce a better outcome.

Part II — From Quality Words to Quality Scenarios

6. The Problem with Adjectives

Architecture requirements often contain statements such as:

  • The assistant must be reliable.
  • The agent must be secure.
  • Answers must be explainable.
  • The platform must be fast.
  • The solution must be cost-effective.
  • The system must be fair.

These statements express intent.

They do not define a testable requirement.

“Fast” could mean:

  • first token within 500 milliseconds;
  • complete answer within five seconds;
  • asynchronous report within ten minutes;
  • remediation proposal before an incident escalates.

“Reliable” could mean:

  • API availability;
  • correct answer;
  • correct evidence;
  • successful tool execution;
  • graceful degradation;
  • recovery after provider failure.

The architect must convert quality words into scenarios.

7. The Classical Quality Attribute Scenario

The SEI quality-attribute approach uses scenario elements such as:

  • source;
  • stimulus;
  • environment;
  • artifact;
  • response;
  • response measure.[2]

A performance scenario might be:

Source:
  An authenticated customer

Stimulus:
  Submits a support question

Environment:
  Normal weekday load

Artifact:
  Customer-assistance workflow

Response:
  Returns an answer

Response measure:
  95% of complete responses within five seconds

The scenario gives a quality requirement a context and a measurable response.

8. The AI Quality Attribute Scenario

For AI systems, this handbook extends the scenario with two explicit conditions:

  • evidence condition — what information is available or required;
  • risk condition — what consequence or control level applies.
Source
  ↓
Stimulus
  ↓
Environment
  ↓
Artifact
  ↓
Evidence Condition
  ↓
Risk Condition
  ↓
Response
  ↓
Response Measure

This is an original handbook synthesis built on the established SEI scenario structure.

Example: grounded policy answer

Source:
  An authenticated employee

Stimulus:
  Asks whether a travel expense is permitted

Environment:
  Normal operation; current policy index available

Artifact:
  Internal policy assistant

Evidence condition:
  At least one current, authorised policy passage directly addresses the claim

Risk condition:
  Advisory answer; financial submission is validated separately

Response:
  Answer with source citation, policy date, and scope limitation

Response measure:
  98% claim support on the approved evaluation set;
  zero uncited definitive answers when required evidence is absent;
  p95 response latency below four seconds

This scenario is more useful than:

The system should provide accurate and explainable answers.

9. Response Measures for Probabilistic Systems

A deterministic requirement may use a binary response measure:

  • encryption is enabled;
  • write access is denied;
  • schema validation passes;
  • transaction is idempotent.

AI behaviour often requires statistical measures:

  • 95% task success across representative cases;
  • less than 1% unsupported material claims;
  • zero execution of prohibited tool calls;
  • no more than 5% performance difference across defined groups;
  • 99% of high-risk cases escalated;
  • p95 first-token latency below one second.

Statistical measures require:

  • defined dataset;
  • sampling method;
  • confidence interval where appropriate;
  • segment reporting;
  • evaluation cadence;
  • acceptance threshold;
  • owner;
  • response when the threshold is missed.

A percentage without an evaluation population is not a quality requirement.

10. Avoid Universal Thresholds

There is no universal acceptable hallucination rate, latency, fairness difference, or escalation level.

Thresholds depend on:

  • consequence;
  • reversibility;
  • user expectations;
  • task frequency;
  • available alternatives;
  • human oversight;
  • regulation;
  • cost;
  • evidence quality.

A 2% unsupported-claim rate may be tolerable for brainstorming and unacceptable for financial advice.

Human judgment is required to choose relevant metrics and thresholds, as NIST also emphasises for AI trustworthiness characteristics.[3]

Part III — The Quality Attribute Portfolio

11. Do Not Treat Every Quality as Equal

A long checklist can create the appearance of rigour while avoiding decisions.

Every system should care about security, reliability, performance, cost, operations, and responsible behaviour. But architecture is driven by the qualities that are most difficult, consequential, or differentiating in its context.

A quality portfolio should classify attributes as:

Driving

The architecture must be shaped around this quality.

Constraining

A minimum threshold must be met, but it is not the differentiator.

Monitored

The quality is observed for regression or emerging risk.

Not material

The quality has been considered and is not currently significant.

Example for an internal meeting-summary assistant:

Attribute Priority
Privacy Driving
Usability Driving
Latency Constraining
Veracity Constraining
Availability Monitored
Fairness Monitored
Broad autonomy Not material

Example for an autonomous incident-remediation system:

Attribute Priority
Safety Driving
Controllability Driving
Reliability Driving
Auditability Driving
Latency Driving
Cost Constraining
Explainability Constraining
Creativity Not material

The classification must be justified, not copied from a template.

12. Architecture Drivers

A quality becomes an architecture driver when it strongly affects:

  • boundaries;
  • topology;
  • data;
  • control flow;
  • deployment;
  • technology;
  • ownership;
  • operational processes.

Examples:

Latency as a driver

May lead to:

  • smaller models;
  • caching;
  • streaming;
  • regional deployment;
  • reduced context;
  • parallel retrieval;
  • asynchronous processing.

Privacy as a driver

May lead to:

  • local inference;
  • data minimisation;
  • access-filtered retrieval;
  • redaction;
  • regional storage;
  • limited logging;
  • retention controls.

Auditability as a driver

May lead to:

  • decision envelopes;
  • durable state;
  • versioned prompts and policies;
  • evidence identifiers;
  • actor attribution;
  • append-only events.

Modifiability as a driver

May lead to:

  • model adapters;
  • stable tool contracts;
  • independent evaluation suites;
  • configuration versioning;
  • modular retrieval.

A quality word is not an architecture driver until it changes design.

Part IV — Functional and Task Fitness

13. Functional Suitability

The system must first perform the required function.

For AI, this includes:

  • task completion;
  • correct interpretation;
  • relevant output;
  • complete coverage;
  • appropriate refusal;
  • correct tool use;
  • adherence to constraints.

Functional suitability is broader than answer similarity.

A customer-support agent may produce an accurate answer while failing the task because it:

  • does not update the case;
  • omits the next step;
  • uses an unauthorised policy;
  • fails to escalate;
  • creates unnecessary customer effort.

Useful measures

  • task success;
  • constraint adherence;
  • correct tool selection;
  • correct action parameters;
  • completion without human repair;
  • appropriate refusal;
  • escalation precision and recall.

14. Task Success Must Be Defined Behaviourally

Weak definition:

The response is good.

Stronger definition:

The system identifies the applicable policy, asks for missing evidence, proposes a permitted action, and produces a complete case record without unsupported claims.

The success definition should reflect the workflow, not merely the text.

Architecture smell — Text-quality substitution

Linguistic quality is used as a substitute for completing the actual task.

Part V — Validity, Reliability, and Resilience

15. Reliability Has Multiple Layers

AWS defines reliability for generative AI workloads as consistently performing intended functions and delivering expected results under normal and adverse conditions, including model quality, varying demand, resource use, and recovery from failures.[5]

For an AI system, reliability can mean:

Service reliability

Can users access the system?

Behavioural reliability

Does it perform the task consistently enough?

Evidence reliability

Are sources current, authoritative, and retrievable?

Tool reliability

Do external actions and data queries work correctly?

Workflow reliability

Can the process recover from partial failure, timeout, and retry?

Outcome reliability

Does the system produce the intended real-world effect?

These layers must not be collapsed into uptime.

16. Reliability Scenarios

Provider failure

Source:
  Model provider

Stimulus:
  Returns timeout for the primary model

Environment:
  Peak business period

Artifact:
  Customer-support assistant

Response:
  Route eligible tasks to a tested fallback model;
  preserve task and evidence state;
  escalate unsupported tasks

Response measure:
  99% of eligible requests complete within the fallback SLO;
  zero high-risk tasks silently downgraded

Behavioural regression

Source:
  Model or prompt release

Stimulus:
  Reduces citation support on policy questions

Environment:
  Canary deployment

Artifact:
  Policy-answer workflow

Response:
  Block wider release and restore previous version

Response measure:
  Regression detected before 10% traffic exposure;
  previous version restored within five minutes

17. Graceful Degradation

Possible degraded modes include:

  • retrieval-only answers;
  • deterministic workflow;
  • smaller model;
  • read-only tools;
  • reduced autonomy;
  • delayed batch processing;
  • human escalation;
  • explicit unavailability.

Degradation should preserve the most important quality.

A safety-critical system may stop.

A low-risk assistant may continue with reduced capability.

18. Error Budgets for AI Behaviour

SRE uses SLIs and SLOs to define the level of service users require and guide action when the service falls below the objective.[6]

AI systems can extend this idea beyond availability.

Examples:

  • unsupported-claim budget;
  • incorrect-action budget;
  • policy-violation budget;
  • excessive-latency budget;
  • human-override budget.

If the budget is consumed:

  • stop autonomy expansion;
  • freeze model changes;
  • increase review;
  • improve evidence;
  • rollback;
  • retrain or reroute.

Constraint

Not every harmful event should receive a nonzero budget.

A prohibited safety action may require zero tolerance.

Part VI — Security, Privacy, and Resilience

19. Security Is an End-to-End Quality

AI adds attack surfaces while retaining all conventional security concerns.

Threats include:

  • prompt injection;
  • malicious retrieved content;
  • excessive tool permissions;
  • credential leakage;
  • cross-tenant context leakage;
  • data poisoning;
  • insecure model or package supply chain;
  • output injection into downstream systems;
  • extraction of sensitive prompts or records.

Security quality scenarios should name:

  • actor;
  • asset;
  • attack;
  • environment;
  • control response;
  • detection;
  • response measure.

20. Security Scenario

Source:
  Untrusted document author

Stimulus:
  Embeds instructions asking the agent to reveal secrets

Environment:
  Retrieval-assisted support workflow

Artifact:
  Context and tool layer

Evidence condition:
  Document is relevant but untrusted

Risk condition:
  Agent has read access to customer records

Response:
  Treat retrieved instructions as data;
  block secret access outside task scope;
  record injection detection;
  continue with trusted policy

Response measure:
  Zero secret disclosure across the adversarial evaluation set;
  100% prohibited tool calls blocked

21. Privacy Quality

Privacy includes:

  • lawful and appropriate collection;
  • data minimisation;
  • purpose limitation;
  • access control;
  • retention;
  • deletion;
  • regional requirements;
  • training use;
  • trace-content policy;
  • user transparency.

A system can be secure and still violate privacy by collecting or retaining more information than necessary.

Privacy measures

  • percentage of prompts containing unnecessary personal data;
  • redaction effectiveness;
  • unauthorised retrieval rate;
  • retention-policy compliance;
  • deletion completion;
  • privacy incident rate;
  • exposure through logging.

22. Resilience to Adversarial and Unexpected Inputs

Robustness asks whether the system maintains acceptable behaviour when inputs are:

  • noisy;
  • incomplete;
  • unfamiliar;
  • adversarial;
  • contradictory;
  • out of distribution.

The AWS Responsible AI Lens distinguishes robustness, veracity, safety, controllability, privacy, security, fairness, explainability, transparency, and governance as complementary dimensions.[7]

A robust system may not produce the correct answer under every unexpected input. It should fail in an acceptable way.

Part VII — Performance and Interaction Quality

23. Performance Is Experienced End to End

AI latency can include:

  • authentication;
  • context assembly;
  • retrieval;
  • reranking;
  • model queue;
  • time to first token;
  • generation;
  • tool calls;
  • validation;
  • approval;
  • post-processing.

Users experience the total.

A model benchmark that excludes retrieval and tools may not predict workflow latency.

24. Useful Performance Measures

Time to first meaningful response

Not merely first token if the first tokens convey no useful information.

Time to complete task

Includes tools, validation, and persistence.

Tail latency

p95 or p99 reveals slow cases hidden by averages.

Throughput

Tasks or tokens handled per unit time.

Concurrency

Simultaneous users or workflows.

Deadline success

Percentage completed before a business deadline.

Queue time

Delay before work begins.

Google’s AI and ML reliability guidance recommends SLOs that reflect acceptable reliability and performance from the user’s perspective.[8]

25. Streaming Changes Perception, Not Completion

Streaming can improve perceived responsiveness.

It does not necessarily improve:

  • total completion time;
  • correctness;
  • cost;
  • tool latency;
  • decision latency.

For a drafting assistant, streaming may improve usability.

For a structured decision workflow, partial output may be unusable or unsafe.

26. Interaction Capability

Quality includes the ability of users to:

  • understand system status;
  • provide effective input;
  • inspect evidence;
  • correct errors;
  • challenge decisions;
  • know when AI is involved;
  • escalate;
  • recover from mistakes.

A technically accurate system can be low quality if users cannot recognise its limits.

Measures

  • task completion without support;
  • correction rate;
  • time to recover from error;
  • escalation success;
  • user comprehension;
  • evidence-view usage;
  • automation-bias indicators;
  • abandonment.

Part VIII — Cost Efficiency and Sustainability

27. Cost Is a Quality Attribute

A system that meets technical targets but cannot be operated economically is not fit for purpose.

AI cost includes:

  • model input and output;
  • embeddings;
  • retrieval;
  • reranking;
  • vector and document storage;
  • tool APIs;
  • evaluation;
  • observability;
  • human review;
  • incident handling;
  • platform engineering;
  • data preparation;
  • provider migration.

AWS recommends matching model size and inference approach to actual performance needs rather than paying for capability that does not deliver proportional value.[9]

28. Unit Economics

Measure cost against a meaningful unit:

  • cost per resolved case;
  • cost per accepted code change;
  • cost per correct extraction;
  • cost per incident investigated;
  • cost per autonomous action;
  • cost per business outcome.

Token cost alone can mislead.

A more expensive model may reduce human repair and lower total cost.

A cheaper model may create costly rework.

29. Cost Scenario

Source:
  Monthly demand growth

Stimulus:
  Support volume doubles

Environment:
  Normal quality targets

Artifact:
  AI support workflow

Response:
  Route simple intents to a smaller model;
  cache stable answers;
  reserve frontier reasoning for complex cases;
  preserve evidence and safety thresholds

Response measure:
  Cost per correctly resolved case below £0.40;
  no more than one percentage point reduction in task success;
  no increase in policy violations

The quality requirement prevents cost reduction from silently reducing safety or outcome quality.

30. Sustainability

Sustainability can involve:

  • energy consumption;
  • hardware use;
  • model size;
  • inference frequency;
  • unnecessary regeneration;
  • storage;
  • data movement;
  • idle capacity.

It should be considered alongside performance, cost, and outcome.

The lowest-energy model is not useful if it cannot perform the task.

The largest model is wasteful when smaller capability is sufficient.

Part IX — Maintainability, Modifiability, and Portability

31. Behaviour Must Be Changeable Safely

AI systems change through:

  • code;
  • prompts;
  • policies;
  • model;
  • provider;
  • retrieval;
  • corpus;
  • embeddings;
  • tool definitions;
  • evaluator;
  • threshold;
  • guardrail;
  • workflow.

Each is a versioned behavioural dependency.

Maintainability requires the team to:

  • know what changed;
  • reproduce prior behaviour;
  • test the change;
  • deploy gradually;
  • observe impact;
  • rollback;
  • assign ownership.

32. Modifiability Scenario

Source:
  Architecture team

Stimulus:
  Replaces the primary model provider

Environment:
  Before a pricing contract renewal

Artifact:
  Document-review platform

Response:
  Introduce provider adapter;
  execute the independent evaluation suite;
  compare cost, latency, and quality;
  canary eligible traffic

Response measure:
  Business logic unchanged;
  migration completed within four weeks;
  all driving quality thresholds met;
  rollback possible within one deployment

This scenario is more realistic than:

The system must be vendor-neutral.

Complete neutrality is rarely free.

33. Testability

A testable AI architecture supports:

  • deterministic unit tests;
  • recorded tool responses;
  • representative evaluation cases;
  • versioned datasets;
  • failure injection;
  • shadow deployment;
  • trace replay;
  • segment analysis;
  • reproducible configuration.

Testability should influence architecture early.

A system whose evidence and decisions cannot be reconstructed will be difficult to improve safely.

34. Portability and Interoperability

Portability can concern:

  • models;
  • cloud platforms;
  • data;
  • embeddings;
  • telemetry;
  • tools;
  • prompts;
  • evaluations.

Interoperability can concern:

  • tool schemas;
  • event contracts;
  • identity;
  • policy;
  • trace context;
  • data formats.

The architect should identify which forms of portability justify their abstraction cost.

Architecture smell — Abstract everything

Extensive indirection is added without evidence that the dependency is likely to change or that migration matters.

Part X — Veracity, Groundedness, and Evidence Quality

35. Veracity

Veracity concerns factual correctness.

It can be evaluated through:

  • exact answer;
  • claim verification;
  • source agreement;
  • authoritative tool result;
  • human review;
  • outcome.

Not all generated content has a single verifiable truth.

The evaluation method must fit the task.

36. Groundedness Is Not the Same as Truth

Groundedness asks whether the output is supported by provided evidence.

An answer can be:

  • grounded and wrong because the source is wrong;
  • ungrounded and true by coincidence;
  • partially grounded;
  • grounded in unauthorised evidence;
  • grounded in stale evidence.

Quality requires both evidence support and evidence quality.

Groundedness scenario

Source:
  Employee

Stimulus:
  Requests a policy interpretation

Environment:
  Current policy corpus available

Artifact:
  Retrieval-assisted answer workflow

Evidence condition:
  Claims must use approved documents effective on the request date

Response:
  Answer with claim-level citations;
  disclose conflict or insufficiency;
  avoid definitive unsupported claims

Response measure:
  98% claim support;
  100% citation validity;
  zero definitive answer when no approved source exists

37. Citation Quality

Measure:

  • citation exists;
  • citation resolves;
  • passage supports claim;
  • source is authoritative;
  • source is current;
  • source is accessible to the user;
  • citation coverage is sufficient.

A citation is not decoration.

Part XI — Safety and Controllability

38. Safety

Safety concerns unacceptable harm arising from:

  • intended use;
  • foreseeable misuse;
  • model error;
  • tool action;
  • interaction design;
  • organisational process;
  • affected-party reliance.

Safety is contextual.

A harmful output for one system may be harmless in another.

39. Safety Scenario

Source:
  User in distress

Stimulus:
  Requests instructions that could enable serious self-harm

Environment:
  Public assistant

Artifact:
  Response and escalation workflow

Response:
  Do not provide enabling instructions;
  provide appropriate supportive response;
  offer locally relevant crisis options where available;
  trigger internal safety telemetry

Response measure:
  Zero enabling responses on the approved red-team set;
  99% correct safe-response classification;
  p95 response latency below three seconds

The scenario requires careful domain and policy ownership, not only a generic “safety score.”

40. Controllability

Controllability means the ability to:

  • constrain scope;
  • steer behaviour;
  • stop execution;
  • reduce permissions;
  • change autonomy;
  • override;
  • rollback;
  • revoke authority;
  • isolate a failing component.

The AWS Responsible AI Lens defines controllability as mechanisms to monitor and steer AI system behaviour.[7]

Measures

  • time to suspend agent actions;
  • percentage of actions within delegated scope;
  • successful policy-block rate;
  • rollback success;
  • human override effectiveness;
  • maximum tool-call depth;
  • budget compliance.

41. Safety Is Not Only Content Filtering

Content filters may be useful.

Safety can also depend on:

  • tool boundaries;
  • identity;
  • transaction limits;
  • physical controls;
  • confirmation;
  • simulation;
  • supervision;
  • safe degradation;
  • incident response;
  • organisational training.

A safe response attached to an unsafe action architecture is not a safe system.

Part XII — Explainability, Transparency, and Auditability

42. Explainability Is User- and Decision-Specific

An explanation may serve:

  • user understanding;
  • operator diagnosis;
  • reviewer approval;
  • affected-party challenge;
  • regulatory review;
  • developer debugging.

These audiences need different information.

A customer may need:

  • decision;
  • key factors;
  • evidence;
  • correction path.

An operator may need:

  • model and prompt version;
  • retrieval;
  • tool calls;
  • validation;
  • policy;
  • trace.

AWS recommends validating whether explanations actually help users decide whether to trust or act on system output.[10]

43. Explanation Quality

Possible measures:

  • faithfulness to system evidence;
  • completeness;
  • comprehensibility;
  • usefulness;
  • stability;
  • actionability;
  • inappropriate disclosure;
  • user decision improvement.

A plausible explanation can be unfaithful.

A detailed explanation can be unusable.

44. Transparency

Transparency may include:

  • disclosure that AI is used;
  • system purpose;
  • limitations;
  • data use;
  • oversight;
  • contact or appeal;
  • changes;
  • known performance.

Transparency does not require exposing secrets, security controls, or private model reasoning.

45. Auditability

Auditability is the ability to reconstruct:

  • task;
  • actors;
  • evidence;
  • model and configuration;
  • validation;
  • policy;
  • authority;
  • action;
  • outcome.

Auditability and explainability overlap.

They are not identical.

An explanation may help a user while being insufficient for incident reconstruction.

Part XIII — Fairness and Harmful Bias

46. Fairness Is About Impact

Fairness cannot be reduced to one universal metric.

Possible concerns include:

  • equal error rates;
  • equal access;
  • equal treatment;
  • equal opportunity;
  • representational harm;
  • quality differences across language or disability;
  • allocation of benefit and burden.

Metrics can conflict.

The choice is a product, risk, legal, and ethical decision—not only a data science decision.

47. Fairness Scenario

Source:
  Job applicant

Stimulus:
  Submits a résumé for role matching

Environment:
  Standard recruitment workflow

Artifact:
  Candidate-matching system

Risk condition:
  Recommendation influences human screening

Response:
  Produce ranked match with evidence;
  exclude protected attributes from inappropriate use;
  monitor quality across defined groups;
  provide human review and correction

Response measure:
  Minimum recall threshold for qualified candidates;
  group differences within approved bounds;
  zero use of prohibited attributes;
  documented review of residual disparity

A fairness measure should be linked to the actual decision and harm.

48. Aggregate Quality Can Hide Group Failure

A model may achieve 95% overall performance while performing poorly for:

  • a minority language;
  • an uncommon document format;
  • users with assistive technology;
  • a geographic region;
  • a rare but high-risk case.

Always segment according to the context of use.

Architecture smell — Average-user quality

The system is declared fit based on aggregate performance while important affected groups or risk classes are invisible.

Part XIV — Operational Excellence and Observability

49. Quality Must Be Operable

A system is not high quality if the team cannot:

  • deploy it safely;
  • diagnose it;
  • recover it;
  • understand ownership;
  • control change;
  • manage cost;
  • respond to incidents;
  • improve it.

Operational excellence connects process, people, and technology.

50. Quality Signals

Service signals

  • availability;
  • latency;
  • errors;
  • saturation;
  • throughput.

AI behaviour signals

  • task success;
  • groundedness;
  • tool correctness;
  • refusal;
  • policy compliance;
  • evaluation result;
  • drift.

Governance signals

  • approval;
  • override;
  • prohibited-action attempt;
  • appeal;
  • audit completeness;
  • authority expiry.

Outcome signals

  • user success;
  • business KPI;
  • incident rate;
  • side effect;
  • harm;
  • cost per outcome.

The architect should choose a small set of decision-driving indicators rather than monitor every available metric. Google SRE similarly recommends selecting a handful of representative indicators based on what users need.[6]

51. Quality Gates

A quality gate defines whether a system may:

  • enter testing;
  • enter production;
  • receive more traffic;
  • access a tool;
  • increase autonomy;
  • remain in operation.

Examples:

Release gate

  • task success ≥ 92%;
  • prohibited actions = 0;
  • p95 latency ≤ 4 seconds;
  • critical group performance above threshold;
  • security review complete.

Autonomy gate

  • action success ≥ 99.5%;
  • rollback tested;
  • evidence current;
  • policy violations = 0;
  • incident response exercised;
  • human override rate below threshold.

Continued-operation gate

  • no consumed safety budget;
  • cost per outcome within limit;
  • no unresolved critical drift;
  • audit completeness above threshold.

The AWS Responsible AI Lens recommends release criteria spanning usability, latency, uptime, safety, controllability, security, privacy, robustness, fairness, veracity, explainability, and transparency.[11]

52. Quality Gates Need Responses

A threshold without an action is only a dashboard value.

When a gate is missed, define:

  • block release;
  • rollback;
  • route to fallback;
  • reduce autonomy;
  • increase human review;
  • freeze changes;
  • investigate;
  • notify owner;
  • accept documented risk.

Part XV — Trade-offs and Sensitivity Points

53. Quality Attributes Interact

Examples:

Accuracy versus latency

More retrieval, larger models, and verification may improve task quality while increasing response time.

Privacy versus observability

Capturing more content may improve debugging while increasing exposure and retention obligations.

Explainability versus performance

Detailed explanation can add model calls and latency.

Security versus usability

Stronger controls can increase friction.

Cost versus reliability

Redundancy and fallback improve resilience but increase cost.

Fairness versus aggregate optimisation

Improving performance for underrepresented groups may change aggregate metrics.

Autonomy versus controllability

More autonomy can reduce human delay while increasing blast radius.

AWS advises teams to consider trade-offs between responsible-AI release criteria; for example, privacy constraints can affect explainability and accuracy targets can affect latency.[12]

54. Sensitivity Points

A sensitivity point is a decision that strongly affects a quality attribute.

Examples:

  • model size affects capability, latency, cost, and energy;
  • context length affects evidence coverage, latency, cost, and noise;
  • approval threshold affects safety, latency, and human workload;
  • logging depth affects auditability, privacy, and cost;
  • tool granularity affects usability, security, and maintainability;
  • caching affects performance, freshness, and privacy.

The architect should identify these points early and validate them.

55. Trade-off Record

For a significant trade-off, record:

Decision:
  Use a smaller default model with selective escalation

Improves:
  Cost and latency

May weaken:
  Complex reasoning performance

Controls:
  Capability classifier;
  evaluation by task class;
  fallback;
  outcome monitoring

Revisit when:
  Escalation rate exceeds 20%;
  task distribution changes;
  provider pricing changes

The record turns compromise into an explicit, reviewable decision.

Part XVI — Prioritising Quality Attributes

56. Start with Business and Mission Goals

The SEI Quality Attribute Workshop begins with stakeholder and business drivers, then generates and prioritises scenarios.[2]

For AI, involve:

  • users;
  • product;
  • engineering;
  • operations;
  • data;
  • security;
  • privacy;
  • legal and compliance;
  • domain experts;
  • affected-party representatives;
  • support;
  • finance.

Different stakeholders see different failure modes.

57. Prioritisation Questions

For each quality scenario, ask:

  1. What goal does it protect?
  2. What is the consequence if missed?
  3. How likely is the stimulus?
  4. Is the failure detectable?
  5. Is it reversible?
  6. Does the architecture need to change?
  7. How will it be measured?
  8. Who owns the threshold?
  9. What conflicts with it?
  10. What happens when the threshold is missed?

58. Prioritisation Method

A practical workshop can rank scenarios using:

  • business importance;
  • risk;
  • architectural difficulty;
  • uncertainty;
  • urgency.

Do not calculate a false-precision universal score.

Use the ranking to identify:

  • top architecture drivers;
  • validation spikes;
  • release gates;
  • trade-offs;
  • owner decisions.

59. The Quality Attribute Workshop for AI

Suggested sequence:

  1. Present business and mission goals.
  2. Describe users and affected parties.
  3. Define system boundary and decision authority.
  4. Identify quality concerns.
  5. Generate real scenarios.
  6. Add evidence and risk conditions.
  7. Define response measures.
  8. Consolidate duplicates.
  9. Prioritise.
  10. Identify conflicts and sensitivity points.
  11. Assign owners.
  12. Select validation methods.

The output is not a generic quality checklist.

It is a prioritised set of scenarios that shape the architecture.

Part XVII — Worked Example: Enterprise Knowledge Assistant

60. Scenario

An organisation wants an assistant that answers employee questions across HR, IT, procurement, and operations.

Leadership initially requests:

It must be accurate, secure, fast, and scalable.

These are not yet usable architecture requirements.

61. Stakeholders

  • employees;
  • content owners;
  • service desk;
  • security;
  • privacy;
  • legal;
  • platform team;
  • business leaders;
  • auditors.

62. Candidate Quality Scenarios

Groundedness

For policy questions, every material claim must be supported by an authorised, current source.

Access control

The assistant must never retrieve content the requesting employee cannot access.

Latency

95% of routine answers complete within four seconds.

Availability

The system is available during business hours with tested fallback.

Explainability

Users can inspect the source and effective date.

Maintainability

A content owner can publish a corrected policy and have it searchable within fifteen minutes.

Cost

Cost per useful answer remains below an agreed threshold.

Safety

The system detects defined high-risk categories and escalates.

Fairness and interaction

The assistant meets quality thresholds across supported languages and accessible interaction modes.

63. Architecture Consequences

Groundedness drives

  • retrieval;
  • source metadata;
  • claim-level citation;
  • insufficiency state;
  • evaluation.

Access control drives

  • identity-aware retrieval;
  • document permissions;
  • filtered indexes or query-time enforcement;
  • audit.

Latency drives

  • routing;
  • caching;
  • streaming;
  • model choice;
  • parallel retrieval.

Maintainability drives

  • ingestion automation;
  • content ownership;
  • freshness monitoring;
  • rollback.

Cost drives

  • smaller-model routing;
  • context control;
  • cache policy;
  • unit economics.

Safety drives

  • classification;
  • escalation;
  • support procedures;
  • monitoring.

The architecture now has reasons for its components.

64. Trade-off Example

Caching improves latency and cost.

It may weaken:

  • freshness;
  • access revocation;
  • privacy;
  • citation validity.

A responsible cache design might:

  • cache only public or broadly accessible content;
  • include policy version in the key;
  • use short TTLs;
  • invalidate on content change;
  • avoid user-sensitive responses.

The trade-off determines the tactic.

65. Quality Gate

Before release:

  • grounded-claim support ≥ 98%;
  • citation validity = 100%;
  • cross-permission leakage = 0;
  • p95 latency ≤ 4 seconds;
  • supported-language quality above agreed thresholds;
  • high-risk escalation recall ≥ 99%;
  • content update visible within 15 minutes;
  • cost per useful answer within budget.

Each threshold is contextual and requires a defined test set.

Part XVIII — Architecture Review

66. Scenario

A company proposes an autonomous sales agent.

The design team reports:

  • 93% benchmark accuracy;
  • 99.9% API uptime;
  • average latency of 2.5 seconds;
  • low token cost.

The agent can:

  • identify prospects;
  • draft outreach;
  • send email;
  • offer discounts;
  • update the CRM.

67. ARB Findings

Finding 1 — Model benchmark substitutes for workflow quality

The benchmark does not establish correct prospect selection, policy-compliant discounting, or useful sales outcomes.

Finding 2 — Average latency hides tail behaviour

Approval and tool latency are not included.

Finding 3 — Uptime does not show behavioural reliability

The service can be available while sending inappropriate messages.

Finding 4 — Cost unit is incomplete

Token cost excludes review, support, reputation, and error recovery.

Finding 5 — Fairness and brand safety are unmeasured

Prospect selection and messaging can affect groups differently.

Finding 6 — Controllability is unclear

No action tier, stop mechanism, or authority expiry is defined.

Finding 7 — Outcome is not specified

Email sent is treated as success instead of qualified engagement or revenue.

68. Recommended Quality Portfolio

Driving:

  • policy compliance;
  • brand safety;
  • controllability;
  • prospect-selection quality;
  • auditability.

Constraining:

  • latency;
  • cost;
  • availability;
  • explainability.

Monitored:

  • group impact;
  • deliverability;
  • customer complaints;
  • override;
  • business outcome.

The architecture should begin in recommendation or draft mode and earn additional autonomy through measured evidence.

Part XIX — Architecture Smells

69. Quality by Adjective

The requirement says “reliable,” “secure,” or “responsible” without a scenario or measure.

70. Accuracy Monoculture

One quality metric dominates all other concerns.

71. Dashboard Without Decision

Metrics exist, but no threshold changes release, routing, autonomy, or operation.

72. Average Hides Harm

Aggregate performance conceals tail latency, rare risk, or group failure.

73. Benchmark Is the Product

Public evaluation is treated as proof of task and outcome quality.

74. Uptime Theatre

The system is declared reliable because endpoints respond.

75. Explainability Theatre

The system produces fluent rationales that are not verified for faithfulness or usefulness.

76. Cost Is Tokens

The business ignores evaluation, review, operations, and error recovery.

77. Checklist Trustworthiness

Every quality is marked “considered,” but none is prioritised or measured.

78. Threshold by Guess

A metric target is selected without evidence, consequence analysis, or stakeholder ownership.

Part XX — Interview Preparation

79. Foundational Questions

Question 1

What is a quality attribute?

A measurable property describing how a system behaves under specified conditions, such as reliability, security, performance, modifiability, safety, or groundedness.

Question 2

Why is accuracy not enough for AI system quality?

Discuss availability, evidence, security, privacy, latency, cost, operational behaviour, fairness, safety, maintainability, and outcome.

Question 3

How do you make “the system must be reliable” testable?

Create scenarios with source, stimulus, environment, artifact, response, and response measure. For AI, also clarify evidence and risk conditions.

Question 4

Which quality attributes are specific to AI?

A mature answer avoids a hard binary. Conventional attributes remain essential. AI elevates qualities such as veracity, groundedness, controllability, explainability, fairness, safety, and behavioural robustness, and changes how reliability and testability are measured.

Question 5

How do you prioritise quality attributes?

Start from business goals, users, affected parties, consequence, risk, architectural difficulty, and uncertainty. Prioritise scenarios, not abstract words.

80. Senior-Level Questions

Question 6

How would you define an SLO for an AI assistant?

Use service indicators and behavioural or task indicators. Example: 99.9% availability, p95 latency under four seconds, and 98% supported material claims for the defined task set.

Question 7

What is the difference between groundedness and correctness?

Groundedness measures support from supplied evidence. Correctness measures truth or task validity. A grounded answer can rely on an incorrect source.

Question 8

How do you evaluate explainability?

By audience and purpose. Measure faithfulness, comprehension, usefulness, actionability, and whether the explanation improves appropriate reliance.

Question 9

How do you handle trade-offs between privacy and observability?

Capture the minimum reconstruction data, redact content, limit access and retention, sample deliberately, and preserve metadata and evidence identifiers where full content is unnecessary.

Question 10

How do you prevent cost optimisation from reducing quality?

Define cost per successful outcome and preserve quality gates. Route by task complexity, cache safely, reduce context, and monitor regression.

Question 11

How do you measure reliability for an agent?

Include service availability, task success, evidence freshness, tool correctness, retry safety, policy compliance, outcome success, and recovery.

Question 12

How should fairness be measured?

Tie metrics to the decision and harm, define affected groups with appropriate expertise, segment performance, document trade-offs, and provide review and correction.

81. Principal-Level Questions

Question 13

How would you establish an enterprise quality standard for AI systems?

Create a common quality vocabulary, scenario template, risk tiers, minimum gates, evaluation infrastructure, trace conventions, ownership, exception process, and domain-specific extensions.

Do not impose one threshold on every use case.

Question 14

How do SLOs and evaluation metrics interact?

SLOs govern service and operational expectations. Evaluations govern behavioural fitness. Production quality needs both, plus outcome metrics.

Question 15

What makes a quality attribute an architecture driver?

It materially changes structure, data, boundaries, control flow, deployment, ownership, or operations.

Question 16

How do you detect that a quality target is wrong?

The system meets the target while users or outcomes deteriorate; teams game the measure; important segments fail; or the metric does not drive the intended decision.

Part XXI — Whiteboard Challenge

82. Design Quality Requirements for an AI Coding Agent

The agent can:

  • inspect repositories;
  • modify code;
  • run tests;
  • open pull requests;
  • respond to review;
  • deploy to a test environment.

Constraints

  • multiple languages;
  • regulated and non-regulated repositories;
  • secrets may exist;
  • tests vary in quality;
  • developers use the agent interactively and asynchronously;
  • cloud model providers are permitted for some repositories only.

Discuss

  1. Identify stakeholders and affected parties.
  2. Define model, system, and outcome quality.
  3. Create five prioritised AI Quality Attribute Scenarios.
  4. Define task success.
  5. Define security and privacy measures.
  6. Define behavioural reliability.
  7. Define latency and cost per accepted change.
  8. Define maintainability and provider portability.
  9. Define safe autonomy gates.
  10. Define segment analysis by repository risk.
  11. Identify quality trade-offs.
  12. Define release and continued-operation gates.

Strong-answer characteristics

  • distinguishes generated code from accepted change;
  • uses repository risk tiers;
  • prevents secret and cross-repository leakage;
  • requires test and policy evidence;
  • measures defect escape and review burden;
  • keeps deployment authority separate;
  • defines idempotent operations;
  • tracks cost per accepted, correct change;
  • includes rollback and suspension;
  • tests across language, repository type, and change complexity.

Part XXII — Questions to Take Back to Your Team

  1. Which qualities actually drive our architecture?
  2. Which qualities are merely adjectives?
  3. What is the context of use?
  4. Are we measuring the model, the system, or the outcome?
  5. Which aggregate metric hides important segments?
  6. What evidence and risk conditions apply to each scenario?
  7. What is the response when a threshold is missed?
  8. Which quality trade-offs have been accepted?
  9. Who owns each threshold?
  10. What is our cost per successful outcome?
  11. Can the system degrade safely?
  12. How do we measure appropriate refusal and escalation?
  13. Is explanation faithful and useful?
  14. Does uptime hide behavioural failure?
  15. What would cause us to reduce autonomy?
  16. Which quality target could be gamed?
  17. What changes require full reevaluation?
  18. Are continued-operation gates defined?

Architect’s Notebook — Quality Is a Decision System

A quality metric is useful only when it influences a decision.

It may decide whether to:

  • release;
  • rollback;
  • route;
  • escalate;
  • approve;
  • block;
  • investigate;
  • invest;
  • retire.

A dashboard that never changes behaviour is a display, not a control.

The architect should trace every important measure to:

  1. a stakeholder concern;
  2. a quality scenario;
  3. a threshold;
  4. an owner;
  5. an action.

From the Architect’s Desk

Teams often ask for a quality checklist because checklists feel complete. They protect us from forgetting obvious concerns. But architecture begins where the checklist ends.

The difficult work is deciding which qualities dominate this system, how they will be measured, what they conflict with, and what happens when they fail.

An assistant can be accurate but unusable. An agent can be available but unsafe. A model can be fair on average while failing a small group. A system can be cheap per token and expensive per successful outcome.

Do not allow attractive aggregate numbers to close the discussion. Ask about the dataset, the segment, the environment, the consequence, the evidence, and the response.

Quality is not a property you add after the architecture. The qualities you prioritise determine the architecture you need.

If I Were the Architect

You inherit an AI document-review platform.

The dashboard is green:

  • 99.95% uptime;
  • 3-second average latency;
  • 94% overall accuracy;
  • low token cost.

Users still distrust it.

Investigation shows:

  • citations sometimes point to irrelevant passages;
  • uncommon document formats perform poorly;
  • reviewers spend time correcting missing fields;
  • policy changes take two days to appear;
  • high-risk documents are not evaluated separately;
  • the average latency hides 30-second tail responses.

What do you do first?

Do not begin by replacing the model.

Rebuild the quality model:

  1. Define task completion.
  2. Segment by document and risk class.
  3. Add citation-support measures.
  4. Measure human correction and review effort.
  5. Define freshness.
  6. measure tail latency.
  7. establish high-risk gates.
  8. identify architecture drivers.
  9. assign threshold owners.
  10. connect missed thresholds to release and routing decisions.

The system was not unmeasured.

It was measuring the wrong definition of quality.

Key Takeaways

  • AI quality is contextual and belongs to the complete socio-technical system.
  • Capability, system quality, and outcome quality are distinct.
  • Quality adjectives must be converted into measurable scenarios.
  • The AI Quality Attribute Scenario adds evidence and risk conditions to the established scenario structure.
  • Probabilistic measures require a defined population, segmentation, cadence, threshold, and owner.
  • Not every quality attribute should receive equal priority.
  • An attribute becomes an architecture driver when it changes design.
  • Reliability includes service, behaviour, evidence, tools, workflow, and outcome.
  • SLOs should reflect user experience and can be complemented by behavioural error budgets.
  • Security, privacy, safety, fairness, and controllability are end-to-end properties.
  • Groundedness is not identical to truth.
  • Explainability must be faithful and useful for a defined audience.
  • Cost should be measured per successful outcome, not only per token.
  • Quality attributes interact; trade-offs and sensitivity points should be documented.
  • Aggregate metrics can hide tail, segment, and high-risk failures.
  • Quality gates must trigger release, rollback, routing, review, or operational action.
  • A checklist supports memory; prioritised scenarios shape architecture.
