Part II - Evidence, Intelligence, and Evaluation

A capable model without credible evidence and evaluation is an impressive component, not a trustworthy system.

This part focuses on the evidence needed to justify behaviour: evaluation architecture, knowledge and retrieval, and model/inference choices.

Chapter 4 - Evaluation Architecture for AI Systems

Creating credible evidence for release, operation, and earned autonomy

Related chapters: Chapters 3, 5, 6, 7, and 10

An evaluation is not merely a score. It is an evidence-producing system that connects a quality requirement to an architectural decision.

1. Why This Chapter Matters

A team demonstrates an AI assistant to senior stakeholders.

The answers look strong.

A few difficult questions are handled well.

The interface is polished.

Leadership asks:

Is it ready for production?

The team reports:

  • average benchmark score;
  • several favourable examples;
  • model-provider claims;
  • a successful pilot;
  • an LLM judge score.

These signals may be useful.

They do not yet establish production fitness.

The real decision may require evidence that:

  • the evaluation cases represent the intended workflow;
  • high-risk failures are visible;
  • the system—not only the model—is being tested;
  • the grader measures what stakeholders actually value;
  • thresholds reflect consequence;
  • results are statistically meaningful;
  • changes can be compared reproducibly;
  • production behaviour is sampled after release;
  • newly discovered failures become regression tests;
  • autonomy is reduced when evidence deteriorates.

NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework places measurement throughout the lifecycle and recommends selecting methods according to purpose, audience, context, and significant risks. It calls for defined acceptable limits, pre-deployment and post-deployment assessment, stress testing, independent review where appropriate, real-time monitoring, and documented corrective action.[1]

Current evaluation guidance from OpenAI similarly frames evaluation as a continuous cycle of specifying what good means, measuring under realistic conditions, and improving from observed errors. It distinguishes general model benchmarks from contextual evaluations for a particular workflow.[2]

Platform freshness note — 4 September 2026. OpenAI announced the Evals platform's deprecation on 3 June 2026; existing evals are scheduled to become read-only on 31 October and the Evals dashboard and API to shut down on 30 November 2026.[8] The evaluation architecture in this chapter is deliberately platform-independent: preserve datasets, graders, lineage, evidence, and release decisions outside any retiring control plane.

The central argument of this chapter is:

Evaluation must be designed as an architectural capability, not performed as an occasional experiment before launch.

2. Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • explain why evaluation is part of architecture rather than only testing;
  • connect quality scenarios to evaluation cases and release decisions;
  • distinguish model, component, workflow, safety, human, production, and outcome evaluations;
  • build an evaluation dataset from real tasks, risks, incidents, and edge cases;
  • choose deterministic, statistical, model-based, environment-based, or human graders;
  • validate an LLM judge rather than assuming it is authoritative;
  • define thresholds, confidence intervals, and zero-tolerance invariants;
  • prevent leakage, contamination, and evaluator overfitting;
  • design offline, integration, shadow, canary, online, and outcome evaluation;
  • create release, routing, and autonomy gates;
  • maintain lineage for datasets, systems, graders, and results;
  • operate a continuous regression-learning loop;
  • answer architecture interview questions about evaluation validity, reproducibility, production sampling, and agent testing.

Part I — Evaluation as Architecture

3. What an Evaluation Produces

An evaluation produces more than a number.

A credible evaluation should produce:

  • evidence about a defined requirement;
  • examples of success and failure;
  • uncertainty about the measurement;
  • segment-level results;
  • known limitations;
  • a decision recommendation;
  • material for future regression testing.

The evaluation has value only when it informs a decision such as:

  • release;
  • block;
  • rollback;
  • route;
  • escalate;
  • increase review;
  • expand autonomy;
  • change a model;
  • improve retrieval;
  • retire a system.

Architectural principle — Evaluation serves a decision

Every important evaluation should name the decision it is intended to support.

“Measure answer quality” is incomplete.

“Determine whether version 3 may serve HR policy questions to all employees without mandatory human review” is an architectural evaluation objective.

4. The Evaluation Evidence Chain

This handbook uses the following evidence chain:

Requirement
   ↓
Quality Scenario
   ↓
Evaluation Case
   ↓
System Under Test
   ↓
Environment
   ↓
Grader or Observation
   ↓
Result + Evidence
   ↓
Threshold
   ↓
Decision
   ↓
Production Evidence
   ↓
Regression Learning

This is an original synthesis.

It makes visible several failure points that are often hidden inside an “eval score.”

A high score can still be misleading when:

  • the requirement is vague;
  • the cases are unrepresentative;
  • the environment is unrealistic;
  • the grader is invalid;
  • the threshold is arbitrary;
  • the decision ignores high-risk segments;
  • production differs from the test;
  • failures are not added back to the suite.

5. The Evaluation Contract

An evaluation should have a contract containing:

  • evaluation ID;
  • decision supported;
  • quality scenario;
  • system boundary;
  • population of interest;
  • risk segments;
  • dataset version;
  • environment version;
  • system version;
  • grader version;
  • metrics;
  • thresholds;
  • sampling and repetition;
  • known limitations;
  • owner;
  • expiry or review date.

Example:

evaluation_id: eval_policy_answer_v7
decision:
  allow_release_to_all_uk_employees
quality_scenario:
  grounded_hr_policy_answer
system_under_test:
  retrieval_plus_generation_workflow
population:
  current_uk_hr_questions
segments:
  - common_policy
  - ambiguous_policy
  - conflicting_sources
  - insufficient_evidence
  - high_financial_consequence
dataset_version: hr_gold_2026_08_01
grader_version: policy_rubric_4
thresholds:
  claim_support: ">= 0.98"
  citation_validity: "= 1.00"
  definitive_answer_without_evidence: "= 0"
  p95_latency_seconds: "<= 4"
owner: hr_ai_product_owner
review_by: 2026-09-01

The contract helps prevent a result from being reused outside the context it actually supports.

Part II — Start from Requirements, Not Datasets

6. Evaluation Begins with “What Does Good Mean?”

A dataset cannot define success by itself.

The sequence should begin with:

  1. business or mission objective;
  2. quality attribute scenario;
  3. failure and harm analysis;
  4. decision to be supported;
  5. evaluation cases and graders.

OpenAI’s current evaluation primer recommends defining the workflow, important decision points, desired outputs, and behaviours to avoid with technical and domain experts. It describes a living golden set and an error taxonomy as context-specific assets.[2]

Weak starting point

We found a public benchmark for question answering.

Strong starting point

The assistant must answer current travel-policy questions with supported claims, recognise insufficient evidence, and never treat an advisory response as financial approval.

The stronger statement can produce relevant cases.

7. Evaluation Questions

Before building the suite, ask:

  • What decision will the result support?
  • What is the actual unit of work?
  • What failure matters most?
  • Which failures are common?
  • Which failures are rare but severe?
  • Which users or groups could be missed by averages?
  • What evidence is available?
  • What does appropriate refusal look like?
  • Which behaviour is deterministic?
  • Which judgment requires domain expertise?
  • What production outcome matters?
  • When will this evaluation become stale?

8. The Unit of Evaluation

Possible units include:

  • one response;
  • one claim;
  • one retrieved passage;
  • one tool call;
  • one workflow;
  • one conversation;
  • one completed task;
  • one real-world outcome;
  • one user session;
  • one decision.

The correct unit should match the quality requirement.

A response-level score may miss that:

  • the correct tool was never called;
  • the wrong record was updated;
  • the user needed three retries;
  • the final outcome failed;
  • a policy breach occurred during an intermediate step.

Agent evaluations increasingly require multi-turn tasks, tools, environments, and state-based grading rather than a single prompt and answer. Anthropic’s current agent-evaluation guidance describes evals as a task plus grading logic, with more complex agent cases judged by the resulting environment and tests.[3]

Part III — The Evaluation Portfolio

9. No Single Evaluation Is Sufficient

A production AI system needs a portfolio.

Deterministic checks

Hard invariants and exact behaviours.

Component evaluations

Models, retrieval, tools, classifiers, and validators.

Workflow evaluations

End-to-end task completion.

Adversarial evaluations

Malicious, unusual, and stress conditions.

Human evaluations

Expert judgment, preference, usability, and impact.

Production evaluations

Real inputs and outputs sampled after release.

Outcome evaluations

Whether the system improved the real-world objective.

Outcome Evaluation
        ▲
Production Evaluation
        ▲
Human and Adversarial Evaluation
        ▲
Workflow Evaluation
        ▲
Component Evaluation
        ▲
Deterministic Invariants

This is not a maturity hierarchy in which upper layers replace lower layers.

Each layer answers a different question.

10. Deterministic Checks

Use deterministic checks wherever success can be expressed exactly.

Examples:

  • JSON schema;
  • citation ID exists;
  • tool name is allowed;
  • refund amount is within limit;
  • SQL is read-only;
  • expected file was created;
  • unit tests pass;
  • prohibited action was not attempted;
  • approval token is valid;
  • evidence is not expired.

Benefits:

  • fast;
  • reproducible;
  • explainable;
  • suitable for continuous integration;
  • resistant to grader subjectivity.

Architectural principle — Deterministic before interpretive

Do not use a probabilistic grader to judge a condition that can be checked deterministically.

11. Component Evaluations

Model evaluation

Does the selected model have the required capability?

Retrieval evaluation

  • recall;
  • ranking;
  • source authority;
  • freshness;
  • permission correctness.

Tool evaluation

  • selection;
  • parameters;
  • result handling;
  • retry;
  • idempotency.

Validator evaluation

Does the validator catch the failures it is intended to catch?

Router evaluation

Does traffic reach the correct model, workflow, or escalation path?

Component evaluation supports diagnosis.

A workflow failure may be caused by retrieval rather than reasoning.

12. Workflow Evaluation

Workflow evaluation tests the actual system boundary.

It may include:

  • authentication;
  • task framing;
  • context;
  • retrieval;
  • model;
  • tools;
  • validation;
  • authority;
  • persistence;
  • user response.

The case should reflect a real task.

Example:

Given an incident alert, deployment history, current telemetry, and a read-only diagnostic tool, identify the likely cause, cite supporting evidence, and produce a permitted remediation proposal.

The grader may inspect:

  • final recommendation;
  • evidence;
  • tool trace;
  • policy;
  • environment state;
  • task completion.

13. Adversarial and Stress Evaluation

Evaluate:

  • prompt injection;
  • conflicting evidence;
  • corrupted documents;
  • stale data;
  • tool timeout;
  • duplicate event;
  • model refusal;
  • high load;
  • long conversations;
  • unusual language;
  • misleading user claims;
  • permission boundary;
  • repeated retries;
  • provider failure.

NIST recommends stress testing under likely and extreme conditions, testing against past incidents and near-misses, and documenting conditions under which the system fails safely.[1]

14. Human Evaluation

Human evaluation is appropriate when quality depends on:

  • domain judgment;
  • appropriateness;
  • usefulness;
  • tone;
  • explanation;
  • fairness;
  • user trust;
  • subtle safety;
  • business process.

Human evaluation still needs design.

Define:

  • evaluator qualifications;
  • rubric;
  • training;
  • examples;
  • disagreement process;
  • number of reviewers;
  • blinding;
  • sampling;
  • compensation;
  • fatigue controls;
  • privacy.

Human judgment is not automatically consistent or unbiased.

15. Production and Outcome Evaluation

Offline evaluation predicts.

Production evaluation observes.

Outcome evaluation confirms whether the system improved the intended condition.

Examples:

  • repeat-contact rate;
  • incident restoration time;
  • accepted code changes;
  • defect escape;
  • successful refund resolution;
  • user correction rate;
  • business conversion;
  • safety incidents.

Offline evals complement rather than replace A/B testing, product experimentation, and production measurement.[2]

Part IV — Building the Evaluation Dataset

16. Dataset Sources

Cases may come from:

  • historical tasks;
  • expert-authored examples;
  • support tickets;
  • incidents;
  • user research;
  • production logs;
  • synthetic generation;
  • adversarial exercises;
  • policy changes;
  • near-misses;
  • known model failures;
  • regulatory scenarios.

The source affects validity.

A synthetic dataset may improve coverage but fail to reproduce real ambiguity.

Historical data may reflect old workflows and past bias.

Production logs may contain sensitive information.

17. Dataset Roles

Golden set

Authoritative examples reviewed by domain experts.

Regression set

Known failures that must not return.

Challenge set

Rare, adversarial, or high-difficulty cases.

Calibration set

Used to validate graders and thresholds.

Holdout set

Kept separate from iterative development.

Live sample

Recent production cases used to test continued fitness.

These sets may overlap operationally, but their roles should be explicit.

18. Represent the Task Distribution

A dataset should represent:

  • common cases;
  • difficult cases;
  • high-risk cases;
  • boundary cases;
  • insufficient evidence;
  • conflicting evidence;
  • affected groups;
  • languages;
  • environments;
  • tool failures;
  • expected refusals.

Do not mirror frequency blindly.

A rare catastrophic failure deserves deliberate over-sampling.

Architectural principle — Frequency and consequence both shape coverage

The evaluation distribution should reflect ordinary use and intentionally amplify rare, consequential failures.

19. Error Taxonomy

An error taxonomy converts failures into categories.

Example:

Evidence
  - missing source
  - stale source
  - unsupported claim
  - invalid citation

Reasoning
  - incorrect synthesis
  - premature conclusion
  - wrong decomposition

Action
  - wrong tool
  - invalid parameters
  - duplicate side effect

Governance
  - missed escalation
  - policy violation
  - expired authority

Outcome
  - task incomplete
  - harmful side effect
  - user rework

Track:

  • frequency;
  • severity;
  • segment;
  • trend;
  • detection;
  • remediation.

OpenAI recommends reviewing early outputs to build an error taxonomy and continuously adding newly discovered failures to the evaluation process.[2]

20. Labels and Reference Answers

Some cases have exact references.

Others require:

  • accepted alternatives;
  • required elements;
  • prohibited elements;
  • rubric;
  • state transition;
  • outcome.

Do not force open-ended work into one canonical answer when several answers can be correct.

Example:

required:
  - identify current policy
  - cite effective source
  - ask for missing receipt
prohibited:
  - invent approval
  - expose another employee's data
acceptable_outcomes:
  - request_evidence
  - escalate_policy_conflict

21. Dataset Contamination and Leakage

Evaluation loses value when the system has been optimised directly against the test cases.

Risks include:

  • prompt examples copied into the eval;
  • fine-tuning data includes holdout cases;
  • grader prompt leaks expected answer;
  • developers manually tune for visible cases;
  • public benchmark appears in model training;
  • production case enters both training and testing without separation.

Controls:

  • dataset access boundaries;
  • holdout sets;
  • versioning;
  • lineage;
  • periodic unseen cases;
  • external review;
  • rotated challenge sets.

Architecture smell — Memorising the exam

The evaluation score improves because the system has learned the test set rather than the underlying task.

Part V — Choosing Graders

22. A Grader Is a Measurement Instrument

A grader may be:

  • deterministic code;
  • exact match;
  • unit or integration test;
  • statistical metric;
  • policy rule;
  • environment-state check;
  • human reviewer;
  • LLM judge;
  • business outcome.

Every instrument has:

  • scope;
  • error;
  • bias;
  • cost;
  • latency;
  • reproducibility.

The grader itself must be evaluated.

23. Deterministic Graders

Use for:

  • exact values;
  • structured fields;
  • allowed actions;
  • test pass/fail;
  • environment state;
  • policy invariants;
  • citation existence;
  • latency;
  • cost.

Do not use semantic similarity when exact correctness is available.

24. Reference-Based Graders

Compare output against a reference using:

  • exact match;
  • token or field overlap;
  • numeric tolerance;
  • semantic similarity;
  • required elements.

Risks:

  • valid alternatives penalised;
  • superficial wording rewarded;
  • reference contains error;
  • semantic similarity ignores contradiction.

25. Rubric-Based Human Graders

A rubric should define:

  • criterion;
  • scale;
  • examples;
  • critical failures;
  • tie or uncertainty;
  • reviewer evidence.

Example:

Groundedness
0 — material claims unsupported or contradicted
1 — mixed support; important gap
2 — all material claims supported by approved evidence

Avoid scales with distinctions reviewers cannot apply consistently.

26. LLM-as-a-Judge

An LLM judge can scale evaluation of open-ended outputs.

It is useful when:

  • criteria can be expressed clearly;
  • human reference labels exist for calibration;
  • volume makes full human review impractical;
  • decisions are not based solely on one unvalidated score.

Known limitations include:

  • position bias;
  • verbosity or style preference;
  • self-preference;
  • prompt sensitivity;
  • reasoning limitations;
  • correlated failure with the generator.

The MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena research showed useful agreement with human preferences while also documenting position, verbosity, self-enhancement, and reasoning biases.[4]

Architectural principle — The judge is not ground truth

Treat an LLM judge as a calibrated measurement instrument, not an oracle.

27. Validating an LLM Judge

Create a calibration dataset labelled by qualified humans.

Measure:

  • agreement;
  • false pass;
  • false fail;
  • segment performance;
  • consistency across repeated runs;
  • sensitivity to output order;
  • sensitivity to length and style;
  • sensitivity to rubric wording;
  • disagreement severity.

Controls may include:

  • randomising pair order;
  • pointwise and pairwise checks;
  • reference-guided grading;
  • multiple judges;
  • repeated trials;
  • human audit;
  • deterministic checks first.

OpenAI recommends regular domain-expert audits of LLM graders and direct review of system logs.[2]

28. Environment Graders

For agents, inspect the resulting environment.

Examples:

  • repository tests pass;
  • file contents changed correctly;
  • ticket exists once;
  • database remains consistent;
  • service state improved;
  • prohibited resource untouched.

Environment grading is often stronger than judging the final explanation.

A coding agent can provide a convincing summary while producing broken code.

29. Outcome Graders

Outcome grading measures the real-world effect.

Examples:

  • incident resolved;
  • customer did not recontact;
  • change accepted;
  • payment dispute avoided;
  • decision appealed;
  • user completed task.

Outcome evaluation may be delayed and confounded.

It remains necessary because execution quality can diverge from business value.

Part VI — Statistical Design

30. An Evaluation Result Is an Estimate

A score from a finite dataset contains uncertainty.

A one-point difference may reflect:

  • genuine improvement;
  • different case difficulty;
  • random model variation;
  • grader noise;
  • small sample;
  • segment mix.

Report more than the mean.

Where appropriate, include:

  • sample size;
  • distribution;
  • confidence interval;
  • standard error;
  • segment results;
  • repeated-run variance;
  • effect size;
  • paired comparison.

Research on statistical reporting for model evaluations recommends uncertainty measures such as standard errors and confidence intervals, particularly when comparing systems on the same cases.[5]

31. Paired Comparison

When comparing version A and B, run both on the same cases.

For each case, record:

  • A passes, B passes;
  • A passes, B fails;
  • A fails, B passes;
  • both fail.

This exposes whether improvement is broad or merely shifts failures.

Averages can hide regression on high-risk cases.

32. Repeated Trials

Probabilistic systems may vary across runs.

Repeat selected cases when:

  • sampling is enabled;
  • tool timing varies;
  • agent plans vary;
  • judge output varies;
  • the consequence is high.

Measure:

  • pass probability;
  • variance;
  • worst observed path;
  • tool-call distribution;
  • cost distribution.

Do not assume one successful run proves reliability.

33. Sample Size

Sample size should reflect:

  • required precision;
  • expected variance;
  • number of segments;
  • rarity of failure;
  • decision consequence;
  • evaluation cost.

A small suite can support rapid development.

A release or autonomy decision may require larger and more targeted evidence.

Constraint

Large datasets do not correct invalid cases or graders.

Validity comes before volume.

34. Statistical and Practical Significance

A change can be statistically detectable but operationally irrelevant.

Ask:

  • Is the difference meaningful to users?
  • Does it change the release decision?
  • Does it justify cost or latency?
  • Which failure classes improved?
  • Did any critical segment regress?

Part VII — Evaluation Stages

35. Development Evaluation

Fast feedback during design:

  • unit checks;
  • small golden set;
  • prompt experiments;
  • component tests;
  • local traces.

Goal:

Find obvious failures quickly.

36. Integration Evaluation

Test model, retrieval, tools, policies, and state together.

Goal:

Verify components cooperate under realistic conditions.

37. End-to-End Evaluation

Test complete user or system tasks.

Goal:

Measure task completion across the production-like workflow.

38. Shadow Evaluation

Run the new system on real inputs without allowing it to affect users or state.

Compare against:

  • current system;
  • human decision;
  • known outcome.

Goal:

Observe realistic behaviour without production authority.

39. Canary Evaluation

Expose a controlled subset of eligible traffic.

Use:

  • segment limits;
  • rollback;
  • quality gates;
  • technical and behavioural monitoring.

Goal:

Validate assumptions under real operation with bounded risk.

40. Online Evaluation

Sample real production behaviour.

Use:

  • deterministic checks;
  • model graders;
  • human review;
  • user feedback;
  • outcome linkage.

Goal:

Detect drift, emergent failure, and contextual mismatch.

NIST recommends comparing pre-deployment and post-deployment performance, monitoring in real time, and adapting measurement as risks and context change.[1]

41. Outcome Evaluation

Observe whether the system improves the intended result.

Goal:

Confirm value and unintended effects.

Evaluation should not stop at launch because the deployment environment can differ from the test environment.

Part VIII — Release and Autonomy Gates

42. Thresholds Must Trigger Decisions

Example release gate:

Deterministic invariants:
  prohibited action attempts = 0
  citation validity = 100%

Statistical thresholds:
  task success >= 92%
  claim support >= 98%
  p95 latency <= 4 seconds

Segment thresholds:
  every high-risk category >= 99% escalation recall

Operational requirements:
  rollback tested
  owner assigned
  production sampling enabled

43. Zero-Tolerance Gates

Use zero tolerance when:

  • any occurrence is unacceptable;
  • the invariant can be measured reliably;
  • risk justifies blocking.

Examples:

  • cross-tenant data exposure;
  • prohibited production command;
  • unapproved financial action;
  • invalid authority token.

Do not misuse zero tolerance for subjective metrics whose measurement is noisy.

44. Routing Gates

Evaluation can govern routing.

Example:

  • small model for routine cases;
  • stronger model for complex reasoning;
  • human review for insufficient evidence;
  • deterministic workflow for exact calculation.

The routing classifier and thresholds must also be evaluated.

45. Autonomy Gates

Before increasing autonomy, require evidence for:

  • task success;
  • action correctness;
  • policy compliance;
  • adverse cases;
  • idempotency;
  • rollback;
  • outcome;
  • monitoring;
  • incident response.

Architectural principle — Evaluation is the currency of autonomy

Autonomy should increase only when evaluation and production evidence justify the additional authority.

46. Continued-Operation Gates

A system may pass release and later become unfit.

Trigger reduction or suspension when:

  • safety failure occurs;
  • evaluator score falls;
  • evidence freshness degrades;
  • cost exceeds limit;
  • override rate rises;
  • drift is detected;
  • outcome worsens;
  • policy changes;
  • incident remains unresolved.

Part IX — Evaluation Lineage and Reproducibility

47. What Must Be Versioned

  • evaluation contract;
  • dataset;
  • case;
  • reference;
  • rubric;
  • grader;
  • model;
  • prompt;
  • policy;
  • retrieval index;
  • tools;
  • environment;
  • code;
  • configuration;
  • seed where relevant.

Without lineage, a score cannot be reproduced or compared.

48. Evaluation Result Record

run_id: evalrun_2026_08_06_001
evaluation_id: eval_policy_answer_v7
system_version: app_3.4.1
model: model_provider_x_version_y
prompt_version: prompt_18
retrieval_index: hr_index_2026_08_05
dataset_version: hr_gold_2026_08_01
grader_version: rubric_4_judge_2
cases: 640
repetitions: 3
results:
  task_success: 0.943
  claim_support: 0.986
  unsupported_definitive_answers: 0
decision: canary_10_percent
limitations:
  - insufficient Welsh-language cases

49. Evaluation Drift

The evaluation itself can become stale because:

  • business process changes;
  • user population changes;
  • policy changes;
  • model capability changes;
  • new attack patterns emerge;
  • graders no longer correlate with experts;
  • production tasks shift;
  • old edge cases become common.

Evaluate the evaluation.

50. Metric Gaming

Once a metric governs release, teams and systems optimise toward it.

Possible effects:

  • verbose answers score better;
  • agent refuses difficult tasks to avoid error;
  • routing sends hard cases away;
  • humans label ambiguous cases as acceptable;
  • system optimises citations rather than usefulness.

Use:

  • balanced metrics;
  • outcome checks;
  • challenge sets;
  • human audits;
  • periodic rubric review;
  • failure analysis.

Architecture smell — Score over purpose

The system improves the evaluation while becoming worse at the real task.

Part X — Independent Evaluation and Governance

51. Evaluation Ownership

Roles may include:

  • product owner;
  • domain expert;
  • evaluation engineer;
  • data scientist;
  • safety or risk;
  • security;
  • operations;
  • affected-party representative;
  • independent reviewer.

The development team should not be the only group defining success for a consequential system.

NIST recommends independent assessors or separate testing teams where appropriate and emphasises clear accountability for measurement and course-correction.[1]

52. Independence Is Proportional to Risk

Low-risk internal assistant:

  • product and domain review may be sufficient.

High-impact decision system:

  • independent validation;
  • risk oversight;
  • external testing;
  • affected-party feedback;
  • formal sign-off may be required.

Independence reduces correlated incentives and assumptions.

53. Evaluation Review Board

An organisation may establish an evaluation review for:

  • high-risk release;
  • autonomy increase;
  • critical model change;
  • major data change;
  • new user population;
  • unresolved evaluator limitation.

The review should examine:

  • evaluation contract;
  • dataset representativeness;
  • grader validity;
  • thresholds;
  • segment results;
  • failures;
  • production plan;
  • residual risk.

Part XI — Evaluating Agents

54. Agent Evaluation Is State and Trajectory Evaluation

An agent can reach the correct final result through an unsafe path.

It can also take a reasonable path and fail because a tool is unavailable.

Evaluate:

  • final state;
  • tool calls;
  • permissions;
  • number of steps;
  • retries;
  • policy;
  • cost;
  • latency;
  • intermediate side effects;
  • recovery;
  • escalation.

55. Agent Task Environment

An agent evaluation needs:

  • initial state;
  • tools;
  • permissions;
  • hidden ground truth;
  • success state;
  • prohibited states;
  • time and budget;
  • grader.

Example:

initial_state:
  repository_commit: abc123
task:
  fix failing invoice parser
tools:
  - read_file
  - edit_file
  - run_tests
prohibited:
  - network_access
  - modify_payment_code
success:
  - target_tests_pass
  - regression_tests_pass
  - no_prohibited_files_changed
budget:
  tool_calls: 30
  elapsed_minutes: 20

56. Outcome and Trajectory Grading

Outcome grader

Did the environment reach the correct state?

Trajectory grader

Was the path acceptable?

Examples:

  • no secret access;
  • no prohibited tool;
  • no unbounded loop;
  • appropriate escalation;
  • efficient plan.

Outcome grading should usually dominate for task success.

Trajectory grading is necessary for safety, policy, and efficiency.

57. Stochastic Agent Evaluation

Run repeated trials to observe:

  • success probability;
  • path diversity;
  • rare unsafe behaviour;
  • tool-call distribution;
  • cost;
  • time;
  • escalation.

One deterministic-looking transcript can hide unstable behaviour.

Anthropic’s agent-evaluation guidance highlights the importance of tasks, environments, and graders for multi-turn systems rather than relying on single-response scoring.[3]

Part XII — Worked Example: Incident-Remediation Agent

58. Evaluation Objective

Determine whether the agent may recommend production rollbacks for stateless services.

Not yet execute them autonomously.

59. Quality Scenarios

Diagnosis

Identify the causal deployment with supported telemetry.

Safety

Do not recommend rollback when a database migration makes it unsafe.

Evidence

Cite current deployment and metric evidence.

Policy

Request approval for production action.

Performance

Produce recommendation within three minutes.

60. Dataset

  • common deployment regressions;
  • dependency outage;
  • stale telemetry;
  • conflicting metrics;
  • database migration;
  • multiple simultaneous changes;
  • no evidence;
  • malicious log entry;
  • tool timeout;
  • previous failed rollback;
  • near-miss from production.

Segments:

  • low risk;
  • high risk;
  • ambiguous;
  • insufficient evidence;
  • adversarial.

61. Graders

Deterministic

  • prohibited tools not called;
  • recommendation schema valid;
  • cited evidence IDs exist;
  • approval required;
  • rollback target exists.

Environment

  • diagnostic queries are read-only;
  • no production state changes;
  • task completes within budget.

Domain rubric

  • likely cause;
  • evidence relevance;
  • alternative hypothesis;
  • risk recognition;
  • remediation appropriateness.

Human audit

Incident experts review:

  • high-risk cases;
  • grader disagreement;
  • novel failures;
  • production samples.

62. Gate

prohibited production action = 0
unsafe rollback recommendation = 0
high-risk escalation recall >= 99%
supported diagnosis >= 95%
p95 completion <= 3 minutes
LLM grader agreement with experts >= approved threshold

Decision:

  • recommendation mode only;
  • canary with selected incident teams;
  • production sampling enabled;
  • autonomy review after evidence threshold.

63. Learning Loop

Every:

  • incorrect diagnosis;
  • unsafe recommendation;
  • operator override;
  • incident outcome;
  • tool failure;
  • new runbook;

is reviewed for addition to:

  • regression set;
  • challenge set;
  • rubric;
  • policy;
  • architecture.

Part XIII — Architecture Review

64. Scenario

A company has an AI recruitment assistant.

The team reports:

  • 91% overall score;
  • LLM judge average 4.4/5;
  • 2,000 synthetic cases;
  • no major demo failures.

The system screens résumés and recommends candidates.

65. ARB Findings

Finding 1 — Decision is undefined

The evaluation does not state whether the system is being approved for recommendation, ranking, or automatic rejection.

Finding 2 — Dataset lacks production validity

Synthetic cases may not represent actual résumés, roles, or applicant groups.

Finding 3 — Aggregate score hides impact

Performance by role, language, disability-related format, and affected group is unknown.

Finding 4 — LLM judge is unvalidated

Agreement with qualified recruiters is not measured.

Finding 5 — Outcome is missing

The system may optimise similarity while reducing qualified-candidate recall.

Finding 6 — No zero-tolerance controls

Use of prohibited attributes and unauthorised rejection are not deterministic gates.

Finding 7 — No production plan

No shadow comparison, appeal, override, or continued monitoring exists.

66. Recommended Evaluation Architecture

  • define decision authority;
  • build real, permissioned historical and expert-authored cases;
  • segment by role and affected group;
  • deterministic checks for prohibited features;
  • human-calibrated rubric;
  • holdout and challenge sets;
  • recruiter baseline;
  • shadow evaluation;
  • candidate recall and downstream outcome;
  • appeal and override analysis;
  • independent review;
  • production sampling;
  • clear release constraints.

Part XIV — Architecture Smells

67. Demo as Evaluation

A curated conversation is treated as evidence of production fitness.

68. Benchmark Substitution

A public model benchmark is treated as evaluation of the application workflow.

69. One Score to Rule Them All

A single aggregate score hides risk, segments, and failure types.

70. The Judge Is the Truth

An LLM grader is used without human calibration or bias testing.

71. Test Set as Product Specification

The team tunes directly to visible cases until the suite no longer measures generalisation.

72. Offline Completion

Evaluation stops when the system is released.

73. Synthetic Comfort

Synthetic cases are abundant but fail to represent real ambiguity and consequence.

74. Threshold Without Owner

A metric exists, but no stakeholder owns the decision or response.

75. Green Average, Red Tail

Mean performance passes while high-risk or minority segments fail.

76. Evaluation Without Lineage

Results cannot be reproduced because model, prompt, data, tools, or graders were not versioned.

77. Grading the Explanation

The judge rewards a convincing narrative rather than task outcome or evidence.

78. Autonomy by Accuracy

A high answer score is used to justify action authority without tool, policy, rollback, or outcome evaluation.

Part XV — Interview Preparation

79. Foundational Questions

Question 1

What is an eval?

A structured test that runs a defined AI system on representative cases and applies grading or observation to produce evidence for a decision.

Question 2

Why are model benchmarks insufficient?

They measure general capability under benchmark conditions, not the complete workflow, organisation-specific data, tools, risks, users, or outcomes.

Question 3

What belongs in an evaluation case?

Input, initial state, evidence, environment, expected or acceptable outcomes, prohibited outcomes, segment, risk, and grading method.

Question 4

When should you use an LLM judge?

For scalable grading of open-ended qualities when criteria are clear and the judge is calibrated against humans. It should not replace deterministic checks or expert review for high-risk decisions.

Question 5

What is a golden set?

A living set of representative examples and expert judgments defining expected quality for a specific workflow.

80. Senior-Level Questions

Question 6

How do you validate an LLM judge?

Compare against qualified human labels; measure agreement, false passes, false fails, segments, repeatability, position and style sensitivity; audit periodically.

Question 7

How do you evaluate an agent?

Use a realistic task environment, tool permissions, success and prohibited states, deterministic outcome tests, trajectory checks, repeated trials, cost, latency, and escalation.

Question 8

What is the difference between offline and online evaluation?

Offline uses controlled cases before or outside production. Online evaluates real behaviour and outcomes after deployment. Both are required.

Question 9

How do you prevent overfitting to evals?

Holdouts, challenge rotation, lineage, unseen production samples, external review, outcome metrics, and separation of training and evaluation data.

Question 10

How do you set an evaluation threshold?

Start from the quality scenario, consequence, baseline, human performance, measurement error, segment risk, and acceptable residual risk—not an arbitrary percentage.

Question 11

How do you handle nondeterminism?

Repeat trials where relevant, report variance and pass probability, control configuration, compare paired cases, and inspect worst-case trajectories.

Question 12

Should every failure be added to the regression set?

Add material, representative, or recurring failures. Avoid uncontrolled growth and duplicates; preserve taxonomy, ownership, and dataset balance.

81. Principal-Level Questions

Question 13

How would you create an enterprise evaluation platform?

Provide:

  • dataset registry;
  • case schema;
  • environment execution;
  • grader registry;
  • lineage;
  • model and prompt versioning;
  • traces;
  • segment reporting;
  • statistical analysis;
  • release gates;
  • production sampling;
  • human review queues.

Keep domain definitions and thresholds with product and risk owners.

Question 14

What should be centralised versus domain-owned?

Centralise infrastructure, standards, security, lineage, and common graders.

Domain teams own:

  • success;
  • cases;
  • severity;
  • rubrics;
  • thresholds;
  • outcome.

Question 15

How does evaluation support earned autonomy?

It provides task, safety, policy, action, recovery, and outcome evidence needed to justify authority. Production evidence must continue after autonomy is granted.

Question 16

What is evaluator validity?

The extent to which the evaluator actually measures the intended property and supports the intended decision.

Question 17

How do you evaluate a system when ground truth is unavailable?

Use triangulation: domain rubrics, pairwise comparison, human judgment, environment outcomes, downstream metrics, consistency checks, and explicit uncertainty.

Part XVI — Whiteboard Challenge

82. Design Evaluation Architecture for an AI Coding Agent

The agent can:

  • inspect a repository;
  • write code;
  • run tests;
  • respond to review;
  • open a pull request;
  • deploy to a sandbox.

Constraints

  • multiple languages;
  • unreliable existing tests;
  • regulated repositories;
  • secrets;
  • asynchronous runs;
  • model changes;
  • cost limit;
  • no production deployment authority.

Discuss

  1. Define the release decision.
  2. Define quality scenarios.
  3. Identify deterministic invariants.
  4. Build golden, regression, challenge, holdout, and live sets.
  5. Define task environments.
  6. Choose outcome and trajectory graders.
  7. Validate LLM-based code-quality judges.
  8. Measure pass probability across repeated trials.
  9. Segment by repository risk and task type.
  10. Define cost per accepted correct change.
  11. Design shadow and canary evaluation.
  12. Define production sampling and incident learning.
  13. Version all evaluation dependencies.
  14. Create autonomy gates for additional tools.

Strong-answer characteristics

  • evaluates accepted changes, not generated text;
  • uses unit, integration, security, and policy checks;
  • inspects prohibited file access;
  • tests real repository environments;
  • measures review burden and defect escape;
  • calibrates subjective code-quality rubrics;
  • keeps holdouts;
  • tracks model and prompt changes;
  • uses paired comparison;
  • prevents deployment authority;
  • links production incidents to regression cases.

Part XVII — Questions to Take Back to Your Team

  1. Which decision does each evaluation support?
  2. Is the system boundary explicit?
  3. Does the dataset represent real use and severe risk?
  4. Which cases are golden, regression, challenge, holdout, and live?
  5. Which checks can be deterministic?
  6. Has the grader itself been evaluated?
  7. Are results segmented?
  8. Is uncertainty reported?
  9. Are repeated trials needed?
  10. Can the run be reproduced?
  11. What happens when a threshold is missed?
  12. Does the suite test the workflow or only the model?
  13. Are production inputs sampled?
  14. Are outcomes measured?
  15. How are new failures added?
  16. Could the system be gaming the metric?
  17. Which evaluations become stale after a policy or model change?
  18. What evidence justifies the current autonomy level?

Architect’s Notebook — Evaluation Is Organisational Memory

A regression suite is more than test data.

It records:

  • what the organisation has learned;
  • which failures matter;
  • how experts define quality;
  • which trade-offs were accepted;
  • what the system must never repeat.

Without this memory, teams rediscover the same failures after every model, prompt, provider, or workflow change.

Evaluation becomes a durable asset when it preserves judgment—not only data.

From the Architect’s Desk

AI teams are often tempted to believe that better models will eventually make evaluation less important. The opposite is more likely. As capability increases, systems are trusted with more varied tasks, more tools, and more authority. The number of plausible outputs grows, and so does the cost of being confidently wrong.

A good evaluation architecture does not promise certainty. It shows what has been tested, under which conditions, with which instrument, and for which decision. It makes gaps visible.

Do not ask only whether the new version scored higher. Ask which cases changed, which risks remain, whether the judge is valid, whether the result is meaningful, and what production evidence will challenge the conclusion.

The purpose of evaluation is not to create a green dashboard. It is to make better release, routing, governance, and investment decisions.

When evaluation works, every failure makes the organisation harder to surprise in the future.

If I Were the Architect

You inherit an enterprise assistant with a large evaluation suite.

It has 20,000 cases and passes 96%.

Yet incidents continue.

You discover:

  • most cases are synthetic;
  • the suite tests final text only;
  • the LLM judge was never calibrated;
  • high-risk cases are less than 1% of the set;
  • no results are segmented;
  • prompts have been tuned against the full suite;
  • production outcomes are not linked;
  • old cases reference retired policies.

What do you do first?

Do not add another 10,000 cases.

Rebuild the evidence chain:

  1. State the decisions the suite must support.
  2. Map cases to quality scenarios and risks.
  3. Quarantine stale and contaminated cases.
  4. Create holdout and challenge sets.
  5. Add deterministic and environment graders.
  6. Calibrate subjective graders.
  7. Segment results.
  8. Run repeated trials where necessary.
  9. Establish release and continued-operation gates.
  10. Sample production and add material failures to regression.

The organisation did not lack evaluation volume.

It lacked evaluation architecture.

Key Takeaways

  • Evaluation is an architectural capability that produces evidence for decisions.
  • The Evaluation Evidence Chain connects requirement, scenario, case, system, environment, grader, threshold, decision, production evidence, and learning.
  • An evaluation contract defines scope, versions, metrics, thresholds, owner, and limitations.
  • Model benchmarks do not establish workflow fitness.
  • A production system requires deterministic, component, workflow, adversarial, human, production, and outcome evaluation.
  • Datasets should include golden, regression, challenge, calibration, holdout, and live roles.
  • Coverage should reflect frequency and amplify rare consequential failures.
  • Graders are measurement instruments with error and bias.
  • Deterministic checks should precede probabilistic judgment.
  • LLM judges require human calibration, bias testing, and ongoing audit.
  • Agent evaluation should inspect environment state, trajectory, authority, cost, and repeated trials.
  • Results should report uncertainty, segments, and practical significance.
  • Evaluation should progress through development, integration, end-to-end, shadow, canary, online, and outcome stages.
  • Thresholds must trigger release, rollback, routing, review, or autonomy decisions.
  • Evaluation lineage is necessary for reproducibility.
  • Production monitoring challenges—not merely confirms—offline evidence.
  • Newly discovered failures should strengthen regression memory.
  • Evaluation is the currency of earned autonomy.

- Do not treat LLM judges as ground truth.
- Do not use one aggregate score for high-risk decisions.
- Preserve deterministic zero-tolerance gates where measurement is reliable.
- Keep holdout and production evidence separate from development tuning.
- Do not imply statistical confidence corrects invalid cases or graders.
- Evaluation must continue after release.
- Domain experts and affected stakeholders must share ownership of important
  definitions and thresholds.

References

https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/measure/

https://openai.com/index/evals-drive-next-chapter-of-ai/

https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents

[4] Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685
