Chapter 6 - Model and Inference Architecture

Matching capability to task, risk, latency, cost, and control

Related chapters: Chapters 4, 7, 10, and 12

The best model is not the model with the highest general benchmark score. It is the model configuration that satisfies the task’s quality bar within the system’s risk, latency, cost, privacy, and operating constraints.

1. Why This Chapter Matters

Model selection is one of the most visible decisions in an AI system.

It is also one of the easiest decisions to frame badly.

Teams ask:

  • Which model is smartest?
  • Which model has the largest context window?
  • Which provider leads the current benchmark?
  • Should we use an open model?
  • Should we host it ourselves?
  • Can one model handle every task?
  • Can a router choose automatically?

These questions matter.

They become architectural only when connected to:

  • the task;
  • the required capability;
  • acceptable failure;
  • evidence and evaluation;
  • latency;
  • throughput;
  • cost;
  • privacy;
  • authority;
  • deployment;
  • operations;
  • change.

A frontier model may be unnecessary for routine extraction.

A small model may be unsafe for complex policy interpretation.

A locally hosted model may improve data control while creating a platform the organisation cannot reliably operate.

A fallback may restore availability while silently weakening structured output, tool use, safety behaviour, or supported context length.

Current architecture guidance increasingly treats model choice as a portfolio decision. Microsoft recommends evaluating each model in the workload individually and distinguishes predictable design-time selection from dynamic runtime routing. AWS advises mapping task complexity to the smallest model that meets its quality bar, with escalation to more capable models when required.[1][2]

Inference architecture is equally important. Production systems must control:

  • queueing;
  • prefill;
  • token generation;
  • context and output limits;
  • batching;
  • cache;
  • memory;
  • accelerator use;
  • routing;
  • quotas;
  • failover;
  • observability.

The central argument of this chapter is:

A model is a behavioural dependency. Inference architecture governs how that dependency is selected, configured, supplied, observed, scaled, and replaced.

2. Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • describe a model as a behavioural dependency rather than a library;
  • create a capability profile for a task class;
  • select models through contextual evaluation rather than benchmark reputation;
  • compare hosted, managed, self-hosted, open, and proprietary options;
  • decide when one model, a model portfolio, or a routing layer is appropriate;
  • design routing, escalation, fallback, and degraded modes;
  • create an explicit inference contract;
  • explain how decoding parameters affect behaviour and reproducibility;
  • distinguish context capacity from effective task performance;
  • break latency into queue, prefill, decode, tool, and validation stages;
  • explain batching, KV cache, PagedAttention, prompt caching, speculative decoding, quantisation, and parallelism;
  • define inference SLOs and cost-per-outcome metrics;
  • design model versioning, canary, rollback, and reevaluation;
  • identify false portability created by incomplete model abstractions;
  • answer architecture interview questions about model serving, routing, self-hosting, optimisation, resilience, and vendor dependency.

Part I — The Model as a Behavioural Dependency

3. Models Are Not Ordinary Libraries

A conventional library generally exposes defined functions whose behaviour changes when the library or configuration changes.

A model is different.

Its observable behaviour can depend on:

  • provider;
  • model family;
  • model snapshot;
  • training and alignment;
  • system instructions;
  • tools;
  • retrieved evidence;
  • prompt ordering;
  • sampling;
  • reasoning budget;
  • context length;
  • output limit;
  • platform policy;
  • server-side implementation;
  • safety filters.

Two models exposing similar chat or responses APIs may differ materially in:

  • instruction hierarchy;
  • tool-call format;
  • schema adherence;
  • refusal;
  • reasoning;
  • multilingual performance;
  • context use;
  • citation support;
  • latency;
  • token accounting;
  • data handling.

A model adapter can make APIs look similar.

It cannot make behaviour identical.

Architectural principle — Portability is behavioural

A model is portable only when the replacement passes the system’s evaluations, quality gates, policy checks, and operating requirements—not merely when it accepts the same request schema.

4. The Behavioural Dependency Record

For every production model, record:

  • provider and service;
  • model family;
  • exact version or alias;
  • release and retirement status;
  • supported input modalities;
  • supported output and tool features;
  • context and output limits;
  • data region and retention commitments;
  • safety and policy behaviour;
  • evaluation results;
  • known weak tasks;
  • latency and cost profile;
  • fallback;
  • owner;
  • review date.

Example:

model_id: support_reasoner_primary
provider: provider_a
model_reference: model-family-version
task_classes:
  - ambiguous_policy
  - multi_document_synthesis
features:
  structured_output: true
  tool_use: true
  vision: false
limits:
  max_context_tokens: 128000
  max_output_tokens: 8000
routing:
  fallback: support_reasoner_secondary
risk_constraints:
  - no autonomous financial action
evaluation:
  suite: support_eval_v12
  last_passed: 2026-08-03
owner: customer_ai_platform

The record belongs in configuration and governance, not only in a slide deck.

5. Model Capability Is Task-Specific

A model can be strong at:

  • coding;
  • extraction;
  • classification;
  • multilingual interaction;
  • tool use;
  • long-document synthesis;
  • visual understanding;
  • planning.

The same model can be weak at another task.

A public benchmark may indicate general capability.

It does not establish:

  • organisation-specific policy interpretation;
  • correct tool selection;
  • quality under the actual prompt and context;
  • safety under the delegated authority;
  • cost at expected traffic;
  • latency under production load;
  • performance after quantisation;
  • behaviour through a compatibility layer.

The selection must use Chapter 4’s evaluation architecture.

Part II — Model Capability Profiles

6. Define the Task Before the Model

A model-selection decision should begin with:

  • task class;
  • input;
  • expected output;
  • evidence;
  • reasoning complexity;
  • tool use;
  • risk;
  • latency;
  • volume;
  • cost;
  • privacy;
  • language and modality;
  • failure response.

Weak requirement:

We need the strongest available model.

Stronger requirement:

For routine English-language invoice extraction, return twelve typed fields with at least 99% field validity, p95 completion under two seconds, and cost below £0.02 per document. Ambiguous documents must escalate.

The stronger requirement creates a candidate set.

7. The Model Capability Profile

This handbook introduces the Model Capability Profile:

Task
  + Input and Modality
  + Reasoning Complexity
  + Evidence and Tools
  + Output Contract
  + Risk and Failure Policy
  + Latency and Throughput
  + Privacy and Residency
  + Cost Boundary
  = Required Capability Profile

It is an original synthesis.

Example:

task_class: routine_incident_summary
input:
  modality: text
  typical_tokens: 6000
  maximum_tokens: 20000
reasoning:
  complexity: moderate
  tool_use: read_only
output:
  format: structured_summary_v3
risk:
  consequence: advisory
  unsupported_claim: refuse_or_flag
performance:
  first_token_p95_ms: 1000
  completion_p95_ms: 6000
volume:
  peak_requests_per_minute: 120
privacy:
  data_class: internal
cost:
  maximum_per_task_gbp: 0.05

The profile should be stable enough to compare candidates while allowing the model portfolio to evolve.

8. Capability Dimensions

Task competence

Can the model perform the domain task?

Instruction following

Does it obey system constraints and output requirements?

Evidence use

Does it use supplied evidence and recognise insufficiency?

Tool use

Can it select and call allowed tools correctly?

Structured output

Can it produce valid, useful structures?

Robustness

How does it behave under unusual, incomplete, or adversarial input?

Safety and policy

Does it preserve required boundaries?

Language and modality

Does performance hold for required languages, images, audio, code, or tables?

Operational fit

Does it meet latency, throughput, availability, and cost needs?

Change fit

Can the model be versioned, evaluated, observed, and replaced?

9. The Smallest Sufficient Model

A useful default is:

Choose the smallest and least operationally expensive model that consistently meets the task’s quality and risk thresholds.

“Smallest” can mean:

  • fewer parameters;
  • lower reasoning effort;
  • cheaper service tier;
  • lower precision deployment;
  • specialised model;
  • local model;
  • deterministic mechanism instead of a generative model.

AWS’s agentic guidance recommends classifying tasks by reasoning complexity and mapping each class to the smallest model that meets its quality bar.[2]

Constraint

The smallest model is not automatically the cheapest system.

A weaker model may increase:

  • retries;
  • escalation;
  • tool errors;
  • human repair;
  • context size;
  • workflow length;
  • incidents.

Measure cost per successful outcome.

Part III — One Model or a Portfolio?

10. The Single-Model Architecture

A single model simplifies:

  • integration;
  • prompts;
  • evaluation;
  • observability;
  • routing;
  • support;
  • procurement.

It is appropriate when:

  • tasks are similar;
  • volume is moderate;
  • requirements are stable;
  • one model meets all quality bars;
  • portability is not a strong driver;
  • operational simplicity matters more than marginal optimisation.

Risks

  • overpaying for simple tasks;
  • dependency concentration;
  • capacity bottleneck;
  • model weakness in one modality;
  • broad blast radius during change.

11. The Model Portfolio

A portfolio can include:

  • small fast model;
  • strong reasoning model;
  • vision model;
  • embedding model;
  • classification model;
  • safety model;
  • local privacy-sensitive model;
  • fallback provider.

Benefits:

  • task fit;
  • cost control;
  • resilience;
  • specialisation;
  • data control.

Costs:

  • more evaluations;
  • routing complexity;
  • inconsistent behaviour;
  • prompt variants;
  • fragmented observability;
  • procurement and governance;
  • harder incident diagnosis.

A portfolio should exist because tasks differ—not because many models are available.

12. Static Selection

The application explicitly maps a known task to a known model.

Invoice Extraction ──► Extraction Model
Policy Reasoning    ──► Reasoning Model
Image Inspection   ──► Vision Model

Benefits:

  • predictable;
  • auditable;
  • easy to evaluate;
  • stable cost;
  • easier safety analysis.

Use for:

  • critical paths;
  • regulated workflows;
  • well-understood task classes;
  • strict residency;
  • model-specific tools.

13. Dynamic Routing

A routing component selects from an approved model set at runtime.

Possible routing inputs:

  • task class;
  • estimated complexity;
  • user tier;
  • latency target;
  • budget;
  • language;
  • modality;
  • privacy;
  • model health;
  • quota;
  • prior failure;
  • confidence or validation state.

Microsoft describes automatic model selection as moving model choice from a static design-time decision into an operational concern, while retaining manual selection for critical paths where predictability is more important.[1]

Risks

  • router misclassification;
  • unstable cost;
  • difficult reproducibility;
  • routing bias;
  • safety differences;
  • unsupported feature selection;
  • feedback loops;
  • opaque provider optimisation.

The router must be evaluated like any other decision component.

14. The Routing Policy

A routing policy should define:

  • approved models;
  • eligible task classes;
  • excluded data classes;
  • quality threshold;
  • cost boundary;
  • latency target;
  • fallback order;
  • escalation condition;
  • maximum attempts;
  • observability fields;
  • expiry and version.

Example:

policy_id: coding_route_v4
rules:
  - when:
      task: documentation
      repository_risk: low
    use: small_code_model
  - when:
      task: architecture_change
    use: reasoning_code_model
  - when:
      validation: failed
      attempts: 1
    escalate_to: reasoning_code_model
constraints:
  prohibited_models:
    - unapproved_external
  maximum_model_calls: 3
  preserve:
    - structured_output
    - tool_policy
    - data_residency

15. Routing Is a Quality Trade-off

Dynamic routing can optimise:

  • cost;
  • latency;
  • capacity;
  • task quality.

It can weaken:

  • predictability;
  • auditability;
  • reproducibility;
  • safety consistency.

The architecture should identify which quality is driving the router.

“Use AI to select the AI” is not a sufficient rationale.

Part IV — Escalation, Fallback, and Degraded Modes

16. Escalation

Escalation moves a task to a more capable or more expensive path.

Triggers may include:

  • low task confidence;
  • invalid structure;
  • missing evidence;
  • complex intent;
  • tool failure;
  • high-risk classification;
  • human request;
  • small-model failure.
Small Model
    │
    ├── pass validation ─► continue
    └── fail or high risk ─► stronger model / human

The escalation policy should avoid repeatedly paying for two models when a task can be classified correctly upfront.

17. Fallback

Fallback preserves service when the preferred model is unavailable or unsuitable.

Causes:

  • provider outage;
  • quota;
  • region;
  • rate limit;
  • model retirement;
  • high latency;
  • safety block;
  • feature failure.

Architectural principle — Fallback changes behaviour

A fallback is not merely a traffic event. It is a behavioural change that must preserve the task’s minimum quality, safety, policy, and data requirements.

The secondary model may have:

  • shorter context;
  • different tool semantics;
  • weaker schema adherence;
  • different safety policy;
  • different language performance;
  • different data region.

Fallback eligibility must be evaluated.

18. Degraded Modes

Sometimes no model can preserve full capability.

Degraded modes include:

  • smaller-context response;
  • retrieval-only result;
  • deterministic workflow;
  • no tool execution;
  • read-only action;
  • asynchronous processing;
  • human review;
  • explicit temporary unavailability.

A degraded mode should be named and observable.

It should not masquerade as normal service.

19. Cascades and Their Risks

A cascade may try:

  1. small model;
  2. stronger model;
  3. alternate provider;
  4. human.

Risks:

  • compounded latency;
  • repeated token cost;
  • inconsistent answers;
  • duplicated tool calls;
  • state loss;
  • privacy expansion;
  • difficult traces.

Use one durable task ID and record each attempt.

Tool execution should be separated from candidate generation so a retry does not repeat side effects.

Part V — The Inference Contract

20. Model Configuration Is Part of Behaviour

A model name alone does not define a production inference.

Behaviour also depends on:

  • version;
  • system instructions;
  • temperature;
  • top-p;
  • maximum output;
  • stop conditions;
  • reasoning effort;
  • tool definitions;
  • response schema;
  • seed where supported;
  • timeout;
  • retry;
  • content filters;
  • context policy;
  • cache policy.

This handbook introduces the Inference Contract.

21. The Inference Contract

contract_id: support_reasoning_v8
model_policy: support_router_v5
task_class: policy_interpretation
configuration:
  temperature: 0.1
  top_p: 1.0
  max_output_tokens: 3000
  reasoning_budget: medium
output:
  schema: supported_answer_v4
  strict_validation: true
tools:
  allowed:
    - policy_search
    - employee_profile_read
  maximum_calls: 4
context:
  maximum_tokens: 60000
  evidence_required: true
reliability:
  timeout_ms: 12000
  retries: 1
  fallback: policy_reasoner_secondary
safety:
  financial_approval: prohibited
observability:
  capture:
    - model_version
    - route
    - token_usage
    - latency_breakdown
    - validation

The contract is an original synthesis.

It makes model behaviour:

  • reviewable;
  • versioned;
  • testable;
  • comparable;
  • auditable.

22. Decoding Parameters

Temperature

Controls randomness in token selection.

Lower temperature can improve repeatability.

It does not guarantee factuality or correctness.

Top-p and top-k

Restrict the candidate token distribution.

Changing them alters style and variability.

Maximum output

Constrains latency, cost, and runaway generation.

Too small a limit can truncate required output.

Stop conditions

Can prevent unwanted continuation.

Incorrect stop sequences can cut valid output.

Reasoning budget or effort

Some models expose controls that trade additional computation for task quality.

These controls should be evaluated by task, not set globally.

23. Reproducibility Has Limits

Even with fixed parameters, outputs can vary because of:

  • server-side changes;
  • distributed execution;
  • tool timing;
  • retrieval;
  • dynamic routing;
  • provider implementation;
  • nondeterministic kernels.

Production reproducibility should mean:

  • configuration is recorded;
  • versions are known;
  • evidence and tools are traceable;
  • acceptance is statistical;
  • failures can be reconstructed.

It does not mean every token must always be identical.

24. Structured Outputs

Structured output features can constrain generated content to a schema.

Benefits:

  • reliable parsing;
  • validation;
  • safer integration;
  • clearer failure handling.

OpenAI’s structured-output guidance distinguishes schema-constrained generation from ordinary JSON generation.[3]

Constraint

A valid schema does not prove:

  • correct values;
  • supported claims;
  • permitted action;
  • safe decision.

Structure is one layer of validation.

Part VI — Context Capacity and Effective Context

25. Maximum Context Is Not Effective Context

A model may support a large token window.

That does not mean every task should use it.

Long context increases:

  • prefill latency;
  • input cost;
  • memory;
  • irrelevant information;
  • conflict;
  • prompt-injection surface;
  • cache sensitivity.

The effective context is the amount and organisation of information the model can use reliably for the task.

Chapter 5’s evidence architecture should determine what enters context.

26. Context Strategies

  • retrieve only relevant evidence;
  • summarise old interaction;
  • maintain structured state;
  • use tools for live data;
  • cache stable prefixes;
  • split tasks;
  • use long context only when relationships across the whole corpus matter.

A larger context window is a capability.

It is not an information architecture.

27. Context-Length Evaluation

Evaluate across:

  • typical length;
  • high percentile;
  • maximum supported case;
  • conflicting evidence;
  • source position;
  • repeated facts;
  • irrelevant distractors.

Measure:

  • task success;
  • claim support;
  • latency;
  • cost;
  • truncation;
  • tool use.

Part VII — The Anatomy of Inference Latency

28. Latency Is a Pipeline

Client
  ↓
Gateway and Queue
  ↓
Context Assembly
  ↓
Prefill
  ↓
First Token
  ↓
Decode
  ↓
Tools
  ↓
Validation
  ↓
Complete Response

Useful measures:

  • queue time;
  • time to first token;
  • inter-token latency;
  • output tokens per second;
  • time to complete;
  • total task latency.

29. Prefill and Decode

Prefill

The model processes the input context and builds internal key-value state.

Prefill grows with input size and compute.

Decode

The model generates output tokens sequentially.

Decode is strongly affected by:

  • output length;
  • memory bandwidth;
  • batching;
  • cache;
  • decoding method.

Optimising only tokens per second may not improve first-token latency.

30. User-Perceived Latency

Different workflows value different measures.

Interactive assistant

  • first meaningful token;
  • smooth streaming;
  • interruption.

Structured extraction

  • full valid result;
  • no value in partial output.

Agentic workflow

  • total time to outcome;
  • tools and approvals dominate.

Batch processing

  • throughput and deadline;
  • first token irrelevant.

31. Latency Budgets

Allocate the end-to-end target:

Gateway                100 ms
Retrieval               400 ms
Prefill                 800 ms
Decode                 2500 ms
Validation              200 ms
Reserve                1000 ms
-----------------------------
p95 budget             5000 ms

The budget exposes which stage requires optimisation.

Part VIII — Throughput, Batching, and Memory

32. Throughput Is Not Latency

A system can achieve high throughput while individual users wait too long.

Batching increases hardware utilisation by grouping work.

It can also increase queue delay.

Choose based on:

  • request arrival;
  • latency SLO;
  • input/output length;
  • model size;
  • accelerator;
  • cost.

33. Static and Continuous Batching

Static batching

Wait for a group, process together.

Simple but inefficient when sequence lengths differ.

Continuous or in-flight batching

Add and remove requests as generation progresses.

Improves utilisation for variable-length generation.

Modern inference engines expose in-flight batching, cache management, parallelism, quantisation, and decoding controls as serving concerns.[4]

34. The KV Cache

Autoregressive transformers reuse previous attention keys and values during generation.

The KV cache grows with:

  • active requests;
  • context length;
  • generated tokens;
  • model layers;
  • hidden dimensions;
  • precision.

KV-cache pressure often limits concurrency before model weights do.

Monitor:

  • cache utilisation;
  • eviction;
  • reuse;
  • active sequences;
  • rejected requests;
  • preemption.

35. PagedAttention

The PagedAttention work applied virtual-memory-style paging to KV-cache management. The vLLM system reported reduced memory waste and higher serving throughput at comparable latency by allocating cache in blocks and sharing cache where possible.[5]

Architectural lesson:

Memory management and scheduling can materially change serving economics without changing the model.

Treat serving engine choice as part of inference architecture.

36. Prefix and Prompt Caching

Repeated stable prompt prefixes can be cached.

Examples:

  • system instructions;
  • policy corpus;
  • tool definitions;
  • long documents;
  • shared conversation prefix.

Prompt caching can reduce repeated processing, cost, and latency. Current provider implementations may use automatic or explicit cache semantics with provider-specific eligibility and lifetime rules.[6][7]

Cache design questions

  • Which prefix is stable?
  • What invalidates it?
  • Is it tenant-specific?
  • Does it contain sensitive data?
  • What is the cache lifetime?
  • Is a hit observable?
  • Does model or configuration change invalidate it?

Cache efficiency depends on prompt structure.

Dynamic content placed before shared static content can destroy reuse.

37. Cache Safety

A cache key should include relevant:

  • model;
  • model version;
  • tenant;
  • policy version;
  • prompt prefix;
  • tool version;
  • safety configuration;
  • data classification.

Incorrect cache reuse can cause:

  • cross-tenant leakage;
  • stale policy;
  • wrong tool schema;
  • hidden behavioural change.

Part IX — Inference Optimisation

38. Optimise After Measurement

Common optimisations include:

  • smaller model;
  • shorter context;
  • shorter output;
  • routing;
  • caching;
  • batching;
  • quantisation;
  • speculative decoding;
  • parallelism;
  • hardware change;
  • asynchronous execution.

Each can alter quality, latency, cost, or operations.

Use Chapter 4’s evaluations before and after optimisation.

39. Quantisation

Quantisation stores or computes model values at lower precision.

Potential benefits:

  • lower memory;
  • higher throughput;
  • cheaper hardware;
  • larger model on limited devices.

Potential costs:

  • quality regression;
  • hardware-specific performance;
  • calibration effort;
  • unsupported operators;
  • more deployment variants.

GPTQ and AWQ are influential post-training approaches for low-bit weight quantisation.[8][9]

Architectural rule

Quantised models are new behavioural artifacts and must pass the relevant evaluation suite.

Do not inherit the full-precision model’s approval automatically.

40. Speculative Decoding

Speculative decoding uses a faster draft mechanism to propose multiple future tokens and a target model to verify them.

The aim is to reduce sequential decoding latency while preserving the target distribution. Google reported substantial inference speedups in early work and subsequent product use.[10]

Suitability depends on:

  • draft-target alignment;
  • workload;
  • output length;
  • hardware;
  • implementation overhead.

It is a serving optimisation, not a substitute for a smaller sufficient model.

41. Parallelism

Large models may require or benefit from:

  • tensor parallelism;
  • pipeline parallelism;
  • data parallelism;
  • expert parallelism;
  • multi-instance serving;
  • multi-node serving.

Parallelism introduces:

  • communication overhead;
  • topology sensitivity;
  • more failure modes;
  • scheduling complexity.

NVIDIA’s TensorRT-LLM serving stack exposes tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism alongside cache, scheduling, quantisation, and decoding options.[4]

42. Prefill–Decode Disaggregation

Some large-scale systems separate prefill and decode onto different resources.

Potential benefits:

  • independent scaling;
  • hardware specialisation;
  • queue isolation.

Costs:

  • transfer of KV state;
  • more networking;
  • orchestration;
  • failure complexity.

Use when workload scale and traffic shape justify the platform complexity.

43. Batch and Asynchronous Inference

Real-time endpoints are not required for every task.

Use asynchronous or batch processing when:

  • user is not waiting;
  • payload is large;
  • deadline is minutes or hours;
  • throughput matters more than first-token latency;
  • capacity can be scheduled.

This can reduce cost and smooth demand.

The product must communicate progress and failure.

Part X — Hosted, Managed, Self-Hosted, and Edge

44. Hosted Model API

The provider operates the model and infrastructure.

Benefits:

  • rapid adoption;
  • limited infrastructure;
  • elastic access;
  • frontier capabilities;
  • managed upgrades.

Costs and risks:

  • vendor dependency;
  • variable quotas;
  • model changes;
  • data commitments;
  • regional availability;
  • pricing;
  • limited low-level control.

45. Managed Dedicated Deployment

A cloud platform operates a deployment with stronger capacity or isolation controls.

Benefits:

  • enterprise integration;
  • provisioned capacity;
  • regional choice;
  • monitoring;
  • support.

Costs:

  • platform coupling;
  • reserved cost;
  • deployment configuration;
  • cloud-specific features.

46. Self-Hosted Model

The organisation operates weights and serving infrastructure.

Benefits:

  • control;
  • customisation;
  • isolation;
  • data locality;
  • predictable use of owned capacity;
  • access to open models.

Costs:

  • accelerators;
  • serving engine;
  • scaling;
  • upgrades;
  • security;
  • reliability;
  • optimisation;
  • on-call support;
  • model and licence governance.

AWS’s inference guidance explicitly distinguishes serverless, managed, and self-managed inference choices because each carries different operational and performance responsibilities.[11]

47. Edge and On-Device Inference

Use cases:

  • disconnected operation;
  • very low network latency;
  • privacy;
  • local personalisation;
  • low-volume specialised task.

Constraints:

  • memory;
  • power;
  • model size;
  • update;
  • observability;
  • device diversity;
  • physical extraction risk.

Quantisation and specialised runtimes may make edge inference possible, but quality and update control remain architectural concerns.

48. The Self-Hosting Decision

Self-host when several conditions align:

  • data or sovereignty requires it;
  • suitable model exists;
  • traffic supports the economics;
  • latency or offline operation requires locality;
  • customisation creates material value;
  • organisation can operate the platform;
  • hardware and licence risk are acceptable.

Do not self-host only because API unit price appears high.

Compare total cost:

Hardware or Cloud Compute
+ Serving Platform
+ Capacity Headroom
+ Engineering
+ Security
+ Monitoring
+ Upgrades
+ Incidents
+ Evaluation
+ Support

Part XI — Model Gateways and Abstractions

49. Why Use a Gateway?

A gateway can centralise:

  • authentication;
  • quotas;
  • routing;
  • retries;
  • circuit breakers;
  • observability;
  • cost attribution;
  • policy;
  • model aliases;
  • version control;
  • cache;
  • provider selection.

Azure’s architecture guidance notes that gateways can move retry, circuit breaker, safe deployment, and observability responsibilities away from many clients.[12]

50. Gateway Trade-offs

Benefits:

  • central control;
  • simpler clients;
  • cross-provider governance;
  • migration point;
  • standard telemetry.

Costs:

  • additional hop;
  • central failure domain;
  • platform ownership;
  • hidden provider features;
  • lowest-common-denominator APIs;
  • routing complexity.

The gateway should solve explicit cross-cutting requirements.

It should not become an unbounded AI platform.

51. False Portability

Compatibility layers may ignore or transform:

  • instruction roles;
  • strict schema features;
  • prompt caching;
  • reasoning controls;
  • tool semantics;
  • safety options;
  • streaming events;
  • token usage;
  • error codes.

Anthropic’s OpenAI SDK compatibility guidance, for example, documents fields that are unsupported, transformed, or ignored and recommends native APIs for some guarantees.[13]

Architectural principle — Abstract the stable intent

Abstract business intent, task contracts, evidence, tools, evaluations, and telemetry. Do not assume every model-specific capability should be hidden behind one universal request object.

52. Adapter Boundaries

A useful architecture separates:

Business Task
      ↓
Canonical Task Contract
      ↓
Model Policy and Routing
      ↓
Provider Adapter
      ↓
Native Provider API

The adapter translates only what can be translated safely.

Provider-specific capabilities remain explicit where they matter.

Part XII — Reliability and Capacity

53. Failure Modes

  • model endpoint unavailable;
  • region unavailable;
  • rate limit;
  • quota exhausted;
  • overloaded deployment;
  • very high latency;
  • malformed response;
  • provider safety refusal;
  • context limit;
  • tool feature unavailable;
  • model retired;
  • routing failure.

54. Reliability Tactics

  • timeout;
  • bounded retry;
  • circuit breaker;
  • load shedding;
  • queue;
  • fallback;
  • alternate region;
  • alternate provider;
  • provisioned capacity;
  • degraded mode;
  • asynchronous processing.

AWS supports cross-region inference profiles to use capacity across approved regions for traffic bursts and availability, while Azure provides model-router and gateway patterns for approved fallback sets and routing.[14][15]

55. Retry Carefully

Retry when failure is likely transient.

Avoid uncontrolled retries when:

  • request is expensive;
  • timeout outcome is unknown;
  • tool calls may have occurred;
  • provider is overloaded;
  • fallback would be better;
  • deadline is exceeded.

Use a total request budget.

56. Capacity Modes

Possible modes:

  • pay-per-request;
  • shared on-demand;
  • provisioned throughput;
  • dedicated endpoint;
  • serverless;
  • autoscaled self-hosting;
  • batch capacity.

Select based on:

  • baseline traffic;
  • peak;
  • latency;
  • predictability;
  • cost;
  • availability;
  • commitment.

57. Admission Control

When demand exceeds capacity:

  • reject low-priority work;
  • queue batch jobs;
  • reduce output length;
  • route to smaller model;
  • disable optional reasoning;
  • preserve high-risk workflows;
  • notify users.

Do not let overload degrade every task equally.

Part XIII — Privacy, Residency, and Security

58. Data Path

Map:

User
  ↓
Gateway
  ↓
Logs and Cache
  ↓
Provider Region
  ↓
Model Service
  ↓
Tools and Evidence
  ↓
Telemetry

For each stage, record:

  • data classification;
  • encryption;
  • region;
  • retention;
  • training use;
  • operator access;
  • deletion;
  • tenant isolation.

59. Privacy-Aware Routing

Routing may be constrained by:

  • user consent;
  • data class;
  • country;
  • customer contract;
  • model provider;
  • endpoint type;
  • zero-retention requirement;
  • local deployment.

Privacy should filter eligible models before cost or quality optimisation.

60. Secrets and Tools

Do not place long-lived credentials in model-visible context.

Use:

  • scoped tool services;
  • credential broker;
  • short-lived tokens;
  • workload identity;
  • policy enforcement;
  • audit.

The inference layer proposes tool calls.

The tool layer authorises and executes.

Part XIV — Cost Architecture

61. Cost Components

Hosted API

  • input;
  • cached input;
  • output;
  • reasoning;
  • image or audio;
  • tool;
  • premium tier;
  • provisioned capacity.

Self-hosted

  • accelerator;
  • CPU and memory;
  • storage;
  • network;
  • idle headroom;
  • engineering;
  • support.

Workflow

  • retrieval;
  • reranking;
  • repeated attempts;
  • validators;
  • human review;
  • incidents.

62. Useful Cost Measures

  • cost per request;
  • cost per successful task;
  • cost per accepted action;
  • cost per active user;
  • cost per outcome;
  • cost of fallback;
  • cost of human repair;
  • idle-capacity cost.

Measure by:

  • task class;
  • model;
  • tenant;
  • route;
  • environment;
  • team.

63. Cost Controls

  • small default model;
  • classification;
  • output limits;
  • context budget;
  • cache;
  • batch;
  • route by complexity;
  • asynchronous work;
  • spend budget;
  • quota;
  • anomaly alert;
  • stop loops.

Cost controls should preserve quality gates.

Part XV — Inference Observability and SLOs

64. Request-Level Trace

Record:

  • task ID;
  • route;
  • model and version;
  • provider;
  • region;
  • configuration;
  • input and output tokens;
  • cached tokens;
  • queue;
  • time to first token;
  • decode;
  • complete latency;
  • retries;
  • fallback;
  • validation;
  • cost;
  • outcome link.

Content capture remains subject to privacy policy.

65. Inference Metrics

Reliability

  • success rate;
  • timeout;
  • rate limit;
  • fallback rate;
  • region failure;
  • invalid response.

Performance

  • queue time;
  • TTFT;
  • inter-token latency;
  • tokens per second;
  • total completion;
  • throughput.

Resource

  • GPU utilisation;
  • memory;
  • KV cache;
  • batch size;
  • cache hit;
  • eviction;
  • queue depth.

Behaviour

  • task success;
  • schema pass;
  • tool correctness;
  • escalation;
  • refusal;
  • segment performance.

Cost

  • unit cost;
  • route cost;
  • wasted retry;
  • idle capacity.

NVIDIA Triton exposes model and serving metrics, including LLM-specific cache and in-flight batching metrics, illustrating that serving internals belong in operational observability.[16]

66. Inference SLO Example

Routine support tasks:
  availability >= 99.9%
  p95 TTFT <= 1 second
  p95 complete <= 5 seconds
  task success >= 94%
  schema validity = 100%
  fallback rate <= 2%
  cost per successful task <= £0.05

A service SLO without task quality is incomplete.

A task-quality target without availability and latency is also incomplete.

67. Route-Level Monitoring

Report by route:

  • selection count;
  • pass rate;
  • escalation;
  • cost;
  • latency;
  • segment;
  • failure.

A global average can hide a poor low-cost route.

Part XVI — Model Change and Lifecycle

68. Model Changes Are Behavioural Releases

Changes include:

  • new snapshot;
  • new alias target;
  • provider migration;
  • quantisation;
  • serving engine;
  • reasoning setting;
  • context limit;
  • tool feature;
  • routing policy;
  • system prompt.

Each can change behaviour.

69. Change Classification

Low

  • infrastructure patch with no model or configuration change;
  • validated capacity increase.

Medium

  • prompt-cache configuration;
  • inference parameter within tested bounds;
  • serving optimisation with identical model.

High

  • model version;
  • provider;
  • quantisation;
  • fine-tune;
  • routing change;
  • fallback;
  • context strategy;
  • safety policy.

High changes require broad reevaluation.

70. Canary and Shadow

Shadow

Send production-like requests without affecting users or actions.

Compare:

  • output;
  • latency;
  • cost;
  • safety;
  • route.

Canary

Expose bounded eligible traffic.

Use:

  • rollback;
  • segment limits;
  • gates;
  • monitoring.

71. Model Rollback

Rollback requires:

  • previous model available;
  • previous configuration;
  • compatible provider API;
  • prompt version;
  • evaluation result;
  • routing policy;
  • cache invalidation;
  • index compatibility.

A provider may retire a model, making rollback impossible.

Design migration windows and alternate recovery.

72. Reevaluation Triggers

  • model version;
  • provider;
  • quantisation;
  • prompt hierarchy;
  • tool schema;
  • context policy;
  • safety control;
  • reasoning budget;
  • routing;
  • data region;
  • serving engine;
  • major traffic change.

Architectural principle — Approval does not transfer automatically

A model’s production approval applies to the evaluated artifact and configuration. It does not automatically transfer to a replacement, quantised version, fallback, or compatibility endpoint.

Part XVII — Worked Example: Enterprise Coding Assistant

73. Scenario

An organisation wants an assistant that:

  • explains code;
  • drafts tests;
  • fixes small defects;
  • proposes architecture changes;
  • opens pull requests.

Repositories have different risk levels.

74. Capability Profiles

Documentation

  • low risk;
  • moderate context;
  • low latency;
  • small model eligible.

Unit-test generation

  • repository tools;
  • structured patch;
  • validation required;
  • medium model.

Defect repair

  • code reasoning;
  • test execution;
  • repeated tool calls;
  • stronger model.

Architecture change

  • broad context;
  • high consequence;
  • strong reasoning;
  • mandatory human review.

75. Routing

Task Classification
      │
      ├── explain / document ─► fast code model
      ├── tests              ─► standard code model
      ├── defect repair      ─► reasoning code model
      └── architecture       ─► reasoning model + architect review

Constraints:

  • regulated repositories use approved endpoints;
  • no production deployment;
  • failed validation escalates once;
  • tool permissions remain independent of model.

76. Inference Contracts

Documentation route:

  • low reasoning;
  • short output;
  • no write tools.

Defect route:

  • deterministic patch schema;
  • bounded tool calls;
  • test tools;
  • maximum elapsed time;
  • no secret access;
  • human approval for pull request.

77. Evaluation

Measure:

  • accepted correct change;
  • tests;
  • regression;
  • prohibited access;
  • review burden;
  • latency;
  • cost per accepted change;
  • performance by language and repository risk.

The strongest model is not used universally.

The architecture allocates capability where its value exceeds its cost and risk.

Part XVIII — Architecture Review

78. Scenario

A company proposes a universal model gateway.

It:

  • exposes one OpenAI-compatible API;
  • routes every request dynamically;
  • chooses the cheapest acceptable model;
  • retries across three providers;
  • hides the selected model from applications;
  • uses a common system prompt;
  • reports only total latency and tokens.

79. ARB Findings

Finding 1 — “Acceptable” is undefined

No contextual evaluation or task-specific quality bar exists.

Finding 2 — Dynamic routing is opaque

Applications cannot reproduce or explain behaviour.

Finding 3 — Cheapest routing can violate risk

Privacy, safety, and tool support must filter eligibility before cost.

Finding 4 — Compatibility hides semantic differences

Role handling, schema, tools, caching, reasoning, and safety can differ.

Finding 5 — Retry can multiply cost and latency

No total attempt budget exists.

Finding 6 — Fallback is unevaluated

Secondary models may not preserve minimum behaviour.

Finding 7 — Observability is insufficient

Route, model version, fallback, validation, and cost per successful task are missing.

Finding 8 — Gateway blast radius is large

Failure affects every AI workload.

80. Recommended Redesign

  • explicit task classes;
  • approved model portfolio;
  • capability profiles;
  • static routing for critical paths;
  • dynamic routing only within evaluated sets;
  • privacy and policy eligibility filters;
  • versioned routing policy;
  • provider-native adapters;
  • bounded attempts;
  • safety-preserving fallback;
  • route-level trace;
  • canary;
  • per-product ownership.

Part XIX — Architecture Smells

81. Benchmark Crown

The model with the highest public score is selected without task evaluation.

82. Frontier Everywhere

The most capable and expensive model handles routine work.

83. Cheap Model Tax

A cheap model increases retries, repair, and workflow cost.

84. Router Without Policy

Dynamic selection exists without task classes, constraints, or evaluation.

85. Fallback by API Shape

A model is considered a valid fallback because its endpoint is compatible.

86. Gateway as Platform Monolith

Every AI responsibility accumulates in one proxy.

87. Context Window as Architecture

A large context window replaces evidence selection and state design.

88. Quantisation by Assumption

A compressed model inherits production approval without reevaluation.

89. Tokens per Second Theatre

Serving throughput improves while task latency or quality worsens.

90. Cache Without Identity

Shared prefixes or responses cross tenant or policy boundaries.

91. Self-Hosting by Unit Price

API cost is compared with GPU cost while engineering and reliability are ignored.

92. Model Alias Surprise

A mutable provider alias changes behaviour without a controlled release.

Part XX — Interview Preparation

93. Foundational Questions

Question 1

How do you select a model?

Start from task, quality, risk, latency, cost, privacy, and operations. Build a candidate set and evaluate the complete workflow.

Question 2

Why not use the strongest model for everything?

Cost, latency, capacity, privacy, and operational complexity. Smaller models may satisfy routine tasks, while stronger models are reserved for complexity or risk.

Question 3

What is a model router?

A policy component that selects an approved model based on task and operational conditions. It must be evaluated, versioned, and observed.

Question 4

What is the difference between escalation and fallback?

Escalation seeks more capability. Fallback preserves service after unavailability or failure. They may use similar models but serve different purposes.

Question 5

Why is a compatible API not enough for portability?

Behaviour, tools, schema guarantees, instructions, safety, context, and operational semantics differ.

94. Senior-Level Questions

Question 6

When should a smaller model be the default?

When it meets the task’s quality and risk thresholds with better cost, latency, capacity, or privacy. Validate total outcome cost.

Question 7

How do you design a safe fallback?

Choose from an evaluated set, preserve policy and residency, revalidate context and output, record degraded mode, and avoid repeating side effects.

Question 8

How would you decide between hosted and self-hosted inference?

Compare capability, data control, latency, traffic economics, hardware, licensing, platform maturity, reliability, staffing, and lifecycle burden.

Question 9

What should an inference contract contain?

Task class, model policy, configuration, context limit, output schema, tools, budgets, timeout, retry, fallback, safety, and telemetry.

Question 10

How do context length and output length affect inference?

Longer context increases prefill, memory, and cost. Longer output increases decode latency and cost. Effective context matters more than advertised limit.

Question 11

What is KV cache pressure?

Memory used to retain attention state for active sequences can limit concurrency. Efficient cache management and scheduling improve throughput.

Question 12

When is quantisation appropriate?

When memory or compute reduction creates value and the resulting artifact meets task and risk evaluations on target hardware.

95. Principal-Level Questions

Question 13

How would you design an enterprise model gateway?

Start with cross-cutting requirements: identity, routing, quotas, policy, telemetry, cost, reliability. Preserve provider-native capabilities, avoid a lowest-common-denominator API, and make the gateway highly available and product-owned.

Question 14

How do you prevent routing from becoming opaque?

Version policy, log route inputs and result, use approved sets, segment metrics, support replay, and provide static routing for critical paths.

Question 15

How do you manage model retirement?

Track lifecycle, evaluate replacements early, maintain migration windows, canary, rollback where possible, update prompts and tools, and communicate behavioural change.

Question 16

What are the main levers for inference cost?

Model size, reasoning, context, output, routing, caching, batching, quantisation, hardware, capacity mode, retries, and human repair.

Question 17

How do you define inference reliability?

Endpoint availability plus task quality, feature compatibility, routing, capacity, fallback behaviour, and degraded-mode correctness.

Question 18

What changes require reevaluation?

Any change that can alter behaviour: model, provider, quantisation, serving engine, prompt, tool, context, routing, safety, or inference configuration.

Part XXI — Whiteboard Challenge

96. Design Model and Inference Architecture for a Multi-Tenant AI Platform

The platform serves:

  • customer support;
  • document extraction;
  • coding assistance;
  • incident diagnosis;
  • executive summarisation.

Constraints

  • different data-residency requirements;
  • three cloud providers;
  • open and proprietary models;
  • bursty demand;
  • strict cost allocation;
  • high-risk tools;
  • provider retirement;
  • some offline and edge use.

Discuss

  1. Define task and capability profiles.
  2. Decide single model versus portfolio.
  3. Separate static and dynamic routing.
  4. Define privacy eligibility.
  5. Create inference contracts.
  6. Design escalation, fallback, and degraded modes.
  7. Define gateway responsibility.
  8. Select managed versus self-hosted modes.
  9. Define latency and capacity architecture.
  10. Apply caching, batching, quantisation, and speculative decoding.
  11. Define observability.
  12. Define canary and rollback.
  13. Define model retirement.
  14. Define cost per successful outcome.
  15. Identify gateway and provider failure modes.

Strong-answer characteristics

  • task-specific evaluation;
  • smallest sufficient model;
  • risk-aware routing;
  • explicit provider adapters;
  • strict tool boundary;
  • tested fallback;
  • durable task state;
  • total attempt budget;
  • route-level observability;
  • capacity modes;
  • privacy before optimisation;
  • lifecycle and reevaluation;
  • no universal model abstraction.

Part XXII — Questions to Take Back to Your Team

  1. What task classes exist?
  2. What capability does each require?
  3. Is the current model larger than necessary?
  4. Which routes are static and which are dynamic?
  5. What evidence validates the router?
  6. Does fallback preserve safety, tools, context, and residency?
  7. Is model configuration versioned?
  8. Which context is stable enough to cache?
  9. What invalidates the cache?
  10. What is the latency breakdown?
  11. What limits throughput: weights, KV cache, queue, or tools?
  12. Does quantisation pass the full evaluation?
  13. What is total cost per successful task?
  14. Why are we self-hosting?
  15. Can the gateway fail safely?
  16. Are provider-specific features being hidden?
  17. Which alias can change without our release?
  18. What is the model retirement plan?
  19. Which changes trigger reevaluation?
  20. Can we explain every route and fallback?

Architect’s Notebook — Intelligence Is a Portfolio Decision

The model-selection discussion often begins as though one model must win.

That is rarely the real decision.

An organisation may need:

  • one default;
  • a small specialist;
  • a strong escalation path;
  • a privacy-sensitive local option;
  • an alternate capacity provider;
  • a no-model degraded mode.

The architecture should allocate intelligence like any other constrained resource.

Use more capability where it changes the outcome.

Do not purchase, host, or invoke intelligence that the task cannot justify.

From the Architect’s Desk

Model choice attracts attention because model names are visible, comparable, and easy to debate. Inference architecture is less visible. It appears in queueing, context, cache, routing, memory, retries, capacity, and the uncomfortable details of what happens when the preferred model is not available.

That invisible structure determines whether an impressive model becomes a dependable product.

Do not ask only whether a replacement model is smarter. Ask whether it follows the same contracts, uses evidence correctly, preserves policy, meets latency, operates in the right region, and survives the evaluation that justified the original design.

A fallback that produces an answer is not necessarily a successful fallback. A gateway that accepts every provider is not necessarily portable. A self-hosted model is not necessarily controlled if the organisation cannot patch, observe, and recover it.

Treat model capability as a resource. Treat model behaviour as a dependency. Treat every inference configuration as a release.

If I Were the Architect

You inherit a platform that sends every request to one frontier model.

The model performs well.

But:

  • costs are growing;
  • p95 latency is high;
  • simple tasks dominate volume;
  • one region creates a capacity bottleneck;
  • compliance requires local processing for some users;
  • the provider will retire the current version in sixty days;
  • no fallback has passed evaluation.

What do you do first?

Do not immediately add a router.

  1. Classify real task distribution.
  2. define capability profiles.
  3. establish quality and risk gates.
  4. identify tasks eligible for smaller or local models.
  5. evaluate candidate routes.
  6. define inference contracts.
  7. test fallback and degraded modes.
  8. introduce route-level telemetry.
  9. plan model migration and canary.
  10. optimise cache, context, and output before adding serving complexity.

A router without task architecture moves uncertainty rather than reducing it.

Key Takeaways

  • A model is a behavioural dependency.
  • Model selection starts with task, quality, risk, latency, cost, privacy, and operations.
  • A Model Capability Profile defines the required capability before candidate selection.
  • The smallest sufficient model is a useful default, but total outcome cost matters.
  • A single model optimises simplicity; a portfolio optimises task fit and resilience at greater operational cost.
  • Static routing favours predictability; dynamic routing favours adaptability.
  • The router is a decision component and requires evaluation.
  • Escalation seeks capability; fallback preserves service.
  • Fallback must preserve minimum behaviour, not merely API availability.
  • An Inference Contract versions model configuration, context, tools, budgets, reliability, safety, and telemetry.
  • Structured output validates shape, not truth.
  • Maximum context is not effective context.
  • Inference latency includes queue, prefill, decode, tools, and validation.
  • Throughput optimisation can conflict with individual latency.
  • KV-cache management, continuous batching, and serving engines materially affect economics.
  • Prompt caching requires deliberate prefix, identity, and invalidation design.
  • Quantised models are new behavioural artifacts and require reevaluation.
  • Speculative decoding and parallelism are serving tactics, not architecture goals.
  • Hosted, managed, self-hosted, and edge inference carry different control and operating burdens.
  • Gateways centralise cross-cutting controls but can create false portability and a large failure domain.
  • Cost should be measured per successful task or outcome.
  • Model changes, fallbacks, routing changes, quantisation, and serving changes are behavioural releases.
  • Production approval does not automatically transfer to a replacement model.
