Part III - Controlled Agency

As systems gain memory, tools, and the ability to act over time, architecture must make authority, state, security, governance, privacy, and recovery explicit.

This part moves from responses to sustained action under bounded authority.

Chapter 7 - Workflow and Agent Architecture

Orchestration, state, tools, humans, and durable control

Related chapters: Chapters 2, 6, 8, 10, and 13

Use deterministic workflow for what the system already knows how to control. Use agentic reasoning only where the next useful step genuinely depends on evidence discovered at runtime.

1. Why This Chapter Matters

The word agent is now applied to systems with very different behaviour.

An “agent” may be:

  • a model that calls one search tool;
  • a fixed chain of prompts;
  • a workflow with a few dynamic branches;
  • a long-running software-development process;
  • a customer-service assistant with delegated actions;
  • a group of specialised agents that exchange tasks;
  • an autonomous service that monitors signals and changes production state.

This ambiguity creates architecture problems.

Teams adopt an agent framework before deciding:

  • whether the task is actually dynamic;
  • which steps must remain deterministic;
  • where state lives;
  • how failures are recovered;
  • how tool actions are authorised;
  • how loops stop;
  • how human intervention works;
  • whether one agent is sufficient;
  • whether multiple agents create value greater than their coordination cost.

Anthropic distinguishes workflows, in which models and tools follow predefined code paths, from agents, in which models dynamically direct their own process and tool use. Its production guidance recommends starting with the simplest solution and increasing complexity only when the task requires it.[1]

OpenAI similarly describes agents as systems that combine models, tools, instructions, guardrails, and orchestration to accomplish work, while advising teams to maximise a single agent before introducing multi-agent complexity.[2]

Current cloud architecture guidance treats agent systems as a continuum: deterministic chains, single agents making bounded decisions, and multi-agent systems with specialised coordination. More autonomy creates more state, handoff, observability, reliability, and governance obligations.[3][4]

The central argument of this chapter is:

An agent is not the architecture. The architecture is the control system around the model loop: task framing, workflow, state, tools, policy, durability, human authority, observation, and recovery.

2. Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish deterministic workflow, agentic workflow, and autonomous agent;
  • decide when an agent is unnecessary;
  • design a deterministic workflow skeleton around probabilistic decision points;
  • define an agent run contract with objective, scope, budgets, state, tools, and stop conditions;
  • separate conversational context from durable workflow state;
  • model an agent as explicit state transitions rather than an endless chat;
  • select sequential, routing, parallel, evaluator, handoff, orchestrator-worker, and multi-agent patterns;
  • determine when multiple agents are justified;
  • design tool contracts, authority checks, retries, and side-effect boundaries;
  • implement checkpoints, durable waits, replay, and recovery;
  • prevent duplicate effects when interrupted or resumed;
  • design meaningful human approval and intervention;
  • bound loops by steps, time, cost, and progress;
  • create dead-letter and manual-recovery states;
  • observe trajectory, state, actions, and outcomes;
  • evaluate long-running and multi-agent systems;
  • answer architecture interview questions about orchestration, state, checkpointing, human-in-the-loop, concurrency, and agent reliability.

Part I — Workflow Before Agent

3. Start with the Work

Before selecting an agent framework, map the work.

Ask:

  • What is the objective?
  • Which steps are known?
  • Which decisions are conditional?
  • Which information becomes available only at runtime?
  • Which actions change state?
  • Which steps require authority?
  • Which failures can be retried?
  • Which steps may wait for hours or days?
  • Which parts can run concurrently?
  • What proves completion?

A workflow may already be sufficient.

Example:

Receive Invoice
      ↓
Validate Supplier
      ↓
Extract Fields
      ↓
Check Duplicate
      ↓
Apply Approval Rules
      ↓
Route or Post

AI may improve field extraction. That does not require the entire process to become agent-directed.

Architectural principle — Agentic only where necessary

Place probabilistic control only at decision points whose useful next step cannot be defined reliably in advance.

This keeps policy, authority, irreversible state changes, financial limits, audit, retry, and completion inside explicit workflow control.

4. Three Control Modes

Deterministic workflow

The sequence and branches are defined in code or configuration.

A → B → C
      ├── condition X → D
      └── condition Y → E

Use when:

  • process is known;
  • auditability matters;
  • variation is bounded;
  • exact policy applies;
  • predictable latency and cost matter.

Agentic workflow

The workflow skeleton is explicit, but a model chooses within bounded decision points.

Validate Task
     ↓
Agent Chooses Diagnostic Tool
     ↓
Deterministic Validation
     ↓
Approval if Required
     ↓
Controlled Execution

Use when interpretation is dynamic, tools vary by evidence, planning is useful, and actions remain bounded.

Autonomous agent

The model can plan, choose tools, revise its approach, and continue until completion or a stop condition.

Use when the task path cannot be enumerated economically, environment feedback matters, experimentation or search is required, and controls and recovery justify the autonomy.

The categories are a continuum, not rigid product labels.

5. The Deterministic Workflow Skeleton

This handbook introduces the Deterministic Workflow Skeleton:

Objective and Task Contract
          ↓
Deterministic Preconditions
          ↓
Probabilistic Decision Point
          ↓
Tool or Evidence Acquisition
          ↓
Deterministic Validation and Policy
          ↓
Durable State Transition
          ↓
Human Authority if Required
          ↓
Controlled Action
          ↓
Outcome Observation

The skeleton provides the stable rails. The model supplies judgment only where variation creates value.

Benefits include easier evaluation, bounded failure, explicit state, clear ownership, meaningful approval, recoverable execution, lower cost, and simpler observability.

Over-constraining every step can remove the flexibility that justified an agent. The design goal is not maximum determinism. It is deliberate allocation of control.

Part II — The Agent Loop

6. A Minimal Agent Loop

A basic agent loop is:

Observe
   ↓
Decide
   ↓
Act
   ↓
Observe Result
   ↓
Continue or Stop

OpenAI’s technical description of the Codex loop shows a model receiving instructions and tool definitions, producing either tool calls or a final assistant message that terminates the loop.[5]

The loop appears simple. Production behaviour depends on the harness around it.

7. The Harness

An agent harness is the software system that enables the model to act.

It typically handles:

  • initial instructions;
  • context construction;
  • model calls;
  • tool exposure;
  • tool execution;
  • state;
  • budgets;
  • validation;
  • retries;
  • interruption;
  • tracing;
  • completion.

Anthropic describes long-running managed agents using separable concepts such as a session or append-only record of activity, a harness that invokes the model and routes tools, and a sandbox where actions occur.[6]

This separation is architecturally useful:

  • the model is the decision component;
  • the harness is the control component;
  • the sandbox or tool environment is the action boundary.

8. The Agent Run Contract

This handbook introduces the Agent Run Contract.

run_id: incident_7432_agent_run_1
objective: identify cause and propose safe remediation
requesting_principal: incident_commander_482
subject: checkout-api-production
scope:
  allowed:
    - inspect_telemetry
    - inspect_deployment
    - propose_remediation
  prohibited:
    - database_write
    - execute_production_change
state:
  checkpoint_policy: after_each_tool
  expiry: 2026-08-06T18:00:00Z
tools:
  allowed:
    - metrics_query
    - logs_query
    - deployment_read
budgets:
  model_calls: 12
  tool_calls: 20
  elapsed_minutes: 15
  cost_gbp: 1.50
stop_conditions:
  - supported_remediation_proposed
  - insufficient_evidence
  - approval_required
  - budget_exhausted
  - unrecoverable_tool_failure

The contract should also define model and inference policy, evidence requirement, risk class, human intervention, output, outcome measure, and retention.

The run contract gives the loop a boundary.

9. Termination Is a Design Responsibility

An agent should not stop merely because the model emits final prose.

Completion must be checked against:

  • task success;
  • required artifacts;
  • state;
  • validation;
  • evidence;
  • policy;
  • outcome;
  • budget.

Possible termination states:

  • completed;
  • completed with limitations;
  • insufficient evidence;
  • human input required;
  • approval required;
  • budget exhausted;
  • cancelled;
  • failed;
  • expired.

Architecture smell — Polite completion

The agent declares success in natural language even though the required state or outcome was not achieved.

Part III — State Architecture

10. Conversation Is Not Workflow State

Conversation history may contain user messages, model responses, tool results, and summaries.

It should not be the only record of task status, approval, action, retry, evidence, ownership, or completion.

A consequential workflow needs explicit durable state.

11. State Categories

Task state

  • objective;
  • scope;
  • current stage;
  • owner;
  • deadline;
  • completion criteria.

Evidence state

  • sources;
  • freshness;
  • conflicts;
  • insufficiency;
  • provenance.

Decision state

  • proposal;
  • validation;
  • policy;
  • confidence;
  • approval.

Action state

  • requested;
  • authorised;
  • executing;
  • succeeded;
  • uncertain;
  • compensated.

Conversation state

  • interaction history;
  • user clarification;
  • preferences;
  • explanations.

Operational state

  • attempts;
  • budgets;
  • checkpoint;
  • error;
  • lease;
  • worker.

These categories can share storage. They should remain conceptually distinct.

12. The Agent State Envelope

An Agent State Envelope records the durable state required to resume and audit a run.

run_id: run_7432
task:
  status: awaiting_approval
  objective: restore checkout
evidence:
  current:
    - telemetry_937
    - deployment_482
decision:
  proposed_action: rollback_4_8_2
  validation: passed
authority:
  required: incident_commander
  approval_status: pending
action:
  status: not_started
execution:
  checkpoint: propose_remediation
  attempts: 1
  budgets_remaining:
    model_calls: 5
    tool_calls: 9
trace_id: trace_abc

This is an original handbook synthesis, not a universal standard. It provides a design checklist.

13. Store Raw State, Render Context

Durable state should preserve structured facts.

Context can be rendered from those facts for each model call.

Prefer:

{
  "deployment_version": "4.8.2",
  "error_rate": 0.17,
  "approval_status": "pending"
}

over storing only:

“The latest deployment may be causing elevated errors, and approval is pending.”

Structured state is easier to validate, update, query, migrate, audit, and render differently.

LangGraph’s architecture guidance similarly recommends storing raw data in state and formatting prompts at execution time.[7]

14. State Ownership

For each state item, define:

  • authoritative writer;
  • permitted readers;
  • version;
  • conflict rule;
  • retention;
  • expiry;
  • audit.

The model may propose a state change. The workflow should apply it through validated transitions.

15. State Machines

A state machine makes control explicit.

Requested
   ↓
Planning
   ↓
Gathering Evidence
   ↓
Proposing
   ↓
Validating
   ↓
Awaiting Approval
   ↓
Executing
   ↓
Observing
   ↓
Completed

Exceptional states:

  • insufficient evidence;
  • rejected;
  • expired;
  • cancelled;
  • failed;
  • compensating;
  • dead letter.

Transitions should have guards.

Awaiting Approval → Executing
only if:
  approval is valid
  evidence is current
  policy still permits
  action has not already run

Part IV — Workflow Patterns

16. Prompt Chaining

A task is split into a known sequence.

Extract
   ↓
Classify
   ↓
Draft
   ↓
Validate

Use when steps are stable, each stage has a clear contract, and intermediate validation improves quality.

Risks include cumulative latency, error propagation, repeated context, and over-fragmentation.

17. Routing

A classifier or model sends work to a specialised path.

Request
  ├── Billing
  ├── Technical
  └── Account

Use when categories have different prompts, tools, policies, models, or owners.

Evaluate the router and fallback.

18. Parallelisation

Independent tasks run concurrently.

             ┌─► Security Review
Input ───────┼─► Cost Review
             └─► Reliability Review
                   ↓
                Synthesis

Use when subtasks do not depend on one another, can be merged, benefit from separate perspectives, and justify concurrency cost.

Avoid when tasks require cumulative context or strict ordering.

19. Orchestrator–Worker

A controller decomposes work and delegates to workers.

Objective
   ↓
Orchestrator
   ├── Worker A
   ├── Worker B
   └── Worker C
          ↓
       Synthesis

Use when subtask count is not known in advance, parallel research or inspection is useful, and workers have bounded roles.

Anthropic uses orchestrator-worker as a distinct workflow pattern for tasks whose subproblems are dynamic.[1]

Risks include poor decomposition, duplicated work, context loss, expensive fan-out, and weak synthesis.

20. Evaluator–Optimizer

One component generates. Another evaluates and returns feedback.

Generate
   ↓
Evaluate
   ├── pass → complete
   └── revise → Generate

Use when quality criteria are explicit and iterative improvement adds value. Run deterministic checks first.

Bound iteration count, cost, evaluator confidence, and improvement threshold.

Avoid endless self-critique.

21. Handoff

One agent transfers responsibility to another.

The handoff should carry:

  • task;
  • reason;
  • evidence;
  • state;
  • authority;
  • completed work;
  • unresolved questions;
  • budgets;
  • expected response.

A handoff is not simply “Agent B, take over.” It is a contract.

22. Group Collaboration

Multiple agents exchange messages or proposals.

Patterns include group chat, debate, voting, shared board, and manager-led discussion.

Use cautiously.

Risks include long transcripts, duplicated reasoning, social convergence, unclear authority, difficult attribution, and high cost.

Azure’s agent-design guidance catalogues sequential, concurrent, handoff, group-chat, and dynamic manager patterns, each with distinct coordination and human-in-the-loop characteristics.[3]

Part V — Single Agent or Multiple Agents?

23. Prefer One Agent When Possible

A single agent with clear tools is easier to evaluate, trace, secure, operate, tune, and recover.

OpenAI recommends maximising the capabilities of a single agent before moving to multi-agent designs because additional agents introduce new coordination and evaluation complexity.[2]

24. When Multiple Agents Are Justified

Multi-agent architecture may be justified by:

Independent parallel work

Subtasks can be executed simultaneously.

Context isolation

Different domains require separate bounded context.

Specialised tools or authority

Agents need distinct permissions or operating environments.

Independent review

A separate role provides valuable challenge.

Scale

A coordinator distributes work across many tasks.

Organisational boundaries

Different teams own different domains or policies.

25. Weak Reasons for Multiple Agents

  • the framework supports it;
  • prompts are getting long;
  • agent names make the demo intuitive;
  • “collaboration” sounds intelligent;
  • one model is assigned several personas;
  • a deterministic step is presented as an agent.

Many named agents can still be one model producing a longer conversation.

26. Multi-Agent Costs

  • additional model calls;
  • handoff errors;
  • conflicting state;
  • duplicated tools;
  • coordination latency;
  • distributed failure;
  • trace complexity;
  • security boundaries;
  • evaluation combinations.

AWS’s Agentic AI Lens notes that multi-agent systems introduce coordination overhead, handoff complexity, and distributed failure modes and therefore require controlled orchestration and defined fallback chains.[4][8]

27. The Multi-Agent Justification Test

Before adding an agent, answer:

  1. What independent responsibility does it own?
  2. What state does it own?
  3. What tools or authority differ?
  4. Why can a function or workflow node not do this?
  5. How is handoff validated?
  6. What happens if it fails?
  7. How is its contribution evaluated?
  8. Does the improvement justify the cost?

If the answers are weak, use a workflow node.

Part VI — Tool Architecture

28. Tools Are Contracts

A tool should define purpose, input schema, output schema, preconditions, permissions, idempotency, side effects, errors, timeout, retry, audit, and version.

Weak tool:

execute_command(command)

Stronger tool:

restart_service(
  service_id,
  environment,
  approval_id,
  idempotency_key
)

Tool design constrains the agent’s action space.

29. Tool Descriptions Are Behavioural Interfaces

The model uses descriptions to decide when to call, which parameters to provide, and what to expect.

Descriptions should state intended use, exclusions, required evidence, side effects, and error meaning.

Anthropic’s tool-design guidance recommends monitoring real tool-call patterns and designing tools around the workflows agents actually perform.[9]

30. Separate Proposal from Execution

Agent proposes tool call
        ↓
Schema validation
        ↓
Policy and authority
        ↓
Idempotency check
        ↓
Execution
        ↓
Result recorded

The model should not possess raw credentials or bypass the tool service.

31. Tool Result Integrity

Tool results should include tool version, source, timestamp, status, data, pagination, freshness, error, and correlation ID.

The agent should not infer success from an ambiguous response.

32. Tool Failure Policy

Retryable

  • transient timeout;
  • rate limit;
  • temporary unavailability.

Repairable

  • invalid parameter;
  • missing field;
  • stale version.

Escalating

  • permission denied;
  • policy conflict;
  • unknown target.

Terminal

  • prohibited action;
  • expired task;
  • unsupported operation.

The workflow, not the model alone, should map errors to recovery.

Part VII — Durable Execution

33. Why Durability Matters

Agent runs may last seconds, hours, days, or weeks.

They may wait for human approval, an external system, scheduled time, data arrival, rate-limit reset, or another team.

A process should not need to remain alive while waiting.

Microsoft’s Durable Task guidance for agents describes long-running sessions, human-in-the-loop waits, checkpointing, and recovery across crashes and scaling events.[10][11]

34. Checkpoints

A checkpoint records state after a meaningful boundary.

Examples:

  • after evidence retrieval;
  • after tool result;
  • before approval;
  • after execution;
  • before long wait.

A checkpoint enables resume, recovery, audit, replay, debugging, and human inspection.

LangGraph persistence saves graph state as checkpoints and supports human-in-the-loop, replay, memory, and fault recovery.[12]

35. Replay Is Re-Execution

A durable workflow may reconstruct execution by replaying deterministic workflow logic.

Workflow code that is replayed must not perform uncontrolled side effects.

External effects should be isolated in activities or tools whose results are recorded.

Temporal describes durable execution as resuming application state after failures, potentially after long periods.[13]

Framework semantics differ. The architectural concern is constant:

  • know what re-executes;
  • know what is recorded;
  • isolate side effects;
  • use idempotency.

36. Interrupt and Resume

A workflow may interrupt for approval, correction, missing evidence, user choice, or policy exception.

The interrupt should persist state, pending action, evidence, expiry, reviewer role, and allowed decisions.

LangGraph’s interrupt mechanism saves state and waits until execution is resumed. Its documentation warns that side effects before an interrupt must be idempotent because the node may re-execute on resume.[14]

37. Idempotency

An idempotent action produces no additional unintended effect when repeated with the same key.

Use for ticket creation, payment request, deployment, email scheduling, and record update.

A checkpoint does not prevent duplicate external effects by itself. The action service must participate.

38. Compensation

Some actions cannot be rolled back exactly.

Define compensation, manual repair, notification, residual harm, and owner.

Create Case
   ↓
Notify Customer
   ↓
Reserve Refund
   ↓
Failure
   ↓
Cancel Reservation
   ↓
Send Correction

The model can propose compensation. The workflow should own it.

39. Dead-Letter State

A run should enter a dead-letter or manual-recovery state when retry budget is exhausted, state is inconsistent, tool outcome is unknown, compensation fails, schema cannot migrate, approval expires repeatedly, or no safe continuation exists.

Record the last checkpoint, error, completed effects, pending effects, recovery instructions, and owner.

Architecture smell — Infinite resilience

The workflow retries indefinitely instead of admitting that automated recovery has failed.

Part VIII — Human Intervention

40. Human-in-the-Loop Has Several Meanings

A human may provide missing information, approve an action, edit a proposal, reject, select an option, take over, audit later, or change policy.

These are different control mechanisms.

41. Approval

An approval request should present task, proposed action, subject, evidence, risk, reversibility, alternatives, expiry, prior actions, and expected outcome.

The reviewer needs authority and time.

AWS recommends tiered oversight based on impact and reversibility and warns against routing every action to human review because of fatigue and rubber-stamping.[15]

42. Edit and Resume

The reviewer may modify tool arguments, scope, evidence, plan, or output.

The workflow should preserve original proposal, edit, reviewer, reason, and resumed state.

43. Takeover

For high uncertainty or failure, a human may become the active controller.

The handoff should include full durable state, action ledger, evidence, unresolved issue, and suggested next steps.

The system should not continue acting concurrently unless explicitly designed.

44. Approval Expiry

Approval may become invalid when evidence changes, target state changes, time expires, policy changes, or a different action is proposed.

Revalidate immediately before execution.

Part IX — Loops, Budgets, and Progress

45. Why Agents Loop

An agent may loop because a tool failed, evidence is insufficient, the plan is weak, the environment changed, an evaluator requests revision, or the goal is not met.

Loops create adaptability. They also create unbounded cost and risk.

46. Budget Dimensions

Bound:

  • model calls;
  • tool calls;
  • elapsed time;
  • token use;
  • cost;
  • retries;
  • parallel workers;
  • context growth;
  • approval waits;
  • generated artifacts.

Budgets should vary by task and risk.

47. Progress Detection

An agent is not progressing merely because it is producing messages.

Progress signals include new evidence, completed subtask, reduced uncertainty, valid artifact, state transition, failed hypothesis eliminated, or outcome improved.

Track repeated tool calls, queries, errors, plans, and states.

48. Loop Policies

Continue

New evidence or meaningful progress.

Repair

Correct parameters or context.

Replan

Current approach is invalid.

Escalate

Task exceeds capability or authority.

Stop

Objective met, unsafe, expired, or budget exhausted.

Architectural principle — Every loop needs a stopping rule

Agentic persistence is useful only while each iteration can create meaningful new information or progress.

Part X — Long-Running Work

49. Context Windows Are Not Project Memory

Long-running work cannot depend on one ever-growing conversation.

Use external artifacts:

  • task plan;
  • progress file;
  • decision log;
  • repository;
  • issue tracker;
  • test results;
  • state database;
  • summaries;
  • checkpoints.

Anthropic’s long-running-agent work uses explicit progress artifacts and incremental state across context windows rather than expecting a model to retain the entire project mentally.[16]

50. Session, Workspace, and State

Session

Chronological record of interaction and actions.

Workspace

Files, code, documents, or sandbox state.

Workflow state

Structured progress, ownership, and control.

Memory

Selected information intended to influence future reasoning.

Do not treat them as interchangeable.

51. Context Compaction

When context grows:

  • summarise completed work;
  • preserve unresolved decisions;
  • retain evidence references;
  • remove obsolete detail;
  • keep tool and policy instructions;
  • maintain structured task state.

Validate compaction. A summary can lose constraints or invent completion.

52. Incremental Deliverables

Long runs should produce reviewable artifacts such as plans, partial results, tests, diffs, evidence sets, and decision records.

This reduces risk and supports recovery.

Part XI — Concurrency and Coordination

53. Parallel Work

Parallel workers can reduce latency when subtasks are independent.

Control worker count, scope, evidence access, tool permissions, deadlines, and merge.

54. Shared State Risks

Concurrent agents may overwrite, duplicate, read stale state, produce conflicting actions, or exceed budgets.

Use ownership, optimistic concurrency, locks, compare-and-set, event logs, partitioned work, and merge rules.

Do not ask the model to resolve every race condition conversationally.

55. Work Allocation

Possible patterns:

  • fixed partition;
  • queue;
  • capability-based routing;
  • auction;
  • manager assignment.

Prefer simple deterministic allocation when possible.

56. Synthesis

Synthesis should deduplicate, resolve conflicts, preserve dissent, track source, and validate completion.

A manager agent may synthesise. The workflow should enforce output and evidence requirements.

Part XII — Memory Boundaries

57. Short-Term Context

Information needed for the current reasoning step. It should be task-scoped.

58. Working Memory

Structured scratch state for the current run: hypotheses, plan, completed steps, and pending questions.

Working memory is not necessarily trusted evidence.

59. Long-Term Memory

Information retained across runs: preferences, prior outcomes, user-approved facts, and recurring procedures.

It needs provenance, consent, expiry, update, deletion, and conflict policy.

60. Organisational Memory

Durable assets such as runbooks, evaluation failures, incident lessons, policies, decision records, and tool contracts.

This is usually more valuable than unconstrained model-generated memory.

61. Memory Write Policy

The agent should not persist every inference.

Define eligible fact, authority, approval, scope, retention, confidence, source, and correction.

Architecture smell — Memory as truth

A model-generated summary is persisted and later treated as authoritative evidence.

Part XIII — Observability and Evaluation

62. What to Trace

  • run ID;
  • objective;
  • state transitions;
  • model calls;
  • tool calls;
  • evidence;
  • decisions;
  • validation;
  • approval;
  • retries;
  • checkpoints;
  • handoffs;
  • cost;
  • latency;
  • outcome.

AWS recommends distributed tracing and decision-artifact storage because agent actions across tools and services are otherwise difficult to reconstruct.[17]

63. Agent Metrics

Completion

  • task success;
  • incomplete runs;
  • time to outcome.

Trajectory

  • steps;
  • tool calls;
  • retries;
  • replans;
  • loops;
  • prohibited actions.

State

  • checkpoint age;
  • stuck states;
  • dead letters;
  • approval wait.

Human

  • approval;
  • rejection;
  • edit;
  • takeover;
  • review latency.

Cost

  • per run;
  • per success;
  • fan-out;
  • wasted retries.

64. Evaluate Outcome and Trajectory

Evaluate final state, path, permissions, actions, cost, recovery, repeated trials, and outcomes.

A correct outcome through an unsafe path is not acceptable.

A reasonable path with failed infrastructure may be recoverable.

65. Multi-Agent Evaluation

Test individual agents, handoffs, coordinator, state consistency, failure isolation, synthesis, fallback, and concurrency.

Do not rely only on end-to-end success.

66. Chaos and Failure Injection

Inject tool timeout, model refusal, checkpoint failure, duplicate event, stale state, worker crash, reviewer delay, coordinator failure, and conflicting evidence.

Observe recovery.

Part XIV — Worked Example: Insurance Claim Investigation

67. Scenario

An insurer wants an AI system to investigate a complex property claim.

The system may read documents, identify missing evidence, request external data, compare policy, flag fraud indicators, draft recommendation, and route to an adjuster.

It cannot approve or reject the claim autonomously.

68. Workflow Skeleton

Receive Claim
     ↓
Deterministic Eligibility Check
     ↓
Agent Plans Evidence Review
     ↓
Parallel Document and External Checks
     ↓
Evidence Qualification
     ↓
Agent Drafts Findings
     ↓
Deterministic Policy Validation
     ↓
Human Adjuster Review
     ↓
Decision Recorded

69. Agent Run Contract

  • objective: complete investigation pack;
  • scope: claim documents and approved sources;
  • prohibited: claim decision and customer payment;
  • tool calls: bounded;
  • active time: two hours;
  • elapsed time: five days;
  • checkpoints: after each evidence group;
  • stop: complete pack, conflict, missing evidence, budget, or escalation.

70. State

  • claim facts;
  • evidence requests;
  • received documents;
  • policy version;
  • fraud flags;
  • unresolved conflicts;
  • reviewer status;
  • action log.

Conversation is a presentation. State is durable and structured.

71. Parallel Workers

Possible workers:

  • document extraction;
  • weather verification;
  • repair-cost review;
  • policy coverage.

Each has bounded evidence, no decision authority, structured output, and a deadline.

A deterministic coordinator tracks completion.

72. Human Review

The adjuster sees claim summary, evidence, conflicts, missing information, model recommendations, policy checks, and provenance.

The reviewer can accept findings, request more evidence, edit, reject, or take over.

73. Recovery

If the external weather tool fails:

  • retry with bounded policy;
  • use alternate approved source;
  • checkpoint other completed work;
  • mark evidence incomplete;
  • do not fabricate;
  • escalate before recommendation.

74. Evaluation

Measure investigation completeness, evidence validity, policy correctness, missed escalation, prohibited decision, adjuster correction, time, cost, and repeated-run stability.

Part XV — Architecture Review

75. Scenario

A company proposes a multi-agent procurement system.

It contains planning, supplier, negotiation, compliance, finance, manager, and critic agents.

All agents use the same model, share one conversation, access the same tools, write to shared memory, retry freely, and send purchase orders after manager-agent approval.

76. ARB Findings

Finding 1 — Roles are theatrical

Agents do not have distinct authority, state, or capabilities.

Finding 2 — Shared conversation is the state store

Approval, action, and evidence are not durable.

Finding 3 — Manager approval is probabilistic

A model approves other model outputs.

Finding 4 — Tool access is excessive

Every agent can use every tool.

Finding 5 — Shared memory is ungoverned

Generated summaries become truth.

Finding 6 — Retries can duplicate orders

No idempotency or action ledger exists.

Finding 7 — Loops are unbounded

No cost, time, or progress stop exists.

Finding 8 — Human authority is unclear

The procurement owner appears only after model approval.

77. Recommended Redesign

  • deterministic procurement workflow;
  • one agent for ambiguous supplier research;
  • one independent compliance service;
  • authoritative finance and sanctions tools;
  • durable state;
  • evidence packet;
  • human approval before purchase order;
  • narrow idempotent action;
  • bounded retries;
  • explicit dead-letter state;
  • outcome monitoring.

Multi-agent design may be reintroduced only if independent parallel research demonstrably justifies it.

Part XVI — Architecture Smells

78. Agent by Renaming

A function or prompt step is called an agent without independent control.

79. Workflow Avoidance

A known business process is delegated to a model because explicit states feel less fashionable.

80. Chat as Database

Conversation history is the authoritative record of state, approval, and action.

81. Multi-Agent Theatre

Several personas share the same model, tools, state, and authority.

82. Infinite Loop with a Budget Dashboard

The system reports cost but has no enforced stop.

83. Approval After Action

The agent acts and then asks a human to confirm.

84. Retry Equals Recovery

The workflow repeats the same failing action without changing state or strategy.

85. Memory Without Provenance

Generated summaries are persisted as facts.

86. Checkpoint Without Idempotency

State can resume, but external effects can repeat.

87. Agent Owns Policy

The same probabilistic component plans, approves, executes, and audits.

88. Handoff by Prose

Agents exchange natural-language summaries without structured state, responsibility, or acceptance.

89. Parallelism Without Independence

Tasks run concurrently despite shared ordering or state dependencies.

Part XVII — Interview Preparation

90. Foundational Questions

Question 1

What is the difference between a workflow and an agent?

A workflow follows predefined control paths. An agent dynamically decides its next steps and tools within constraints.

Question 2

When should you not use an agent?

When the process is known, rules are explicit, exact control is required, or a deterministic workflow provides the needed value.

Question 3

Where should agent state live?

Consequential task, evidence, decision, authority, and action state should be durable and structured outside the conversation.

Question 4

What is an agent harness?

The control software around the model that builds context, invokes models, routes tools, stores state, enforces budgets, interrupts, and traces.

Question 5

How do you stop an agent loop?

Explicit success, insufficiency, approval, failure, expiry, and enforced budgets for calls, tools, time, cost, and progress.

91. Senior-Level Questions

Question 6

How do you make a long-running agent recoverable?

Durable state, checkpoints, idempotent tools, recorded results, replay-safe workflow code, compensation, expiry, and dead-letter recovery.

Question 7

What happens when a workflow resumes after human approval?

Load the checkpoint, validate approval and current evidence, prevent duplicate effects, and continue through an explicit transition.

Question 8

When is multi-agent architecture justified?

Independent parallel work, context isolation, specialised authority or tools, independent review, scale, or organisational ownership.

Question 9

How do you design a handoff?

Transfer task, state, evidence, authority, completed work, unresolved questions, budgets, and acceptance criteria.

Question 10

How do you evaluate an agent?

Test final state and trajectory, tools, permissions, policy, cost, latency, recovery, repeated trials, and outcomes.

Question 11

Why are checkpoints insufficient for exactly-once actions?

A state checkpoint does not guarantee an external side effect did not already occur. The action service needs idempotency or reconciliation.

Question 12

How do you design human-in-the-loop?

Define intervention type, evidence, authority, expiry, edit/reject paths, resumption, audit, and escalation.

92. Principal-Level Questions

Question 13

How would you define an enterprise agent runtime?

Provide task contracts, identity, state, checkpoints, tool registry, policy, budgets, approval, telemetry, evaluation, isolation, and recovery—without centralising domain decisions.

Question 14

What should be deterministic in an agent architecture?

Authentication, authority, hard policy, limits, state transitions, idempotency, audit, and irreversible actions. Models interpret and propose.

Question 15

How do you prevent a multi-agent system from becoming a distributed monolith?

Bound responsibilities, state ownership, tool access, handoff contracts, failure isolation, versioning, and independent evaluation.

Question 16

How do you handle concurrent agents updating shared state?

Partition ownership, optimistic concurrency, locks or compare-and-set, event logs, and deterministic merge policies.

Question 17

What is the relationship between memory and state?

State controls the workflow. Memory influences reasoning. Memory is not automatically authoritative or durable.

Question 18

How do you design for agent cancellation?

Persist cancellation intent, stop new work, revoke authority, handle in-flight tools, compensate where needed, and reach an auditable terminal state.

Part XVIII — Whiteboard Challenge

93. Design a Long-Running Software-Migration Agent

The system must inspect several repositories, create a migration plan, modify code, run tests, open pull requests, respond to review, coordinate human approvals, and operate over several days.

Constraints:

  • different repository owners;
  • regulated services;
  • unreliable tests;
  • tool outages;
  • model context limits;
  • no production deployment;
  • cost and time budgets.

Discuss:

  1. Define workflow and agentic decision points.
  2. Create the run contract.
  3. Define durable state.
  4. Define workspace and session.
  5. Select orchestration patterns.
  6. Decide single versus multiple agents.
  7. Define tool contracts and permissions.
  8. Define checkpoints and replay.
  9. Prevent duplicate effects.
  10. Design approval and takeover.
  11. Handle context compaction.
  12. Define progress artifacts.
  13. Define loops and stop conditions.
  14. Define dead-letter recovery.
  15. Evaluate outcome and trajectory.
  16. Observe cost, state, and outcome.

Strong answers include workflow before agent, explicit repository ownership, deterministic branch and approval logic, durable task and action state, idempotent pull-request actions, bounded sandbox, no production tools, progress files, tests and policy as deterministic validators, human review, cancellation, repeated-trial evaluation, and incident recovery.

Part XIX — Questions to Take Back to Your Team

  1. Which steps are genuinely dynamic?
  2. Which steps should be deterministic?
  3. Is the agent loop bounded?
  4. What proves completion?
  5. Where does durable state live?
  6. Are approval and action recorded outside chat?
  7. What re-executes after resume?
  8. Are side effects idempotent?
  9. What is the dead-letter state?
  10. When does a human take over?
  11. What makes each agent independent?
  12. Who owns shared state?
  13. Are handoffs structured?
  14. How are conflicts merged?
  15. Which memory is authoritative?
  16. How does the agent show progress?
  17. How is a run cancelled?
  18. What happens when the coordinator fails?
  19. Are trajectory and outcome evaluated?
  20. What complexity would disappear if one agent were removed?

Architect’s Notebook — The Agent Is the Variable Part

The model loop is the variable part of the system.

Everything around it should reduce ambiguity:

  • the task;
  • tools;
  • permissions;
  • state;
  • budgets;
  • transitions;
  • approval;
  • recovery;
  • outcome.

This does not weaken the agent. It gives the agent a useful environment in which its flexibility can create value without becoming the only control mechanism.

From the Architect’s Desk

The most convincing agent demonstrations often make the architecture disappear. A request is entered, the model thinks, tools move, and the result arrives. That seamlessness is a product achievement. It is not permission to leave the control system implicit.

Long-running work will cross process restarts, model changes, tool failures, human delay, and partial completion. A conversation transcript cannot carry all of those responsibilities.

Put durable truth in state. Put authority in policy and identity. Put side effects behind narrow tools. Put flexibility in the agent loop.

Use multiple agents when responsibilities are independently valuable—not when a diagram needs more boxes.

The goal is not to build the most autonomous system. It is to build the least complicated control system capable of completing the work safely, reliably, and with evidence.

If I Were the Architect

You inherit an agent that resolves support tickets.

It works well for simple cases.

The product team now wants it to update accounts, issue credits, contact external suppliers, continue over several days, and coordinate specialised agents.

The current implementation stores only conversation history and tool logs.

What do you do first?

Do not add more agents.

  1. Define task classes and authority.
  2. Design the deterministic workflow skeleton.
  3. Create durable task, evidence, decision, and action state.
  4. Define the Agent Run Contract.
  5. Make tools narrow and idempotent.
  6. Add checkpoints and expiry.
  7. Define approval, takeover, and cancellation.
  8. Define loop and cost budgets.
  9. Create dead-letter recovery.
  10. Evaluate the single-agent system under the new workflow.

Only then decide whether specialised agents create independent value.

Key Takeaways

  • Workflow architecture should precede agent selection.
  • Deterministic workflow controls known process; agentic reasoning handles runtime uncertainty.
  • The Deterministic Workflow Skeleton places probabilistic decisions inside explicit preconditions, validation, state, authority, action, and outcome.
  • An agent loop requires a harness.
  • The Agent Run Contract bounds objective, scope, state, tools, budgets, and termination.
  • Natural-language completion is not proof of task completion.
  • Conversation is not durable workflow state.
  • Task, evidence, decision, action, conversation, and operational state should be distinguished.
  • Store structured raw state and render model context from it.
  • Prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-worker, evaluator-optimizer, handoff, and collaboration serve different needs.
  • Prefer one agent until multiple agents have independently justified responsibilities.
  • Tool design constrains the action space.
  • Proposal, authority, and execution should remain separate.
  • Durable execution requires checkpoints, replay awareness, idempotency, compensation, and dead-letter recovery.
  • Human-in-the-loop includes information, approval, edit, rejection, takeover, and audit.
  • Every loop needs budgets and a stopping rule.
  • Context windows are not project memory.
  • Long-running work needs external progress artifacts and durable state.
  • Concurrency requires explicit state ownership and merge control.
  • Memory influences reasoning; state controls workflow.
  • Evaluate agent outcome and trajectory.
  • The agent is the variable part of a controlled system.

ARB Review Record

Decision ID: ARB-CH-007
Subject: Chapter 7 — Workflow and Agent Architecture
Outcome: Accepted with constraints for user review

Primary contribution:
Places agents inside durable, stateful, policy-governed workflows and defines
when deterministic, single-agent, and multi-agent patterns are appropriate.

Grounded foundations:
- Anthropic workflow and agent patterns.
- OpenAI agent-design guidance and Codex agent loop.
- Azure agent orchestration patterns.
- AWS Agentic AI Lens orchestration, oversight, and observability.
- Microsoft Durable Task agent guidance.
- LangGraph persistence and interrupts.
- Temporal durable execution.
- Long-running agent harness guidance.

Original synthesis requiring explicit labelling:
- Deterministic Workflow Skeleton.
- Agent Run Contract.
- Agent State Envelope.
- Multi-Agent Justification Test.
- “The agent is the variable part.”
- “Every loop needs a stopping rule.”

Constraints:
- Do not define every model-and-tool workflow as an agent.
- Do not make conversation history authoritative workflow state.
- Do not recommend multi-agent architecture without independent responsibilities.
- Do not imply checkpointing guarantees exactly-once effects.

- Do not use human review as a universal substitute for risk design.
- Treat framework APIs as implementation examples, not enduring architecture.
