Chapter 10 - Operational Assurance: Observability, Incidents, and Continuous Control

Knowing whether an AI system remains healthy, trustworthy, controlled, and valuable

Related chapters: Chapters 4, 7, 8, 9, and 12

Deployment is not the end of assurance. It is the point at which the system begins producing the evidence needed to justify continued operation.

1. Why This Chapter Matters

An AI service returns HTTP 200.

The request completed.

The model generated an answer.

The trace contains no exception.

The system can still have failed.

It may have:

  • answered the wrong question;
  • relied on stale evidence;
  • selected an inappropriate tool;
  • acted outside delegated authority;
  • produced a valid schema containing incorrect values;
  • completed the workflow without improving the real-world outcome;
  • created an unfair or unsafe pattern that is visible only across many cases;
  • consumed ten times the expected cost through repeated reasoning loops.

Traditional operational signals remain essential. Availability, latency, errors, saturation, queue depth, dependency health, and resource consumption still determine whether the service can run.

They do not fully describe whether a probabilistic system is behaving acceptably.

NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework calls for post-deployment monitoring, response and recovery planning, user and stakeholder feedback, incident communication, decommissioning, change management, and continual improvement.[1][2]

Current agentic-AI guidance likewise recommends end-to-end traces covering model operations, tools, memory, and handoffs; behavioural baselines; structured and protected audit trails; workflow-specific KPIs; automated recovery; and break-glass procedures.[3][4]

OpenTelemetry’s GenAI semantic-conventions work is developing common spans, metrics, and events for model calls, retrieval, agents, workflows, plans, tool execution, usage, and evaluation results.[5]

These sources point toward a broader operating discipline.

The central argument of this chapter is:

Operational assurance is the continuing production of evidence that an AI system remains within its technical, behavioural, authority, risk, and outcome boundaries—and the capability to intervene when it does not.

2. Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish monitoring, observability, evaluation, and operational assurance;
  • define operational expectations before deployment;
  • connect technical health, behavioural quality, control status, and outcomes;
  • create service, task, safety, and business indicators;
  • use SLOs and behavioural error budgets without normalising unacceptable harm;
  • detect model, data, evidence, tool, workflow, policy, and outcome drift;
  • classify AI incidents by consequence rather than by component failure alone;
  • create an AI Incident Envelope for coordinated response;
  • contain harmful capability before completing root-cause analysis;
  • design degraded modes, rollback, reconciliation, and outcome verification;
  • turn incidents, overrides, complaints, and near misses into regression tests;
  • continuously monitor security, governance, and evidence controls;
  • design workflow-specific dashboards and actionable alerts;
  • establish operational review cadences and ownership;
  • identify signals that justify suspension or retirement;
  • answer architecture interview questions about AI observability, incident response, drift, behavioural SLOs, postmortems, and continued-operation gates.

Part I — From Monitoring to Operational Assurance

3. Monitoring

Monitoring answers known questions through predefined signals.

Examples:

  • Is the endpoint available?
  • Is p95 latency below the target?
  • How many tool calls failed?
  • Has the fallback rate increased?
  • Has the escalation threshold been breached?

Monitoring works well when the failure is anticipated and measurable.

4. Observability

Observability is the ability to understand internal behaviour from the signals a system emits.

It helps answer questions that were not fully predicted before the incident.

The familiar signals remain:

  • metrics;
  • logs;
  • traces;
  • events;
  • profiles;
  • artifacts.

For AI systems, observability also needs:

  • model and configuration version;
  • evidence sources;
  • retrieval results;
  • task and route;
  • reasoning or decision stage;
  • tool calls;
  • authority decisions;
  • validation;
  • human intervention;
  • evaluation result;
  • outcome link.

Microsoft describes AI observability as extending logs, metrics, and traces with evaluation and governance so teams can understand production quality, safety, and operational health.[6]

5. Evaluation

Evaluation measures fitness against a defined requirement.

It may be:

  • offline;
  • in CI/CD;
  • shadow;
  • canary;
  • sampled in production;
  • outcome based.

Evaluation answers:

Does this behaviour meet the required quality threshold?

Observability provides the evidence needed to diagnose why it did or did not.

6. Operational Assurance

Operational assurance combines:

  • expectations;
  • telemetry;
  • evaluation;
  • control monitoring;
  • incident response;
  • recovery;
  • outcome verification;
  • governance review.

It answers:

Should this system continue operating with its present scope and authority?

Architectural principle — Assurance decays

Operational confidence decays unless it is renewed by current production evidence.

A successful release evaluation becomes weaker evidence when:

  • users change;
  • policy changes;
  • the model changes;
  • sources become stale;
  • tools evolve;
  • traffic scales;
  • attackers adapt;
  • the business process changes.

7. The Operational Assurance Loop

This handbook introduces the Operational Assurance Loop:

Expected Behaviour
       ↓
Operational Signals
       ↓
Detection and Diagnosis
       ↓
Containment
       ↓
Recovery
       ↓
Outcome Verification
       ↓
Regression Learning
       ↓
Governance Reassessment
       └───────────────► Expected Behaviour

This is an original synthesis.

The loop connects Chapters 3–9:

  • quality attributes define expected behaviour;
  • evaluation defines measurement;
  • evidence architecture supports diagnosis;
  • model and workflow architecture enable rollback and degraded operation;
  • security enables containment;
  • governance determines authority to continue.

8. The Operational Assurance Contract

For each critical workflow, define:

assurance_id: refund_agent_uk_v5
workflow: customer_refund_resolution
owners:
  service: customer_platform
  outcome: customer_operations
  risk: payments_risk_owner
expectations:
  availability: 99.9%
  task_success: 96%
  unauthorised_refund: 0
  complaint_recontact_rate: <= 4%
segments:
  - standard_refund
  - high_value
  - vulnerable_customer
  - insufficient_evidence
signals:
  - service_metrics
  - workflow_traces
  - production_evaluation
  - approval_events
  - customer_outcomes
responses:
  warning: increase_sampling
  critical: disable_refund_tool
review_cadence: weekly
expiry: 2026-11-01

The contract should include:

  • expected behaviour;
  • relevant population and segments;
  • indicators and thresholds;
  • owners;
  • alert response;
  • evidence retention;
  • review cadence;
  • expiry or reassessment trigger.

A dashboard without an assurance contract can accumulate data without creating an operating decision.

Part II — The Operational Signal Model

9. Three Planes and a Cross-Cutting Control Status

Chapter 2 introduced three observability planes:

  • technical;
  • behavioural;
  • outcome.

Chapter 10 retains them.

Governance and security controls are treated as cross-cutting control status, not a separate outcome plane.

Technical Plane ───────────────┐
Behavioural Plane ─────────────┼──► Operational Assurance
Outcome Plane ─────────────────┘
          ▲
          │
Control Status across every plane

This avoids two errors:

  • treating governance as a dashboard detached from behaviour;
  • treating policy compliance as a substitute for useful outcomes.

10. Technical Plane

Signals include:

  • availability;
  • error rate;
  • latency;
  • queue time;
  • throughput;
  • saturation;
  • rate limits;
  • provider health;
  • cache;
  • token use;
  • tool availability;
  • checkpoint age;
  • worker health;
  • storage and network.

Technical signals answer whether the system can execute.

11. Behavioural Plane

Signals include:

  • task success;
  • groundedness;
  • citation validity;
  • tool selection;
  • action correctness;
  • refusal;
  • escalation;
  • policy adherence;
  • loop length;
  • route quality;
  • evaluator score;
  • human correction;
  • performance by segment.

Behavioural signals answer whether the system is doing the intended work in an acceptable way.

12. Outcome Plane

Signals include:

  • issue resolution;
  • repeat contact;
  • incident restoration time;
  • accepted code change;
  • defect escape;
  • complaint;
  • appeal;
  • customer loss;
  • business benefit;
  • harmful side effect;
  • human workload;
  • fairness impact;
  • cost per successful outcome.

Outcome signals answer whether the work improved the real situation.

13. Cross-Cutting Control Status

Control status includes:

  • valid authority;
  • policy version;
  • approval freshness;
  • model approval;
  • tool registry status;
  • evaluation recency;
  • exception expiry;
  • evidence freshness;
  • credential validity;
  • audit completeness;
  • inventory ownership;
  • containment readiness.

A system can be technically healthy and behaviourally strong while operating under an expired exception or unapproved model.

That is an operational failure.

14. Telemetry Context

Correlate every critical run with:

  • task ID;
  • user and workload identity;
  • tenant;
  • workflow;
  • model and version;
  • route;
  • prompt or configuration version;
  • evidence IDs;
  • tool versions;
  • policy version;
  • approval;
  • deployment;
  • trace ID;
  • outcome ID.

Without shared context, teams manually join unrelated logs during an incident.

AWS recommends end-to-end trace propagation across model calls, tools, memory, and agent handoffs.[3]

15. GenAI Semantic Conventions

OpenTelemetry’s GenAI conventions define developing telemetry models for:

  • chat and generation;
  • embeddings;
  • retrieval;
  • agent invocation;
  • workflow invocation;
  • planning;
  • tool execution;
  • usage;
  • evaluation events.[5]

They improve interoperability.

They do not define:

  • your task success;
  • your harm model;
  • your authority policy;
  • your business outcome.

Use standard telemetry for common operations and domain attributes for the meaningful workflow.

16. Content Capture and Privacy

Capturing prompts, responses, retrieved documents, tool arguments, and memory can improve diagnosis.

It can also expose:

  • personal data;
  • secrets;
  • commercial information;
  • protected decisions;
  • security controls.

Define:

  • whether content is captured;
  • which fields are redacted;
  • sampling;
  • encryption;
  • access;
  • retention;
  • deletion;
  • incident preservation;
  • tenant boundary.

Prefer identifiers, hashes, structured summaries, and evidence references when full content is unnecessary.

Part III — SLOs and Behavioural Error Budgets

17. Start with the User and Outcome

Google SRE guidance recommends reliability goals based on what users need, rather than every available infrastructure metric.[7]

For AI systems, the user experiences:

  • availability;
  • delay;
  • correctness;
  • evidence;
  • safety;
  • recovery;
  • outcome.

An SLO should describe the service level the user or business requires.

18. Service-Level Indicators

Examples:

Technical

  • successful request ratio;
  • p95 time to first token;
  • p95 completion time;
  • tool success;
  • recovery time.

Behavioural

  • task success;
  • supported-claim ratio;
  • correct-action ratio;
  • escalation recall;
  • appropriate-refusal ratio.

Outcome

  • successful resolution;
  • repeat-contact ratio;
  • human repair;
  • adverse incident;
  • cost per outcome.

An indicator needs:

  • event definition;
  • denominator;
  • data source;
  • segment;
  • measurement window;
  • owner.

19. Behavioural SLO Example

For eligible standard refund cases over 28 days:

- at least 96% are resolved without human repair;
- 100% of issued credits are within delegated amount;
- at least 99% of insufficient-evidence cases escalate;
- no unauthorised customer account is modified;
- p95 workflow completion is below 90 seconds.

This is stronger than:

The agent should be accurate and fast.

20. Error Budgets

An error budget is the amount of allowed unreliability before operating policy changes.

Google’s example policy halts nonessential releases when the service exceeds its error budget and requires a postmortem when one incident consumes a large share.[7]

AI systems can define budgets for:

  • task failure;
  • unsupported claim;
  • wrong escalation;
  • human repair;
  • excessive latency;
  • fallback;
  • cost overrun.

If consumed:

  • freeze autonomy increases;
  • block model changes;
  • increase sampling;
  • restore prior version;
  • require human review;
  • investigate.

21. Zero-Tolerance Events

Do not assign a routine error budget to every failure.

Examples that may require zero tolerance:

  • cross-tenant disclosure;
  • unauthorised payment;
  • prohibited production action;
  • use of expired authority;
  • irreversible action without approval.

A zero-tolerance control should be:

  • clearly defined;
  • deterministically measurable;
  • operationally actionable.

Noisy subjective metrics should not be presented as perfect invariants.

22. Behavioural Error-Budget Policy

Document:

  • SLO;
  • budget window;
  • high-risk segments;
  • freeze conditions;
  • exception owner;
  • restart criteria;
  • postmortem trigger.

Architectural principle — Budget changes authority

A behavioural error budget has value only when consuming it changes release, routing, review, or autonomy.

Part IV — Drift and Change Detection

23. Input Drift

Changes in:

  • user language;
  • task mix;
  • document format;
  • geography;
  • adversarial input;
  • customer segment.

Input drift may make the evaluation set unrepresentative.

24. Evidence Drift

Changes in:

  • source content;
  • authority;
  • freshness;
  • permission;
  • index coverage;
  • ranking;
  • citation resolution.

The model can remain unchanged while answer quality deteriorates.

25. Model and Configuration Drift

Changes in:

  • provider alias;
  • model snapshot;
  • prompt;
  • reasoning budget;
  • tool description;
  • safety filter;
  • route;
  • cache;
  • quantisation.

Some changes are intentional releases.

Others are unplanned configuration drift.

26. Behavioural Drift

Changes in:

  • task success;
  • response style;
  • refusal;
  • tool pattern;
  • loop length;
  • citation use;
  • group performance;
  • human override.

Behavioural drift is measured against a baseline and current expectation.

27. Outcome Drift

Changes in:

  • resolution;
  • customer behaviour;
  • business result;
  • complaint;
  • harm;
  • operator workload.

A system can maintain its behavioural metric while the surrounding workflow changes and the outcome declines.

28. Policy and Control Drift

Changes in:

  • regulation;
  • internal policy;
  • risk appetite;
  • exception;
  • owner;
  • approval;
  • authorised tool;
  • credential.

Control drift should be monitored as actively as model drift.

29. Baselines

A baseline should state:

  • time period;
  • population;
  • model and configuration;
  • traffic mix;
  • evaluation set;
  • known limitations.

A baseline must not adapt so quickly that slow degradation becomes normal.

Use:

  • fixed reference baseline;
  • recent operational baseline;
  • release comparison;
  • high-risk segment baseline.

30. Change Annotations

Annotate dashboards and traces with:

  • deployment;
  • model change;
  • prompt change;
  • source update;
  • policy update;
  • tool release;
  • incident;
  • traffic change.

This reduces time spent guessing whether a metric movement followed a known change.

Part V — What Counts as an AI Incident?

31. AI Incident Definition

An AI incident is an event or pattern in which an AI system:

  • causes or risks unacceptable harm;
  • violates authority, policy, or obligation;
  • fails a critical task or outcome;
  • exposes data;
  • becomes unavailable;
  • behaves outside its approved envelope;
  • consumes uncontrolled resources;
  • produces evidence that continued operation is no longer justified.

Not every low evaluation score is an incident.

Not every incident produces an exception.

32. Incident Classes

Service incident

Availability, latency, dependency, or capacity failure.

Model incident

Unexpected model behaviour, refusal, regression, or provider change.

Evidence incident

Stale, poisoned, inaccessible, conflicting, or incorrectly ranked evidence.

Tool and action incident

Wrong tool, duplicate effect, incorrect parameters, partial execution.

Workflow and state incident

Stuck state, replay error, lost checkpoint, invalid transition, orphaned run.

Security incident

Injection, data exposure, credential abuse, unauthorised capability.

Governance incident

Expired approval, unowned system, policy violation, unreviewed material change.

Outcome incident

Harm, unfairness, business deterioration, complaint pattern.

Consumption incident

Runaway loops, fan-out, quota exhaustion, unexpected cost.

One event can occupy several classes.

33. Severity

Severity should consider:

  • consequence;
  • affected people or systems;
  • reversibility;
  • active authority;
  • duration;
  • detectability;
  • data sensitivity;
  • legal obligation;
  • likelihood of spread;
  • availability of safe fallback.

A wrong internal summary and an unauthorised payment should not share severity because they both involve “incorrect output.”

34. Pattern Incidents

Some incidents emerge statistically:

  • one language performs worse;
  • complaint rate increases gradually;
  • high-value cases receive fewer escalations;
  • reviewer override rises;
  • a source becomes systematically stale.

The incident may not have one start time.

Declare it when evidence crosses the defined threshold.

Part VI — Incident Response

35. Incident Roles

Adapt established incident-management roles.

Incident Commander

Owns coordination and priorities.

Operations Lead

Executes technical containment and recovery.

AI or Domain Lead

Interprets behavioural, evidence, model, and outcome signals.

Communications Lead

Coordinates internal, customer, regulator, and affected-party communication.

Security, Privacy, or Governance Lead

Joins according to incident type.

The delivery team should not simultaneously investigate, approve continued operation, and communicate impact without independent challenge for major incidents.

36. The AI Incident Envelope

This handbook introduces the AI Incident Envelope:

incident_id: ai_inc_2026_041
system: refund_agent_uk
status: contained
severity: critical
first_signal: unauthorised_high_value_credit
affected:
  customers: 3
  transactions: 4
active_authority:
  refund_tool: revoked
versions:
  model: provider_model_2026_08
  prompt: refund_v17
  policy: refund_policy_6
suspected_stages:
  - evidence
  - authority
containment:
  - disabled_refund_tool
  - switched_to_advisory_mode
unknowns:
  - duplicate_transactions
owners:
  incident_commander: operations_lead
  accountable_owner: customer_operations_director

The envelope contains:

  • identity and severity;
  • affected systems and parties;
  • observed signals;
  • current versions;
  • active authority;
  • completed and uncertain actions;
  • containment;
  • owners;
  • communication;
  • evidence preservation.

37. Response Phases

Detect
  ↓
Declare
  ↓
Contain
  ↓
Diagnose
  ↓
Recover
  ↓
Verify Outcome
  ↓
Communicate
  ↓
Learn

The phases may overlap.

Containment should not wait for perfect diagnosis when authority can create ongoing harm.

38. Contain Before Explain

For consequential incidents:

  • revoke tool access;
  • reduce autonomy;
  • switch to read-only;
  • stop routing;
  • pause queue;
  • isolate model or source;
  • require human review;
  • disable egress.

Architectural principle — Contain before explain

When harmful capability remains active, reduce the blast radius before completing the root-cause narrative.

This is original handbook synthesis.

39. Degraded Modes

Possible modes:

  • advisory only;
  • retrieval only;
  • deterministic workflow;
  • approved model only;
  • no external communication;
  • human review;
  • delayed batch;
  • temporary unavailability.

A degraded mode should be:

  • predesigned;
  • tested;
  • visible to users and operators;
  • protected from silent capability expansion.

40. Break-Glass Operations

Break-glass runbooks preserve critical business operation when the AI path is unsafe or unavailable.

They should include:

  • manual process;
  • access;
  • contacts;
  • data needed;
  • decision authority;
  • time target;
  • reconciliation;
  • return-to-service criteria.

AWS recommends rehearsing manual fallback procedures before incidents occur.[4]

41. Unknown Side Effects

A timeout does not always mean an action failed.

The system may have:

  • sent an email;
  • created a ticket;
  • initiated a payment;
  • changed a record.

Mark the outcome as unknown until reconciled.

Do not retry a consequential action blindly.

42. Communication

Communicate:

  • what is known;
  • what is uncertain;
  • affected population;
  • containment;
  • expected next update;
  • user action;
  • correction or recourse;
  • owner.

NIST includes communication with affected actors and communities in incident response and recovery.[1]

Part VII — Diagnosis

43. Diagnose by Stage

Use the AI Decision Pipeline:

  • intent;
  • context;
  • evidence;
  • reasoning;
  • validation;
  • authority;
  • action;
  • outcome;
  • learning.

Ask:

Which stage first diverged from expected behaviour?

This avoids replacing the model when the actual failure is stale evidence, wrong policy, or duplicate action.

44. Reconstruct the Run

A useful trace should answer:

  • what task was requested;
  • which identity acted;
  • which model and route ran;
  • which evidence entered context;
  • which tools executed;
  • which validation passed;
  • which authority applied;
  • what state changed;
  • what outcome followed.

The trace should preserve links to protected evidence without requiring every operator to access sensitive content.

45. Evaluation During Diagnosis

Run:

  • the incident case;
  • similar cases;
  • previous version;
  • fallback;
  • high-risk segments;
  • repeated trials.

An LLM judge can assist triage.

It should not be the sole authority deciding whether a critical incident is resolved.

46. Evaluator Incidents

The evaluator can fail through:

  • drift;
  • prompt change;
  • correlated model failure;
  • stale rubric;
  • unrepresentative sampling;
  • hidden segment weakness.

A production score can improve while real quality worsens.

Compare automated scores with:

  • human audit;
  • outcomes;
  • complaints;
  • deterministic checks.

47. Provider and Alias Changes

Verify:

  • actual response model;
  • provider route;
  • endpoint;
  • region;
  • model alias;
  • safety policy;
  • token and latency pattern.

A compatibility API may hide an upstream change.

Chapter 6 established that behavioural approval does not automatically transfer to a replacement artifact.

Part VIII — Recovery and Outcome Verification

48. Recovery Patterns

  • retry after verified transient failure;
  • fail over to evaluated model;
  • restore prior prompt or policy;
  • rebuild index;
  • revoke poisoned source;
  • repair workflow state;
  • compensate action;
  • require human reprocessing;
  • reduce scope;
  • retire capability.

Recovery should address the failed control, not merely clear the alert.

49. Rollback

Rollback may require:

  • model;
  • prompt;
  • route;
  • tool;
  • source index;
  • policy;
  • workflow code;
  • memory;
  • cache;
  • deployment.

Record compatibility dependencies.

A previous model may no longer be available.

Design alternate recovery paths.

50. State and Action Reconciliation

Identify:

  • completed actions;
  • duplicate actions;
  • partial actions;
  • unknown actions;
  • approvals used;
  • affected records;
  • compensation required.

The final service status can be green while business records remain wrong.

51. Outcome Verification

Verify:

  • user outcome;
  • affected-party correction;
  • business state;
  • financial state;
  • security state;
  • audit completeness;
  • residual risk.

Architectural principle — Recovery ends at the outcome

An AI incident is not resolved when the endpoint recovers. It is resolved when the affected real-world state is understood and corrected or explicitly accepted.

52. Continued-Operation Gate

Before restoring full authority, require:

  • causal hypothesis;
  • containment effectiveness;
  • repaired control;
  • evaluation pass;
  • affected-state reconciliation;
  • monitoring;
  • owner approval;
  • communication;
  • follow-up plan.

Possible decisions:

  • full restore;
  • limited restore;
  • canary;
  • advisory only;
  • remain suspended;
  • retire.

Part IX — Post-Incident Learning

53. Blameless but Accountable

A postmortem should avoid personal blame while still assigning ownership for corrective action.

Google SRE guidance treats a postmortem as a factual learning artifact and emphasises official ownership of actions.[8][9]

Include:

  • summary;
  • impact;
  • timeline;
  • detection;
  • response;
  • contributing factors;
  • control failures;
  • what went well;
  • what did not;
  • action items;
  • owners;
  • dates.

54. The Incident-to-Evaluation Loop

Incident or Near Miss
        ↓
Failure Taxonomy
        ↓
Regression Case
        ↓
Control or Architecture Change
        ↓
Evaluation
        ↓
Canary
        ↓
Production Monitoring

Every material incident should strengthen:

  • evaluation;
  • controls;
  • runbooks;
  • operating assumptions.

Architectural principle — Incidents must change the system

Every material incident should change at least one control, evaluation, or documented operating assumption.

55. Near Misses and Overrides

Learn from:

  • human rejection;
  • corrected tool parameter;
  • blocked action;
  • prompt-injection denial;
  • customer complaint;
  • unusual escalation;
  • evaluator disagreement;
  • almost-consumed budget.

Near misses provide evidence before harm occurs.

56. Runbook Evolution

Runbooks should include:

  • symptoms;
  • dashboard;
  • queries;
  • likely causes;
  • containment;
  • recovery;
  • verification;
  • escalation;
  • owner.

Test runbooks through:

  • tabletop;
  • game day;
  • chaos exercise;
  • shadow incident.

Operational knowledge should not remain in the memory of one engineer.

57. Action-Item Quality

Weak:

Improve monitoring.

Stronger:

Add a deterministic alert for high-value refund actions without current approval; owner Payments Platform; due 21 August; test through staging incident scenario.

Track:

  • owner;
  • due date;
  • status;
  • risk reduced;
  • verification.

Part X — Continuous Control Monitoring

58. Why Monitor Controls?

Controls can fail silently.

Examples:

  • an approval expires;
  • a policy service is bypassed;
  • a model alias changes;
  • a tool is added without review;
  • a retention job stops;
  • an exception becomes permanent;
  • evaluation is stale.

Operational assurance should observe whether the controls themselves remain active and effective.

59. Governance Controls

Monitor:

  • named owner;
  • current risk tier;
  • approval date;
  • review date;
  • impact assessment;
  • exception expiry;
  • material change;
  • recourse availability;
  • inventory completeness.

60. Security Controls

Monitor:

  • workload identity;
  • credential lifetime;
  • policy decision;
  • tool registry;
  • egress;
  • sandbox;
  • denied actions;
  • audit integrity;
  • containment test.

61. Evidence and Data Controls

Monitor:

  • source freshness;
  • permission sync;
  • provenance;
  • index coverage;
  • retention;
  • deletion;
  • memory expiry;
  • poisoned content;
  • citation validity.

62. Evaluation Controls

Monitor:

  • last run;
  • dataset freshness;
  • segment coverage;
  • grader calibration;
  • holdout integrity;
  • threshold;
  • failed gate;
  • production sample rate.

63. Control Effectiveness

A control can exist but fail to reduce risk.

Examples:

  • reviewers approve everything;
  • prompt-injection detector has high false negatives;
  • fallback never succeeds;
  • appeal takes months;
  • logs cannot reconstruct action.

Measure outcomes of controls, not only configuration.

Part XI — Cost, Capacity, and Consumption Operations

64. Consumption Signals

Monitor:

  • model calls per task;
  • tool calls;
  • reasoning steps;
  • input and output tokens;
  • cache hit;
  • fan-out;
  • retries;
  • human review;
  • cost;
  • capacity;
  • quota.

Agentic systems can amplify small errors into large consumption.

AWS recommends monitoring operational boundaries and implementing automatic cutoffs for runaway behaviour.[4]

65. Runaway Patterns

  • repeated tool failure;
  • evaluator–optimizer loop;
  • multi-agent debate;
  • recursive delegation;
  • cache miss;
  • oversized context;
  • provider retry storm;
  • duplicate queue delivery.

Controls:

  • total attempt budget;
  • time budget;
  • cost budget;
  • worker limit;
  • circuit breaker;
  • admission control;
  • cancellation.

66. Capacity Planning

Plan for:

  • normal volume;
  • burst;
  • provider quota;
  • fallback capacity;
  • human-review capacity;
  • break-glass manual capacity;
  • incident replay;
  • batch backlog.

A fallback path that cannot support incident traffic is not a reliable fallback.

67. Cost Incidents

Treat unexpected cost as an incident when it:

  • threatens business operation;
  • indicates loops or abuse;
  • consumes shared quota;
  • hides quality regression;
  • bypasses budget policy.

Contain cost without silently routing high-risk tasks to an unsuitable model.

Part XII — Dashboards, Alerts, and Operating Cadence

68. Workflow-Specific Dashboards

A useful dashboard follows the critical path:

Request
  ↓
Evidence
  ↓
Model
  ↓
Validation
  ↓
Authority
  ↓
Tool
  ↓
Outcome

Show:

  • volume;
  • latency by stage;
  • failures;
  • route;
  • evaluation;
  • authority;
  • outcome;
  • cost;
  • deployment changes.

AWS recommends workflow-specific dashboards rather than generic infrastructure views.[3]

69. Alert Design

An alert should be:

  • actionable;
  • owned;
  • tied to user or risk impact;
  • severity appropriate;
  • resistant to noise;
  • linked to a runbook.

Avoid paging on:

  • every evaluator fluctuation;
  • low-confidence single sample;
  • metrics without response.

Page when immediate action can reduce consequence.

Create tickets or reviews for slower trends.

70. When Evaluation Becomes an Alert

A production evaluation result can trigger an alert when:

  • the evaluator is validated;
  • sample size is sufficient;
  • threshold is meaningful;
  • segment is material;
  • false-alarm policy exists;
  • response is defined.

A noisy LLM-judge score should not wake an operator without corroboration.

71. Operating Cadence

Real time

  • critical security and authority;
  • service health;
  • runaway consumption;
  • prohibited action.

Daily

  • failed workflows;
  • stuck state;
  • fallback;
  • cost anomalies;
  • evidence freshness.

Weekly

  • behavioural quality;
  • segments;
  • incidents;
  • overrides;
  • complaints;
  • control status.

Monthly or quarterly

  • outcomes;
  • governance assurance;
  • third-party change;
  • impact assessment;
  • retirement;
  • investment.

72. Ownership

Define owners for:

  • service;
  • model and evaluation;
  • evidence;
  • tools;
  • security;
  • outcome;
  • governance;
  • incident command.

A cross-functional system still needs clear primary ownership.

73. On-Call Readiness

Operators need:

  • task and workflow understanding;
  • model limitations;
  • safe degraded modes;
  • containment authority;
  • runbooks;
  • access to domain experts;
  • communication templates;
  • regular exercises.

Do not page a traditional infrastructure team for an AI behavioural incident without the evidence and expertise needed to respond.

Part XIII — Worked Example: Customer-Service Refund Agent

74. Scenario

The agent can:

  • read order and delivery data;
  • interpret refund policy;
  • request evidence;
  • recommend or issue low-value credits;
  • escalate high-value or ambiguous cases.

75. Assurance Contract

Technical:

  • 99.9% availability;
  • p95 completion below 90 seconds.

Behavioural:

  • 96% correct resolution;
  • 99% insufficient-evidence escalation;
  • zero credit above delegated amount.

Outcome:

  • repeat contact below 4%;
  • complaint rate below threshold;
  • no disproportionate failure in vulnerable-customer segment.

Control:

  • current policy;
  • valid workload identity;
  • approved tool;
  • fresh authority;
  • evaluation within thirty days.

76. Incident

A policy change lowers the permitted automatic credit from £30 to £20.

The retrieval index updates.

The deterministic tool policy remains at £30.

The model cites the new policy but issues £25 credits.

Technical dashboards remain green.

Behavioural evaluation finds policy inconsistency.

Outcome monitoring identifies four incorrect credits.

77. Response

  1. Declare authority and policy incident.
  2. Disable automatic refund tool.
  3. Continue in advisory mode.
  4. identify affected transactions.
  5. confirm policy and gateway versions.
  6. correct tool limit.
  7. add deterministic control test.
  8. reconcile customer accounts.
  9. rerun regression and canary.
  10. accountable owner approves restored delegation.

The model was not the root cause.

The policy–control mapping drifted.

78. Learning

Add:

  • policy-version consistency check;
  • control-drift alert;
  • regression case;
  • monthly authority review;
  • dashboard showing policy and tool versions.

The incident improves governance, evaluation, and operations.

Part XIV — Architecture Review

79. Scenario

A company launches a multi-agent operations platform.

It has:

  • infrastructure dashboards;
  • model latency and token charts;
  • complete conversation logs;
  • an LLM judge scoring a sample of answers;
  • a monthly governance report.

It lacks:

  • task success;
  • outcome linkage;
  • control status;
  • incident taxonomy;
  • degraded modes;
  • authority revocation;
  • regression learning.

80. ARB Findings

Finding 1 — Availability substitutes for success

No workflow or outcome SLO exists.

Finding 2 — Content logging creates risk

Full conversations are retained without minimisation.

Finding 3 — Judge validity is unknown

The score cannot safely trigger operational decisions.

Finding 4 — Control drift is invisible

Expired approvals and unreviewed changes are not monitored.

Finding 5 — Incidents have no AI classification

Behavioural and authority failures are handled as software bugs.

Finding 6 — No containment path

Operators cannot reduce autonomy or revoke tools quickly.

Finding 7 — Recovery stops at endpoint health

Downstream actions are not reconciled.

Finding 8 — Learning is manual

Incidents do not become evaluation cases or control improvements.

81. Recommended Redesign

  • operational assurance contracts;
  • technical, behavioural, and outcome signals;
  • cross-cutting control monitoring;
  • end-to-end trace correlation;
  • privacy-aware content capture;
  • behavioural SLO policy;
  • AI incident envelope;
  • containment and degraded modes;
  • outcome verification;
  • incident-to-evaluation loop;
  • governance continued-operation gate.

Part XV — Architecture Smells

82. HTTP 200 Success

Transport success is treated as task success.

83. Infrastructure-Only Observability

CPU, latency, and errors are visible; behaviour and outcomes are not.

84. Dashboard Without Authority

Operators can see a problem but cannot reduce autonomy or disable a tool.

85. LLM Judge Pager

A noisy unvalidated evaluator directly pages on-call staff.

86. Green Average, Hidden Segment

Aggregate quality passes while a consequential segment fails.

87. Adaptive Baseline Amnesia

The baseline moves until slow degradation appears normal.

88. Endpoint Recovery Theatre

The service recovers while incorrect real-world state remains.

89. Retry Storm as Resilience

Repeated model or tool calls amplify an outage.

90. Audit as Data Lake

Everything is logged without privacy, purpose, or retrieval design.

91. Control Exists, Effect Unknown

The organisation verifies configuration but not whether the control reduces risk.

92. Postmortem Without Regression

The incident is documented but cannot be detected in future testing.

93. Permanent Degraded Mode

A temporary safe fallback becomes an unreviewed operating model.

Part XVI — Interview Preparation

94. Foundational Questions

Question 1

What is the difference between monitoring and observability?

Monitoring answers predefined questions through known signals. Observability supports understanding unexpected behaviour through correlated telemetry.

Question 2

What is operational assurance?

The ongoing production of evidence that an AI system remains within technical, behavioural, authority, risk, and outcome boundaries, combined with the ability to intervene.

Question 3

Why is HTTP 200 insufficient for an AI workflow?

It shows transport or endpoint success, not correct intent, evidence, tool use, policy, action, or outcome.

Question 4

What should an AI trace contain?

Task, identities, model and configuration, evidence, tools, validation, authority, state transitions, cost, latency, and outcome linkage.

Question 5

What is behavioural drift?

A material change in task, evidence, tool, refusal, escalation, safety, or segment performance over time.

95. Senior-Level Questions

Question 6

How would you define an SLO for an AI agent?

Combine technical service indicators with task, safety, authority, and outcome indicators for a defined population and window.

Question 7

When should an evaluation metric become an operational alert?

When the evaluator is valid, sampling is sufficient, the threshold maps to risk, and a defined response can reduce impact.

Question 8

How do you detect drift without hiding slow degradation?

Use a fixed reference baseline alongside recent baselines, segment results, and change annotations.

Question 9

How do you respond to an AI behavioural incident?

Declare, contain authority, preserve evidence, diagnose by decision stage, recover, reconcile real-world effects, verify outcome, and add regression learning.

Question 10

Why is rollback not always sufficient?

External effects, memory, caches, evidence indexes, and business records may remain changed and require reconciliation.

Question 11

How do you monitor governance controls in production?

Observe approval freshness, model and tool approval, policy version, exception expiry, evaluation recency, owner, and continued-operation gate status.

Question 12

How do you control runaway agent cost?

Enforce model, tool, time, token, worker, and cost budgets; use circuit breakers, admission control, cancellation, and route policy.

96. Principal-Level Questions

Question 13

How would you design enterprise AI observability?

Standardise common trace context and GenAI operations while allowing products to define task, risk, control, and outcome signals. Provide privacy controls, workflow dashboards, evaluation integration, and incident response.

Question 14

How should AI incidents be classified?

By consequence and failed boundary across service, model, evidence, tool, workflow, security, governance, outcome, and consumption—not only by component.

Question 15

How do SLOs, evaluation gates, and governance gates interact?

SLOs govern ongoing service; evaluations measure behavioural fitness; governance gates decide authority. A breach can trigger freeze, rollback, reduced autonomy, or suspension.

Question 16

What is continuous control monitoring?

Automated or regular evidence that required controls remain configured, current, effective, and linked to appropriate response.

Question 17

How do you prove an AI incident is resolved?

Show containment, corrected cause, successful evaluation, reconciled affected state, outcome verification, current controls, and accountable approval.

Question 18

How do you create organisational learning from incidents?

Convert failures into taxonomy, regression tests, control changes, runbooks, owner actions, and governance reassessment.

Part XVII — Whiteboard Challenge

97. Operate a Multi-Tenant Agent Platform

The platform hosts:

  • customer support agents;
  • coding agents;
  • procurement agents;
  • incident-remediation agents;
  • internal research agents.

Constraints

  • several models and providers;
  • dynamic routing;
  • shared tool gateway;
  • regulated tenants;
  • human approvals;
  • high-volume traffic;
  • cost limits;
  • third-party evidence sources.

Discuss

  1. Define operational assurance contracts.
  2. Design trace context.
  3. Define technical, behavioural, outcome, and control signals.
  4. Create SLO and error-budget policy.
  5. Detect drift.
  6. Define incident taxonomy and severity.
  7. Create the AI Incident Envelope.
  8. Design containment and degraded modes.
  9. Design rollback and reconciliation.
  10. Define production evaluation and sampling.
  11. Monitor governance and security controls.
  12. Design dashboards and alerts.
  13. Define cost and capacity controls.
  14. Define incident roles and communication.
  15. Create postmortem and regression learning.
  16. Define continued-operation and retirement gates.

Strong-answer characteristics

  • task and outcome signals;
  • route and model visibility;
  • tenant segmentation;
  • privacy-aware tracing;
  • validated evaluators;
  • control status;
  • immediate authority reduction;
  • idempotent reconciliation;
  • behavioural error budgets;
  • workflow-specific dashboards;
  • automated cutoffs;
  • manual break glass;
  • incident-to-evaluation loop;
  • accountable restart.

Part XVIII — Questions to Take Back to Your Team

  1. What does success mean after the endpoint responds?
  2. Which outcome proves the workflow helped?
  3. Which high-risk segments are hidden by averages?
  4. Can every model, tool, evidence, and policy version be reconstructed?
  5. Which control can silently expire?
  6. Which evaluator is trusted without calibration?
  7. What causes immediate reduction of autonomy?
  8. Can operators disable a capability without redeploying the whole system?
  9. What is the safest degraded mode?
  10. Can external side effects be reconciled?
  11. Which incidents have no runbook?
  12. When did the baseline last change?
  13. Which costs indicate a loop or abuse?
  14. Does the dashboard map to the workflow?
  15. Which alerts have no action?
  16. Do postmortems create regression tests?
  17. Who approves return to full operation?
  18. What evidence justifies continued operation?
  19. Which system should be retired rather than repaired?
  20. Can affected parties receive correction and recourse?

Architect’s Notebook — Operations Is the Continuing Architecture Review

Architecture review is often treated as a meeting before implementation.

Production reveals:

  • actual traffic;
  • actual failures;
  • actual users;
  • actual workarounds;
  • actual cost;
  • actual harm.

Operational assurance is the architecture review that never ends.

It asks repeatedly:

  • Is the system still solving the intended problem?
  • Are the assumptions still true?
  • Are controls still effective?
  • Is authority still justified?
  • Should the system change, narrow, or stop?

From the Architect’s Desk

AI observability becomes complicated when teams try to record everything. The more useful question is: which signal would change an operating decision?

Trace the workflow, not merely the model call. Measure the outcome, not merely the fluent response. Monitor the control, not merely the policy document.

During an incident, do not wait for a perfect explanation while harmful authority remains active. Contain first. Preserve evidence. Reconcile the real-world effect.

A mature system does not avoid every failure. It detects important failure, limits consequence, recovers deliberately, and becomes harder to surprise the next time.

If I Were the Architect

You inherit an AI agent platform with excellent infrastructure monitoring.

The dashboards show:

  • availability;
  • latency;
  • token use;
  • provider errors.

Yet users report:

  • incorrect actions;
  • stale answers;
  • unexplained escalation;
  • rising human correction;
  • cost spikes.

What do you do first?

Do not add another generic dashboard.

  1. Define critical workflows and outcomes.
  2. create operational assurance contracts.
  3. correlate task, model, evidence, tool, authority, and outcome.
  4. add production evaluation by risk segment.
  5. monitor policy and approval freshness.
  6. create an AI incident taxonomy.
  7. establish containment and degraded modes.
  8. define behavioural error-budget responses.
  9. turn incidents and overrides into regression cases.
  10. require accountable continued-operation review.

The organisation did not lack telemetry.

It lacked an operational model for deciding what the telemetry meant.

Key Takeaways

  • Deployment begins, rather than completes, operational assurance.
  • Monitoring, observability, evaluation, and assurance serve different purposes.
  • Operational confidence decays unless renewed by current evidence.
  • The Operational Assurance Loop connects expected behaviour, signals, response, recovery, learning, and governance.
  • Technical, behavioural, and outcome planes must be observed together.
  • Control status cuts across all operational planes.
  • Common semantic conventions improve correlation but do not define domain success.
  • Content capture must balance diagnosis with privacy.
  • AI SLOs should combine service, task, safety, authority, and outcome.
  • Behavioural error budgets should change release or autonomy policy.
  • Some events require deterministic zero tolerance.
  • Drift can affect input, evidence, model, behaviour, outcome, and policy.
  • AI incidents should be classified by consequence and failed boundary.
  • The AI Incident Envelope supports coordinated response and reconstruction.
  • Contain harmful capability before completing root-cause analysis.
  • Endpoint recovery does not prove real-world recovery.
  • Continued operation requires outcome verification and accountable approval.
  • Incidents, near misses, overrides, and complaints should strengthen evaluation and controls.
  • Continuous control monitoring checks whether governance and security remain active and effective.
  • Consumption and cost can become reliability incidents.
  • Workflow-specific dashboards outperform generic AI dashboards.
  • Operational assurance is the continuing architecture review.

ARB Review Record

Decision ID: ARB-CH-010
Subject: Chapter 10 — Operational Assurance
Outcome: Accepted with constraints for user review

Primary contribution:
Defines operational assurance as the continuing production of evidence that an
AI system remains within technical, behavioural, authority, risk, and outcome
boundaries, combined with intervention and learning capabilities.

Grounded foundations:
- NIST AI RMF Measure and Manage guidance.
- AWS Agentic AI Lens operational excellence and recovery guidance.
- OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions.
- Microsoft AI observability guidance.

- Google Cloud AI/ML reliability and operational-excellence guidance.

Original synthesis requiring explicit labelling:
- Operational Assurance Loop.
- Operational Assurance Contract.
- AI Incident Envelope.
- control status as cross-cutting operational evidence.
- “operational confidence decays.”
- “contain before explain.”
- “recovery ends at the outcome.”

Constraints:
- Do not treat infrastructure health as task or outcome success.
- Do not treat one LLM judge as the incident authority.
- Do not capture sensitive content without purpose and controls.
- Do not let adaptive baselines hide gradual degradation.
- Do not assign error budgets to unacceptable deterministic violations.
- Preserve fast containment and manual break glass.
- Require reconciliation of external effects.
- Connect material incidents to regression and governance reassessment.
