Chapter 11 - Data and Privacy Architecture for AI Systems

Purpose, lineage, minimisation, memory, deletion, and recourse

Related chapters: Chapters 5, 8, 9, and 12

AI data should never be governed as one undifferentiated asset. Training data, evaluation data, retrieval evidence, model context, memory, telemetry, and generated artifacts serve different purposes and require different access, retention, deletion, and privacy controls.

1. Why This Chapter Matters

AI systems create unusually complex data paths.

A customer question may become:

  • a request log;
  • model context;
  • retrieved evidence;
  • a tool call;
  • an agent checkpoint;
  • short-term memory;
  • a quality-evaluation sample;
  • an incident trace;
  • a fine-tuning candidate;
  • an analytics event;
  • a cached response.

The original record may be deleted.

Derived copies may remain.

A user may agree to receive a service.

That does not automatically mean their data may be used for:

  • model training;
  • evaluator calibration;
  • product analytics;
  • long-term memory;
  • unrelated research;
  • another customer’s retrieval index.

An organisation may protect a database with encryption while allowing sensitive information to enter:

  • prompts;
  • traces;
  • caches;
  • screenshots;
  • model-provider logs;
  • generated files;
  • support tickets.

Privacy is therefore not simply:

Keep the database secure.

Security protects against unauthorised access and alteration.

Privacy also asks:

  • Why is the data being processed?
  • Is the processing expected?
  • Is the data necessary?
  • Can the person understand and influence the use?
  • Can the information be linked back to them?
  • How long will it persist?
  • Which derived artifacts exist?
  • Can rights and deletion requests be fulfilled?
  • What happens when the purpose changes?

The GDPR’s data-processing principles include lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity, confidentiality, and accountability.[1]

NIST frames privacy as enterprise risk management concerned with problems individuals may experience because systems process data. Its privacy- engineering work adds objectives such as predictability, manageability, and disassociability.[2][3]

ISO/IEC 27701:2025 defines requirements and guidance for establishing, maintaining, and continually improving a privacy information management system for organisations acting as PII controllers or processors.[4]

These foundations become harder—not less relevant—when AI creates many derived representations.

The central argument of this chapter is:

Data and privacy architecture must bind every material data use to a purpose, authority, lifecycle, access boundary, lineage, retention rule, deletion path, and accountable owner.

2. Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish training, validation, evaluation, retrieval, context, memory, telemetry, and generated data;
  • create a purpose contract for each material data use;
  • identify the controller, processor, owner, subject, consumer, and system of record;
  • map data through collection, transformation, derivation, use, sharing, retention, deletion, and recourse;
  • implement data minimisation at collection, retrieval, prompt, tool, memory, and telemetry boundaries;
  • distinguish anonymity, pseudonymisation, tokenisation, encryption, synthetic data, and differential privacy;
  • preserve provenance, consent, licence, authority, and lineage;
  • govern training and evaluation data separately;
  • prevent retrieval and memory from bypassing purpose and access controls;
  • create cross-tenant isolation for indexes, caches, traces, and memory;
  • design retention and deletion propagation across derived artifacts;
  • explain why deletion from source data does not automatically remove model influence;
  • assess residency, sovereignty, transfers, providers, and subprocessors;
  • select privacy-enhancing technologies based on an explicit threat and use case;
  • support access, correction, objection, restriction, deletion, and recourse;
  • evaluate privacy controls and respond to privacy incidents;
  • answer architecture interview questions about minimisation, lineage, unlearning, memory, telemetry, PETs, and individual rights.

Part I — AI Data Is a Portfolio

3. Data Roles

The same field can have different governance depending on its role.

Source data

The authoritative record from which the system reads.

Examples:

  • customer profile;
  • policy document;
  • transaction;
  • medical record;
  • source code.

Training data

Used to change model parameters.

Validation data

Used during development to tune choices or thresholds.

Evaluation data

Used to produce evidence about system quality.

Retrieval data

Indexed or queried to supply evidence at runtime.

Context data

Placed into the model’s current input.

Working state

Temporary structured data used to complete a workflow.

Memory

Information retained to influence future interactions or runs.

Telemetry

Events, traces, metrics, logs, and samples used to operate the system.

Generated artifacts

Outputs such as reports, code, images, decisions, messages, or summaries.

Derived metadata

Embeddings, labels, risk scores, summaries, features, and indexes.

These categories can overlap physically.

They should remain distinct logically because they differ in:

  • purpose;
  • authority;
  • sensitivity;
  • access;
  • retention;
  • deletion;
  • rights handling;
  • acceptable reuse.

4. The System of Record and the System of Influence

A system of record is the authoritative source.

An AI system often creates systems of influence:

  • vector indexes;
  • caches;
  • embeddings;
  • memory;
  • fine-tuned models;
  • summaries;
  • agent state;
  • evaluation sets.

A system of influence may shape decisions without being authoritative.

That creates a dangerous ambiguity.

Example:

HR System of Record
       ↓
Employee Profile Index
       ↓
Assistant Memory
       ↓
Manager Recommendation

If the employee record changes but the index or memory does not, the AI system may continue acting on stale information.

Architectural principle — Derived does not mean harmless

Any artifact that can influence a claim, decision, action, or future model behaviour belongs in the data-governance boundary.

5. Data Actors

For each use, identify:

  • data subject — the person the data concerns;
  • controller or accountable organisation — determines purpose and means;
  • processor or service provider — processes on another’s behalf;
  • data owner — accountable for organisational use and quality;
  • steward — operates definitions, access, and lifecycle;
  • producer — creates or supplies the data;
  • consumer — uses it;
  • model or agent — probabilistic consumer and transformer;
  • third party — external recipient or supplier;
  • rights owner — handles individual requests and recourse.

These are governance roles.

They should map to real technical identities and workflows.

Part II — Purpose and Authority

6. The Data Purpose Contract

This handbook introduces the Data Purpose Contract:

data_use_id: employee_assistant_memory_v2
purpose: remember user-approved communication preferences
data_subject: employee
source: explicit_user_input
authority:
  legal_or_policy_owner: privacy_office
  user_choice: opt_in
permitted_uses:
  - personalise_future_employee_assistant_sessions
prohibited_uses:
  - model_training
  - performance_scoring
  - manager_reporting
sensitivity: internal_personal
scope:
  subject: individual_employee
  tenant: employer_uk
retention: 180_days_from_last_use
rights:
  access: supported
  correction: supported
  deletion: supported
sharing:
  providers:
    - approved_memory_service
residency: uk
owner: employee_ai_product_owner

The contract is an original synthesis.

It binds:

  • purpose;
  • authority;
  • source;
  • scope;
  • permitted and prohibited reuse;
  • sensitivity;
  • sharing;
  • residency;
  • retention;
  • rights;
  • owner.

The contract should be machine-readable where runtime controls depend on it.

7. Purpose Limitation

Purpose answers:

Why is this processing occurring?

Examples:

  • answer a support request;
  • detect fraud;
  • evaluate system quality;
  • remember a preference;
  • train a model;
  • investigate an incident.

A vague purpose such as:

Improve AI.

is too broad to govern architecture.

A useful purpose should be:

  • specific enough to constrain reuse;
  • connected to an accountable outcome;
  • understandable to affected people;
  • testable through controls and evidence.

GDPR purpose limitation requires personal data to be collected for specified, explicit, legitimate purposes and not further processed incompatibly.[1]

The legal interpretation varies by jurisdiction.

The architecture need is universal:

Record why the data exists and prevent silent purpose expansion.

8. Authority Is Not the Same as Availability

A dataset may be technically accessible.

That does not establish authority to use it.

Authority may depend on:

  • consent;
  • contract;
  • legal obligation;
  • legitimate interest;
  • public task;
  • employment context;
  • licence;
  • organisational policy;
  • user choice;
  • research approval.

The architecture should preserve:

  • source;
  • original collection purpose;
  • applicable authority;
  • restrictions;
  • expiry;
  • withdrawal;
  • contractual terms.

EDPB Opinion 28/2024 emphasises case-by-case assessment of personal-data use in AI models, including expectations, necessity, legitimate-interest balancing, anonymity, and the consequences of unlawfully processed development data.[5]

This is not a universal lawful-basis recipe.

Qualified legal and privacy owners must decide applicability.

9. Secondary Use

Secondary use occurs when data collected for one purpose is used for another.

Examples:

  • support conversations used for training;
  • incident traces used for employee performance;
  • customer documents used to evaluate a new model;
  • memory used for advertising;
  • production prompts used in a public benchmark.

Before secondary use, ask:

  1. Is the new purpose compatible and authorised?
  2. Would the individual reasonably expect it?
  3. Is the data necessary?
  4. Can the use be isolated or anonymised?
  5. Are rights and notices preserved?
  6. Does the provider contract permit it?
  7. Does the risk change?
  8. Is a new impact assessment required?

Architecture smell — Improvement as universal consent

A broad claim that data is used to “improve the service” becomes authority for unrelated training, analytics, evaluation, and product development.

Part III — The Data Lifecycle Control Plane

10. Lifecycle

A useful lifecycle is:

Purpose
  ↓
Requirement
  ↓
Collection and Authority
  ↓
Qualification and Classification
  ↓
Transformation and Derivation
  ↓
Use and Sharing
  ↓
Storage and Access
  ↓
Retention and Deletion
  ↓
Evidence and Recourse

This handbook calls the governing layer around that lifecycle the Data Lifecycle Control Plane.

It includes:

  • purpose contracts;
  • classification;
  • access policy;
  • lineage;
  • consent or authority records;
  • retention rules;
  • residency;
  • deletion orchestration;
  • rights workflows;
  • evidence.

It is an original synthesis.

The control plane does not require one central database.

It requires consistent control across distributed data paths.

11. Data Zones

Possible zones:

Authoritative zone

Systems of record and approved source documents.

Preparation zone

Cleaning, labelling, transformation, and quality checks.

Model-development zone

Training, validation, and experimentation.

Evaluation zone

Golden, regression, challenge, and holdout data.

Retrieval zone

Indexes and query-accessible evidence.

Runtime context zone

Data assembled for a specific inference.

Memory zone

Approved retained user or task information.

Telemetry zone

Operational and evaluation records.

Quarantine zone

Data suspected of poisoning, rights conflict, malware, or unauthorised use.

Deletion-pending zone

Data and derived artifacts awaiting propagation and verification.

Zones should have:

  • purpose;
  • identities;
  • ingress;
  • egress;
  • controls;
  • retention;
  • owner.

12. Lineage

Lineage connects a derived artifact to:

  • source;
  • transformation;
  • time;
  • version;
  • authority;
  • owner;
  • consumers.

Example:

Customer Email
   ↓ parsed by parser_v4
Structured Case
   ↓ redacted by policy_12
Training Candidate
   ↓ approved in dataset_7
Fine-Tune Example
   ↓ used in model_ft_3
Production Model

Lineage supports:

  • quality;
  • rights;
  • deletion;
  • incident response;
  • reproducibility;
  • licensing;
  • audit.

A model card without dataset lineage is incomplete.

13. Data Contracts

A data contract can define:

  • schema;
  • meaning;
  • producer;
  • quality;
  • sensitivity;
  • authority;
  • allowed purpose;
  • retention;
  • residency;
  • lineage fields;
  • change policy.

Schema compatibility does not establish purpose compatibility.

Part IV — Data Minimisation

14. Minimisation Is a Design Activity

Data minimisation asks whether data is:

  • adequate;
  • relevant;
  • limited to what is necessary.

It should be applied at every boundary.

Collection minimisation

Do not collect fields without a defined purpose.

Storage minimisation

Do not persist transient context unnecessarily.

Retrieval minimisation

Return only evidence needed for the task.

Prompt minimisation

Do not send full records when selected fields suffice.

Tool minimisation

Expose only required response data.

Memory minimisation

Store only approved durable facts.

Telemetry minimisation

Prefer identifiers and structured metadata where full content is unnecessary.

Retention minimisation

Delete when purpose ends.

The ICO’s current UK guidance treats data protection by design and default as considering privacy from the start and implementing technical and organisational measures throughout processing.[6]

15. Minimisation Versus Data Quality

AI teams sometimes argue:

More data always improves quality.

More data can improve:

  • coverage;
  • representativeness;
  • rare-case detection;
  • evaluation power.

It can also increase:

  • privacy exposure;
  • bias;
  • stale information;
  • irrelevant context;
  • attack surface;
  • retention burden;
  • cost.

The architecture should record the trade-off.

Example:

Need:
  evaluate accessibility performance

Minimum data:
  interaction mode and task success

Not required:
  employee name, manager, full conversation

Additional protected sample:
  reviewed under separate assessment

Data quality and minimisation are not opposites.

They require purpose-specific selection.

16. Context Minimisation

Before model invocation:

  1. Identify the exact reasoning need.
  2. select necessary fields.
  3. remove unrelated identifiers.
  4. enforce tenant and subject scope.
  5. redact or tokenise secrets.
  6. label trust and sensitivity.
  7. set provider eligibility.
  8. define retention.

Example:

Weak:

Send the entire customer account and five years of contact history.

Stronger:

Send the current case, relevant entitlement, last two related interactions, and policy passages.

17. Telemetry Minimisation

Operational teams need enough information to diagnose failures.

They do not automatically need:

  • every prompt;
  • every document;
  • every personal identifier;
  • every model output.

Use layers:

Baseline metadata

  • task ID;
  • route;
  • model;
  • latency;
  • token count;
  • tool;
  • status;
  • policy result.

Protected diagnostic content

Available only for sampled or incident cases under restricted access.

Evidence identifiers

References to source data rather than copies.

Redacted content

Sensitive fields removed or tokenised.

Time-bounded capture

Enabled temporarily during investigation.

Part V — Training and Evaluation Data

18. Data Acquisition

For training or fine-tuning, record:

  • source;
  • collection method;
  • licence;
  • terms;
  • personal-data status;
  • original purpose;
  • consent or authority;
  • geography;
  • age;
  • representativeness;
  • restrictions;
  • removal mechanism.

“Publicly accessible” does not automatically mean:

  • anonymous;
  • licensed for every use;
  • expected to be used for training;
  • free of sensitive data;
  • accurate.

The EDPB specifically identifies public availability, relationship, source, collection context, future uses, and individuals’ awareness as relevant factors in assessing expectations.[5]

19. Training, Validation, and Test Separation

Keep roles explicit.

Training

Changes model parameters.

Validation

Supports tuning and development choices.

Test or holdout

Provides independent evidence.

Privacy consequences differ.

A production incident case added to training may also remain in a regression set.

Lineage should record both roles.

The EU AI Act’s Article 10 provides a current regulatory example for high-risk systems, requiring appropriate governance of training, validation, and testing data, including origin, preparation, assumptions, suitability, gaps, bias, and contextual representativeness.[7]

20. Personal Data in Models

A model may be exposed to personal data through:

  • pretraining;
  • fine-tuning;
  • retrieval;
  • prompt context;
  • memory.

Questions include:

  • Can individuals be identified from the model?
  • Can training data be extracted?
  • Does the model reproduce rare sequences?
  • Is the model accessible publicly?
  • What mitigations and access controls exist?
  • Can affected data be isolated?
  • Is the model considered anonymous?

EDPB Opinion 28/2024 says model anonymity requires a case-by-case assessment and that it should be very unlikely both to identify individuals and to extract their personal data through queries.[5]

Do not describe a model as anonymous merely because records are not stored in rows.

21. Evaluation Data Privacy

Evaluation sets may contain:

  • sensitive production cases;
  • failures;
  • adversarial content;
  • user complaints;
  • human labels.

Controls:

  • purpose contract;
  • restricted access;
  • pseudonymisation;
  • sampling;
  • retention;
  • separation from training;
  • secure annotation;
  • rights handling;
  • provenance.

A golden set can become a high-value privacy target.

22. Annotation

Human annotation can expose data to:

  • employees;
  • contractors;
  • external platforms;
  • model-assisted labelling services.

Define:

  • minimum fields;
  • location;
  • confidentiality;
  • access;
  • reviewer training;
  • quality;
  • deletion;
  • subcontractors;
  • incident process.

Part VI — Retrieval, Context, and Memory

23. Retrieval Data

Chapter 5 established that relevance is not authority.

Privacy adds:

  • relevance is not permission;
  • an index is a derived copy;
  • embeddings can reveal associations;
  • access changes must propagate;
  • deletion must reach chunks and vectors;
  • cache keys need tenant and policy boundaries.

A retrieval index should preserve:

  • source ID;
  • permission;
  • tenant;
  • purpose;
  • sensitivity;
  • effective date;
  • deletion state;
  • lineage.

24. Model Context

Context is temporary from the model’s perspective.

It may still persist in:

  • provider logs;
  • application traces;
  • retries;
  • cache;
  • screenshots;
  • support tools;
  • model state during the session.

Architecture questions:

  • Which provider receives the context?
  • Is the request retained?
  • Is it used for training?
  • Which region processes it?
  • Is prompt caching enabled?
  • Which content appears in telemetry?
  • Can the user request deletion?

25. Memory Write Policy

A memory write should be an explicit event.

Record:

  • candidate fact;
  • source;
  • subject;
  • purpose;
  • user visibility;
  • sensitivity;
  • confidence;
  • scope;
  • expiry;
  • correction;
  • deletion.

Example:

memory_candidate:
  value: prefers concise weekly summaries
  source: explicit_user_statement
  purpose: response_personalisation
  sensitivity: low
  scope: user
  retention_days: 180
  requires_confirmation: true

Do not persist:

  • model speculation;
  • unverified allegations;
  • secrets;
  • transient task details;
  • protected attributes without a justified purpose;
  • another person’s data.

26. Memory and Purpose Drift

Memory can make a future task use data outside the context in which it was provided.

Example:

User mentions a health condition while requesting accessibility help.

Later:

Sales agent uses the condition to alter an offer.

The memory system must enforce:

  • purpose;
  • agent eligibility;
  • subject;
  • sensitivity;
  • scope;
  • expiry.

The fact being remembered does not authorise every future agent to use it.

27. Cross-Tenant Isolation

Isolate:

  • retrieval indexes;
  • namespaces;
  • cache;
  • session;
  • memory;
  • vector metadata;
  • logs;
  • evaluation samples;
  • fine-tunes;
  • exports.

Test for:

  • direct access;
  • semantic retrieval leakage;
  • cache collision;
  • prompt-prefix reuse;
  • telemetry search;
  • support access;
  • backup restoration.

Architecture smell — Tenant ID as privacy architecture

A tenant field exists, but derived stores, caches, traces, and evaluation pipelines do not enforce it consistently.

Part VII — Retention and Deletion

28. Retention Schedule

Retention should be bound to purpose.

Example:

Data role Retention
Runtime prompt no application persistence
Security audit metadata 12 months
Incident diagnostic sample incident closure + 90 days
User-approved memory 180 days since last use
Evaluation failure case until superseded, then reviewed
Training candidate 30 days pending approval
Backup encrypted rotation, 35 days

Retention should also define:

  • legal hold;
  • deletion method;
  • owner;
  • verification;
  • exception;
  • restoration behaviour.

29. The Deletion Propagation Map

This handbook introduces the Deletion Propagation Map:

Deletion or Restriction Request
          ↓
Authoritative Source
          ↓
Derived Records and Features
          ↓
Indexes and Embeddings
          ↓
Caches and Context Stores
          ↓
Memory and Agent State
          ↓
Telemetry and Evaluation Sets
          ↓
Training and Fine-Tune Artifacts
          ↓
Backups and Archives
          ↓
Verification and Recourse

It is an original synthesis.

A deletion workflow should:

  1. identify the subject and scope;
  2. validate the request and exceptions;
  3. locate source and derived artifacts;
  4. stop new processing where required;
  5. remove or restrict accessible copies;
  6. update indexes and caches;
  7. address memory and state;
  8. assess model artifacts;
  9. handle backups;
  10. record completion and residual limitations.

30. Deletion from Models

Deleting a training record does not automatically reverse its influence on model parameters.

Possible responses include:

  • retrain without the data;
  • apply validated machine-unlearning techniques;
  • replace or retire the fine-tune;
  • restrict model access;
  • suppress known outputs;
  • remove retrieval or memory paths;
  • strengthen extraction controls;
  • document residual risk;
  • obtain legal and privacy decision.

The correct action depends on:

  • legal obligation;
  • model exposure;
  • extraction risk;
  • consequence;
  • technical feasibility;
  • alternative controls.

Do not promise deletion from model influence unless the process has been validated.

Architectural principle — Deletion is an evidence claim

A deletion request is complete only when the organisation can state which artifacts were removed, which were restricted, which remain, why they remain, and how residual risk is controlled.

31. Backups

Immediate deletion from every backup may be impractical.

Controls can include:

  • short rotation;
  • encryption;
  • access restriction;
  • no ordinary restoration;
  • deletion reapplication after restore;
  • legal hold tracking;
  • documented delay.

The restoration process must not silently reintroduce deleted data.

32. Caches

Caches can retain:

  • prompt prefixes;
  • responses;
  • retrieval results;
  • tool responses;
  • embeddings.

Keys should include:

  • tenant;
  • user or subject where required;
  • purpose;
  • model;
  • policy;
  • data version;
  • permission version.

Deletion or permission change should invalidate relevant cache entries.

33. Rights Workflow

Depending on applicable law and policy, individuals may need:

  • access;
  • correction;
  • deletion;
  • restriction;
  • objection;
  • portability;
  • explanation;
  • human review;
  • complaint.

The system needs:

  • identity verification;
  • data discovery;
  • derived-artifact mapping;
  • response deadline;
  • exceptions;
  • owner;
  • evidence;
  • recourse.

The ICO’s AI guidance includes individual rights, accountability, transparency, lawfulness, fairness, security, and minimisation. As of 4 September 2026, the ICO states that this guidance is under review because of changes made by the UK’s Data (Use and Access) Act.[8][9]

Current legal interpretation must therefore be checked at the time of use.

Part VIII — Residency, Sovereignty, and Sharing

34. Residency

Residency asks:

Where is data stored or processed?

Map:

  • source storage;
  • model inference;
  • cache;
  • retrieval;
  • telemetry;
  • annotation;
  • support;
  • backup;
  • disaster recovery.

A “regional endpoint” may still involve:

  • global support;
  • metadata transfer;
  • subprocessors;
  • control-plane data;
  • cross-region failover.

35. Sovereignty

Sovereignty is broader than location.

It can include:

  • governing law;
  • operational control;
  • cryptographic control;
  • personnel access;
  • supplier dependency;
  • extraterritorial obligation;
  • ability to exit.

A self-hosted model can still depend on:

  • foreign packages;
  • external model weights;
  • remote telemetry;
  • global support.

36. Transfer Map

Record:

  • exporter;
  • importer;
  • data;
  • purpose;
  • country;
  • legal mechanism;
  • subprocessor;
  • encryption;
  • access;
  • retention;
  • onward transfer;
  • exit.

The transfer map should connect to the Data Purpose Contract.

37. Third-Party Providers

Assess:

  • data used for training;
  • retention;
  • region;
  • subprocessors;
  • human access;
  • abuse monitoring;
  • prompt caching;
  • deletion;
  • model change;
  • incident notice;
  • audit;
  • export;
  • exit.

Contract claims should be verified against actual configuration.

Part IX — Privacy-Enhancing Technologies

38. PETs Are Tactics

Privacy-enhancing technologies include:

  • encryption;
  • pseudonymisation;
  • tokenisation;
  • access control;
  • trusted execution;
  • secure multiparty computation;
  • federated learning;
  • differential privacy;
  • synthetic data.

A PET should address a defined privacy problem.

It should not be added as a generic badge.

39. Encryption

Encryption protects data:

  • at rest;
  • in transit;
  • sometimes during computation.

It does not prevent:

  • authorised misuse;
  • overcollection;
  • purpose drift;
  • model memorisation after decryption;
  • inappropriate output.

Key ownership and access matter.

40. Pseudonymisation and Tokenisation

Replace direct identifiers with controlled references.

Benefits:

  • reduce ordinary exposure;
  • separate identity from task data;
  • support controlled re-linking.

Risks:

  • quasi-identifiers enable re-identification;
  • mapping table compromise;
  • token reused across purposes;
  • linkability across systems.

Pseudonymised data remains personal data when re-identification is reasonably possible.

41. Anonymisation

Anonymisation aims to make identification no longer reasonably likely.

It is context dependent.

Consider:

  • auxiliary data;
  • model queries;
  • uniqueness;
  • future techniques;
  • access;
  • release scale.

EDPB’s AI-model opinion treats anonymity as a case-by-case assessment and requires very low likelihood of identification and extraction.[5]

Do not use “anonymised” as a synonym for removing names.

42. Differential Privacy

Differential privacy provides a mathematical way to bound how much the output of an analysis changes because one person’s data is present.

Possible uses:

  • aggregate analytics;
  • statistics;
  • privacy-preserving training;
  • synthetic-data generation.

Key design choices:

  • privacy unit;
  • neighbouring datasets;
  • epsilon and delta;
  • composition;
  • clipping;
  • randomness;
  • implementation;
  • utility.

NIST SP 800-226 provides final guidance for evaluating differential-privacy guarantees and warns that implementation choices and privacy hazards matter alongside the mathematical claim.[10]

Constraint

Differential privacy is not:

  • encryption;
  • universal anonymity;
  • protection for arbitrary raw-record retrieval;
  • useful without a managed privacy budget.

43. Synthetic Data

Synthetic data can reduce direct use of real records.

It can still:

  • reproduce training examples;
  • preserve sensitive correlations;
  • underrepresent rare groups;
  • hide quality problems;
  • be re-identifiable;
  • retain licence or source concerns.

Evaluate:

  • privacy leakage;
  • membership inference;
  • similarity;
  • utility;
  • subgroup performance;
  • provenance.

Architecture smell — Synthetic means safe

Generated data is treated as non-personal without testing how it was produced or what it reveals.

44. Federated Learning

Federated learning moves some training to distributed data locations and aggregates updates.

It can reduce central collection.

It may still leak information through:

  • gradients;
  • updates;
  • metadata;
  • malicious participants.

It also introduces:

  • coordination;
  • device trust;
  • poisoning;
  • uneven data;
  • operational complexity.

Often it is combined with secure aggregation and differential privacy.

45. Confidential Computing

Trusted execution environments can reduce exposure during computation.

Consider:

  • threat model;
  • attestation;
  • key release;
  • provider trust;
  • side channels;
  • debugging;
  • availability;
  • cost.

Confidential computing protects a processing boundary.

It does not decide whether the processing purpose is acceptable.

46. PET Selection

Use a table:

Privacy problem Candidate tactic
Provider should not see direct identity tokenisation or pseudonymisation
Aggregate statistics reveal individuals differential privacy
Raw data cannot leave organisation federated or local processing
Operator access during processing confidential computing
Unnecessary prompt fields minimisation and field selection
Cross-tenant retrieval identity-aware filtering and isolation

Select using:

  • threat;
  • purpose;
  • data;
  • quality;
  • cost;
  • operating capability;
  • residual risk.

Part X — Privacy Evaluation and Operations

47. Privacy Evaluation

Test:

  • purpose enforcement;
  • data minimisation;
  • permission;
  • cross-tenant isolation;
  • memory write;
  • retention;
  • deletion;
  • rights response;
  • model extraction;
  • provider configuration;
  • telemetry redaction;
  • PET implementation.

Privacy tests should include the complete workflow.

48. Privacy Metrics

Examples:

  • unnecessary fields per request;
  • prompts containing sensitive data;
  • unauthorised retrieval;
  • cross-tenant leakage;
  • memory writes without approval;
  • expired data;
  • deletion completion time;
  • unverified deletion artifacts;
  • rights-request completion;
  • re-identification risk;
  • provider-region violations;
  • diagnostic content access.

Metrics need owners and responses.

49. Privacy Control Evidence

Examples:

  • data-flow map;
  • purpose contracts;
  • access-policy results;
  • retention jobs;
  • deletion ledger;
  • rights cases;
  • provider configuration;
  • model-extraction tests;
  • privacy-budget records;
  • incident exercises.

ISO/IEC 27701:2025 frames privacy management as an accountable, continually improving system for PII controllers and processors.[4]

Evidence should therefore be current, not collected only for certification.

50. Privacy Incident

Possible incidents:

  • sensitive prompt sent to unapproved model;
  • cross-tenant retrieval;
  • memory stores restricted attribute;
  • deleted data restored from backup;
  • production traces exposed;
  • model reproduces personal data;
  • evaluation vendor receives unapproved records;
  • provider uses content outside contract.

Response:

  1. contain processing;
  2. preserve evidence;
  3. identify subjects and data;
  4. map derived artifacts;
  5. revoke access;
  6. assess notification;
  7. delete or quarantine;
  8. repair controls;
  9. add evaluation;
  10. verify residual effects.

Part XI — Worked Example: Employee Knowledge Assistant

51. Scenario

An organisation deploys an assistant that can:

  • answer HR and IT questions;
  • read employee profile fields;
  • summarise support cases;
  • remember preferences;
  • improve from feedback.

52. Data Roles

Source

  • HR system;
  • policy documents;
  • support platform.

Retrieval

  • permission-aware policy index.

Context

  • question;
  • relevant profile fields;
  • approved policy passages.

Memory

  • user-approved communication preferences.

Telemetry

  • route;
  • citations;
  • latency;
  • policy outcome;
  • sampled redacted failures.

Evaluation

  • expert-authored cases;
  • selected production failures after review.

Not permitted

  • employee questions used for model training by default;
  • manager access to private assistant memory;
  • full HR record in every prompt.

53. Purpose Contracts

Profile use:

Determine applicable location and employment category for the current policy answer.

Memory use:

Personalise response style for the employee.

Evaluation use:

Detect policy-answer failures using approved, minimised examples.

Each has different retention and access.

54. Context Assembly

Employee Question
      ↓
Task Classification
      ↓
Required Profile Fields
      ↓
Permission Check
      ↓
Policy Retrieval
      ↓
Redacted Context
      ↓
Model
      ↓
Citation and Privacy Validation

The model never receives unrelated salary, health, or disciplinary data.

55. Deletion Example

The employee deletes a remembered preference.

The workflow removes:

  • active memory record;
  • memory index;
  • cache;
  • future context eligibility.

It does not delete:

  • required security audit metadata;
  • the original conversation where retention is lawfully required,

unless those artifacts are within scope.

The completion record explains the distinction.

56. Evaluation

Test:

  • unnecessary field disclosure;
  • policy permission;
  • memory isolation;
  • deletion;
  • cross-employee access;
  • provider region;
  • telemetry redaction;
  • user understanding.

Part XII — Architecture Review

57. Scenario

A company proposes a central AI data lake.

It will contain:

  • production prompts;
  • tool results;
  • employee documents;
  • customer conversations;
  • generated reports;
  • evaluation labels;
  • agent memory.

The platform team says:

  • data will be encrypted;
  • names will be removed;
  • all data may improve models;
  • retention will be indefinite;
  • every AI team can query it.

58. ARB Findings

Finding 1 — Purpose is undefined

“Improve models” authorises unlimited secondary use.

Finding 2 — Data roles are collapsed

Training, evaluation, telemetry, memory, and evidence have different requirements.

Finding 3 — De-identification is weak

Removing names does not establish anonymity.

Finding 4 — Access is excessive

Every team can access unrelated data.

Finding 5 — Retention is unjustified

Indefinite storage is not connected to purpose.

Finding 6 — Deletion is impossible

No lineage or propagation path exists.

Finding 7 — Encryption is overclaimed

Encryption does not prevent authorised misuse.

Finding 8 — Tenant and subject scope are missing

Derived indexes and exports may cross boundaries.

59. Recommended Redesign

  • data-role inventory;
  • purpose contracts;
  • separate zones;
  • subject and tenant scope;
  • minimised production sampling;
  • governed evaluation sets;
  • opt-in memory;
  • provider eligibility;
  • lineage;
  • retention schedules;
  • deletion orchestration;
  • rights workflow;
  • PETs for defined risks;
  • independent privacy testing.

Part XIII — Architecture Smells

60. AI Data Lake by Default

Every prompt, document, trace, and output enters one reusable store.

61. Improvement as Universal Purpose

A vague improvement claim authorises training, analytics, and evaluation.

62. Public Means Permitted

Accessible data is assumed to be lawful, expected, licensed, and appropriate.

63. Name Removal as Anonymity

Direct identifiers are removed while linkability and extraction remain.

64. Encryption as Privacy

Confidentiality is treated as proof of purpose limitation and minimisation.

65. Prompt as Temporary

Model context is assumed not to persist anywhere.

66. Memory by Convenience

Useful details are stored without purpose, scope, user control, or expiry.

67. Telemetry as Exemption

Operational need becomes permission to retain full content indefinitely.

68. Deletion at the Source

The authoritative record is deleted while indexes, caches, memory, traces, and models remain unexamined.

69. Synthetic Means Safe

Generated data is assumed to carry no privacy or representational risk.

70. Tenant ID as Isolation

A field exists but derived systems do not consistently enforce it.

71. Residency by Endpoint Label

A regional endpoint is treated as proof that all processing and support remain in the region.

Part XIV — Interview Preparation

72. Foundational Questions

Question 1

What is data minimisation in an AI system?

Collect, retrieve, place in context, persist, and expose only the data necessary for a defined purpose.

Question 2

Why should training, retrieval, memory, and telemetry data be governed separately?

They serve different purposes, influence different behaviours, and have different authority, access, retention, deletion, and rights implications.

Question 3

What is purpose limitation?

Data should be collected and used for specified purposes, with incompatible secondary uses requiring new authority and assessment.

Question 4

What is data lineage?

The trace from a source through transformations and derived artifacts to its uses and consumers.

Question 5

Is encrypted data anonymous?

No. Encryption protects access. The data remains identifiable when decrypted.

73. Senior-Level Questions

Question 6

How would you implement deletion for a RAG system?

Delete or restrict the source, derived chunks, embeddings, metadata, caches, memory, evaluation copies, and exports; handle backups; verify propagation.

Question 7

How is pseudonymisation different from anonymisation?

Pseudonymisation replaces identifiers but permits controlled re-linking. Anonymisation aims to make identification no longer reasonably likely.

Question 8

Can personal data remain in model weights?

A model can memorise or reproduce training data. Assess extraction and identification risk, access, lineage, and available retraining or unlearning controls.

Question 9

How do you minimise telemetry without losing observability?

Collect structured metadata by default, protect sampled content, use evidence identifiers, redact sensitive fields, restrict access, and set short retention.

Question 10

When is synthetic data a privacy control?

When generation and testing demonstrate reduced disclosure risk while preserving required utility. Synthetic origin alone is not sufficient.

Question 11

What is differential privacy?

A mathematical framework for bounding how much an output changes because one privacy unit’s data is included, subject to explicit parameters and composition.

Question 12

How do you prevent memory from violating purpose limitation?

Use explicit memory-write policy, purpose and agent scope, user visibility, sensitivity, expiry, correction, and deletion.

74. Principal-Level Questions

Question 13

How would you design an enterprise AI data control plane?

Use purpose contracts, classification, lineage, access, provider eligibility, residency, retention, rights, deletion orchestration, evidence, and product ownership across distributed data zones.

Question 14

How do you reconcile minimisation with representativeness?

Define the decision and affected population, collect only attributes needed to measure and mitigate material risk, isolate sensitive evaluation, and document trade-offs.

Question 15

How do you handle a deletion request when data was used to fine-tune a model?

Trace exposure, stop new use, remove accessible copies, assess extraction and legal risk, retrain or apply validated unlearning where necessary, constrain or replace the model, and document residual limitations.

Question 16

What does data sovereignty add beyond residency?

Control over law, access, operations, keys, suppliers, support, and exit—not only physical location.

Question 17

How do you evaluate model anonymity?

Case-by-case assessment of identification and extraction likelihood under realistic access, auxiliary data, attacks, and future use.

Question 18

Which privacy controls belong in the platform versus the product?

Platform: identity, classification, provider eligibility, encryption, retention, lineage, deletion infrastructure, and audit. Product: purpose, minimum data, affected-party expectations, rights, thresholds, and outcomes.

Part XV — Whiteboard Challenge

75. Design Data and Privacy Architecture for a Personal Enterprise Assistant

The assistant can:

  • read email;
  • access calendar;
  • search documents;
  • remember preferences;
  • draft messages;
  • generate reports;
  • improve from user feedback.

Constraints

  • multiple employers and tenants;
  • confidential documents;
  • external model providers;
  • regional requirements;
  • long-running agents;
  • user deletion requests;
  • evaluation from production failures.

Discuss

  1. Identify every data role.
  2. Create purpose contracts.
  3. Draw the Data Lifecycle Control Plane.
  4. Define source and derived lineage.
  5. Minimise context.
  6. Separate memory from authoritative evidence.
  7. Design tenant isolation.
  8. Define provider eligibility and residency.
  9. Define telemetry layers.
  10. Create retention schedules.
  11. Create the Deletion Propagation Map.
  12. Address fine-tunes and backups.
  13. Select PETs.
  14. Design rights and recourse.
  15. Define privacy evaluation.
  16. Define incident response.

Strong-answer characteristics

  • purpose before collection;
  • separate data roles;
  • no broad training default;
  • permission-aware retrieval;
  • opt-in scoped memory;
  • structured telemetry;
  • derived-artifact lineage;
  • cross-tenant tests;
  • realistic deletion claims;
  • provider and transfer map;
  • rights workflow;
  • privacy assurance evidence.

Part XVI — Questions to Take Back to Your Team

  1. Which data uses have no explicit purpose?
  2. Which data is technically available but not authorised?
  3. Are training and evaluation data separated?
  4. Which production content enters telemetry?
  5. What does the provider retain?
  6. Which context fields are unnecessary?
  7. Which memories were never approved?
  8. Can access revocation reach the retrieval index?
  9. Can a tenant identifier collision leak data?
  10. Which derived artifacts lack lineage?
  11. How does deletion reach embeddings and caches?
  12. What happens to deleted data after backup restoration?
  13. Can model outputs reproduce personal data?
  14. Is synthetic data privacy tested?
  15. Is differential privacy configured and accounted correctly?
  16. Which subprocessors process prompts?
  17. Does residency cover inference, support, and telemetry?
  18. Can individuals access, correct, and challenge data use?
  19. Which privacy controls are continuously monitored?
  20. Can we prove what was deleted and what remains?

Architect’s Notebook — Privacy Is Control Over Association

Privacy is not simply hiding a value.

It is controlling:

  • who can associate the value with a person;
  • which purpose the association serves;
  • which system can use it;
  • how long the association persists;
  • whether it can be corrected;
  • whether it can influence a future decision;
  • whether the person can challenge the use.

AI increases the number of associations.

Architecture must make them visible and governable.

From the Architect’s Desk

AI systems create copies that do not look like copies: embeddings, summaries, labels, memories, checkpoints, fine-tunes, and evaluation cases. Each can preserve influence after the source record changes.

Do not ask only where personal data is stored. Ask where it can affect behaviour.

Minimise before the prompt, not only before the database. Bind memory to a purpose. Treat telemetry as a data product with its own owner and retention. Make deletion a distributed workflow with evidence—not a single SQL statement.

Privacy architecture is the ability to explain why data is present, who can use it, how it became derived, when it will disappear, and what a person can do when the system gets it wrong.

If I Were the Architect

You inherit an AI platform that stores:

  • all prompts;
  • all outputs;
  • tool results;
  • vector indexes;
  • agent memory;
  • evaluation cases;

for “future improvement.”

There is no lineage or deletion workflow.

What do you do first?

Do not begin with a new anonymisation tool.

  1. Inventory data roles and purposes.
  2. stop unauthorised secondary use.
  3. define Data Purpose Contracts.
  4. classify and separate zones.
  5. minimise new collection and telemetry.
  6. add lineage to derived artifacts.
  7. define memory-write policy.
  8. implement retention schedules.
  9. build deletion propagation.
  10. assess provider, residency, and transfer.
  11. test cross-tenant isolation and model extraction.
  12. create rights and recourse workflows.

The first privacy control is deciding which data should never have entered the system.

Key Takeaways

  • AI data is a portfolio of source, training, validation, evaluation, retrieval, context, state, memory, telemetry, generated, and derived data.
  • Derived artifacts remain in scope when they influence claims, decisions, actions, or future model behaviour.
  • Every material use needs purpose, authority, scope, retention, rights, sharing, residency, and ownership.
  • The Data Purpose Contract makes those boundaries explicit.
  • Purpose limitation prevents “improvement” from becoming universal reuse.
  • The Data Lifecycle Control Plane governs distributed data paths.
  • Lineage supports quality, deletion, rights, licensing, and incident response.
  • Data minimisation applies at collection, retrieval, prompt, tool, memory, telemetry, and retention boundaries.
  • More data is not automatically better data.
  • Public availability does not establish permission or expected use.
  • Training, validation, test, and evaluation roles should remain explicit.
  • A model is not anonymous merely because it does not expose database rows.
  • Retrieval indexes, embeddings, caches, context, and memory are derived data stores.
  • Memory requires purpose, subject, scope, user control, and expiry.
  • Cross-tenant isolation must cover every derived store.
  • Retention belongs to purpose, not storage cost.
  • The Deletion Propagation Map turns deletion into a system-wide workflow.
  • Deleting source data does not automatically reverse model influence.
  • Deletion is an evidence claim about what was removed, restricted, retained, and controlled.
  • Residency does not equal sovereignty.
  • PETs should be selected for a defined privacy problem.
  • Encryption does not enforce minimisation or purpose.
  • Differential privacy requires a correctly designed privacy unit, parameters, composition, and implementation.
  • Synthetic data is not automatically safe.
  • Privacy must be evaluated and operated continuously.
  • Privacy is control over association, use, persistence, and recourse.

Decision ID: ARB-CH-011
Subject: Chapter 11 — Data and Privacy Architecture for AI Systems
Outcome: Accepted with constraints for user review

Primary contribution:
Treats AI data as purpose-bound lifecycle classes and connects collection,
authority, lineage, minimisation, retrieval, context, memory, telemetry,
retention, deletion, residency, privacy technologies, and recourse.

Grounded foundations:
- GDPR processing principles.
- NIST Privacy Framework and privacy-engineering objectives.

- EDPB Opinion 28/2024 on personal data in AI models.
- ICO AI and data-protection guidance.

Original synthesis requiring explicit labelling:
- Data Purpose Contract.
- Data Lifecycle Control Plane.
- system-of-influence framing.
- Deletion Propagation Map.
- “derived does not mean harmless.”
- “deletion is an evidence claim.”
- “privacy is control over association.”

Constraints:
- Do not provide universal legal-basis conclusions.
- Do not claim public data is unrestricted.
- Do not claim pseudonymisation or encryption creates anonymity.
- Do not promise model unlearning without validated evidence.
- Keep provider and legal details in the living source layer.
- Require purpose and lineage for derived artifacts.
- Preserve affected-person rights and recourse.
- Keep privacy proportional to context while retaining minimum controls.
