Part IV - Enterprise Scale and Synthesis

Scale does not eliminate context. The enterprise challenge is to share the mechanisms that should be common without centralising the judgments that must remain local.

This part connects the handbook into an enterprise platform model and then tests that model across contrasting end-to-end architectures.

Chapter 12 - AI Platform Architecture

Shared capabilities, product boundaries, and enterprise scale

Related chapters: Chapters 6, 8, 10, 11, and 13

A good AI platform centralises mechanisms that should be consistent and reusable. It does not centralise domain judgment merely because the same model or framework appears in several products.

1. Why This Chapter Matters

The first AI product in an organisation often builds everything itself:

  • model access;
  • retrieval;
  • prompt storage;
  • tool connections;
  • evaluation;
  • tracing;
  • secrets;
  • rate limits;
  • approval flows;
  • cost reporting.

The second product does the same.

By the fifth product, organisations begin asking:

Should we create an AI platform?

The answer is often yes.

The next mistake is to centralise too much.

A platform team may try to own:

  • every prompt;
  • every workflow;
  • every evaluation threshold;
  • every knowledge base;
  • every agent;
  • every business approval rule.

The result is not a platform.

It is a central application team with too many customers.

At the opposite extreme, a platform may expose only:

Here are some API keys and a model endpoint.

Every product then rebuilds:

  • security;
  • evaluation;
  • observability;
  • cost attribution;
  • provider adapters;
  • tool governance;
  • privacy controls.

The result is a fragmented toolchain.

Platform engineering provides a useful general principle: treat the platform as a product for internal developers, provide self-service within a secure and governed framework, and progressively pave common paths rather than demanding that every team solve the same infrastructure problem independently.[1]

Current enterprise AI architectures are converging on shared capabilities. Microsoft Foundry supports multiple projects with isolated access while sharing selected model deployments, network controls, and connected services.[2] AWS’s multi-tenant generative-AI platform guidance describes shared model access, evaluation, prompts, telemetry, and governance as reusable building blocks for multiple lines of business.[3]

The important question is not:

Which vendor has the most complete AI platform?

It is:

Which organisational responsibilities are stable enough to become a shared contract, and which must remain owned by the product because context defines correctness?

The central argument of this chapter is:

AI platform architecture should standardise the path to safe, observable, economical AI while preserving product ownership of intent, domain logic, quality thresholds, authority, and outcomes.

2. Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

  • distinguish an AI platform from an AI product and an infrastructure bundle;
  • decide which capabilities belong in the platform and which remain in the product;
  • separate platform control planes from runtime data paths;
  • design stable platform contracts without forcing a lowest-common-denominator abstraction;
  • create model, evidence, evaluation, tool, identity, policy, workflow, data, privacy, observability, and cost shared capabilities;
  • use gateways appropriately without turning them into a monolith;
  • design multi-tenant isolation, quotas, noisy-neighbour controls, and dedicated escape paths;
  • create paved roads and self-service experiences;
  • define product and platform SLOs;
  • design showback and chargeback for AI consumption;
  • decide when to build, buy, compose, or expose a provider-native capability;
  • govern versions, migrations, and deprecation;
  • define team ownership and support models;
  • recognise platform failure modes;
  • evaluate whether the platform is creating reuse or coupling;
  • answer architecture interview questions about enterprise AI platforms, tenancy, gateways, shared controls, cost allocation, and platform-team boundaries.

Part I — What an AI Platform Is

3. Platform, Product, and Infrastructure

Infrastructure

Provides:

  • compute;
  • network;
  • storage;
  • identity substrate;
  • secrets;
  • databases;
  • clusters.

Infrastructure is necessary.

It does not tell an AI product:

  • which model may receive a sensitive request;
  • which evaluator must pass before release;
  • which tool requires approval;
  • how costs are attributed to a tenant.

AI platform

Provides reusable mechanisms and contracts for building and operating AI products.

Examples:

  • model access;
  • routing;
  • identity propagation;
  • policy enforcement;
  • tool registration;
  • evaluation execution;
  • tracing;
  • data controls;
  • durable runtime;
  • cost attribution.

AI product

Owns an outcome for users or the business.

It defines:

  • intent;
  • domain behaviour;
  • user experience;
  • workflow semantics;
  • quality requirements;
  • business authority;
  • domain evidence;
  • outcome metrics.

Architectural principle — A platform does not own the business outcome

The platform provides mechanisms. The product remains accountable for how those mechanisms are used to create an outcome.

4. Platform as Product

An internal platform has customers.

Those customers are commonly:

  • product teams;
  • engineers;
  • data scientists;
  • AI engineers;
  • security teams;
  • operators.

The platform should have:

  • product manager or accountable owner;
  • roadmap;
  • service boundaries;
  • SLOs;
  • support;
  • documentation;
  • adoption metrics;
  • feedback;
  • deprecation policy.

Microsoft’s platform-engineering guidance explicitly recommends a product mindset, self-service, asset inventories, paved paths, and measurement of the developer experience.[1][4]

A platform no one wants to use is not made successful by mandatory adoption.

Mandatory controls may still be required.

The user experience around those controls remains a product concern.

5. Shared Does Not Mean Centralised Everything

A capability is a strong shared candidate when it has:

  • common policy;
  • common protocol;
  • common infrastructure economics;
  • repeated implementation;
  • clear stable contract;
  • independent lifecycle;
  • strong security or governance value.

A capability is usually product-specific when it depends on:

  • business semantics;
  • domain thresholds;
  • customer experience;
  • workflow meaning;
  • local evidence;
  • business authority;
  • risk appetite;
  • outcome interpretation.

Part II — The Platform Product Boundary

6. The Platform Boundary Test

This handbook introduces the Platform Boundary Test.

Before moving a capability into the platform, ask:

  1. Invariant — What must remain consistent across products?
  2. Reuse — Is the mechanism materially repeated?
  3. Contract — Can it be exposed through a stable interface?
  4. Context — Does correctness depend on domain judgment?
  5. Control — Does centralisation improve security, privacy, governance, or reliability?
  6. Economics — Does sharing create meaningful scale or cost advantage?
  7. Isolation — Can tenants and failure domains remain isolated?
  8. Ownership — Can one team operate the capability with clear SLOs?
  9. Change — Can the capability evolve independently of products?
  10. Escape — Can exceptional products use a governed alternative?

It is an original synthesis.

A capability does not need to satisfy every condition.

The questions expose trade-offs.

7. Strong Platform Candidates

Model gateway and provider adapters

Shared:

  • authentication;
  • quota;
  • model registry;
  • approved-provider policy;
  • routing primitives;
  • cost metadata;
  • telemetry;
  • provider adaptation.

Product:

  • task route;
  • quality bar;
  • inference contract;
  • model escalation semantics.

Identity and credential brokering

Shared:

  • workload identity;
  • user-context propagation;
  • scoped token exchange;
  • secrets boundary;
  • common policy enforcement.

Product:

  • domain action authority;
  • approval semantics;
  • subject scope.

Observability

Shared:

  • trace transport;
  • telemetry schema;
  • correlation;
  • storage;
  • privacy controls;
  • dashboards primitives.

Product:

  • behavioural meaning;
  • outcome metric;
  • product-specific alert thresholds.

Evaluation execution

Shared:

  • dataset registry;
  • evaluator runtime;
  • experiment lineage;
  • comparison;
  • release integration.

Product:

  • golden cases;
  • error taxonomy;
  • acceptable thresholds;
  • human rubric;
  • outcome significance.

8. Weak Platform Candidates

Be cautious about centralising:

  • one universal system prompt;
  • one enterprise agent;
  • one generic memory model;
  • universal business approval;
  • global task taxonomy;
  • one quality threshold;
  • one retrieval corpus;
  • one domain ontology;
  • one “confidence score.”

These concepts are rarely invariant across every product.

Part III — The AI Platform Contract Stack

9. From Product Intent to Providers

This handbook introduces the AI Platform Contract Stack:

Product Intent and Domain Logic
              ↓
Product Workflow and Quality Contract
              ↓
Stable Platform Contracts
              ↓
Shared Control Planes
              ↓
Provider and Runtime Adapters
              ↓
Infrastructure and External Services
              ↓
Evidence, Evaluation, and Operations

The stack is an original synthesis.

Product intent and domain logic

Why the system exists.

Product workflow and quality contract

What the product must achieve and how success is judged.

Stable platform contracts

The interfaces products consume.

Shared control planes

Policy, identity, routing, evaluation, tooling, data, and operations.

Provider adapters

Translate into vendor- or runtime-specific capabilities.

Infrastructure

Compute, storage, network, model services, databases.

Evidence, evaluation, and operations

Close the loop back to product and platform decisions.

10. Control Plane and Data Plane

Control plane

Configures:

  • approved models;
  • policies;
  • tenants;
  • tools;
  • budgets;
  • datasets;
  • evaluation rules;
  • credentials;
  • retention;
  • routing policies;
  • observability destinations.

Data plane

Handles runtime:

  • prompts;
  • model calls;
  • retrieval;
  • tool calls;
  • agent messages;
  • generated outputs.

Separating them can improve:

  • governance;
  • change control;
  • availability;
  • audit.

But the control plane may still sit on the critical path for real-time authorisation.

Design its reliability accordingly.

Part IV — Model Access and Gateway Architecture

11. Why Use a Model Gateway?

A model gateway can centralise:

  • identity;
  • authentication;
  • quota;
  • provider selection;
  • model aliases;
  • routing;
  • retries;
  • circuit breaking;
  • content policy;
  • telemetry;
  • usage reporting;
  • cost allocation.

Azure’s current architecture guidance presents the gateway as an architectural pattern for offloading cross-cutting responsibilities while still preserving provider-specific functionality when necessary.[5][6]

12. What the Gateway Should Not Become

Avoid placing in one request proxy:

  • business workflow;
  • domain prompt;
  • retrieval;
  • human approval;
  • product state;
  • domain validation;
  • every evaluation;
  • arbitrary transformation.

The gateway’s blast radius grows with responsibility.

Architecture smell — Gateway as enterprise brain

The shared proxy gradually becomes the place where every AI behaviour, policy, prompt, workflow, and product decision is implemented.

13. Stable Abstraction Versus Native Features

A common interface can cover stable concepts:

  • model identity;
  • messages;
  • output;
  • token limits;
  • tools;
  • telemetry metadata.

Provider-specific features may include:

  • reasoning controls;
  • cache semantics;
  • native search;
  • audio;
  • computer use;
  • safety features;
  • batch modes;
  • structured outputs;
  • model-specific events.

Chapter 6 established:

Portability is behavioural.

The platform should not hide useful native capability merely to preserve a fiction of perfect interchangeability.

Pattern

Canonical Platform Contract
        ↓
Common Capabilities
        ↓
Provider Adapter
        ├── common behaviour
        └── explicit native extension

14. Gateway Failure Domain

If every AI product depends on one gateway:

  • outage becomes enterprise-wide;
  • bad policy blocks all products;
  • routing error affects many teams;
  • deployment regression has broad blast radius.

Design:

  • regional deployment;
  • independent scaling;
  • bounded policy scope;
  • canary;
  • rollback;
  • circuit breaker;
  • emergency direct or alternate route where justified.

A platform is not successful if it converts many local failures into one global failure.

Part V — Evidence and Retrieval Platform

15. What to Share

Strong shared mechanisms:

  • ingestion pipeline primitives;
  • parsing;
  • metadata schema;
  • embedding service;
  • index provisioning;
  • permission propagation;
  • retrieval API;
  • reranking;
  • citation format;
  • lineage;
  • deletion propagation;
  • observability.

Product teams still own:

  • source authority;
  • corpus selection;
  • freshness requirements;
  • source precedence;
  • domain conflict handling;
  • groundedness threshold.

16. Evidence Contract

A shared retrieval service should accept product requirements such as:

tenant: finance_uk
purpose: policy_answer
subject: employee_482
source_classes:
  - current_policy
freshness:
  maximum_age_days: 7
permission_context:
  user: employee_482
result:
  maximum_chunks: 8
  include_provenance: true

The platform enforces common mechanisms.

The product defines what evidence is meaningful.

17. Shared Index Versus Dedicated Index

Shared

Benefits:

  • efficiency;
  • standard operations;
  • easier onboarding.

Risks:

  • tenant leakage;
  • noisy neighbours;
  • complex deletion;
  • permission mistakes.

Dedicated

Benefits:

  • strong isolation;
  • product tuning;
  • independent lifecycle.

Costs:

  • duplication;
  • operational overhead.

Hybrid

Use shared services with separate indexes or namespaces for standard products, and dedicated deployments for:

  • regulated use;
  • large scale;
  • special latency;
  • data residency;
  • incompatible retrieval methods.

Part VI — Evaluation as a Platform Capability

18. Evaluation Execution Is Reusable

Shared evaluation platform functions:

  • dataset versioning;
  • evaluator registry;
  • deterministic graders;
  • LLM judges;
  • human review interface;
  • experiment lineage;
  • comparison;
  • batch execution;
  • CI/CD integration;
  • production sampling.

AWS’s multi-tenant generative-AI platform guidance explicitly treats evaluation datasets, experiment lineage, human review, evaluator services, and release integration as reusable platform capabilities.[3]

19. Evaluation Meaning Is Local

The platform should not decide:

  • acceptable customer harm;
  • legal threshold;
  • domain correctness;
  • critical failure taxonomy;
  • autonomy level;
  • minimum recall for a medical task.

The product and accountable owner define those.

Architectural principle — Share evaluation machinery, not accountability

The platform can execute the test. It cannot own the meaning of passing.

20. Evaluation Registry

Record:

  • evaluator;
  • version;
  • input contract;
  • score;
  • cost;
  • expected use;
  • known limitations;
  • owner.

Product evaluation plans refer to approved evaluators.

This reduces duplicate implementation without creating universal thresholds.

Part VII — Tool and Capability Platform

21. Tool Registry

A shared tool registry can contain:

  • name;
  • owner;
  • version;
  • schema;
  • side effects;
  • data class;
  • authentication;
  • permission;
  • reliability;
  • risk tier;
  • deprecation;
  • supported tenants.

Chapter 8 established that discovery is not trust.

Registration can become a production gate.

22. MCP as a Protocol Boundary

MCP standardises ways for model applications to access:

  • resources;
  • prompts;
  • tools.

The 2026-07-28 specification keeps explicit authorization guidance for HTTP transports and requires token audience binding, access-token validation, and secure token handling when authorization is used.[7] It also removes protocol-level sessions and the initialization handshake, adds server/discover, carries protocol version and client capabilities per request, moves tasks to the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension, and represents multi-round-trip input with input_required.

Treat protocol compatibility as an explicit contract. Pin and test the version, keep durable business state and authority outside the transport, and make retries idempotent: a broken response stream can require the client to re-issue the work as a new request.

MCP improves interoperability.

It does not answer:

  • whether a tool should exist;
  • who may invoke it;
  • whether an action is permitted;
  • which data may leave the tenant;
  • whether the server is trustworthy.

The platform should enforce those policies around the protocol.

23. Tool Execution Boundary

Recommended flow:

Product or Agent
      ↓
Tool Registry
      ↓
Identity and Policy
      ↓
Schema Validation
      ↓
Execution Service
      ↓
System of Record
      ↓
Audit and Result

The platform owns:

  • authentication;
  • policy mechanics;
  • schema validation;
  • runtime isolation;
  • audit.

The product owns:

  • why this tool is needed;
  • when business authority applies;
  • whether the outcome is acceptable.

24. Tool Lifecycle

Provide:

  • registration;
  • review;
  • publish;
  • version;
  • monitor;
  • deprecate;
  • revoke.

A tool’s schema is an API contract.

Its behavioural risk is larger because models choose when to invoke it.

Part VIII — Identity, Policy, and Credential Services

25. Shared Identity

The platform should provide:

  • workload identity;
  • tenant context;
  • user context;
  • task identity;
  • token exchange;
  • service authentication.

Do not require every product to reinvent:

  • OAuth flows;
  • credential storage;
  • agent identities;
  • audit propagation.

26. Shared Policy Engine

Strong central policy candidates:

  • approved model by data class;
  • tenant isolation;
  • prohibited provider;
  • maximum spend;
  • network destination;
  • tool eligibility;
  • credential lifetime;
  • retention class.

Domain policy remains product-owned:

  • refund threshold;
  • incident-remediation tier;
  • recruitment recommendation rule;
  • clinical escalation.

AWS AgentCore’s current policy capability is one vendor example of enforcing tool authorization at a gateway boundary outside the agent’s model reasoning.[8]

The architectural principle is vendor-independent:

Hard shared constraints belong outside product prompts.

Part IX — State, Memory, and Durable Workflow Services

27. State Infrastructure

A platform can provide:

  • durable state store;
  • checkpoint API;
  • event log;
  • task ID;
  • replay;
  • leases;
  • cancellation;
  • dead-letter queue.

The platform should not define every product state machine.

28. Memory Platform

Shared capabilities:

  • memory storage;
  • namespace;
  • identity;
  • purpose metadata;
  • expiry;
  • retrieval;
  • deletion;
  • encryption.

Product ownership:

  • what is worth remembering;
  • whether user confirmation is needed;
  • sensitivity;
  • future-agent eligibility;
  • semantic meaning.

Architecture smell — Enterprise memory

One cross-product memory store accumulates user facts without product, purpose, or sensitivity boundaries.

29. Workflow Runtime

A durable runtime can provide:

  • retries;
  • timers;
  • checkpoints;
  • queues;
  • cancellation;
  • activity isolation;
  • human waits.

Do not encode product workflow into the runtime platform.

The platform owns reliable execution semantics.

The product owns the state transitions and meaning.

Part X — Data and Privacy Control Plane

30. Shared Data Controls

Chapter 11 introduced the Data Lifecycle Control Plane.

Platform candidates:

  • classification;
  • lineage;
  • retention jobs;
  • tenant isolation;
  • provider eligibility;
  • residency policy;
  • deletion orchestration;
  • rights-discovery APIs;
  • protected telemetry.

Product inputs:

  • purpose;
  • minimum fields;
  • source authority;
  • affected-party expectations;
  • retention justification;
  • recourse.

31. Data as Platform Metadata

Runtime requests should carry metadata such as:

  • tenant;
  • user;
  • purpose;
  • data class;
  • residency;
  • retention class;
  • task ID.

This metadata can drive:

  • provider eligibility;
  • logging;
  • routing;
  • tool access;
  • storage;
  • cost attribution.

Do not infer all governance from prompt content.

Part XI — Observability and Operational Integration

32. Common Telemetry

A platform can standardise:

  • trace propagation;
  • model span;
  • tool span;
  • retrieval span;
  • agent step;
  • token usage;
  • route;
  • evaluator;
  • tenant;
  • cost.

OpenTelemetry’s semantic conventions provide common telemetry naming across systems; the GenAI conventions cover model and agent attributes while allowing content capture to remain opt-in because of cost and privacy concerns.[9][10] Many GenAI attributes remain at Development stability. Isolate them behind a translation layer, version dashboards and collectors, and treat prompts, retrieved text, tool arguments, and tool results as sensitive fields rather than default telemetry.

33. Product Signals

Common telemetry is not enough.

Product-specific signals include:

  • claim support;
  • customer resolution;
  • approval accuracy;
  • defect acceptance;
  • financial outcome;
  • escalation quality.

The platform should provide an extension mechanism.

Architectural principle — Standardise correlation, not meaning

The platform should make signals joinable. The product defines what those signals mean.

34. Incident Integration

Provide common:

  • run ID;
  • trace ID;
  • model version;
  • prompt version;
  • tool version;
  • policy version;
  • tenant;
  • evaluation version.

This lets an incident bridge product, platform, and provider evidence.

Chapter 10’s AI Incident Envelope should be producible from platform telemetry.

Part XII — Multi-Tenancy

35. Tenancy Is More Than Authentication

A tenant boundary can apply to:

  • model quota;
  • budget;
  • memory;
  • retrieval;
  • prompts;
  • tools;
  • evaluation data;
  • telemetry;
  • cache;
  • workflow state;
  • keys.

Design all derived stores accordingly.

36. Deployment Models

Pooled

Many tenants share the same runtime.

Benefits:

  • efficiency;
  • elasticity;
  • simple onboarding.

Risks:

  • noisy neighbour;
  • broad failure;
  • isolation complexity.

Siloed

Dedicated resources per tenant.

Benefits:

  • strong isolation;
  • predictable performance;
  • custom policy.

Costs:

  • expensive;
  • operationally heavy.

Hybrid

Standard tenants pooled.

High-risk, high-volume, or regulated tenants dedicated.

AWS’s current Agentic AI Lens explicitly recommends matching pooled, siloed, or hybrid deployment models to tenant isolation, performance, and cost requirements rather than defaulting to one topology.[11]

37. Noisy-Neighbour Controls

Use:

  • quotas;
  • rate limits;
  • concurrency;
  • queue priority;
  • token budgets;
  • tool limits;
  • storage quotas;
  • cache partition;
  • dedicated capacity tier.

Monitor per tenant.

A pooled platform without fairness controls can become unreliable even when the underlying model provider remains healthy.

38. Tenant Metadata

Every runtime operation should carry tenant context.

Do not rely only on:

  • network location;
  • API key;
  • database schema.

Propagate tenant into:

  • policy;
  • trace;
  • cost;
  • retrieval;
  • memory;
  • tool;
  • evaluation.

Part XIII — Cost and FinOps

39. Cost Attribution

AI cost includes:

  • model input;
  • model output;
  • reasoning;
  • cache;
  • retrieval;
  • reranking;
  • tool;
  • workflow runtime;
  • evaluation;
  • human review;
  • platform overhead.

Attribution needs metadata at request and workflow level.

40. Showback and Chargeback

Showback

Makes cost visible to teams while cost may remain centrally funded.

Chargeback

Moves cost into the responsible team’s financial accounts.

FinOps guidance treats cost allocation as the underlying capability for both showback and chargeback and notes that chargeback is an organisational finance choice, whereas transparent showback is foundational.[12][13]

41. Shared Cost Allocation

Shared platform costs include:

  • gateway;
  • telemetry;
  • cache;
  • platform engineers;
  • evaluation infrastructure;
  • shared retrieval;
  • committed model capacity.

Allocation options:

  • direct usage;
  • tokens;
  • requests;
  • compute;
  • storage;
  • weighted task;
  • fixed subscription;
  • central investment.

Do not create precision theatre.

A simple transparent allocation can be more useful than a mathematically complex model no product trusts.

42. Unit Economics

Report:

  • cost per task;
  • cost per successful task;
  • cost per tenant;
  • cost per user;
  • cost per accepted outcome;
  • platform overhead percentage.

A platform that lowers infrastructure cost but increases integration effort may not create net value.

Part XIV — Paved Roads and Self-Service

43. Golden Path

A golden path can provide:

  1. create AI product project;
  2. select risk and data class;
  3. receive approved model access;
  4. provision evaluation;
  5. register retrieval;
  6. register tools;
  7. enable telemetry;
  8. configure budget;
  9. deploy canary;
  10. produce governance evidence.

Microsoft describes paved or golden paths as supported routes that reduce developer cognitive load while preserving organisational requirements.[1][14]

44. Paved, Not Caged

A good golden path is:

  • easy;
  • documented;
  • secure;
  • observable;
  • supported.

An exception path should exist for:

  • unusual model;
  • specialised hardware;
  • strict latency;
  • local inference;
  • research;
  • novel protocol.

The exception still needs governance.

Architecture smell — Golden cage

The supported path becomes so restrictive that capable teams create shadow infrastructure to deliver real requirements.

45. Self-Service

Provide self-service for:

  • project creation;
  • model access;
  • retrieval store;
  • evaluation suite;
  • tool registration;
  • cost dashboard;
  • trace lookup;
  • policy status.

Self-service should not mean:

everyone is an administrator.

It means safe operations are automated and discoverable.

Part XV — Platform Interfaces and Contracts

46. Interface Forms

  • REST;
  • SDK;
  • CLI;
  • portal;
  • templates;
  • policy as code;
  • infrastructure as code;
  • events.

A platform should expose the interface that matches the consumer workflow.

47. Contract Design

A platform contract should define:

  • identity;
  • tenant;
  • purpose;
  • input;
  • output;
  • errors;
  • policy;
  • SLO;
  • telemetry;
  • version;
  • cost;
  • deprecation.

Example:

model_request:
  tenant: support_uk
  task_class: routine_summary
  data_class: internal
  model_policy: support_default_v4
  budget:
    max_cost_gbp: 0.05
  trace:
    task_id: case_482

The platform can validate the contract without understanding every support policy.

48. Versioning

Platform APIs should support:

  • semantic versioning where practical;
  • compatibility period;
  • migration guide;
  • deprecation date;
  • usage discovery;
  • automated warnings.

Do not silently change:

  • model alias;
  • evaluator;
  • tool;
  • policy;
  • telemetry schema.

49. Escape Hatches

An escape hatch should be:

  • explicit;
  • reviewed;
  • time-bounded where necessary;
  • observable;
  • owned.

Example:

Product uses native provider streaming because the platform adapter does not yet expose a required feature.

The platform learns from repeated escapes.

If several products escape for the same reason, the roadmap should respond.

Part XVI — Build, Buy, or Compose

50. Buy

Use a managed capability when:

  • it is non-differentiating;
  • vendor maturity is high;
  • integration is acceptable;
  • control requirements are met;
  • exit is manageable.

Examples may include:

  • model hosting;
  • trace backend;
  • vector service;
  • evaluation execution.

51. Build

Build when:

  • the capability encodes organisational control;
  • vendor abstraction creates unacceptable lock-in;
  • domain-specific integration is differentiating;
  • cost at scale justifies operation;
  • required isolation is unavailable.

Do not build an LLM gateway because gateways are fashionable.

52. Compose

Most platforms should compose:

  • cloud services;
  • open protocols;
  • internal policy;
  • existing developer platform;
  • third-party observability.

Avoid rebuilding:

  • OAuth;
  • secret stores;
  • workflow engine;
  • metrics pipeline;

unless requirements justify it.

53. The Build–Buy–Expose Test

Ask:

  1. Is this an organisational differentiator?
  2. Is it a governance boundary?
  3. Does the vendor satisfy tenancy and data requirements?
  4. Is provider portability important?
  5. Does the capability have a stable open protocol?
  6. Can we operate it better?
  7. What is exit cost?
  8. What happens during vendor outage?
  9. Will we customise it so heavily that it becomes effectively ours?
  10. Can products use the provider directly under governed policy?

Sometimes the correct answer is:

Do not platform this yet.

Part XVII — Team Topology and Ownership

54. Platform Team

Owns:

  • platform product;
  • common contracts;
  • reliability;
  • security mechanisms;
  • developer experience;
  • roadmap;
  • support;
  • deprecation.

55. Product Team

Owns:

  • business goal;
  • user experience;
  • domain architecture;
  • task quality;
  • business evidence;
  • workflow semantics;
  • product risk;
  • outcome.

56. Enabling and Specialist Teams

May support:

  • AI evaluation;
  • security;
  • privacy;
  • data;
  • FinOps;
  • model optimisation.

The goal is to grow product capability, not create permanent queues for every decision.

57. Responsibility Matrix

Responsibility Platform Product
Approved model registry Own Consume
Product task classification Support schema Own
Model route implementation Provide mechanisms Configure
Evaluation runtime Own Consume
Evaluation threshold Support evidence Own
Tool gateway Own Register/use
Business action authority Enforce contract Own
Trace transport Own Instrument domain signal
Outcome metric Support correlation Own
Tenant isolation Own shared mechanism Validate product use
Cost reporting Own infrastructure Review/optimise

Part XVIII — Reliability of the Platform

58. Platform SLOs

Possible SLOs:

  • model gateway availability;
  • policy latency;
  • retrieval service availability;
  • evaluation queue time;
  • tool registry availability;
  • trace ingestion;
  • onboarding time.

Product SLOs remain separate.

A platform can be green while a product is failing behaviourally.

59. Degraded Modes

Platform degraded modes:

  • one provider unavailable;
  • evaluation delayed;
  • retrieval index read-only;
  • trace backend unavailable;
  • policy engine unavailable.

For security-critical policy:

fail closed

may be appropriate.

For low-risk telemetry:

buffer and retry

may be appropriate.

Classify each capability.

60. Platform Change

A platform change can affect many products.

Use:

  • canary tenants;
  • contract tests;
  • regression;
  • change notice;
  • rollback;
  • version pinning.

The platform’s blast radius makes disciplined rollout more important.

Part XIX — Measuring Platform Value

61. Platform Metrics

Adoption

  • products onboarded;
  • active teams;
  • paved-path usage.

Delivery

  • time to first compliant deployment;
  • onboarding time;
  • support tickets;
  • self-service completion.

Reuse

  • shared capabilities consumed;
  • duplicate services retired;
  • common evaluators reused.

Control

  • policy coverage;
  • unapproved provider use;
  • trace coverage;
  • tenant isolation incidents.

Economics

  • cost allocation;
  • idle capacity;
  • unit cost;
  • platform overhead.

Reliability

  • platform SLO;
  • incident blast radius;
  • recovery.

62. The Platform Value Equation

This handbook proposes a qualitative equation:

Platform Value
≈ Reuse
+ Control Consistency
+ Delivery Acceleration
+ Operating Leverage
− Coupling
− Cognitive Overhead
− Failure Concentration

It is an original synthesis.

Do not turn it into a fake numeric score.

Use it to structure review.

63. Platform Exit Cost

Measure the difficulty of:

  • replacing model provider;
  • replacing gateway;
  • moving evaluation;
  • exporting traces;
  • migrating memory;
  • moving indexes;
  • changing workflow runtime.

A platform can reduce vendor lock-in while increasing internal-platform lock-in.

Both matter.

Part XX — Worked Example: Enterprise AI Platform

64. Scenario

An organisation has:

  • customer-service assistant;
  • coding agent;
  • procurement agent;
  • incident-remediation agent;
  • enterprise knowledge assistant.

Each team currently has:

  • different model SDK;
  • separate vector database;
  • different telemetry;
  • no cost attribution;
  • duplicated security review.

65. Platform Boundary

Shared:

  • model gateway;
  • identity and task metadata;
  • approved model registry;
  • policy engine;
  • tool registry;
  • evaluation runtime;
  • trace pipeline;
  • cost attribution;
  • retrieval provisioning;
  • deletion infrastructure.

Product-owned:

  • prompts;
  • workflow;
  • golden cases;
  • thresholds;
  • evidence sources;
  • tool eligibility;
  • approval rules;
  • outcome.

66. Platform Architecture

Product Applications
  ├── Support
  ├── Coding
  ├── Procurement
  ├── Incident
  └── Knowledge
        │
        ▼
Product Contracts and SDK
        │
        ▼
AI Platform
  ├── Model Access
  ├── Evaluation
  ├── Evidence Services
  ├── Tool Registry
  ├── Identity and Policy
  ├── State and Workflow Runtime
  ├── Data and Privacy Controls
  ├── Observability
  └── Cost and Governance
        │
        ▼
Provider / Runtime Adapters
        │
        ▼
Cloud, Models, Data, Enterprise APIs

67. Tenancy

  • pooled gateway;
  • product-specific retrieval indexes;
  • tenant-scoped memory;
  • shared trace backend with tenant policy;
  • dedicated incident-agent execution for production systems;
  • quotas by product and environment.

68. Golden Paths

Knowledge assistant

  • standard retrieval;
  • read-only tools;
  • evidence evaluation.

Action agent

  • durable workflow;
  • workload identity;
  • tool policy;
  • approval;
  • action trace.

Coding agent

  • sandbox;
  • repository scope;
  • test tools;
  • no production credentials.

The platform provides different paved paths instead of one universal template.

69. Cost

Every request includes:

  • product;
  • tenant;
  • environment;
  • task class.

Costs are joined across:

  • model;
  • retrieval;
  • tools;
  • evaluation;
  • shared infrastructure.

Teams receive showback first.

Chargeback is applied only where organisational finance requires it.

Part XXI — Architecture Review

70. Scenario

A company proposes one enterprise AI platform.

It will:

  • provide one universal API;
  • force every model through one gateway;
  • store all prompts centrally;
  • use one shared vector database;
  • provide one enterprise agent memory;
  • define one evaluation score;
  • approve every tool centrally;
  • charge products per API call.

71. ARB Findings

Finding 1 — Universal API hides behaviour

Provider-native capability is lost.

Finding 2 — Gateway blast radius is excessive

Every product shares the same critical dependency.

Finding 3 — Prompt storage violates minimisation

Telemetry policy is not purpose-specific.

Finding 4 — Shared vector database weakens boundaries

Tenant and source authority become difficult to reason about.

Finding 5 — Enterprise memory creates purpose drift

User information crosses product contexts.

Finding 6 — Evaluation meaning is centralised

One score cannot represent every task.

Finding 7 — Tool governance will bottleneck

Central review owns business meaning it does not understand.

Finding 8 — Per-call pricing distorts behaviour

It ignores model, token, evaluation, and shared costs.

72. Recommended Redesign

  • canonical contracts with native extensions;
  • regional or segmented gateways;
  • product-specific telemetry policy;
  • shared retrieval provisioning with isolated indexes;
  • purpose-scoped memory;
  • shared evaluation runtime with product thresholds;
  • central tool security plus product action authority;
  • workflow-level cost attribution;
  • paved paths plus governed exceptions;
  • explicit SLOs;
  • independent product accountability.

Part XXII — Architecture Smells

73. Platform Before Repetition

The organisation builds a large platform before multiple real products expose shared problems.

74. Gateway as Enterprise Brain

Every workflow and policy is inserted into the request proxy.

75. Lowest-Common-Denominator API

Useful provider features are removed to preserve artificial uniformity.

76. Domain Judgment as Shared Service

The platform owns business thresholds and approval meaning.

77. Enterprise Memory

One memory layer allows information to flow across products and purposes.

78. Shared Everything Tenancy

All stores are pooled because the gateway authenticates requests.

79. Golden Cage

The paved path blocks legitimate requirements, creating shadow platforms.

80. Platform by Mandate

Adoption is measured by compliance rather than usefulness.

81. Cost by Request Count

All requests are treated as economically equal.

82. Escape Hatch Without Feedback

Teams bypass the platform repeatedly, but the platform roadmap never changes.

83. Wrapper as Portability

A thin SDK is treated as proof the organisation can migrate providers.

84. Platform Team as Approval Queue

Every product change requires platform-team interpretation.

Part XXIII — Interview Preparation

85. Foundational Questions

Question 1

What belongs in an enterprise AI platform?

Shared mechanisms with stable contracts: model access, identity, policy, evaluation execution, tool registry, telemetry, data controls, and cost attribution. Domain logic and outcomes remain product owned.

Question 2

What is the difference between an AI platform and an AI product?

The platform provides reusable mechanisms and controls. The product creates and owns a user or business outcome.

Question 3

Why use a model gateway?

To centralise cross-cutting identity, routing, policy, quota, telemetry, and cost concerns while isolating provider integration.

Question 4

What should not go into the model gateway?

Business workflows, product state, domain prompts, approval semantics, and arbitrary product transformation.

Question 5

What is a golden path?

A supported, automated route for common development and deployment tasks that embeds organisational standards without requiring teams to rediscover them.

86. Senior-Level Questions

Question 6

How do you decide whether a capability belongs in the platform?

Test invariant, reuse, stable contract, contextual dependence, control value, economics, isolation, ownership, independent change, and escape needs.

Question 7

How should evaluation be platformised?

Share evaluator execution, datasets, lineage, human-review tooling, and CI/CD integration. Keep domain cases, error taxonomy, thresholds, and accountability with the product.

Question 8

How do you design multi-tenancy for an AI platform?

Define tenant boundaries across models, quotas, retrieval, memory, tools, state, caches, telemetry, and cost. Choose pooled, siloed, or hybrid deployment based on risk and performance.

Question 9

How do you allocate AI platform cost?

Propagate product, tenant, environment, and task metadata; attribute direct consumption; allocate shared costs transparently; use showback universally and chargeback according to finance policy.

Question 10

How do you prevent a platform becoming a lowest-common-denominator abstraction?

Expose a stable common contract plus explicit provider-native extensions and governed escape hatches.

Question 11

Who owns a tool’s business permission?

The platform owns identity and policy mechanisms; the product or domain owner defines when the business action is legitimate.

Question 12

How do you know a golden path is working?

Measure onboarding time, self-service completion, product adoption, support load, policy coverage, reliability, delivery speed, and escape patterns.

87. Principal-Level Questions

Question 13

How would you design a global enterprise AI platform?

Use regional control and data planes, stable product contracts, shared model, identity, evaluation, tool, observability, and data controls; preserve tenant and product boundaries; offer dedicated paths for high-risk workloads.

Question 14

How do you prevent the platform team from becoming a bottleneck?

Product mindset, self-service, paved paths, machine-enforced controls, decentralised domain decisions, documented contracts, and governance based on risk.

Question 15

What should be the platform’s failure boundary?

Segment high-blast-radius capabilities, design regional redundancy, fail closed only for critical control, preserve product degraded modes, and canary platform changes.

Question 16

Build or buy an AI gateway?

Assess differentiating control, vendor capability, tenancy, exit, scale, operations, native features, and failure. Compose where possible instead of building everything.

Question 17

How should AI platform contracts evolve?

Version explicitly, discover consumers, support compatibility windows, publish migration paths, test contracts, canary changes, and deprecate deliberately.

Question 18

How do you prove the platform creates value?

Show reuse, control consistency, faster delivery, operating leverage, lower duplicate work, and acceptable coupling and failure concentration.

Part XXIV — Whiteboard Challenge

88. Design an Enterprise AI Platform for 50 Product Teams

Products include:

  • assistants;
  • coding agents;
  • customer-service automation;
  • document processing;
  • high-impact decision support;
  • operational agents.

Constraints

  • AWS and Azure;
  • several model providers;
  • multiple regions;
  • regulated teams;
  • strong cost pressure;
  • teams need self-service;
  • native provider features evolve quickly;
  • central security and governance.

Discuss

  1. Define platform and product boundaries.
  2. Apply the Platform Boundary Test.
  3. Draw the AI Platform Contract Stack.
  4. Design gateway segmentation.
  5. Define model registry and routing primitives.
  6. Design evidence and evaluation services.
  7. Design tool registry and policy.
  8. Define identity and credential boundaries.
  9. Define durable state and memory.
  10. Integrate data and privacy controls.
  11. Define telemetry and incident integration.
  12. Select tenancy model.
  13. Define quotas and noisy-neighbour control.
  14. Define showback and chargeback.
  15. Design golden paths.
  16. Define build, buy, and escape paths.
  17. Define team topology and SLOs.
  18. Define platform-value metrics.

Strong-answer characteristics

  • product accountability;
  • stable contracts;
  • no universal prompt;
  • shared control planes;
  • native feature escape;
  • segmented failure domains;
  • tenant isolation;
  • domain-owned evaluation thresholds;
  • tool security plus business authority;
  • self-service;
  • cost attribution;
  • adoption feedback;
  • deliberate deprecation.

Part XXV — Questions to Take Back to Your Team

  1. Which AI mechanisms are being rebuilt by multiple teams?
  2. Which “shared” capability still depends on domain judgment?
  3. Which platform API hides useful native behaviour?
  4. What is the gateway blast radius?
  5. Are model and tool policies enforced or merely documented?
  6. Who owns evaluation thresholds?
  7. Are retrieval indexes isolated correctly?
  8. Does memory cross product purposes?
  9. Is tenant context propagated everywhere?
  10. Can one tenant exhaust shared capacity?
  11. Are platform costs attributable to products?
  12. Which teams use shadow AI infrastructure?
  13. Why do they bypass the golden path?
  14. Which escape patterns should become platform features?
  15. Can products migrate off a platform capability?
  16. Which platform changes require product reevaluation?
  17. What is the platform SLO?
  18. Which product outcomes prove platform value?
  19. Is the platform reducing cognitive load?
  20. What would we stop operating if adoption disappeared?

Architect’s Notebook — Standardise Mechanisms, Preserve Judgment

Enterprise reuse is attractive.

So is consistency.

The temptation is to turn every repeated concept into a shared service.

But two products can both use:

  • retrieval;
  • approval;
  • evaluation;

while meaning entirely different things by each.

The platform should standardise:

  • how evidence is retrieved;
  • how approval is recorded;
  • how evaluation is executed.

The product should own:

  • which evidence is authoritative;
  • when approval is required;
  • what quality means.

That boundary is the difference between reuse and centralised confusion.

From the Architect’s Desk

The AI platform should make the safe path easier than the improvised path.

It should remove undifferentiated work: provider integration, identity, policy enforcement, evaluation infrastructure, tool plumbing, telemetry, data controls, cost attribution.

It should not take away the work that defines the product: intent, domain judgment, user experience, quality, authority, and outcomes.

A good platform is opinionated about mechanisms and humble about business meaning.

If teams bypass it repeatedly, do not begin by strengthening the mandate. Inspect the escape. The bypass may be evidence that the platform abstraction is wrong.

If I Were the Architect

You inherit eight AI products.

Every team has:

  • its own model SDK;
  • its own telemetry;
  • separate evaluation scripts;
  • different tool authentication;
  • separate vector databases.

Leadership asks for a central AI platform.

What do you do first?

Do not choose a platform vendor.

  1. Inventory repeated mechanisms.
  2. identify shared invariants.
  3. apply the Platform Boundary Test.
  4. identify domain judgments that must remain local.
  5. choose two or three high-value paved paths.
  6. standardise identity and telemetry first.
  7. create model and cost metadata contracts.
  8. centralise evaluation execution without centralising thresholds.
  9. pilot with real product teams.
  10. measure onboarding, reliability, control, and escape patterns.
  11. expand only where reuse is demonstrated.
  12. retain an explicit exit for exceptional requirements.

The first platform architecture is a set of product boundaries—not a list of services.

Key Takeaways

  • An AI platform is a product providing reusable mechanisms, controls, and contracts to product teams.
  • Infrastructure is not automatically a platform.
  • The product remains accountable for the user or business outcome.
  • Centralise mechanisms where invariants are shared; keep domain judgment where context defines correctness.
  • The Platform Boundary Test exposes reuse, control, economics, isolation, ownership, and contextual-dependence trade-offs.
  • The AI Platform Contract Stack connects product intent to stable contracts, shared control planes, providers, and operations.
  • Gateways should offload cross-cutting concerns, not become enterprise brains.
  • Portability remains behavioural, so native provider features need explicit escape paths.
  • Evidence infrastructure can be shared while evidence authority remains local.
  • Share evaluation machinery, not accountability.
  • Tool registries improve reuse and governance; discovery does not establish trust.
  • Identity, credential brokering, and common hard policy are strong platform capabilities.
  • Workflow runtime can be shared while state machines remain product owned.
  • Memory must remain tenant-, purpose-, and product-scoped.
  • Data and privacy controls require product purpose metadata.
  • Standardise telemetry correlation, not domain meaning.
  • Multi-tenancy spans quota, retrieval, memory, tools, state, caches, evaluation, and observability.
  • Use pooled, siloed, or hybrid tenancy intentionally.
  • Cost attribution must include model, tools, retrieval, evaluation, and shared infrastructure.
  • Showback creates visibility; chargeback depends on organisational finance.
  • Golden paths should be paved, not caged.
  • Self-service means safe automation, not universal administration.
  • Platform contracts require versions, migration, and deprecation.
  • Build, buy, compose, and direct-provider use are all valid choices.
  • A platform team owns platform reliability and developer experience, not product outcomes.
  • Platform value is reuse and control plus delivery leverage, minus coupling, cognitive overhead, and failure concentration.

ARB Review Record

Decision ID: ARB-CH-012
Subject: Chapter 12 — AI Platform Architecture
Outcome: Accepted with constraints for user review

Primary contribution:
Defines the boundary between reusable AI platform mechanisms and product-owned
domain judgment and connects model access, evidence, evaluation, tools,
identity, state, data, telemetry, tenancy, cost, and developer experience
through stable platform contracts.

Grounded foundations:
- Microsoft platform-engineering guidance on product mindset, self-service,
  paved paths, and interfaces.
- Microsoft Foundry resource/project architecture.
- Azure Architecture Center model-gateway guidance.
- AWS Generative AI Lens multi-tenant platform scenario.
- AWS Agentic AI Lens resource reusability, policy, multi-tenancy, and cost.
- Model Context Protocol authorization and tool specifications.
- OpenTelemetry semantic conventions.
- FinOps Foundation allocation, showback, and chargeback guidance.

Original synthesis requiring explicit labelling:
- Platform Boundary Test.
- AI Platform Contract Stack.
- Platform Value Equation.
- “centralise mechanisms, preserve judgment.”
- “share evaluation machinery, not accountability.”
- “standardise correlation, not meaning.”

Constraints:
- Do not make one gateway the location for all product logic.
- Do not hide provider-native capabilities merely for uniformity.
- Preserve product ownership of intent, thresholds, authority, and outcomes.
- Keep tenant isolation explicit across every derived store.
- Treat platform controls as products with SLOs and versions.
- Maintain governed escape hatches.
- Do not treat adoption mandates as evidence of platform value.
- Keep vendor-specific services as living examples rather than the enduring
  architecture.
