Chapter 13 - End-to-End Reference Architectures and Trade-off Case Studies

Applying architectural judgment across six different AI systems

Related chapters: Chapters 0-12

There is no universal AI reference architecture. There are recurring mechanisms whose correct combination depends on context, consequence, reversibility, evidence, autonomy, and scale.

1. Why This Chapter Exists

The previous chapters separated the major responsibilities of AI architecture:

  • architectural judgment;
  • the AI Decision Pipeline;
  • quality attributes;
  • evaluation;
  • evidence;
  • models and inference;
  • workflow and agents;
  • security;
  • governance;
  • operational assurance;
  • data and privacy;
  • enterprise AI platforms.

Real systems do not arrive one chapter at a time.

An architect is asked:

We want an internal knowledge assistant. What should we build?

or:

Can this support agent issue a refund?

or:

Can an AI agent remediate production incidents automatically?

The answer cannot be obtained by selecting a pattern from a catalogue.

The same architectural mechanism can be correct in one system and dangerous in another.

For example:

  • A vector index may be the right evidence mechanism for a knowledge assistant but the wrong source of truth for a current bank balance.
  • Human review may add little value to every low-risk FAQ answer but be essential before a high-impact employment decision.
  • Long-term memory may improve a personal assistant while creating purpose drift in an enterprise decision system.
  • A coding agent may be allowed to write files in an isolated repository but not deploy production code.
  • Automated rollback may be safer than waiting for approval during a narrowly defined production failure, while a novel database repair may require human authority.

Current architecture guidance reaches the same broad conclusion from different directions. Microsoft’s RAG guidance distinguishes simpler fixed retrieval pipelines from agentic retrieval, with permission-aware evidence and evaluation needed for enterprise use.[1] AWS’s Agentic AI Lens emphasises explicit purpose, autonomy, success criteria, bounded authority, human oversight, tracing, containment, and recovery rather than treating all agents alike.[2] NIST’s AI RMF is explicitly contextual and encourages organisations to make go/no-go decisions based on system purpose, risks, impacts, and evidence.[3]

The central argument of this chapter is:

Architecture is the disciplined explanation of why this combination of mechanisms is appropriate for this context—and why plausible alternatives are not.

2. The Architecture Context–Decision Trace

This handbook introduces the Architecture Context–Decision Trace:

Context
   ↓
Quality Drivers
   ↓
Architecture Choice
   ↓
Trade-offs
   ↓
Failure Boundary
   ↓
Evidence
   ↓
ARB Decision

It is an original synthesis.

It is not a score. It is a reasoning trace.

Context

What outcome, users, environment, data, authority, and constraints exist?

Quality drivers

Which qualities dominate—for example groundedness, latency, safety, reversibility, privacy, cost, or maintainability?

Architecture choice

Which mechanisms are selected?

Trade-offs

What becomes slower, more expensive, more complex, or less flexible because of that choice?

Failure boundary

Where is probabilistic failure prevented from becoming unacceptable harm?

Evidence

What demonstrates that the architecture meets the quality bar?

ARB decision

Approve, reject, constrain, pilot, or require more evidence.

3. A Common Review Frame

Each case is reviewed through the same questions:

  1. What business outcome matters?
  2. What is explicitly out of scope?
  3. Which quality scenarios dominate?
  4. What does the AI Decision Pipeline look like?
  5. What evidence is authoritative?
  6. How is system quality evaluated?
  7. Which model capability is required?
  8. Where is workflow deterministic and where is it agentic?
  9. What authority can the system exercise?
  10. Where does durable state live?
  11. Which security boundaries matter?
  12. Which data and privacy constraints apply?
  13. What governance decision is required?
  14. How is the system operated and contained?
  15. Which shared platform capabilities are reused?
  16. What alternatives were rejected?
  17. What does failure look like?
  18. What is the cost of successful operation?

The repeated frame matters. Without it, architecture case studies can become stories whose differences are caused by the author’s presentation rather than the system’s requirements.

Case Study 1 — Enterprise Knowledge Assistant

4. Context

A multinational organisation wants employees to ask questions about:

  • HR policy;
  • travel;
  • IT procedures;
  • procurement;
  • security standards.

The assistant should:

  • find current policy;
  • answer with citations;
  • identify jurisdiction or employee context where relevant;
  • say when evidence is insufficient;
  • route sensitive cases to the correct human or transactional system.

It should not:

  • change employee records;
  • approve expenses;
  • interpret ambiguous policy as law;
  • invent an entitlement;
  • expose documents the employee cannot access.

The dominant characteristic is:

Evidence-heavy, read-mostly, low autonomy.

5. Quality Drivers

Groundedness

Claims must be supported by current authoritative policy.

Permission correctness

The user must not retrieve content outside their access.

Freshness

Superseded policy must not outrank current policy.

Latency

Common questions should return in seconds.

Transparency

The employee should see sources and important limitations.

Cost

Routine questions should not require the most expensive reasoning path.

Example quality scenario:

Source: UK employee
Stimulus: asks whether unused holiday carries forward
Environment: normal business hours
Artifact: employee knowledge assistant
Evidence condition: current UK holiday policy is available
Risk condition: outdated global policy conflicts with current UK policy
Response: retrieve permission-authorised UK source and cite it
Measure:
  correct source class = 100%
  unsupported entitlement claim = 0
  p95 answer latency < 6 seconds

6. Architecture

Employee
   ↓
Intent and Context
   ↓
Permission-Aware Retrieval
   ├── HR Policy
   ├── IT Knowledge
   └── Procurement Guidance
   ↓
Evidence Qualification and Reranking
   ↓
Answer Model
   ↓
Claim–Evidence Validation
   ↓
Cited Answer / Insufficient Evidence / Human Route

The fixed retrieval path is preferable for common single-domain queries. Agentic retrieval is reserved for questions that genuinely require multi-source decomposition, iterative retrieval, or dynamic source selection.

Microsoft’s current RAG guidance similarly distinguishes classic/fixed RAG from agentic retrieval and highlights hybrid retrieval, structured citations, permission-aware knowledge, and evaluation as production concerns.[1][4]

7. AI Decision Pipeline

Intent

Classify policy question, request for action, personal case, or restricted domain.

Context

Use minimum required context such as employee jurisdiction and authenticated identity.

Evidence

Retrieve current source, effective date, permission, and provenance.

Reasoning

Synthesize the evidence.

Validation

Check citations, unsupported claims, source status, and restricted content.

Authority

Answer only. No write authority.

Action

Present answer or route elsewhere.

Outcome

Employee receives correct guidance or a safe escalation.

8. Evaluation

Portfolio:

  • deterministic citation checks;
  • retrieval recall;
  • source-authority tests;
  • outdated-document challenge set;
  • conflicting-policy cases;
  • permission tests;
  • human policy-expert review;
  • production unresolved-query sampling.

Primary unit: claim and answer, not merely model response.

A system can generate fluent text while retrieving the wrong policy.

9. Model and Inference

Use the smallest sufficient model for ordinary policy synthesis. Escalate when evidence conflicts, the query is multi-part, reasoning complexity increases, or the user asks for explanation of policy interaction.

The retrieval layer does more work than model scale for many questions.

A frontier model cannot compensate for missing documents, wrong permissions, stale indexes, or bad source precedence.

10. Security, Governance, and Privacy

Security:

  • user-authenticated retrieval;
  • document-level permission;
  • no broad service-account corpus exposure;
  • external document content treated as untrusted data.

Privacy:

  • minimise employee attributes in context;
  • no long-term memory by default;
  • avoid full prompt logging;
  • deletion and permission changes propagate to indexes.

Governance:

  • accountable policy owners;
  • source publication lifecycle;
  • jurisdiction-aware routing;
  • documented non-goals.

11. Operational Assurance

Monitor no-answer rate, outdated-source use, citation failures, permission denials, retrieval latency, escalation, user correction, and policy-owner complaints.

A healthy HTTP endpoint with increasing outdated-policy use is an unhealthy AI system.

12. Alternatives Considered

Fine-tune on all policy

Rejected as the primary evidence mechanism because policy changes, provenance is difficult, and update/deletion is harder.

Give the model all enterprise documents

Rejected because of context, permission, relevance, cost, and stale evidence.

Agentic retrieval for every query

Rejected because of unnecessary latency, cost, variability, and failure surface.

13. Failure Boundary

The failure boundary is between generated claim and employee reliance on policy guidance.

Controls are authoritative source filtering, claim support, explicit insufficiency, no transactional authority, and escalation.

14. ARB Decision

Approve for production as a read-mostly assistant with permission-aware retrieval, source authority, citations, limited employee context, evaluation by policy segment, no write tools, and monitored freshness.

Do not approve use as the authoritative employment-decision engine.

Case Study 2 — Customer-Service Action Agent

15. Context

A retailer wants an agent to resolve customer-support cases. The agent may read orders, inspect shipment status, answer policy questions, draft messages, issue small credits, cancel eligible orders, and escalate unusual cases.

It may not issue unlimited refunds, modify identity attributes, override fraud blocks, or expose one customer’s data to another.

The dominant characteristic is:

Customer data plus bounded transactional authority.

16. Quality Drivers

  • task completion;
  • policy correctness;
  • customer-data privacy;
  • action correctness;
  • reversibility;
  • cost per resolved case;
  • human escalation quality.

Example:

Source: customer
Stimulus: requests compensation for late delivery
Environment: authenticated support interaction
Artifact: service agent
Evidence condition: order and policy are available
Risk condition: request value exceeds automated authority
Response:
  validate order
  determine eligible compensation
  auto-issue only within delegated limit
  otherwise request human approval
Measures:
  incorrect customer target = 0
  credit above delegated limit = 0
  duplicate credit = 0

17. Architecture

Customer
   ↓
Authenticated Case
   ↓
Deterministic Case Preconditions
   ↓
Agent Diagnosis
   ├── Order Read
   ├── Shipment Read
   └── Policy Evidence
   ↓
Proposed Resolution
   ↓
Policy + Authority Gateway
   ├── answer
   ├── bounded reversible action
   └── human approval
   ↓
Idempotent Action Tool
   ↓
Outcome Verification
   ↓
Customer Communication

This is an agentic workflow, not unconstrained autonomy. The workflow skeleton remains deterministic around identity, policy, money limits, state, action, and audit.

AWS’s current guidance recommends tiered human oversight rather than review of every action or no review at all, with enough context for meaningful decisions and auditable approvals.[5]

18. Evidence Architecture

Authoritative tools:

  • order-management API;
  • payment/credit API;
  • shipment API;
  • policy service.

Do not use vector retrieval for current order status, account balance, or whether a credit already executed.

Use retrieval for policy explanation, support guidance, and procedural knowledge.

This illustrates a Chapter 5 principle:

Semantic relevance is not transactional truth.

19. Authority Model

Tier A — Communicate

May answer and draft.

Tier B — Reversible low-value action

May issue up to a defined low-value threshold where policy conditions are deterministically validated.

Tier C — Human approval

Higher credit, ambiguous identity, repeated claims, or sensitive exception.

Tier D — Prohibited

Bank-account change, fraud override, unrestricted payment.

Separate customer identity, agent workload identity, and approver identity. AWS’s Agentic AI Lens explicitly recommends separating human and agent permissions and preserving attribution.[6]

20. State and Durability

Durable case state includes customer, order, evidence, proposed resolution, action status, idempotency key, approval, communication, and outcome.

Conversation is not the state store.

If the process crashes after issuing a credit, resume must not issue another.

21. Evaluation

Test resolution success, policy adherence, wrong-customer actions, duplicate action, escalation, refusal, injection from customer messages or product descriptions, and repeated stochastic trials.

Evaluate outcome and trajectory.

A successful refund through an unauthorised path is a failed run.

22. Security and Privacy

Controls:

  • task-scoped order access;
  • tool invocation authorization;
  • short-lived credentials;
  • idempotent write tools;
  • source–sink egress controls;
  • minimal customer context;
  • no sensitive memory without purpose;
  • protected action ledger.

Prompt injection can enter from customer message, order note, supplier update, or web content. The model is not the security boundary.

23. Operational Assurance

Monitor resolution rate, escalation, incorrect credit, duplicate action, approval override, cost per resolved case, unusually high tool use, and policy denial patterns.

Containment modes can disable financial actions, continue read-only support, require approval for every write, or pause an affected tool.

24. Alternatives

Fully autonomous support

Rejected initially because of broad policy exceptions, customer-data impact, financial authority, and long-tail cases.

Human approval for every action

Rejected because it creates review fatigue and destroys much of the benefit for narrow deterministic reversible actions.

Workflow with no agent

Viable for narrow issue types where the resolution path can be enumerated.

25. Failure Boundary

Between agent proposal and customer-affecting state change.

The action gateway enforces subject, policy, amount, idempotency, and authority.

26. ARB Decision

Approve bounded action autonomy for narrow reversible actions with deterministic policy, transactional source-of-truth tools, idempotency, action ledger, human escalation, and runtime containment.

Do not equate increased model capability with increased financial authority.

Case Study 3 — Software-Engineering Agent

27. Context

A software organisation wants an agent to inspect repositories, reproduce defects, change code, write tests, run CI, prepare pull requests, and respond to review. It may operate over hours.

It may not deploy production directly, read unrelated credentials, bypass branch protection, or merge high-risk changes without human or repository policy approval.

The dominant characteristic is:

Long-running work in a bounded execution environment with machine-verifiable feedback.

28. Quality Drivers

  • code correctness;
  • test evidence;
  • repository isolation;
  • maintainability;
  • minimal change;
  • reproducibility;
  • secure execution;
  • reviewer efficiency.

The software domain is unusual because much of quality can be checked deterministically through compilers, unit tests, static analysis, type checkers, linters, and integration tests.

OpenAI describes the coding-agent harness as the loop connecting model, instructions, tools, and execution, while current software-agent engineering practice emphasises tests, repository context, environment design, and human control over shipping.[7][8]

29. Architecture

Issue / Specification
      ↓
Repository + Constraints
      ↓
Sandboxed Agent Run
      ├── inspect
      ├── edit
      ├── test
      ├── replan
      └── document
      ↓
Deterministic Validation
      ├── tests
      ├── static analysis
      └── policy
      ↓
Diff and Evidence
      ↓
Pull Request
      ↓
Human / Repository Review
      ↓
Merge

The agent can have broad flexibility inside the workspace while production authority remains outside.

30. Run Contract

Define repository, branch/worktree, task, prohibited paths, network, allowed tools, time, model/tool budgets, required tests, and expected output:

  • diff;
  • test result;
  • explanation;
  • unresolved risk.

Long-running agents need durable external artifacts rather than one ever-growing conversation. Anthropic’s long-running-agent work similarly uses explicit progress artifacts and repeatable harness patterns across context windows.[9]

31. Context Architecture

Context should include repository instructions, relevant code, task specification, test output, architecture documents, and current diff.

Avoid indiscriminately loading the entire repository. Use tools for targeted inspection.

Persist plan, completed steps, test state, decisions, and unresolved issues.

32. Security

Sandbox:

  • repository-specific filesystem;
  • no home credential mounts;
  • restricted egress;
  • no production secrets;
  • resource limits.

Tools:

  • shell;
  • tests;
  • search;
  • version control.

Treat repository content as potentially adversarial, including README, issue, generated fixture, and code comment.

33. Evaluation

Offline:

  • benchmark tasks;
  • known bugs;
  • migration tasks;
  • regression suites.

Run-level:

  • tests passing;
  • issue reproduced;
  • diff scope;
  • prohibited file change;
  • security scanning.

Human:

  • maintainability;
  • architecture;
  • review quality.

Outcome:

  • merged change;
  • escaped defect;
  • rollback;
  • review time.

The product metric should not be lines of code generated.

34. Authority

Agent authority:

  • read and write branch/worktree;
  • run approved tools;
  • create PR.

Human/repository policy:

  • merge;
  • protected environment;
  • release.

The boundary can evolve for low-risk automated maintenance, but autonomy should be earned by task class.

35. Operational Assurance

Monitor task success, retry loops, CI failures, PR rejection, reverted change, sandbox escape attempts, cost per accepted change, context size, and tool failures.

Runaway behaviour can be cut off through elapsed-time, token, tool, test-retry, and file-change budgets.

AWS’s current operational guidance similarly calls for automated cutoffs, fallback, recovery, and consumption monitoring for agentic systems.[10]

36. Alternatives

IDE autocomplete only

Insufficient for multi-step autonomous tasks.

Cloud agent with unrestricted internet and credentials

Rejected for broad production use.

Agent allowed to merge everything

Rejected because the repository is itself a governance boundary.

37. Failure Boundary

Between generated code and accepted repository state.

Controls include tests, static validation, diff review, branch protection, and environment isolation.

38. ARB Decision

Approve autonomous implementation inside an isolated repository environment with human or repository-policy control over integration and production.

Increase autonomy task-by-task, not model-by-model.

Case Study 4 — Operational Remediation Agent

39. Context

An operations team wants an agent to consume alerts, inspect telemetry, correlate recent changes, diagnose incidents, propose remediation, and execute a limited set of safe recovery actions.

Possible actions include restart service, scale stateless workload, roll back a known deployment, or disable a feature flag.

It may not edit production databases manually, disable security controls, invent unrestricted host commands, or hide its action history.

The dominant characteristic is:

High time pressure plus production authority.

40. Quality Drivers

  • mean time to restore;
  • diagnosis accuracy;
  • action safety;
  • reversibility;
  • evidence freshness;
  • auditability;
  • containment;
  • availability.

An operations agent differs from the support agent because the environment changes during reasoning, evidence becomes stale quickly, one wrong action can amplify an outage, and speed sometimes matters more than conversational completeness.

41. Architecture

Alert / Incident
      ↓
Incident State
      ↓
Telemetry Evidence
      ├── metrics
      ├── logs
      ├── traces
      ├── deployment history
      └── runbooks
      ↓
Agent Diagnosis
      ↓
Deterministic Safety Validation
      ↓
Impact–Reversibility Gate
      ├── approved auto-remediation
      ├── human approval
      └── proposal only
      ↓
Idempotent Remediation Tool
      ↓
Outcome Verification
      ↓
Continue / Compensate / Escalate

42. Evidence

Use authoritative live tools for current health, deployment, configuration, and service state. Use retrieval for runbooks, prior incident patterns, and architecture notes.

A retrieved incident from last year should not be treated as current production truth.

43. Autonomy by Impact and Reversibility

Auto

  • restart stateless unhealthy replica;
  • retry known failed job;
  • scale within pre-approved range.

Approval

  • roll back production release;
  • switch major traffic route;
  • disable business capability.

Proposal only

  • destructive data repair;
  • IAM changes;
  • novel shell action.

The current AWS Agentic AI Lens similarly emphasises bounded autonomy, risk-tiered human oversight, traceability, and containment for real-world actions.[2][5]

44. State and Idempotency

Incident state includes alert, hypothesis, evidence, proposed action, approval, execution, outcome, compensation, and timestamps.

Tools require target, environment, approval where needed, idempotency key, and expected precondition.

If the agent resumes after interruption, it must know whether an action already ran.

45. Security

  • dedicated agent workload identity;
  • no human credential impersonation;
  • allowlisted tools;
  • narrow parameter ranges;
  • production network boundary;
  • immutable action log;
  • no unrestricted host shell.

Separate agent and human permissions preserve attribution and reduce privilege inheritance.[6]

46. Evaluation

Simulate known incidents, ambiguous symptoms, misleading log lines, tool timeouts, stale runbooks, duplicate alerts, partial recovery, failed rollback, and injection in log or ticket content.

Evaluate diagnosis, safe action, escalation, time to recovery, prohibited action, and repeated stochastic runs.

47. Operational Assurance

The agent itself belongs inside incident management.

Monitor action rate, auto-remediation success, rollback, human rejection, time to restore, tool denial, consumption anomaly, and repeated failed hypotheses.

AWS’s Agentic AI Lens recommends operational recovery mechanisms, cutoffs, and consumption monitoring because runaway behaviour can affect business operations.[10]

48. Alternatives

Proposal-only copilot

Strong first release: lower risk, less time saving.

Fully autonomous SRE agent

Rejected for broad production capability because actions differ greatly in consequence and reversibility.

Fixed automation only

Keep it for known deterministic failures. Do not replace proven automation with LLM reasoning.

49. Failure Boundary

Between diagnosis/proposed recovery and production state change.

The remediation service owns policy, identity, allowed action, preconditions, idempotency, and audit.

50. ARB Decision

Approve earned autonomy for narrowly defined remediation classes. Begin advisory, then approval-gated, then automatic only for well-evaluated reversible actions.

Case Study 5 — High-Impact Decision-Support System

51. Context

An organisation wants AI to support a consequential human decision. For concreteness, consider candidate screening for employment.

The system may extract application information, compare evidence with job criteria, identify questions, and present recommendation and supporting evidence.

It may not reject an applicant autonomously, infer unsupported protected attributes, hide material uncertainty, or make the accountable hiring decision.

The dominant characteristic is:

The consequence to affected people is high even when the system is only advisory.

52. Quality Drivers

  • task fitness;
  • evidence quality;
  • fairness;
  • privacy;
  • explainability;
  • human oversight;
  • contestability;
  • audit;
  • consistency.

The system’s business value does not justify evaluating only average accuracy. Segment evidence matters. So does the human–AI interaction.

53. Architecture

Application
   ↓
Deterministic Eligibility / Parsing
   ↓
Evidence Extraction
   ↓
Criteria-Mapped Recommendation
   ↓
Validation
   ├── evidence support
   ├── prohibited attributes
   ├── uncertainty
   └── segment checks
   ↓
Reviewer Decision Interface
   ↓
Human Decision
   ↓
Decision Record
   ↓
Applicant Correction / Appeal / Recourse

The model recommendation is not the decision. This is the Chapter 2 distinction made operational.

54. Human Oversight

Meaningful review requires the reviewer to see job criterion, applicant evidence, unsupported fields, limitations, system recommendation, and relevant uncertainty.

The reviewer must be able to override, request more information, reject the AI recommendation, and record reason.

The EU AI Act provides a current example of a legal framework requiring effective human oversight for relevant high-risk systems, with design measures intended to prevent or minimise risk to health, safety, or fundamental rights.[11]

This handbook’s architectural conclusion is broader than one law:

A human approval button is not meaningful oversight.

55. Evidence Architecture

Authoritative:

  • submitted application;
  • validated job criteria;
  • approved hiring policy.

Do not treat historical hiring decision, inferred “culture fit,” or the model’s general knowledge as authoritative candidate evidence.

The recommendation should link each material claim to evidence.

56. Evaluation

Evaluate extraction, recommendation, segment performance, human factors, recourse, and outcome.

Questions include:

  • Did the system identify information correctly?
  • Does it map evidence to job criteria?
  • Are material differences present across relevant groups and application formats?
  • Do reviewers over-rely on recommendations?
  • Can incorrect extraction be corrected?
  • Which errors affect interview opportunity or rejection?

NIST’s AI RMF emphasises contextual risk management, stakeholder impacts, testing, evaluation, documentation, and explicit commissioning decisions.[3]

57. Model Choice

Use a model that meets the evidence and reasoning bar. Do not make higher benchmark score the justification for more decision authority.

The model remains advisory.

A smaller or more specialised model may be preferable where cost, privacy, consistency, or explainability dominate.

58. Data and Privacy

  • purpose-bound applicant data;
  • minimise model context;
  • retention schedule;
  • correction path;
  • no unrelated future memory;
  • strict evaluation-data controls;
  • provenance.

If historical hiring data is used, document purpose, inspect bias, evaluate representativeness, and avoid blindly learning past decisions.

59. Governance

Require accountable business owner, impact assessment, documented risk tier, evaluation thresholds, reviewer training, appeal, material-change review, and third-party model governance.

The architecture cannot defer accountability to the recruiter, model provider, or AI governance committee collectively.

60. Operational Assurance

Monitor reviewer overrides, segment performance, complaints, appeals, incorrect extraction, model changes, quality drift, and decision outcome where appropriate.

An increasing acceptance rate is not automatically a positive system metric.

61. Alternatives

Autonomous screening rejection

Rejected. The evidence and consequence do not justify it.

No AI

A legitimate alternative if process scale is low, evaluation cannot demonstrate benefit, or oversight burden exceeds value.

AI only for extraction

A lower-risk alternative when recommendation quality is not sufficiently evidenced.

62. Failure Boundary

Between AI recommendation and human employment decision.

But that boundary is only real if the reviewer has evidence, the interface avoids automation bias, override is practical, the decision is accountable, and recourse exists.

63. ARB Decision

Approve advisory decision support only, subject to strong segmented evaluation, evidence linkage, meaningful human oversight, privacy, recourse, and continual review.

Reject autonomous negative employment decisions in this architecture.

Case Study 6 — Multi-Tenant Enterprise AI Platform

64. Context

An enterprise wants a shared platform serving knowledge assistants, coding agents, customer-service agents, document workflows, operational agents, and high-impact decision support.

The platform provides model access, identity, evaluation, tool registry, retrieval provisioning, workflow runtime, privacy controls, telemetry, and cost attribution.

It does not own product business outcomes.

The dominant characteristic is:

Shared mechanisms with high failure concentration and many different risk profiles.

65. Quality Drivers

  • tenant isolation;
  • platform availability;
  • developer experience;
  • policy consistency;
  • extensibility;
  • cost transparency;
  • provider flexibility;
  • governance;
  • blast-radius control.

66. Architecture

Product Teams
  ├── Knowledge
  ├── Support
  ├── Coding
  ├── Operations
  └── Decision Support
          ↓
Product Contracts
          ↓
AI Platform
  ├── Model Gateway
  ├── Identity and Policy
  ├── Evaluation Runtime
  ├── Evidence Services
  ├── Tool Registry
  ├── Workflow / State
  ├── Data / Privacy
  ├── Observability
  └── Cost Allocation
          ↓
Provider / Runtime Adapters

Chapter 12’s rule governs the design:

Centralise mechanisms. Preserve judgment.

67. Product Boundary

Platform owns common policy mechanism, identity, approved-provider registry, telemetry transport, evaluation runtime, tool registration, tenancy, and cost attribution.

Product owns business purpose, prompt, workflow meaning, evidence authority, evaluation threshold, action authority, and outcome.

68. Tenancy

Use pooled model gateway, tenant-specific quotas, isolated indexes, purpose-scoped memory, tenant-scoped state, tenant telemetry labels, and dedicated execution for high-risk production actions.

Current AWS guidance similarly treats pooled, siloed, and hybrid models as different isolation/economic choices and recommends per-tenant throttling across shared layers to manage noisy neighbours.[12][13]

69. Evaluation

The platform evaluates gateway correctness, policy latency, tenant isolation, routing, tool registry, telemetry, and cost accuracy.

Products evaluate their task, evidence, and outcomes.

The platform does not publish one “AI quality score” for every product.

70. Security and Privacy

  • separate workload identities;
  • credential broker;
  • deny-by-default tool policy;
  • tenant context end-to-end;
  • provider eligibility by data class;
  • protected telemetry;
  • deletion infrastructure.

A single broad platform service account is rejected.

71. Operational Assurance

Platform SLOs cover gateway, policy, evaluation queue, retrieval provisioning, and trace ingestion.

Product operational assurance remains separate.

A green platform does not prove a green support agent.

72. Cost

Attribute product, tenant, environment, and task. Join inference, retrieval, tool, workflow, evaluation, and shared platform cost.

Measure platform value through reuse, onboarding, control coverage, operating leverage, cognitive load, and failure concentration.

73. Alternatives

One universal enterprise agent

Rejected. Products have incompatible authority, evidence, privacy, and outcomes.

No platform

Rejected at this scale because repeated cross-cutting control becomes wasteful and inconsistent.

Full central product implementation

Rejected because the platform becomes approval queue and domain bottleneck.

74. Failure Boundary

The critical boundary is shared mechanism versus product meaning.

The platform must also segment infrastructure so one gateway or policy failure does not become an uncontrolled enterprise-wide outage.

75. ARB Decision

Approve a shared AI platform as an internal product with stable contracts, tenant isolation, provider extensions, paved paths, product-owned quality and outcomes, segmented failure domains, transparent cost, and governed escape hatches.

Part VII — Comparing the Six Architectures

76. Cross-Case Decision Matrix

Dimension Knowledge Assistant Service Agent Coding Agent Remediation Agent High-Impact Support AI Platform
Primary value Answer Resolve case Produce change Restore service Support human decision Enable teams
Autonomy Low Bounded High in sandbox Earned by action class Advisory Not a business agent
Main evidence Documents APIs + policy Repo + tests Live telemetry + runbooks Applicant + criteria Platform telemetry/contracts
State duration Session Case Hours/days Incident Decision lifecycle Continuous
Write authority None Bounded customer action Branch/PR Bounded production action None to final decision Shared control mechanisms
Human oversight Escalation Risk-tiered Merge/release Impact/reversibility Decision owner Product + platform governance
Reversibility High Mixed High before merge Mixed Low for affected person Depends on capability
Privacy burden Medium High Repo/secrets Operational/security Very high Cross-tenant
Evaluation burden Retrieval + claims Outcome + trajectory Tests + review Simulation + recovery Segmented + human factors Contract + isolation
Main containment Read-only Disable writes Stop sandbox Revoke remediation Disable recommendation Segment capability/tenant
Cost unit Answer Resolved case Accepted change Restored incident Reviewed decision Product/tenant workload

The matrix is not a maturity model. It makes context visible.

77. The Same Pattern Can Reverse

RAG

Strong fit: enterprise knowledge assistant.

Partial fit: support agent for policy.

Weak fit: current transaction truth.

Human approval

Wasteful: every low-risk knowledge answer.

Useful: larger customer credit.

Essential: high-impact decision and high-risk remediation.

Agent autonomy

Unnecessary: straightforward policy lookup.

Valuable: coding exploration.

Conditional: remediation.

Memory

Optional: knowledge-assistant preferences.

Case-scoped: service agent.

External progress state: coding agent.

Dangerous if indiscriminate: high-impact decision support.

Shared platform

Useful mechanism: identity, telemetry, evaluation runtime.

Bad centralisation: product quality threshold and business authority.

78. Consequence and Reversibility Change the Architecture

A recurring relationship emerges:

Higher Consequence
        +
Lower Reversibility
        ↓
More:
  evidence
  validation
  independent review
  bounded authority
  audit
  recourse
  containment

This is not a universal formula. It is a useful design pressure.

A reversible restart of one unhealthy stateless replica can justify more automation than an irreversible employment decision even if both use the same model.

79. Evidence Changes the Architecture

Ask:

What kind of truth does this task require?

Documentary truth

Use authoritative retrieval.

Transactional truth

Use system-of-record tools.

Environmental truth

Use current telemetry.

Code correctness

Use tests and executable feedback.

Human-impact judgment

Use evidence plus accountable human decision and recourse.

A vector database is not the universal answer to “how does the AI know?”

80. Autonomy Is an Architectural Budget

Autonomy is consumed through decision rights, tool access, time, scope, money, affected subjects, and irreversibility.

A more capable model does not automatically receive a larger autonomy budget.

Earn autonomy through evidence for a specific task class.

81. Architecture Mechanisms Are Orthogonal

Do not confuse bigger model, more agent loops, better evidence, and more authority. They solve different problems.

A knowledge assistant with weak retrieval does not become reliable by adding multi-agent debate, more reasoning tokens, or more memory. The weak point is evidence.

Part VIII — Cross-Case Failure Patterns

82. Model Quality Used to Hide Evidence Failure

Symptoms include selecting a stronger model after retrieval misses, increasing reasoning budget, and blaming hallucination on the model.

Question:

Did the system have the necessary authoritative evidence?

83. Agent Added to Avoid Workflow Design

Symptoms include a known process becoming a free-running loop, state living in chat, retries being model decisions, and no stop conditions.

Question:

Which next step genuinely cannot be defined before runtime?

84. Human Review Added Without Human-System Design

Symptoms include a reviewer seeing only AI output, no evidence, no time, default approve, and unmeasured override.

Question:

Can the human actually change the outcome for the right reasons?

85. Shared Platform Used to Avoid Product Accountability

Symptoms include platform-defined thresholds, product teams saying “the platform approved it,” and common model policy substituting for local evaluation.

Question:

Who owns the business outcome?

86. Logging Used as Observability

Symptoms include every prompt being stored while task outcome, state transitions, and alert response remain absent.

Question:

Which signal changes an operational decision?

87. Governance Added After the Architecture

Symptoms include impact assessment after build, permanent exceptions, no change trigger, and approval that does not alter runtime authority.

Question:

Which governance decision is actually enforceable by the system?

Part IX — Architecture Review Heuristics

88. The Five Questions

When time is limited, ask:

1. What is the consequence of being wrong?

Determines evidence, validation, oversight, and recourse.

2. What can the system change?

Determines authority, tool design, idempotency, and security.

3. What is authoritative truth?

Determines retrieval, tools, source precedence, and freshness.

4. What proves success?

Determines evaluation, outcome, and telemetry.

5. What happens when the AI is unavailable or manipulated?

Determines fallback, containment, degraded mode, and manual operation.

89. The Architecture Context–Decision Trace in Practice

Example:

Context:
production incident with high availability pressure

Quality Drivers:
fast restoration + safe action + audit

Choice:
agent diagnoses; deterministic gateway controls remediation

Trade-off:
more integration and policy complexity

Failure Boundary:
model cannot execute arbitrary production command

Evidence:
incident simulations + action success + rollback tests

ARB:
approve only defined reversible remediation classes

The value is not the diagram. It is the defensible chain.

Part X — Architecture Smells

90. Universal Reference Architecture

One diagram is presented as correct for every AI product.

91. Pattern by Fashion

RAG, agents, multi-agent, memory, or a control plane is selected because it is current, not because the task requires it.

92. Model as Architecture

The system description is primarily the model name.

93. Reversibility Blindness

A low-risk reversible action and an irreversible human-impact decision receive the same authority model.

94. Evidence Type Confusion

Documents, transaction APIs, live telemetry, and model memory are treated as equivalent truth sources.

95. Autonomy by Model Upgrade

A stronger model silently receives more tool or decision authority.

96. Human Review Everywhere

Human approval is added to all actions instead of designing risk-tiered authority.

97. Human Review Nowhere

The system relies on model confidence to justify consequential action.

98. Platform as Excuse

A product delegates accountability for quality, privacy, or outcomes to the shared AI platform.

99. Cost per Token as Business Case

Cheaper inference is treated as proof the architecture is economical.

100. Success by Demo

A successful end-to-end demonstration substitutes for evaluation of failure segments and operating recovery.

Part XI — Interview Preparation

101. Foundational Questions

Question 1

Is there a standard AI reference architecture?

There are recurring mechanisms, but their correct combination depends on context, evidence, consequence, reversibility, autonomy, and scale.

Question 2

How do you decide between RAG and tools?

Use retrieval for documentary evidence and semantic discovery. Use authoritative tools for current transactional or environmental truth.

Question 3

When do you need an agent rather than a workflow?

When useful next steps genuinely depend on runtime evidence and cannot be economically enumerated in advance.

Question 4

What determines human oversight?

Consequence, reversibility, uncertainty, authority, evidence, and whether human judgment can meaningfully reduce risk.

Question 5

Does a more capable model justify more autonomy?

No. Autonomy should be granted for a task class based on system evidence and control, not model reputation.

102. Senior-Level Questions

Question 6

Why is a knowledge assistant architecture different from a support action agent?

The assistant mainly needs authoritative evidence and permission-aware retrieval. The action agent also needs identity, durable state, authority, idempotent tools, and outcome verification.

Question 7

Why can coding agents operate with relatively high autonomy?

Their workspace can be isolated and much of correctness can be tested through compilers, tests, static analysis, diffs, and repository governance before production consequence.

Question 8

How do you design operational-agent autonomy?

Classify actions by impact and reversibility, use live evidence, narrow tools, idempotency, explicit authority, outcome verification, and rapid containment.

Question 9

What makes human oversight ineffective?

The reviewer lacks evidence, competence, time, authority, an override path, or the system induces automation bias.

Question 10

Which responsibilities belong in an enterprise AI platform?

Stable cross-cutting mechanisms such as identity, model access, policy enforcement, evaluation runtime, telemetry, tool registration, privacy controls, tenancy, and cost attribution.

Question 11

How do you compare two plausible architectures?

Use quality-attribute scenarios, alternatives, trade-offs, failure boundaries, evidence, and a recorded ARB decision.

Question 12

What is cost per successful outcome?

Total model, retrieval, tool, workflow, evaluation, human, and platform cost divided by completed outcomes that meet the quality bar.

103. Principal-Level Questions

Question 13

How do consequence and reversibility change architecture?

Higher consequence and lower reversibility generally demand stronger evidence, validation, bounded authority, independent review, audit, recourse, and containment.

Question 14

How would you design a portfolio of AI systems with different risk?

Use shared platform mechanisms and governance taxonomy while keeping product-specific quality, authority, evidence, autonomy, evaluation, and outcome decisions.

Question 15

How do you prevent architecture from becoming vendor-driven?

Start from quality and control requirements, define stable contracts, treat provider features as implementation choices, preserve portability where valuable, and document behavioural dependencies.

Question 16

When should a product deliberately avoid AI?

When deterministic software meets the need better, authoritative evidence is unavailable, evaluation cannot justify the risk, operating cost exceeds value, or affected-party consequences cannot be governed acceptably.

Question 17

What does an ARB need to approve an agentic system?

Purpose, quality scenarios, evidence, evaluation, state, authority, tools, security, privacy, operational controls, failure recovery, cost, alternatives, and accountable ownership.

Question 18

What is the most important output of architecture work?

A defensible decision: what the system may do, why the design is appropriate, what trade-offs remain, what evidence supports it, and what conditions trigger change.

Part XII — Whiteboard Challenge

104. Design an AI Claims Platform for an Insurer

The platform supports policy Q&A, claim-document review, fraud signals, settlement recommendation, customer communication, low-value payment, and human adjuster review.

Constraints include several countries, sensitive personal data, high fraud exposure, variable claim value, legacy systems, external repair data, and a desire for shared AI platform capabilities.

Discuss:

  1. Which subproblems should be deterministic, retrieval-based, or agentic?
  2. What evidence is authoritative?
  3. What are the quality scenarios?
  4. What does the AI Decision Pipeline look like?
  5. What autonomy applies by claim and action class?
  6. What human oversight is required?
  7. Where is durable state and how is idempotency enforced?
  8. Which identities and security boundaries apply?
  9. What are the data-purpose contracts?
  10. How is the system evaluated?
  11. How is operational containment designed?
  12. Which capabilities belong in the shared platform?
  13. What are at least two credible alternatives?
  14. Where is the failure boundary?
  15. What is the ARB decision?

A strong answer does not say:

Use an agent with RAG and a vector database.

It explains why some questions use retrieval, current claim status uses authoritative APIs, low-value reversible actions may be automated, settlement decisions remain human-owned, evaluation differs by claim segment, and shared platform mechanisms do not own insurance judgment.

Part XIII — Questions to Take Back to Your Team

  1. Are we using the same architecture for tasks with different consequences?
  2. Which evidence source is actually authoritative?
  3. Which actions are reversible?
  4. Which agent decisions could be deterministic workflow?
  5. Which human approvals add real judgment?
  6. Which approvals are rubber stamps?
  7. Where is durable state?
  8. Can repeated execution duplicate effects?
  9. Is autonomy granted by task evidence or model reputation?
  10. Which failures can be contained without full shutdown?
  11. Which data should never enter context?
  12. Which derived data can still influence future behaviour?
  13. Which shared platform mechanisms reduce duplication?
  14. Which platform responsibilities have absorbed domain judgment?
  15. What is the cost per successful outcome?
  16. Which system-quality metric is currently only a model metric?
  17. What evidence justifies continued operation?
  18. Which current architecture decision would change after a serious incident?
  19. Which rejected alternative should be reconsidered if constraints change?
  20. Can another architect reconstruct why this architecture was approved?

Architect’s Notebook — The Diagram Is the Least Important Part

Architecture diagrams are useful. They show components, boundaries, and flows.

But two identical diagrams can represent different architectures if authority, evidence, quality thresholds, failure response, or governance differ.

The durable architecture artifact is not simply boxes and arrows.

It is:

the set of decisions and evidence that make those boxes and arrows appropriate.

From the Architect’s Desk

When teams ask for a reference architecture, they often want certainty.

Give them reusable mechanisms, not false certainty.

A knowledge assistant, coding agent, remediation agent, hiring assistant, and enterprise platform may all contain a model, retrieval, tools, evaluation, telemetry, and identity. That surface similarity is not enough to make their architecture the same.

The architect’s job is to locate the consequence, the authority, the authoritative evidence, the failure boundary, and the proof.

Patterns help us move faster. Judgment prevents patterns from moving us in the wrong direction.

If I Were the Architect

A senior stakeholder says:

“We have already built one successful AI agent. Reuse that architecture for the next five AI use cases.”

What do you do?

Do not reject reuse. Do not accept the premise.

  1. Reuse platform mechanisms first.
  2. classify each use by consequence and reversibility.
  3. identify authoritative evidence.
  4. define action authority.
  5. write quality scenarios.
  6. decide workflow versus agentic control.
  7. define evaluation.
  8. define human oversight.
  9. define privacy and security.
  10. define operational containment.
  11. compare with the existing architecture.
  12. reuse only the components whose assumptions remain valid.

Architecture reuse should follow invariant assumptions, not visual similarity.

Key Takeaways

  • There is no universal AI reference architecture.
  • Reusable mechanisms are not reusable decisions.
  • The Architecture Context–Decision Trace connects context, quality drivers, choice, trade-offs, failure boundary, evidence, and ARB decision.
  • Use the same review frame across cases to expose genuine architectural differences.
  • Knowledge assistants are primarily evidence systems.
  • Transactional agents require authoritative tools, state, authority, and idempotency.
  • Coding agents benefit from isolated environments and executable feedback.
  • Remediation agents need live evidence, impact/reversibility gates, and rapid containment.
  • High-impact decision support requires meaningful human ownership, segmented evaluation, privacy, and recourse.
  • Enterprise platforms should share mechanisms while preserving product judgment.
  • Documentary, transactional, environmental, executable, and human-impact evidence should not be conflated.
  • Consequence and reversibility change the control burden.
  • Human oversight should be risk-tiered and meaningful.
  • More capable models do not automatically deserve more autonomy.
  • Autonomy is an architectural budget for a task class.
  • Cost should be measured per successful outcome.
  • The model, evidence architecture, workflow, security, and governance are orthogonal design dimensions.
  • A pattern correct in one case can become an architecture smell in another.
  • The most important architecture artifact is a defensible decision supported by evidence.

Decision ID: ARB-CH-013
Subject: Chapter 13 — End-to-End Reference Architectures and Trade-off Case Studies
Outcome: Accepted with constraints for user review

Primary contribution:
Synthesises the handbook through six contrasted architectures and demonstrates
that reusable AI mechanisms must be selected according to context,
consequence, reversibility, evidence, autonomy, and scale.

Grounded foundations:
- Microsoft RAG and permission-aware retrieval guidance.

Original synthesis requiring explicit labelling:
- Architecture Context–Decision Trace.

- autonomy as an architectural budget for a task class.
- “reusable mechanisms are not reusable decisions.”
- “the diagram is the least important part.”

Constraints:
- Do not imply the six cases are universal blueprints.
- Keep logical architecture distinct from service topology.
- Preserve authoritative-tool use for transactional truth.
- Preserve product/domain accountability.
- Treat legal examples as contextual, current references.
- Do not increase autonomy because a model benchmark improves.
- Keep human oversight meaningful and risk-tiered.
- Re-evaluate choices when assumptions change.

Appendix B - Canonical Glossary

Status: Initial cross-chapter terminology baseline

Architecture

The fundamental concepts, properties, relationships, decisions, and principles that shape a system and its evolution. Diagrams are descriptions of architecture, not the architecture itself.

Capability

The ability of a model or system to perform a defined task at the required level.

Confidence

The justified level of reliance the surrounding system or stakeholder may place on an output. It is not an unverified confidence statement produced by a model.

Context

The information available to a model or workflow for the current reasoning or action step, including instructions, evidence, history, tools, and state.

Evidence

Information that legitimately supports, refutes, constrains, or verifies a claim or action for a particular task and context.

Groundedness

The degree to which a claim is supported by supplied evidence. Groundedness does not prove that the evidence is true, current, complete, or authorised.

Retrieval

The process of selecting candidate information from one or more sources in response to a query or task.

RAG

Retrieval-augmented generation: a pattern that combines a generative model with retrieved external knowledge. It is one evidence architecture pattern, not the whole discipline.

Memory

Information retained from previous interactions or activity for later use. Memory is not automatically evidence.

Evaluation

A structured process that executes a defined system on representative cases and applies grading or observation to produce evidence for a decision.

Quality Attribute

A measurable property describing how a system behaves under specified conditions, such as reliability, security, latency, modifiability, safety, or groundedness.

Authority

The legitimate permission to make or execute a decision within defined scope, time, policy, identity, and evidence conditions.

Autonomy

The degree to which a system may choose and execute actions without immediate human approval.

Outcome

The observed real-world condition after a decision or action, distinct from model response or tool completion.

Deterministic Boundary

A point where explicit rules, policy, validation, or transactional mechanisms constrain or execute behaviour rather than relying solely on probabilistic model output.

Model Quality

Measured properties of a model under a defined evaluation.

System Quality

Measured properties of the complete technical workflow, including models, data, tools, controls, security, performance, and operations.

Outcome Quality

The degree to which users, organisations, or affected parties experience the intended benefit without unacceptable harm or side effects.

Model Capability Profile

A task-specific description of the capability, modality, evidence, tool, output, risk, performance, privacy, and cost requirements that a model must satisfy.

Model Routing

The policy-driven selection of an approved model for a task at design time or runtime.

Inference Contract

A versioned specification of the model policy, configuration, context, output, tools, budgets, reliability, safety, and observability used for a task class.

Fallback

A controlled alternative used when the preferred model or endpoint is unavailable or unsuitable. A fallback is a behavioural change and requires evaluation.

Escalation

Movement of a task to a more capable, more controlled, or human path because the current path cannot meet the required quality or risk threshold.

Prefill

The inference phase in which input context is processed and attention state is constructed before output generation.

Decode

The inference phase in which output tokens are generated autoregressively.

KV Cache

Stored attention keys and values reused during autoregressive generation. KV-cache capacity can limit concurrency and throughput.

Quantisation

Reduction of model numerical precision to decrease memory or compute requirements. A quantised model is a distinct evaluated artifact.

Workflow

A controlled sequence of tasks and transitions. In a deterministic workflow, the control path is defined in code or configuration.

Agent

A system in which a model dynamically selects steps or tools to accomplish an objective within defined constraints.

Agent Harness

The software control system that builds context, invokes models, routes tools, manages state, enforces budgets, handles interruption, and returns results.

Durable Execution

Execution that can preserve state and resume after process failure, long waits, or infrastructure interruption.

Checkpoint

A durable snapshot of workflow state at a meaningful execution boundary.

Interrupt

A controlled pause that persists state and waits for external input before resuming.

Handoff

A transfer of task responsibility, state, evidence, authority, and unresolved work from one agent or owner to another.

Dead-Letter State

A durable terminal or manual-recovery state used when automated processing cannot continue safely.

Agent State Envelope

A structured record of task, evidence, decision, authority, action, execution, and trace state required to resume and audit a run.

Agent Workload Identity

A verifiable identity assigned to the software workload running an agent, distinct from the human principal on whose behalf it may act.

Delegated Authority

A bounded permission granted by a principal or policy to perform specified actions for a task, subject, environment, and period.

Capability

A narrow, authorised operation exposed to an agent without necessarily exposing the underlying credential.

Prompt Injection

Adversarial instructions intended to manipulate a model’s behaviour. Indirect prompt injection is delivered through external content that the model reads.

Source–Sink Analysis

Analysis of attacker-influenced inputs and the capabilities that can create harm if those inputs alter system behaviour.

Credential Broker

A trusted service that mediates access to credentials and issues short-lived, narrowly scoped proxy capabilities without exposing real long-lived credentials to the agent.

Proof of Possession

A token mechanism requiring the presenter to demonstrate possession of a cryptographic key, reducing the value of a copied bearer token.

Containment

Actions that limit an agent’s capability or reach during a suspected or confirmed security event.

Non-Repudiation

Evidence sufficient to attribute a request, decision, approval, and action and to resist later denial or alteration.

Governance

The system of direction, decision rights, accountability, policies, controls, evidence, and review used to ensure acceptable AI use.

AI Management System

A structured set of organisational policies, processes, resources, monitoring, and improvement practices for responsible AI development and use.

Accountable Owner

The named human role with authority and responsibility for the decision to operate an AI system and accept its residual risk.

Risk Tier

A contextual classification that determines required evidence, controls, ownership, review, and monitoring.

Impact Assessment

A structured evaluation of intended and unintended effects on individuals, groups, organisations, society, and the environment.

Material Change

A change capable of altering a system’s purpose, behaviour, impact, authority, risk, or obligations sufficiently to require renewed review.

Residual Risk

Risk remaining after controls are applied.

Exception

A time-bounded, authorised deviation from policy with defined scope, risk, compensating controls, ownership, and expiry.

Recourse

A mechanism through which an affected person can seek correction, human review, appeal, or remedy.

Governance Assurance Case

A structured claim, argument, evidence set, limitations, and accountable decision supporting the operation of an AI system.

Operational Assurance

The ongoing production of evidence that an AI system remains within its technical, behavioural, authority, risk, and outcome boundaries, combined with the capability to intervene.

Behavioural SLO

A service-level objective defining acceptable AI task, evidence, tool, refusal, escalation, policy, or action behaviour for a specified population and window.

Control Status

Current evidence that a required policy, approval, identity, evaluation, exception, or security control remains valid and effective.

AI Incident

An event or pattern in which an AI system causes or risks unacceptable harm, violates authority or policy, fails a critical task or outcome, or operates outside its approved envelope.

AI Incident Envelope

A structured record of incident scope, signals, versions, active authority, completed and uncertain effects, containment, ownership, and evidence.

Behavioural Drift

A material change over time in task, evidence, tool, refusal, escalation, safety, action, or segment performance.

Reconciliation

The process of determining and correcting the actual external effects of an interrupted, duplicated, failed, or uncertain operation.

Continued-Operation Gate

A governance and operational decision determining whether an AI system may continue, restore, reduce, suspend, or retire its current scope and authority.

Data Purpose Contract

A structured record binding a data use to its purpose, authority, scope, permitted reuse, sensitivity, sharing, residency, retention, rights, and owner.

Data Lifecycle Control Plane

The distributed policies and services governing purpose, classification, lineage, access, use, retention, deletion, rights, and evidence across AI data paths.

System of Influence

A derived artifact—such as an index, embedding, memory, summary, or model—that can affect future behaviour without being the authoritative system of record.

Data Lineage

The trace from source data through transformations and derived artifacts to consumers and outcomes.

Purpose Limitation

The principle that data is collected for specified purposes and should not be silently reused incompatibly.

Data Minimisation

Limiting collection, retrieval, context, storage, sharing, and retention to what is necessary for a defined purpose.

Pseudonymisation

Replacement or separation of direct identifiers while retaining a controlled ability to re-associate data with a person.

Anonymisation

A context-dependent state in which identification is no longer reasonably likely. Removing names alone is insufficient.

Differential Privacy

A mathematical framework that bounds the privacy effect of including one privacy unit’s data in an analysis, subject to explicit parameters and composition.

Data Residency

The geographic locations in which data is stored or processed.

Data Sovereignty

The legal and operational control over data, including jurisdiction, access, keys, suppliers, and exit—not only physical location.

Deletion Propagation Map

A map and workflow for applying deletion or restriction across source records, derived artifacts, indexes, caches, memory, telemetry, models, and backups.

AI Platform

An internal product that provides reusable AI mechanisms, controls, contracts, and self-service capabilities to product teams.

Platform Boundary

The division between shared platform responsibility and product-owned domain logic, quality, authority, and outcomes.

Paved Path

A supported, automated, governed route for a common development or operational task.

Golden Path

A highly supported paved path optimised for common use cases and low cognitive load.

Control Plane

The mechanisms that configure policy, identity, routing, tenants, budgets, registries, and lifecycle controls.

Data Plane

The runtime path through which prompts, model requests, retrieval, tools, messages, and outputs flow.

Showback

Reporting technology cost to the teams or products that consume it without necessarily posting the cost to their financial accounts.

Chargeback

Assigning technology cost into the consuming team’s financial accounts under organisational finance policy.

Platform Contract

A versioned interface defining identity, tenant, input, output, policy, SLO, telemetry, cost, and compatibility for a shared capability.

Architecture Context–Decision Trace

A reasoning artifact connecting context, quality drivers, architecture choice, trade-offs, failure boundary, evidence, and the resulting architecture-review decision.

Reference Architecture

A reusable architectural example or pattern intended to inform, not replace, context-specific design decisions.

Failure Boundary

The point at which architecture prevents a component’s failure or uncertainty from becoming an unacceptable system consequence.

Autonomy Budget

The bounded decision and action scope delegated to an AI system for a specific task class, subject to evidence, time, tools, consequence, and containment.

Appendix C - Principles Index

Judgment

  • Decisions over diagrams.
  • Architecture optimises decisions under constraints.
  • Software architecture manages complexity; AI architecture manages complexity and uncertainty.
  • Consequence determines control.
  • Match evidence to irreversibility.
  • Stable core, replaceable edge.

Decisions and Quality

  • A model produces a response; a system makes a decision.
  • Do not collapse response, recommendation, decision, and action.
  • Quality belongs to a context.
  • An attribute becomes an architecture driver when it changes design.
  • Structured output is a contract, not proof.

Evaluation and Evidence

  • Evaluation serves a decision.
  • Deterministic before interpretive.
  • The judge is not ground truth.
  • Frequency and consequence both shape evaluation coverage.
  • Context is not evidence.
  • Semantic relevance is not evidence authority.
  • Groundedness is not truth.
  • Insufficient evidence is a valid state.

Models and Workflows

  • The model is a behavioural dependency.
  • Portability is behavioural.
  • Fallback changes behaviour.
  • Approval does not transfer automatically.
  • Agentic only where necessary.
  • Conversation is not durable state.
  • Every loop needs a stopping rule.
  • The agent is the variable part of a controlled system.

Security and Governance

  • The model is never the security boundary.
  • Capability without credential possession.
  • Design for manipulated reasoning.
  • Relevance is not permission.
  • Accountability must terminate.
  • Compliance is a floor.
  • Authority must be withdrawable.
  • Exceptions must expire.

Operations

  • Operational confidence decays unless renewed by evidence.
  • Budget changes authority.
  • Contain before explain.
  • Recovery ends at the outcome.
  • Incidents must change the system.
  • Operational assurance is the continuing architecture review.

Data and Privacy

  • Derived does not mean harmless.
  • Availability is not authority.
  • Minimise at every boundary.
  • Memory requires purpose.
  • Deletion is an evidence claim.
  • Residency is not sovereignty.
  • Privacy is control over association.

AI Platform

  • A platform does not own the business outcome.
  • Centralise mechanisms, preserve judgment.
  • Share evaluation machinery, not accountability.
  • Standardise correlation, not meaning.
  • Golden paths should be paved, not caged.
  • Platform adoption is not platform value.

Reference Architecture and Synthesis

  • There is no universal AI reference architecture.
  • Reusable mechanisms are not reusable decisions.
  • Consequence and reversibility change the control burden.
  • Autonomy is a task-specific architectural budget.
  • Use the evidence type appropriate to the truth required.
  • The most important architecture artifact is a defensible decision.
